## Highlights

*   •A brief review was conducted on the pathobiology of IS and the functional characteristics of MG. 
*   •The discussion focused on the dual effect of MG in the acute ischemic cascade reaction. 
*   •A summary was provided on the relationship between MG and the long-term prognosis following a IS. 
*   •Dynamic intervention of microglial subsets or functions is promising in improving IS prognosis. 

## Abstract

Stroke, the third leading cause of death and disability worldwide, is classified into ischemic or hemorrhagic, in which approximately 85% of strokes are ischemic. [Ischemic stroke](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/brain-ischemia) occurs as a result of arterial occlusion due to embolus or [thrombus](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/thrombus), with ischemia in the perfusion territory supplied by the occluded artery. The traditional concept that ischemic stroke is solely a vascular occlusion disorder has been expanded to include the dynamic interaction between [microglia](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/microglia), astrocytes, neurons, vascular cells, and matrix components forming the “neurovascular unit.” Acute ischemic stroke triggers a wide spectrum of neurovascular disturbances, glial activation, and secondary neuroinflammation that promotes further injury, ultimately resulting in [neuronal death](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/neuronal-death). Microglia, as the resident macrophages in the [central nervous system](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/central-nervous-system), is one of the first responders to ischemic injury and plays a significant role in post-ischemic neuroinflammation. In this review, we reviewed the mechanisms of [microglia](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/microglia) in multiple stages of post-ischemic neuroinflammation development, including acute, sub-acute and chronic phases of stroke. A comprehensive understanding of the dynamic variation and the time-dependent role of microglia in post-stroke neuroinflammation could aid in the search for more effective therapeutics and diagnostic strategies for ischemic stroke.

## Introduction

Stroke is categorized into two types: ischemic and hemorrhagic, with ischemic strokes making up 85% of all stroke cases, while hemorrhagic strokes account for the remaining 15% (Dorňák et al., 2015). The global prevalence of ischemic stroke was 7,630,800 incident cases in 2019, with a noticeable increase in worldwide incident cases of ischemic stroke from 1990 to 2019, corresponding to a total increase of 87.55% (Ding et al., 2022). Ischemic stroke, a complex pathology characterized by the destruction of cerebral tissue following sudden deprivation of blood flow in a particular brain region, is one of the leading causes of older adult mortality and acquired long-term disability worldwide (GBD 2016 Lifetime Risk of Stroke Collaborators et al., 2018). Rapid restoration of blood flow in the ischemic brain is essential to save viable neuronal cells in acute ischemic stroke therapy. Currently, recanalization by intravenous recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rt-PA) thrombolysis and/or mechanical thrombectomy during the stroke window period are the first-line therapeutic regimens for cases of major artery blockage (Fukuoka et al., 2019; Aamir et al., 2021). However, thrombolytic therapies or intravascular recanalization treatment are severely limited by their short therapeutic time window (4.5 h for intravenous thrombolysis and 16–24 h for intravascular recanalization), side effects on brain edema and hemorrhage, and inadequate conditions for practical medical treatment (Powers et al., 2019). Even in developed European countries, only 7.3% of all patients with acute ischemic stroke receive intravenous thrombolysis, and only 1.9% receive intravascular recanalization (GBD 2019 Stroke Collaborators et al., 2021). Therefore, targeting key pathogenic mechanisms to search for new therapeutic options that are effective and have fewer treatment limitations, either alone or in combination, is critically needed.

Ischemic stroke is a complex pathology involving multiple phases, including microglial activation, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, neuroexcitotoxicity, and disruption of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) (Lalkovičová and Danielisová, 2016). Inflammation and immune mechanisms play crucial roles in all stages of ischemic cascade, from acute damage cascades to the subacute and chronic course after ischemic stroke (Kelly et al., 2018; Iadecola et al., 2020). In the brain, the interplay between inflammation and the immune system activation exerts both damaging and protective effects on central nervous system (CNS) functions (Kyritsis et al., 2012; Planas, 2018), depending on the cell types or specific molecules involved in the process, as well as the impaired brain regions and phases after the stroke (Endres et al., 2022). Microglia, the resident macrophages of the CNS that constitute 5–20% of the total glial population, are among the first responders to ischemic injury (Guruswamy and Elali, 2017). Microglial activation and polarization, as well as microglia-mediated inflammatory responses, play vital roles in the occurrence, development, and outcome of brain injury after ischemic stroke (Zhang et al., 2021). Thus, an active research field on the interaction between microglia and neuroinflammation in the development of ischemic stroke not only contributes to better understanding of the pathophysiology but also explore new therapeutic strategies for stroke.

This review will through a microglia perspective to introduce and discuss inflammation and immune mechanisms along the disease continuum from the acute cascades to chronic phase (Fig. 1). First, we will briefly review the pathobiology of ischemic stroke and the functional properties of microglia. Along the timeline of ischemic stroke progression, we will explore how microglia and infiltrating immune cells contribute to either beneficial or detrimental mechanisms of action during acute ischemic cascade. We will also discuss how microglia influence chronic neuroinflammation and adaptive immunity, leading to long-term outcomes after stroke and, in particular, cause specific complications such as post-stroke dementia or even depression.

Well-known traditional risk factors for ischemic stroke include hypertension, diabetes mellitus, smoking, atrial fibrillation, obesity, older age, cardiovascular disorders, and sedentary lifestyle (Ekker et al., 2018; Li et al., 2022, Li et al., 2022; Gyldenkerne et al., 2022). It is particularly concerning that ischemic stroke has emerged as both an important clinical feature and complication in COVID-19, with varying estimates of incidence (Bekelis et al., 2020; Mao et al., 2020; Yaghi et al., 2020). The brain is a vital and highly specialized organ that lacks the ability to repair tissue and regenerate damaged regions (Campbell et al., 2019). Consequently, acute ischemic stroke events are often result in high rates of mortality and disability, posing a great threat to patients' lives. During cerebral ischemia, nervous tissue damage occurs in two regions, the “infarct core” and “ischemic penumbra”. The threshold of cerebral blood flow (CBF) for the “infarct core” is time-dependent, when CBF rates below 10 ml/min/100 g for 2 h, or below 18 ml/min/100g during permanent occlusion causing irreversible infarction due to sudden depolarization and over-excitation of neurons (Jones et al., 1981). Ischemic penumbra is characterized by a CBF threshold of 20 mL/min/100 g, with no observed neuronal death but detectable changes in tissue structure and function, such as cessation of interneuron signal transmission, reduction in cellular aerobic metabolism, and suppression of ion pump function (Jones et al., 1981; Dabrowska et al., 2019; Ermine et al., 2021). The major immediate consequence of acute stroke phase is irreversible neuronal cell death and brain damage in the infarct core within minutes of insult onset (Sekerdag et al., 2018). For decades, the primary focus of ischemic stroke therapy has been on rescuing neurons in the penumbra region to prevent expansion of the infarct core. Although timely and appropriate reperfusion therapy following stroke onset has been shown to rescue neurons in the penumbra region, processes such as reperfusion injury, excitotoxicity, neuroinflammation, and oxidative stress can lead to secondary neuronal cell death (Fisher and Albers, 2013; Zhang et al., 2018; Imran et al., 2021).

Following the acute phase, in the sub-acute phase, there is a gradual expansion of the lesion area and further aggravation of brain damage through secondary ischemia or reperfusion injury. This process evolves over a period of weeks to months following the initial injury and is not a single process of brain tissue damage, but also involves the cleaning of dead cells and inhibition of inflammation to promote tissue repair. The chronic-phase after stroke lasts for months to years and rises the risk of depression, fatigue, dementia and seizures. However, the pathogenic mechanisms underlying these conditions are not well understood. Post-ischemic neuroinflammation plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of stroke and is involved in all stages of the ischemic cascade. Microglia, an immune cell type whose dynamic changes in activity are immediately linked to brain tissue damage, neuronal damage/death, and post-stroke neuroinflammation through the continuum of ischemic stroke, is the focus of our attention.

Microglia, which originate from erythro-myeloid progenitor cells in the yolk sac of the embryo (Utz et al., 2020), are the resident macrophage-like immune cells of the CNS that play a pivotal role in immune surveillance, synaptic scaling, and maintenance of neuroimmune homeostasis. In mice, microglial progenitors emigrate to the CNS as early as embryonic day 8.5–10.5 (Ginhoux et al., 2010; Ginhoux et al., 2013; Askew et al., 2018), which is much earlier than the presence of astrocytes and even before the onset of cortical neurogenesis (Norris and Kipnis, 2019). Unlike bone-marrow-derived macrophages, which enter the CNS only when the BBB is disrupted in disorders, microglia populate the CNS before the BBB is formed and seal the CNS from the periphery (Yong, 2022). The normal homeostasis and viability of microglia are highly dependent on colony-stimulating factor-1 (CSF-1, CD115, or c-fms) receptor signaling, which is triggered by two different cytokine ligands, CSF-1 and interleukin-34 (IL-34). CSF–1R deficient mice are born without microglia, and mice lacking either CSF-1 or IL-34 exhibit a major reduction in the population of microglia, illustrating that CSF-1 and IL-34 can partially compensate for each other under special circumstances (Ginhoux et al., 2006, 2010; Greter et al., 2012). In addition to parenchymal microglia, the CNS myeloid cells include non-parenchymal, border-associated macrophages (BAM), which can be subdivided into perivascular, meningeal, and choroid plexus macrophages and acts as immune sentinel roles in the barrier to entry into the CNS (Prinz et al., 2011; Utz et al., 2020). Microglia have been recognized as critical players in CNS function and development (Prinz et al., 2019). The most important characteristic of microglial cells is their sensitivity to changes in the CNS microenvironment. Resting microglia display a ramified morphology characterized by a relatively small cell body with extensively branched out soma (Frank-Cannon et al., 2009; Neumann et al., 2006). When pathological insults occur, microglia immediately undergo a phenotypic transformation from a resting state to an activated state, develop into an amoeboid-like phagocytic phenotype with an enlarged soma and shortened branches. Activated microglia play a central role in engulfing apoptotic neurons, cellular debris, and invading pathogens to promote neuronal microenvironment maintenance and tissue repair. Historically, the morphological transformation of microglia from ramified to amoeboid was regarded as a reliable indicator of their activation, implicating that the CNS is in a pathological state. Whereas, comprehensive morphometric analysis of microglia in the adult human cortical tissues has confirmed that four major microglial phenotypes co-exist (including primed, reactive, amoeboid, and ramified phenotypes) in individuals without neurological, inflammatory, or psychiatric illnesses (Torres-Platas et al., 2014).

Microglia and other macrophages are a highly heterogeneous population of cells in function and phenotype that are generally categorized into classically activated M1-phenotype with pro-inflammatory properties and the alternatively activated M2-phenotype, which exhibit anti-inflammatory properties (Gordon and Martinez, 2010). As microglia have been deeply studied in various CNS diseases, such as viral encephalitis, ischemic stroke, and Alzheimer's disease, this definition has become obsolete and requires a clearer understand of the associations between microglial morphology and functional states for an updated definition. Although researchers have used various modern biotechnologies (e.g. transcriptomic, epigenomic, and proteomic approaches) to elucidate the diverse microglia states in response to complex pathological changes (Gosselin et al., 2017; Butovsky and Weiner, 2018), there is no consensus reached. Future research directions of microglia diversity involve integrating molecular information at multiple levels of biology, including function, morphology, transcriptome, metabolome, and proteome, through high-dimensional techniques.

Most neurological disorders are closely associated with acute/chronic neuroinflammation regulated by the activation of microglia, which secrete anti- and pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines. The expression of target inflammatory genes induced by activated microglia _via_ various signaling pathways, including toll-like receptor (TLR)4/nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB)/mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs), interferon regulatory factor (IRF)5-IRF4, activators of transcription (STAT) 6, and STAT3 (Cai et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019a, Zhou et al., 2019b; Zhou et al., 2019, 2019; Al Mamun et al., 2020). Therefore, targeting microglia to regulate these signaling cascades as a treatment for neurogenic disorders is promising. Under CNS pathological conditions, microglia can secrete neurotoxic factors (e.g. glutamate) and neurotrophic factors [e.g. insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)], which exert cytotoxic and neuroprotective effects, respectively (Parkhurst et al., 2013; Voet et al., 2019; Pellerin et al., 2021). Moreover, microglia/macrophages are the primary cellular sources of reactive nitrogen species (RNS, e.g. nitric oxide) and reactive oxygen species (ROS, e.g. superoxide anion and hydrogen peroxide) (Baecher-Allan et al., 2018). Several studies have demonstrated that microglia are activated within minutes after ischemic onset and produce multiple proinflammatory factors, such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), which further aggravate neuroinflammation and exacerbate brain damage (Guruswamy and Elali, 2017; Jayaraj et al., 2019). Contradictory to apart from its proinflammatory properties, microglia also represent an endogenous self-protective mechanism that can limit cell damage in the ischemic penumbra upon brain ischemia (Rosito et al., 2014). Overall, microglia exhibite an important regulatory effect in the CNS microenvironment by secreting different pro- or anti-inflammatory signaling molecules. Identifying the diverse phenotypes of microglia in conjunction of their secretion profiles at different stages will help further our understanding of ischemic stroke pathology (Table .1).

The activation of microglia is characterized by morphological changes and decreased interactions with neurons. In addition to the ramified and amoeboid morphological states, researchers have identified at least two other morphological microglia (intermediate and round) coexist in acute phase of ischemic stroke (Thored et al., 2009; Anttila et al., 2017). The morphological changes of microglia are intimately related to their activation states and serve as an indicator of the severity of brain injury. Ramified microglia are predominantly located in the brain parenchyma away from the infarct core, including the contralateral side of the ischemic core and the ipsilateral distal regions. The shape of intermediate microglia is somewhere in between ramified-like and amoeboid-like, characterized by an enlarged soma and short branches. Both intermediate and amoeboid microglia are mainly found in the ischemic penumbra region. Round microglia, the most active phenotype, are spherical and macrophage-like, with the ability to rapidly migrate to the infarct core.

Activated microglia have a dual role in ischemic stroke, polarizing towards either the proinflammatory/neurotoxic M1 phenotype or the anti-inflammatory/neuroprotective M2 phenotype. The upregulation of M1-associated markers CD45, CD11b, and Iba-1 in the cortical ischemic penumbra within 0.5–1 h after MCAO suggests rapid polarization of microglia into M1-type in response to ischemia (Xu et al., 2020). Several studies exploring the temporal kinetics of microglial polarization in ischemic mice have demonstrated that the appearance of M2-microglia occurs as early as 12 h after MCAO, with rapid increases at 1–3 days and reaching a maximum at 3–5 days. M2-polarized microglia are mainly located around the infarct core and begin to convert to M1-like microglia at 7 days after cerebral ischemia, with the quantity of M2-microglia returning to pre-injury levels by day 14 (Hu et al., 2012; Perego et al., 2011). In a tMCAO model of transgenic mice (CX3CR1 GFP/+), authors used the specific marker Tmem119 to distinguish resident microglia from infiltrating monocytes and found that blood monocytes-derived macrophages start to be infiltrated into the CNS at day 3 after ischemic stroke (Park et al., 2021). Therefore, the acute inflammatory response after stroke is mainly mediated by microglia.

Several comprehensive literatures have discussed microglial biology in ischemic stroke (Ceulemans et al., 2010; Endres et al., 2022; Spiteri et al., 2022). Herein, we focus on the dynamic effects of microglia at different stages of ischemic stroke. As the development and outcome of ischemic stroke are tightly related to individual patient differences (e.g., gender, age, complications, and severity of disease), ischemic stroke is roughly divided into three periods (Endres et al., 2022): the acute phase (hours), subacute phase (days to weeks), and chronic phase (weeks to years) (Fig. 1). Further investigation into the dynamics of microglial activation profiles and the influence of immunotherapy on microglial function is needed to better evaluate its therapeutic effect in ischemic stroke and provide guidance for clinical treatment.

**Intravascular events** Acute ischemic stroke results from focal cerebral ischemia, mainly occurs secondary to atherosclerosis and embolism, and can also develop from other conditions including moya-moya disease, Call-Fleming syndrome, hypercoagulability, and vasculitis (Mendelson and Prabhakaran, 2021). The normal functioning of the brain relies on a constant supply of glucose and oxygen from the circulatory system. When cerebral blood supply is interrupted, the ischemic brain experiences irreversible damage in a hypoxic and energy-deficient environment, resulting in the formation of an infarct core within hours (Moskowitz et al., 2010). Following arterial occlusion, hypoxia and ROS in the vascular lumen immediately trigger the clotting cascade, leading to leukocyte recruitment, complement system activation, platelet aggregation, and inflammatory reactions (Peerschke et al., 2010; McGarry et al., 2018). Subsequently, perivascular mast cells and macrophages are activated, releasing vasoactive factors [e.g., histamine and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)] and pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α and IL-1β), respectively (Konsman et al., 2007; Lindsberg et al., 2010; Parrella et al., 2019). The chemotactic peptide C5a, interacting with complement receptors CD88 expressed on mast cells, promotes the secretion of MMPs (MMP-9 and MMP-2), which can hydrolyze matrix protein and further disrupt the BBB (Iadecola and Anrather, 2011). The subsequent infiltration of blood-derived immune cells is closely related to the time of BBB breakdown after stroke, with an increase in vascular permeability peaking at 3–6 h and delayed BBB opening occurring at 48–72 h (Abo-Ramadan et al., 2009; Prakash and Carmichael, 2015).

**Extravascular events** In the cerebral parenchyma, hypoxia/ischemia leads to a shift in cellular metabolism towards anaerobic respiration, resulting in decreased adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production and the accumulation of lactic acid. Depletion of ATP induces dysfunction of the sodium potassium pump (Na+/K+ ATPase) and calcium (Ca 2+) ATPase, subsequent reductions of transcellular transport leads to the intracellular accumulation of calcium, sodium, and water. Furthermore, excessive secretion of presynaptic excitatory glutamate upon cell membrane depolarization, allows for more extracellular Ca 2+ influx through N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA)-gated channels. ROS produced by oxidative stress cause more cellular damage due to lipid peroxidation of membranes and DNA. Overall, the combined effects of energy deficiency, acidosis, excessive glutamate, intracellular Ca 2+ accumulation, membranes lipid peroxidation, and nitric oxide (NO) neurotoxicity disrupt vital cell components, ultimately causing cell death. Neurons are more vulnerable than glia and other cells, exhibiting earlier onset of dysfunction and/or faster death after acute ischemic insult (Lipton, 1999). Resting microglia constantly perform dynamic surveillance of the brain parenchyma to detect neuronal damage or death _via_ microglia-neuron tight junction, such as specialized somatic purinergic junctions (Cserép et al., 2020). Neuronal injury and death initiates a new stage of innate immune response in the CNS (Fig. 2).

When neurons are damaged or dying, they release damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) such as purine pyrimidines and nucleotides [uridine triphosphate (UTP), ATP, and their catabolites], high-mobility group box 1 protein (HMGB1), heat shock proteins (HSPs), preoxiredoxins, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), and mitochondrial N-formyl peptides (mtNFPS). These molecules can activate pattern recognition receptors (PPRs) on immune cells in the brain and recruit peripheral immune cells into the CNS (Garcia-Bonilla and Iadecola, 2012; Benakis et al., 2015; Petrovic-Djergovic et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2016). Toll-like receptors (TLRs), particularly TLR4 and TLR2, and nucleotide-binding and oligomerization domain-like receptors (NLRs) are the PPRs involved in microglial activation. High levels of extracellular ATP and UTP can activate the NLRP3 inflammasome and enhance caspase-1 activity in microglia _via_ P2X7 receptors binding, leading to the production and secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Bours et al., 2006). This entire process of purinergic excitotoxicity is initiated and progressively intensified within 20 min after ischemia, and then returns to baseline at around 4 h. HMGB1, a nuclear protein, can be released from damaged or necrotic neurons or secreted by activated microglia and astrocytes after ischemic stroke (Ye et al., 2019). Extracellular HMGB1 binds to multiple microglia surface receptors, such as TLR2, TLR4, and RAGE (receptor for advanced glycation end products) triggering inflammatory responses through the NF-κB signaling pathway, which increases the production of proinflammatory cytokines [TNF-α, interleukin (IL)-1, IL-6 and IL-8] and the expression of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) (Qiu et al., 2010; Fang et al., 2012). HSPs, a group of molecular chaperones, are produced by cells in response to stressful conditions and functions as a detector of misfolded protein. HSP 70 can exert both protective and detrimental effects depending on their location. Intracellular HSP 70 can inhibit cellular damage signaling cascades, including NF-κB, MMPs, and ROS. On the contrary, extracellular Hsp70 exhibits pro-inflammatory effects similar to those of HGMB1. Activated microglia or recruited macrophages recognize extracellular HSP 70 and activate TLRs on microglia/macrophages, stimulating the releases of pro-inflammatory cytokines _via_ NF-κB and associated pathways. Peroxiredoxins (Prxs), a class of thiol-based peroxidases, acts as ROS scavengers in the cytoplasm. Prxs such as Prx-1, Prx-2, Prx-5 and Prx-6 are released from injured and dying neurons 12 h after an acute ischemic event onset and lead to increased expression of pro-inflammatory factors like IL-23 from microglia/macrophages by TLR-2 and TLR-4 ligation. IL-23 can stimulate γδT cells to produce IL-17, playing a central role in recruiting neutrophils into the CNS. Mitochondrial DAMPs, especially mtNFPS and mtDNA, are involved in the initiation and activation of NLRP3 inflammasome, leading to neuroinflammation and neuronal cells death (He et al., 2020). These events cause more blood-derived leukocyte infiltration and exacerbate brain tissue damage, leading to the generation of more DAMPs. Thus, a vicious circle is formed and sustained.

As mentioned above, M2-type microglia can be found in the ischemic region during the acute phase of stroke. These microglia release anti-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-10 and TGF-β) and neurotrophic factors [e.g., neuronal growth factor (NGF), insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF1) and BDNF], which contribute to the resolution of inflammation (Ortega-Gómez et al., 2013), tissue reconstruction and repair, angiogenesis (Sica and Mantovani, 2012), and proliferation of neural precursor cells. Recently, PLX5622, a small molecule CSF–1R inhibitor, has been used to specifically deplete CNS microglia _in vivo_ without affecting peripheral monocytes and macrophages (Kokona et al., 2018; Mrdjen et al., 2018). Depletion of microglia by PLX5622 results in an increased infarct volume and neuronal injury, as well as a reduction of neurons and astrocytes in young and aged male mice at 24h MCAO (Szalay et al., 2016; Marino Lee et al., 2021). These findings indirectly indicate that the neuroprotective and tissue repair effects of M2-microglia are vitally important for ischemic stroke recovery. The activation of M2-microglia is also regulated by injured neurons, which releases vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and lipocalin-2 as a “distress signal” that shifts microglia into potentially pro-recovery forms (Xing et al., 2014; Esposito et al., 2018). IL-10 and TGF-β, produced by M2-type microglia, are multiacting anti-inflammatory factors that promote the polarization of microglia towards an anti-inflammatory phenotype and provide an anti-inflammatory microenvironment for tissue repair after stroke.

Post-ischemic microglia exhibit biphasic effects on astrocytes, oligodendrocytes (OLs), and brain microvascular endothelial cells through their function of different phenotypes. In response to CNS pathological changes, **astrocytes** undergo a unique transformation into a reactive state, termed “astrogliosis”. Zamanian et al. have classified reactive astrocytes into two subtypes: a detrimental subtype called “A1-specific” and a beneficial subtype called “A2-specific”, using a similar classification method to activated microglia (Zamanian et al., 2012). Researchers (Liddelow et al., 2017; Jha et al., 2019) have provided evidence supporting that microglia respond faster to pathological stimuli than astrocytes, determining the fate of astrocytes, inducing either A1-specific or A2-specific astrocytosis. Activated M1-microglia produce proinflammatory factors, such as IL-1β, TNF-α, and complement component 1 subcomponent q (C1q), which can induce A1 reactive astrocytes. The synergistic action of M1-microglia and A1-astrocytes further aggravates neuroinflammation, contributing to oligodendrocyte and neuronal death (Liddelow et al., 2017). Conversely, A2 astrocytes induced by anti-inflammatory M2-microglia exert attenuated inflammatory and neuroprotective effeccts after stroke. An _in vitro_ study (Baxter et al., 2021) showed that neuron/astrocyte co-culture increased the production of TGF-β2, which functions as a secreted factor mediating microglial signature gene induction. Furthermore, astrocytes and neurons combine to provide immunomodulatory cures, inhibiting primed microglial responses to weak inflammatory stimuli (without affecting the maximum response) and, in turn, suppressing the influences of inflammation on the astrocytes and neurons themselves, thus, forming a negative feedback loop (Baxter et al., 2021).

**Oligodendrocytes**, the only myelin-forming cells of the CNS, are highly susceptible to ischemic injury. Conspicuous swelling of OLs occurs as early as 30 min after MCAO, followed by massive lethal injury to OLs within 3 h (Pantoni et al., 1996). Demyelination leads to axonal dysfunction and structure changes; therefore, remyelination is critical for the successful functioning of regenerated nerves. Migration and proliferation of oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs), recognition of target axons, differentiation of OPCs into mature oligodendrocytes, membrane outgrowth, axonal wrapping, and myelin compaction are all essential for the remyelination of ischemic region. Microglia participate in both myelin injury and remyelination during ischemic stroke. TNF-α plays a key role in OL death under _in vitro_ and _in vivo_ conditions (Yang et al., 2011) and is primarily released by M1-microglia after ischemic stroke. The anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-13, IL-10, TGF-α, and IL-33) secreted by M2-microglia decrease the death of OLs and promote the proliferation and differentiation of OPCs to counteract ischemic injury (Miron et al., 2013; Dai et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2021). **Brain microvascular endothelial cells (BMECs),** interconnected with tight junctions, form the primary barrier of the BBB. Disruption of the BBB leads to blood-derived immune cell infiltration into the CNS, recognized as a hallmark event in the pathological course of ischemic stroke (Arba et al., 2021).

Activated microglia's pro-inflammatory effects accelerate BBB disruption mainly through the following mechanisms. Firstly, neuroinflammation mediated by activated microglia leads to microvascular endothelial cell damage and enhances the permeability of the BBB (Häußler et al., 2020). Secondly, dysfunction and injury of neurons and glial initiated by cerebral ischemia can further cause BMEC atrophy and sparse microvessels since their mutual nutritional support for BMECs is impaired (Zegeye et al., 2020). Thirdly, M1-microglia produce proinflammatory mediators (e.g., TNF-α, IL-6, MMPs, and IL-1β) and chemokines (CCL2-5, CXCL-1, and CXCL-10) that disrupt the integrity of the BBB by redistributing tight-junction proteins and altering actin cytoskeletal organization in BMECs (Hu et al., 2022). Similarly, M2-type microglia exert opposite protective effects on the BBB through the secretion of remodeling factors, such as IL-8, TGF-beta1, IL-10, MMP-9, and VEGF after ischemic stroke (Imai et al., 2007; Crain et al., 2013; Rosenberg, 2009).

Accumulated tissue debris and dead cells in ischemic infarct core limit brain repair. Microglia and subsequent infiltrating peripheral monocytes/macrophages constitute the predominant phagocytes to remove them to facilitate brain remodeling (Iadecola and Anrather, 2011). Whether dying neurons are engulfed is regulated by a network of “help me”, “find me” and “eat me” signals. Damaged neurons secrete CX3CL1, which serves as a “help me” signal to modulate microglia phagocytosis (Suzumura, 2013). Dying neurons in the lesion area amplifies CX3CL1 production, which evokes “eat-me” signals that are recognized by microglia expressing complement C3a receptor (C3aR), resulting in phagocytosis of the dying but still viable neurons (Surugiu et al., 2019).

In brief, the acute phase pathological changes of ischemic stroke can be categorized into intravascular events (involving interactions between platelets and leukocytes) and extravascular brain parenchymal events (involving interactions between glia and neurons). Microglia serve as the central hub for intercellular communication and play a dual role in the development of the disease.

During the subacute phase, which occurs in the few days to weeks following ischemic stroke onset, the lesion continues to develop, and subsequent events are closely linked to the interaction between microglia and infiltrating peripheral immune cells. BBB disruption triggers vasogenic brain edema, a type of extracellular edema characterized by the extravasation and extracellular accumulation of fluid in the cerebral parenchyma. This typically occurs at 12 h and peaks about 72–96 h after the initial damage in MCAO mice (Gelderblom et al., 2009; Stokum et al., 2015). The secretion of pro-inflammatory and neurotoxic mediators by M1 microglia facilitates the infiltration of peripheral blood immune cells into the ischemic region. This recruitment of peripheral immune cells to the CNS, results in a dynamic cross-regulation of their respective phenotypes (Fig. 3). Previous investigations have shown that the infiltration of the penumbra by peripheral innate immune cells (macrophages, neutrophils, and dendritic cells) precedes the subsequent influx of adaptive immune cells (B and T lymphocytes) into the brain lesion area in ischemia reperfusion mice models (Gelderblom et al., 2009; Endres et al., 2022).

**Neutrophil** Neutrophilic granulocytes are among the first peripheral innate immune cells to infiltrate the cerebral ischemic region, closely followed by monocytes. A temporal study by Gelderblom and colleagues demonstrated that neutrophils infiltrate the brain parenchyma within 12 h, overwhelm the ischemic hemisphere by Day 3, and decline notablely by Day 7 post-reperfusion (Gelderblom et al., 2009). Higher neutrophil counts in ischemic stroke patients are associated with more severe symptoms and larger infarct volumes, while elevated neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratios are linked to worse functional outcomes. (Guo et al., 2016). Pro-inflammatory mediators, such as IL-1beta, IL-6, TNF-α, released by activated microglia can promote the secretion of adhesion molecules, including intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1) and vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM-1)], which facilitate neutrophil endothelial transmigration (Popović et al., 2012). Activated microglia engulf infiltrating neutrophils at the peri-infarction cortex, as evidenced by the process of phagocytosis in which amoeboid activated microglia internalize one or several infiltrated neutrophils has been observed _in vivo_ (Neumann et al., 2018). Microglia depletion induced by feeding the mice long-term with PLX5622 increases the numbers of neutrophils in the cerebral ischemic tissue and exacerbates brain damage, supporting the view that microglia contribute to neutrophil removal (Otxoa-de-Amezaga et al., 2019). Post-ischemia, neutrophils infiltrating the peri-infarction exhibit phenotypic heterogeneity, including pro-inflammatory N1-subtype neutrophils and alternative N2-subtype neutrophils associated with neuroprotection and inflammatory resolution (Silvestre-Roig et al., 2016; Fridlender et al., 2009). While the exact phenotype targeted by microglia remains unclear, these findings provide valuable insights into the role of neutrophils and microglia in cerebral ischemia.

**Macrophage** Chemical signals associated with neuronal death, microglia activation, and BBB leakage lead to the dynamic recruitment of immature monocytes into the ischemic penumbra and their subsequent differentiation into mature, specific macrophages. Immature monocytes infiltrate the peri-infarct region within 24 h of tMCAO (Gliem et al., 2012), with the number of infiltrating monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) peaking at 3–5 days post-insult before rapidly declining. MDMs remain higher at 7 days compared to contralateral side, reaching control values at 14 days (Wattananit et al., 2016). Circulating monocytes mainly exist in two different phenotypes, “inflammatory” and “patrolling”, and infiltrate the ischemic region to contribute to inflammation or damaged brain tissue repair in a distinct manner. Inflammatory-phenotype monocytes express CCR2+Ly6C hi in mice or CCR2+CD14+CD16− in humans, while patrolling-phenotype monocytes express CX3CR1+Ly6C lo in mice or CX3CR1+CD14+/−CD16+ in humans. A histological study (Garcia-Bonilla et al., 2016) of tMCAO in green fluorescent protein (GFP) transgenic bone marrow chimeric mice revealed that inflammatory monocytes predominate during the early subacute phase (3–5 days), and “patrolling” monocytes number strikingly increased during the late subacute phase (14 and 28 days). The secondary accumulation of “patrolling” monocytes is most likely due to a phenotypic switch of “inflammatory” monocytes rather than infiltration of blood borne“patrolling” monocytes (Garcia-Bonilla et al., 2016). In the early subacute phase, “inflammatory” MDMs and resident microgliarelease factors to mediate CNS inflammation and contribute to the removal of neutrophils, cellular debris, and apoptotic cells. Microglia and monocyte-derived macrophages exhibit temporal activation and polarization that presents an antagonistic situation in ischemic stroke, potentially maintaining a homeostasis of the microenvironment (Fig. 4). Despite significant efforts to define the temporal and phenotype changes of microglia and infiltrating monocytes/macrophages after ischemic stroke, the distinct functional consequences of their polarization remain largely unstudied. Understanding the molecular mechanisms controlling the differentiation of pro-versus anti-inflammatory microglia and MDM subsets and the interaction between different subtypes is crucial to shed light on the mechanism of ischemic damage and post-stroke brain repair.

**Dendritic cell** Dendritic cells (DCs) are professional antigen presenting cells (APCs) that bridge the innate and adaptive immune systems by priming naive T cell responses (Banchereau and Steinman, 1998). Although the CNS has traditionally been described as an immune-privileged site without DCs due to the stringent brain-blood barrier (Preusser et al., 2015), mounting experimental evidence suggests that CNS resident microglia can differentiate into a DC-like subtype expressing the DC surface marker CD11c and exert antigen-presentation functions in response to brain damage or disease (Felger et al., 2010; Butovsky et al., 2006). The number of DC-like microglia increases at 24–72 h post-ischemia, as evidenced by the up-regulation of major histocompatibility complexes (MHC) II and co-stimulatory molecules (CD80 and CD86), and they accumulate in the peri-infarction area in proximity to recruited T-cells (Felger et al., 2010). In contrast, peripheral DCs primarily infiltrate the ischemic infarct core at 72 h after MCAO (Felger et al., 2010). Despite the definition of DC-like microglia as brain-DCs is controversial, microglia mediate the recruitment of peripheral DCs and microglia-DCs interaction plays a critical role in antigen presentation, setting the foundation for adaptive immune responses. These current findings highlight the need to further explore the relationship between microglia and peripheral DCs post-ischemia/reperfusion.

**T-cell** T lymphocytes infiltrate the brain earlier than B cells post-stroke, with infiltration data from MCAO mice showing that T lymphocytes appear in the brain at 24 h and reach their peak within the first week after insult onset, while post-ischemic B lymphocytes enter the brain after 7days (Gelderblom et al., 2009; Grønberg et al., 2013; Korf et al., 2022). Both types of lymphocytes persists in the brain parenchyma for at least 1 month following experimental MCAO (Doyle et al., 2017; Xie et al., 2019) and up to 3 months (Li et al., 2021; Heindl et al., 2021) in ischemic stroke patients. T lymphocytes are also heterogeneous in the cerebral ischemic region, with different T cell subpopulations having distinct respective effector functions in response to pathological conditions. In the early stage of T-lymphocytic infiltration, largely proinflammatory subtypes of CD4+ helper T lymphocytes (Th1 and Th17), CD8+ cytotoxic T cells, and γδ T cells in the brain worsen impaired tissue (Shichita et al., 2009; Selvaraj et al., 2021). Depletion of CD4+ T cells has been shown to reduce circulating levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IFN-γ, CXCL-10, CCL-2, and CXCL-1 (Harris et al., 2020), indicating the detrimental role of CD4+ T cells after stroke. Although microglia/macrophages are act as the main source of TNF-α production following an ischemic stroke, CD3+CD4−CD8− T cells also contribute to the secretion of TNF-α from day 1 to day 3 and are found near the Iba1+ microglia (Meng et al., 2019). The presence of TNF-α stimulates the polarization of microglia to a pro-inflammatory phenotype, ultimately exacerbating inflammation following the stroke. Conversely, the subsequent differentiation of T cells into regulatory T lymphocytes (Tregs) and Th2 lymphocytes mainly contribute to anti-inflammation and neuroprotection (Liesz et al., 2015; Ito et al., 2019). The release of osteopontin by Tregs plays a crucial role in inducing a reparative phenotype change in microglia, which in turn enhances the differentiation of oligodendrocyte precursor cells and facilitates the repair of white matter (Shi et al., 2021). M1-type microglia initiate proinflammatory T lymphocyte responses by releasing chemokines (CXCL9 and CXCL10), proinflammatory factors (IL-6 and IL-23), and other neurotoxic substances (Mantovani et al., 2004; J. Wang et al., 2015). The mediators of inflammation released by T cells, including IFN-γ and TNF-α from Th1 cells and IL-17 from Th17 cells or γδ T cells, in turn, promote microglia/macrophages polarization into a proinflammatory phenotype (Shichita et al., 2009; De Marchi et al., 2021). The secretion of IL-17 from γδ T cells is dependent on IL-23, as evidence by IL-17 production is significantly reduced in Il-23−/− mice (Shichita et al., 2009), and IL-23p19 knockdown suppressed IL-17 mRNA and protein levels (Zheng et al., 2015). On the other hand, the anti-inflammatory phenotype of microglia/macrophages are promoted by Treg-derived (e.g. IL-10, TGFβ) and/or Th2-derived (e.g. IL-4 and IL-13) factors, resulting in subsequently increased production of anti-inflammatory cytokines and neurotrophic factors contribute to resolution of acute neuroinflammation (Heneka et al., 2014). M2-type microglia further activate the recruitment and differentiation of Treg/Th2 cells by releasing cytokines (such as IL-4, IL-10 and TGF-β) and chemokines (such as CCL24, CCL22 and CCL17), sequentially diminishing the inflammatory response (Brea et al., 2014). Nevertheless, it should be noted that Tregs may cause microvascular dysfunction and consequently thrombus formation and secondary infarct growth in the acute phase after experimental ischemic stroke by interacting with endothelial cells and platelets (Schuhmann et al., 2015).

**B-cell** Under physiological conditions, B cells are detectable and scarce in the CNS (including cerebrospinal fluid, meninges, and possibly brain parenchyma), but are transported in larger quantities to CNS tissues in response to injury or disease (Comi et al., 2021). Ren et al. (2011) showed that B cell deficient (μMT−/−) mice developed larger infarct volumes, higher mortality, and more severe functional deficits among mice after tMCAO, suggesting a potentially protective role for B cells during the early stage of acute ischemic injury after stroke. B cell deficient mice that received B cells from IL-10+ mice had reduced infarct size, less severe functional deficits, and lower mortality in the brain 48 h after MCAO (Bodhankar et al., 2013; Ortega et al., 2020), while the transfer of B cells from IL-10 deficient mice did not (Ren et al., 2011). These findings indicate that the beneficial effect of B cells depend on their secretion of the anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective cytokine IL-10 into the post-infarct brain. The immune suppressive function of B cell is attributed to relatively rare populations of regulatory B cells (Bregs), in particular, IL-10-producing B cells also referred to as regulatory “B10” cells (Candando et al., 2014). CXCL13 (also called B cell-attracting chemokine-1) and its receptor CXCR5 are responsible for the migration of B cells (Ansel et al., 1999; Rupprecht et al., 2009). Microglia, among other cells, serve as the main source of CXCL13 in the CNS (Esen et al., 2014) and may exert a pivotal role in the regulation of B cell infiltration. Besides microglia/macrophages and DCs, B cells also acts as antigen presenting cells capable of presenting antigenic fragments to T-cells in complex with cell surface MHC II molecules to facilitate the activation of the adaptive immune response (Kooy-Winkelaar et al., 2011). B cell deficient mice showed a greater quantity of proinflammatory microglia in the ipsilateral hemisphere after MCAO at 48 h, hinting at an inhibitory action of B cells for M1-type microglial activation (Ren et al., 2011). B cells exhibit multiphenotypic characteristics and carry out diverse functions following a stroke. Selvaraj and colleagues conducted a systematic review on the heterogeneity of B cell functions in stroke, highlighting their multiphenotypic characteristics and diverse roles in response to ischemic and hypoxic conditions (Selvaraj et al., 2016). As a result, we have focused our attention on more recent research in this field. In both young and aged brain, there is a significant increase in the population of CD11b high B cells on post-MCAO day 7. This increase is closely associated with the anticipated activation of microglia subsequent to a stroke, as evidenced by elevated expression of CD45 and MHC-II, along with reduced expression of Tmem119 and P2RY12 (Honarpisheh et al., 2020; Ronaldson and Davis, 2020). This is a scientific review article published in *Neurochemistry International* (Volume 169, October 2023, Article 105584) titled "Time-dependent dual effect of microglia in ischemic stroke" by Ping-long Fan, Sha-sha Wang, Shi-feng Chu, and Nai-hong Chen. The article reviews the dual (both protective and detrimental) role of microglia in ischemic stroke across acute, subacute, and chronic phases.

**Key Background Data:**
- Stroke is the third leading cause of death and disability worldwide; ~85% of strokes are ischemic.
- Global incidence of ischemic stroke was 7,630,800 cases in 2019, with an 87.55% increase from 1990 to 2019.
- Microglia constitute 5–20% of the total glial population and are resident macrophages of the CNS.
- Current first-line therapies are limited: intravenous thrombolysis has a 4.5-hour window; intravascular recanalization has a 16–24-hour window. Only 7.3% of acute ischemic stroke patients in developed European countries receive intravenous thrombolysis, and only 1.9% receive intravascular recanalization.

**Microglial Biology:**
- Microglia originate from erythro-myeloid progenitor cells in the embryonic yolk sac, emigrating to the CNS as early as embryonic day 8.5–10.5 in mice.
- Their survival depends on CSF-1R receptor signaling (via CSF-1 and IL-34 ligands).
- Resting microglia have a ramified morphology; upon activation they transform to amoeboid-like phagocytic phenotypes.
- Microglia are classified into M1 (pro-inflammatory/neurotoxic) and M2 (anti-inflammatory/neuroprotective) phenotypes, though this classification is increasingly viewed as oversimplified.

**Temporal Dynamics of Microglial Polarization:**
- M1-microglia upregulate markers (CD45, CD11b, Iba-1) within 0.5–1 hour after MCAO.
- M2-microglia appear as early as 12 hours after MCAO, increase at 1–3 days, peak at 3–5 days, and begin converting to M1-like microglia at 7 days, returning to pre-injury levels by day 14.
- Blood monocyte-derived macrophages infiltrate the CNS at day 3 post-stroke.

**Dual Effects Across Disease Phases:**

*Acute phase:*
- Activated microglia produce proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α) that exacerbate brain damage, but M2-microglia release anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-10, TGF-β) and neurotrophic factors (NGF, IGF-1, BDNF) that promote tissue repair and neuroprotection.
- Depletion of microglia using PLX5622 (CSF-1R inhibitor) increases infarct volume and neuronal injury, demonstrating their protective role.
- Microglia interact bidirectionally with astrocytes (inducing A1 detrimental or A2 beneficial reactive states), oligodendrocytes (participating in both myelin injury and remyelination), and brain microvascular endothelial cells (affecting BBB integrity).
- DAMPs (ATP, UTP, HMGB1, HSPs, peroxiredoxins, mitochondrial DNA) released by injured neurons activate microglia via TLRs and NLRP3 inflammasomes, initiating neuroinflammation.

*Subacute phase:*
- Microglia mediate infiltration of peripheral immune cells including neutrophils (infiltrating within 12h, peaking by day 3), monocyte-derived macrophages (peaking at 3–5 days), dendritic cells (24–72h), T cells (appearing at 24h, peaking within first week), and B cells (entering after 7 days).
- M1-microglia release chemokines promoting leukocyte recruitment; M2-microglia promote anti-inflammatory phenotypes in infiltrating cells.
- B cells play a protective role through IL-10 secretion; B cell-deficient mice develop larger infarcts and worse outcomes.
- Microglia serve as the main CNS source of CXCL13, regulating B cell migration.

*Chronic phase:*
- Post-stroke neuroinflammation contributes to long-term complications including depression, fatigue, dementia, and seizures.
- The review emphasizes that dynamic intervention of microglial subsets or functions is a promising therapeutic strategy.

**Conclusions:**
- Microglia play a time-dependent dual role in ischemic stroke, acting as both drivers of neuroinflammation and key mediators of tissue repair.
- Understanding the dynamic variation of microglial phenotypes at different stroke stages could aid in developing more effective therapeutic and diagnostic strategies.

# Review article

Functions and mechanisms of microglia/macrophages in neuroinflammation and neurogenesis after stroke

Author links open overlay panel Xiao-Yi Xiong, Liang Liu, Qing-Wu Yang

Show more

Add to Mendeley

[https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pneurobio.2016.05.001](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pneurobio.2016.05.001 "Persistent link using digital object identifier")[Get rights and content](https://s100.copyright.com/AppDispatchServlet?publisherName=ELS&contentID=S030100821630003X&orderBeanReset=true)

## Highlights

*   •We discuss microglial and macrophage morphologies and phenotypic changes in response to acute [brain damage](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/brain-injury) and repair in the context of stroke. 
*   •We argue that future translational studies should be targeting multiple key regulating molecules with a concept of “therapeutic time window”. 
*   •We suggest that constructing new experimental stroke models should be considered. 
*   •We suggest that identifying new gene signatures for circulating immune cells when they enter into the [CNS](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/central-nervous-system) should be considered. 
*   •We suggest that exploring the endogenous [neuroprotective](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/neuroprotective-agent) mechanisms responsible for brain repair should be considered. 

## Abstract

Microglia/macrophages are the major immune cells involved in the defence against brain damage. Their morphology and functional changes are correlated with the release of danger signals induced by stroke. These cells are normally responsible for clearing away dead neural cells and restoring neuronal functions. However, when excessively activated by the damage-associated molecular patterns following stroke, they can produce a large number of proinflammatory cytokines that can disrupt neural cells and the blood-brain barrier and influence neurogenesis. These effects indicate the important roles of microglia/macrophages in the pathophysiological processes of stroke. However, the modifiable and adaptable nature of microglia/macrophages may also be beneficial for brain repair and not just result in damage. These distinct roles may be attributed to the different microglia/macrophage phenotypes because the M1 population is mainly destructive, while the M2 population is neuroprotective. Additionally, different gene expression signature changes in microglia/macrophages have been found in diverse inflammatory milieus. These biofunctional features enable dual roles for microglia/macrophages in brain damage and repair. Currently, it is thought that the proper inflammatory milieu may provide a suitable microenvironment for neurogenesis; however, detailed mechanisms underlying the inflammatory responses that initiate or inhibit neurogenesis remain unknown. This review summarizes recent progress concerning the mechanisms involved in brain damage, repair and regeneration related to microglia/macrophage activation and phenotype transition after stroke. We also argue that future translational studies should be targeting multiple key regulating molecules to improve brain repair, which should be accompanied by the concept of a “therapeutic time window” for sequential therapies.

## Introduction

Over the past decades, an increasing amount of research data from experimental and clinical stroke studies have helped us to understand the complex factors relating to the pathophysiological processes of stoke, including ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) and subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Once ischemia occurs, along with the cerebral blood flow reduction and energy deprivation the native microglia undergo morphological changes (Davalos et al., 2005, Dunn et al., 2001, Gyoneva et al., 2009, Masuda et al., 2011) in preparation for the forthcoming immune response. When reperfusion begins, microglia become activated in the penumbra and start to expand cellular protrusions towards the adjacent blood vessels. Subsequently, these perivascular activated microglia start to engulf endothelial cells via phagocytosis, which allows the entrance of blood serum components (Jolivel et al., 2015). The morphological and phenotypic changes in the native microglia in the brain represent an initiation of the events in response to stroke, which are accompanied by the subsequent infiltration of macrophages. Recently, these two immune cells have been found to be derived from the same origin (Ginhoux et al., 2010) and to have similar biofunctions, such as producing inflammatory mediators and clearing cellular debris. However, these two types of cells can play different roles in the injured brain, which may involve different patterns of gene expression (Butovsky et al., 2014). For example, microglia may protect the injured brain while macrophages concomitantly damage the brain under the same circumstances (Yamasaki et al., 2014).

The immune system is considered to play a significant role in determining the condition of the brain and the survival of patients following stroke (Iadecola and Anrather, 2011). Microglia/macrophages are the major cells in an organism's immune system, and they play important roles in CNS repair and regeneration (Hanisch and Kettenmann, 2007). In addition to their neuroprotective roles, microglia/macrophages are also the major producers of proinflammatory cytokines, which can greatly inhibit brain repair and neurogenesis (Ekdahl et al., 2003, Smith et al., 2012). Therefore, the dual roles of microglia and infiltrating macrophages hamper the brain's restoration after stroke. The inflamed microenvironment greatly influences the phenotypic changes in microglia/macrophages, which results in different gene expression patterns and biofunctions in the same brain tissue. This may be explained by the findings that the M1 phenotype of microglia/macrophages induced for instance by lipopolysaccharide (LPS) mainly exhibits destructive effects on the brain, while the M2 phenotype inducible by IL-4 exhibits neuroprotective effects on the brain (Hu et al., 2015). Therefore, these results suggest that, in general, promoting the M2 phenotype and inhibiting the M1 phenotype can be beneficial to brain recovery after stroke.

Furthermore, promoting effective neurogenesis is gradually becoming an important therapeutic method for the treatment of stroke because the dead and lost neurons in the cortical lesions need to be replaced by new-born neurons to replenish and reconstruct the neuronal connections. Recent studies show that microglia/macrophages are involved in each step of neurogenesis. For example, microglia/macrophages produce trophic factors to guide cell migrations (Batchelor et al., 2002), but they can also produce inflammatory cytokines to reduce the survival of new-born neurons (Liu et al., 2007). Therefore, understanding the details of the roles and mechanisms of microglia/macrophages in neurogenesis after stroke would provide help in promoting novel and exciting therapeutic approaches for brain repair.

In this review article, we discuss microglial and macrophage morphologies and phenotypic changes in response to acute brain damage and repair in the context of stroke. Given these modifiable and adaptable functions of microglia/macrophages, we argue that future translational studies should be targeting multiple key regulating molecules involved in changes in microglia/macrophage activation and polarization and that the studies should incorporate the concept of a “therapeutic time window” for sequential therapies. Finally, we also give some suggestions for further research, such as constructing new experimental stroke models, identifying new gene signatures for circulating immune cells when they enter into the CNS, and exploring the endogenous neuroprotective mechanisms responsible for brain repair, which may quicken the forward pace of research.

This is a review article published in Progress in Neurobiology (Volume 142, July 2016, Pages 23-44) by Xiao-Yi Xiong, Liang Liu, and Qing-Wu Yang, titled "Functions and mechanisms of microglia/macrophages in neuroinflammation and neurogenesis after stroke." DOI: 10.1016/j.pneurobio.2016.05.001. The article is highly cited (634 citations) and contains 302 references.

KEY FINDINGS AND ARGUMENTS:
- Microglia/macrophages are the major immune cells involved in defending the brain against damage following stroke (ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, and subarachnoid hemorrhage).
- Microglia and macrophages share the same origin (derived from primitive macrophages during brain development per fate mapping analysis by Ginhoux et al., 2010) and have similar biofunctions, but can play different roles in the injured brain due to different gene expression patterns.
- These cells have dual roles: normally they clear dead neural cells and restore neuronal function, but when excessively activated by damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) after stroke, they produce proinflammatory cytokines that disrupt neural cells and the blood-brain barrier and influence neurogenesis.
- The M1 microglia/macrophage phenotype (induced by LPS) is mainly destructive, while the M2 phenotype (induced by IL-4) is neuroprotective. In general, promoting M2 and inhibiting M1 phenotypes is beneficial to brain recovery after stroke.
- Microglia/macrophages are involved in each step of neurogenesis: they produce trophic factors that guide cell migration, but can also produce inflammatory cytokines that reduce the survival of new-born neurons.
- Neurogenesis occurs in two brain regions: the subgranular zone (SGZ) of the hippocampus and the subventricular zone (SVZ) of the lateral ventricles; neuroblasts must migrate to replenish lost neurons.

KEY RECOMMENDATIONS FOR FUTURE RESEARCH:
1. Future translational studies should target multiple key regulating molecules involved in microglia/macrophage activation and polarization, incorporating the concept of a "therapeutic time window" for sequential therapies.
2. Constructing new experimental stroke models should be considered (since successful approaches in experimental models have largely failed to translate to clinical trials, partly because stroke populations are predominantly elderly with comorbidities like hypertension).
3. Identifying new gene signatures for circulating immune cells when they enter the CNS should be considered.
4. Exploring endogenous neuroprotective mechanisms responsible for brain repair should be considered.

FUNDING: Supported by the National Natural Science Fund for Distinguished Young Scholars (81525008) and the National Basic Research Program of China (973 Program) (2014CB541605).

The article also covers: sterile inflammation as a critical element of stroke pathobiology, microglial activation mechanisms (including perivascular microglia engulfing endothelial cells via phagocytosis after reperfusion), microglia/macrophage polarization factors (e.g., CD14 deficiency, PPARgamma, PACAP, Ly6C(hi) monocytes), and promising therapeutic perspectives including targeting the NLRP3 inflammasome, Notch signaling, and various other molecules.

## Abstract

Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is a significant health problem with high mortality and morbidity rates, partly due to limited treatment options. Hematoma after ICH causes neurological deficits due to the mass effect. Hemorrhage catalyzes secondary damage, resulting in increased neurological damage, poor prognosis, and treatment problems. This review evaluates the role of immunotherapeutic approaches in ICH based on original full-text and review articles on the pathophysiology and immunotherapy of ICH, with emphasis on the modulation of microglia/macrophage polarization to the M2 subtype. In this review, we concluded that the pathophysiology of injury progression after ICH is complex and multifaceted. Inflammation plays a dominant role in secondary injuries. Furthermore, cells involved in the inflammatory process have dual roles in pro-inflammatory/destructive and anti-inflammatory/healing. While the role of inflammation in the pathophysiology makes the immune system a therapeutic target in ICH, the dual role of cells makes them a therapeutic target that can modulate anti-inflammatory/healing. Resident microglia (and even macrophages migrating from a peripheral source) are important therapeutic targets for modulation because of their role in the initiation phase and in shaping immunity. Although clinical results remain poor, experimental and clinical trial data seem promising for deciphering the pathophysiology of ICH and providing treatment options.

## 1. Introduction

Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is one of the most dangerous types of strokes [[1](#B1-ctn-09-00004)]. Approximately 15 million strokes are reported worldwide annually. Despite accounting for up to 20% of all stroke cases (over 2 million worldwide), ICH is associated with a higher mortality rate than ischemic stroke or subarachnoid hemorrhage, with mortality rates reaching 54% after the index event [[2](#B2-ctn-09-00004)]. More than half of the fatal events occur in the first 2 days [[3](#B3-ctn-09-00004)]. Among those who survive, only approximately 20% regain functional independence [[4](#B4-ctn-09-00004)]. In addition to being associated with high mortality and morbidity, ICH also has fewer treatment options than ischemic stroke. The incidence increases significantly with advanced age, and the majority of patients are over 65 years of age [[3](#B3-ctn-09-00004),[4](#B4-ctn-09-00004)]. In the United States alone, ICH is estimated to incur an annual healthcare cost of USD 12.7 billion [[2](#B2-ctn-09-00004)]. Therefore, it is a significant burden not only in terms of health but also in terms of social and economic aspects [[5](#B5-ctn-09-00004)].

Hematoma after ICH can catalyze primary damage caused by the mass effect and secondary damage caused by the inflammatory reaction, resulting in poor prognosis and treatment problems for patients [[6](#B6-ctn-09-00004)]. The treatment of ICH remains a major challenge. Current medical treatments are based on lowering the blood and intracranial pressure and/or hemostatic therapy [[3](#B3-ctn-09-00004),[7](#B7-ctn-09-00004),[8](#B8-ctn-09-00004)]. In addition to having the highest mortality rate, ICH is the least treatable subtype of stroke [[3](#B3-ctn-09-00004)].

The severity, location, and extent of the hemorrhage affect both the prognosis and management of the disease. A larger initial blood volume and progressive growth in the hematoma volume are associated with worse functional outcomes and increased mortality rate [[9](#B9-ctn-09-00004)]. The middle cerebral artery (MCA), part of the circle of the Willis anastomotic system that supplies blood to a wide area of brain tissue, is highly vulnerable and is associated with the majority of stroke-related disability [[10](#B10-ctn-09-00004),[11](#B11-ctn-09-00004)].

It is important to understand the pathophysiological mechanisms associated with the occurrence and progression of ICH to choose the best treatment [[12](#B12-ctn-09-00004)]. Following the initial injury, secondary injuries occur in which complex mechanisms involving many cells and molecules play a role. Furthermore, crosstalk between the cells involved in this process and their mutual influence on each other’s phenotype and function is noteworthy for secondary injury in ICH [[13](#B13-ctn-09-00004)].

Disruption of the blood–brain barrier (BBB) is a key role in the progression of ICH pathophysiology. Disruption of the BBB results in the uncontrolled flow of blood-borne cells, macromolecules, and fluid into the brain, resulting in devastating malignant brain edema and life-threatening hemorrhagic transformation ([Figure 1](#fig_body_display_ctn-09-00004-f001)). Rapid activation of blood-borne immune cells further enhances impaired BBB damage, as they cause microvascular dysregulation and increase BBB permeability by secreting inflammation-associated molecules. There in an extensive inflammatory response in the brain after ICH, involving both the proliferation of resident microglia (Mig) and the recruitment of circulating leukocytes such as monocytes, neutrophils, lymphocytes, and macrophages (Møs) [[14](#B14-ctn-09-00004)]. The production of specific chemokines within a few hours at the site of injury facilitates the selective recruitment, adhesion, and migration of leukocytes through interactions with chemokine receptors expressed in circulating immune cells. This contributes to the development of secondary brain damage [[15](#B15-ctn-09-00004)].

![Ctn 09 00004 g001](/ctn/ctn-09-00004/article_deploy/html/images/ctn-09-00004-g001-550.jpg)

**Figure 1.**
Illustration of the anatomical structure of the BBB and immune cell migration as a result of permeability disruption. (**A**) brain vessel, (**B**) anatomical structure of the BBB, (**C**) migration of immune cells through the damaged barrier in the brain vessel.

The weakness of current therapeutic approaches and the knowledge that the basic pathophysiological mechanisms underlying poor prognosis are immunologically initiated have made attempts to find effective immunotherapeutic targets for ICH a hot research topic [[12](#B12-ctn-09-00004)]. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the role of an immunotherapeutic approach in ICH, mainly emphasizing the modulation of microglia/macrophage polarization to the M2 subtype, in light of recent data. For these reasons, important immunological mechanisms and therapeutic strategies have been summarized.

## 2. Inflammatory Response to Intracerebral Hemorrhage (ICH)

ICH is a common form of hemorrhagic stroke with poor prognosis and limited therapeutic options. Primary and secondary brain damage occur because of bleeding. Primary damage develops as a result of the mass effect and physical disruption of the brain parenchyma. The fundamental factors for secondary damage are neuroinflammatory reactions and the release of clot components. Infiltrating white blood cells, including resident microglia and peripheral leukocytes, has been suggested [[16](#B16-ctn-09-00004)].

Hematoma formation after ICH usually stimulates an inflammatory reaction via activated microglia/macrophages (Mig/Møs), which induces inflammatory signaling pathways. Therefore, these cells contribute to the activation of the immune cascade and secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines [[12](#B12-ctn-09-00004),[17](#B17-ctn-09-00004)]. The onset of ICH disrupts the integrity of the BBB and exposes the brain parenchyma to neurotoxic substances and immune cells, ultimately increasing the risk of secondary brain injury. Subsequently, the secretion of cytokines triggers innate immunity. The movement of circulating immune cells, especially neutrophils, into the brain parenchyma and meninges further damages brain cells by secreting numerous destructive substances, such as cytokines, reactive oxygen species (ROS), matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). In the later period, the activation of acquired immunity triggered by the spread of dead cell-derived antigens exacerbates the systemic immune response, eventually leading to the emergence of systemic negative effects, such as systemic immune response syndrome and cardiac disfunction [[18](#B18-ctn-09-00004)].

The inflammatory response following cerebral hemorrhage is particularly deleterious in the acute phase because the surrounding tissue is destroyed by proteases (such as matrix metalloproteinases, primarily MMP-2, 3, and 9) and ROS secreted by infiltrating leukocytes [[1](#B1-ctn-09-00004),[19](#B19-ctn-09-00004)]. The accumulation of microglia, macrophages, and T lymphocytes occurs later, significantly affecting the immune response. These cells have subtypes that lead to a pro-inflammatory (destructive) or anti-inflammatory (regenerative) state [[3](#B3-ctn-09-00004)]. The BBB is a unique anatomical interface between the blood and central nervous system (CNS) formed by endothelial cells (ECs), the end legs of astrocytes, and pericytes embedded in the capillary basement membrane. Extravasation of peripheral immune cells (PICs) occurs by binding to adhesion molecules, such as vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1) and intercellular cell adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1), expressed by EC and pericytes. Although these adhesion molecules are expressed at extremely low levels under resting conditions, their levels increase exponentially after any damage signal [[1](#B1-ctn-09-00004),[19](#B19-ctn-09-00004)]. In addition to these molecules, many other immunological or non-immunological molecules play a vital role in cell migration, signaling pathways, shaping the immune mechanism, and crosstalk between immune cells [[1](#B1-ctn-09-00004),[15](#B15-ctn-09-00004),[18](#B18-ctn-09-00004)].

## 3. Immune Cells in ICH

The immune cells involved in brain hemorrhage normally fall into two categories: The first category is neuroglia, including microglia and astrocytes, which occur naturally in the brain tissue and are involved in the innate immune response. The other category is leukocytes, which includes neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, and lymphocytes. Leukocytes migrate from the bloodstream, are recruited at the site of cerebral hemorrhage, and play an important role in the acquired immune reaction [[20](#B20-ctn-09-00004),[21](#B21-ctn-09-00004)]. The different roles of cells involved in the pathophysiology of ICH are summarized in [Table 1](#table_body_display_ctn-09-00004-t001).

### 3.1. Local Immune Cells

#### 3.1.1. Microglia

Microglia constitute the largest population of immune cells in the brain. Their highly ramified structures allow them to constantly scan the surrounding environment [[3](#B3-ctn-09-00004),[16](#B16-ctn-09-00004)]. In experimental models, microglia are activated within minutes after brain injury, while peripheral macrophages infiltrate 1–2 days later [[1](#B1-ctn-09-00004),[22](#B22-ctn-09-00004),[23](#B23-ctn-09-00004)]. It is difficult to distinguish between activated microglial cells and macrophages, which have high phagocytic properties. Furthermore, both expressed similar cellular surface markers, including CD11b and Iba-1 [[24](#B24-ctn-09-00004)]. Both microglia and macrophages are divided into M1 (pro-inflammatory, classically activated) and M2 (anti-inflammatory, alternatively activated) [[12](#B12-ctn-09-00004),[25](#B25-ctn-09-00004)]. The M1 subtypes are generally active in the early stages of damage, while the M2 subtypes are usually effective in the later resolution period, usually after day three, and gradually reach their peak after day seven [[12](#B12-ctn-09-00004)].

M1 microglia, whose activation is typically induced by IFN-γ and lipopolysaccharide (LPS), produce inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β, and IL-12, and chemokines such as CC-2 [[26](#B26-ctn-09-00004)]. These cells also produce enzymes such as NADPH oxidase (ROS producing) and inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) (NO producing), MHC-II molecules, integrins (such as CD11b and CD11c), co-stimulatory molecules (such as CD36, CD45, and CD47), and Fc receptors, which contribute to neurological damage [[27](#B27-ctn-09-00004)]. M2 microglia, which are typically induced by cytokines such as IL-4 and IL-13, express cytokines such as IL-10 and TGF-β, and growth factors such as insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), fibroblast growth factor (FGF), colony stimulating factor (CSF) -1, and neurotrophic growth factors (NGFs) ([Figure 2](#fig_body_display_ctn-09-00004-f002)) [[26](#B26-ctn-09-00004),[28](#B28-ctn-09-00004)].

![Ctn 09 00004 g002](/ctn/ctn-09-00004/article_deploy/html/images/ctn-09-00004-g002-550.jpg)

**Figure 2.**
