## Abstract

Stroke is a leading cause of death and long-term disability worldwide. Astrocytes structurally compose tripartite synapses, blood–brain barrier, and the neurovascular unit and perform multiple functions through cell-to-cell signaling of neurons, glial cells, and vasculature. The crosstalk of astrocytes and other cells is complicated and incompletely understood. Here we review the role of astrocytes in response to ischemic stroke, both beneficial and detrimental, from a cell–cell interaction perspective. Reactive astrocytes provide neuroprotection through antioxidation and antiexcitatory effects and metabolic support; they also contribute to neurorestoration involving neurogenesis, synaptogenesis, angiogenesis, and oligodendrogenesis by crosstalk with stem cells and cell lineage. In the meantime, reactive astrocytes also play a vital role in neuroinflammation and brain edema. Glial scar formation in the chronic phase hinders functional recovery. We further discuss astrocyte enriched microRNAs and exosomes in the regulation of ischemic stroke. In addition, the latest notion of reactive astrocyte subsets and astrocytic activity revealed by optogenetics is mentioned. This review discusses the current understanding of the intimate molecular conversation between astrocytes and other cells and outlines its potential implications after ischemic stroke. “Neurocentric” strategies may not be sufficient for neurological protection and recovery; future therapeutic strategies could target reactive astrocytes.

Keywords:

[astrocyte](/search?q=astrocyte); [crosstalk](/search?q=crosstalk); [gliotransmitter](/search?q=gliotransmitter); [regeneration](/search?q=regeneration); [stroke](/search?q=stroke)

## 1. The Way of Astrocyte Crosstalk with Other Cells

Astrocytes are the most abundant glial cell type; they are traditionally considered a kind of “supporting cell” and play a major role in maintaining homeostasis. Astrocytes have long been thought of as “passive” cells, implying that they just “listen” but never “talk”. However, emerging evidence demonstrates that astrocytes are also active participants in brain activity and are essential for cell–cell communication in the neural tissue. During ischemic stroke, the brain undergoes drastic changes and homeostasis breakdown, leading to severe injury. The role of astrocytes during this process is highly complex. Astrocytes show both beneficial and deleterious roles depending on different timepoints, different regions, and different aspects of stroke pathology. Exploring the communication of astrocytes and other cells during different stages of ischemic stroke and its influence on stroke outcomes is of great significance. This review paper discusses the recent advances in the study of astrocytes’ crosstalk with other cells in spatial and temporal dynamics under ischemic insults based on results from experimental animal studies.

Astrocytes have the structural basis for modulating homeostasis in larger brain regions and crosstalk with various cells as follows.

First, astrocytes are morphologically complex and branched with numerous fine processes, which envelop and directly contact with almost all parenchymal cells, including neurons, microglia, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, and immune cells, in the central nervous system [[1](#B1-life-12-00910)]. Astrocytes dynamically change in response to alterations in their environment. Astrocytes can rapidly extend and retract fine processes to engage and disengage from motile postsynaptic dendritic spines with higher average motility than their dendritic spine counterparts [[2](#B2-life-12-00910)].

Second, astrocytes are extensively coupled into homocellular or heterocellular networks via gap junction channels. Intracellular calcium changes in astrocytes can propagate to fine processes and other glial cells through gap junctions [[3](#B3-life-12-00910),[4](#B4-life-12-00910)]. The calcium dynamics convey powerful signals due to their influence on protein kinases, ion channels, and vesicular release. Therefore, astrocytes can function as a syncytium of interconnected cells [[5](#B5-life-12-00910)].

Third, astrocytes express a large repertoire of receptors, responding to all neurotransmitters, neuromodulators, hormones, growth factors, chemokines, and steroids by changing cytosolic Ca2+ or cAMP [[6](#B6-life-12-00910)], which gives astrocytes the ability to detect microenvironment changes. They also release glutamate, D-serine, ATP [[7](#B7-life-12-00910)], GABA [[8](#B8-life-12-00910)], prostaglandins, and neuropeptides, generally called “gliotransmitters”. These gliotransmitters have been shown to modulate other glial, neuronal, or vascular cells [[9](#B9-life-12-00910)]. In addition, a wide range of factors is secreted by astrocytes to modulate microenvironments. Astrocyte-derived exosomes are also one of the most significant ways of communication between astrocytes and surrounding cells [[10](#B10-life-12-00910)]. The major ways of cell communication and microenvironment regulation by astrocytes are shown in [Figure 1](#fig_body_display_life-12-00910-f001).

![Life 12 00910 g001](/life/life-12-00910/article_deploy/html/images/life-12-00910-g001-550.jpg "Life 12 00910 g001")

**Figure 1.**
The major ways of astrocytic cell–cell communication and microenvironment regulation. Reactive astrocytes secrete a wide range of factors modulating the microenvironment and communicating with other cells, including gliotransmitters (glutamate, ATP, and D-serine), growth factors (e.g., BDNF, GDNF), inflammatory cytokines (e.g., interleukins, TNF-α, TGF-β), chemokines (e.g., CXCL12), metabolites (e.g., lactate), and enzymes (e.g., MMPs). Apart from small molecules, they can even send mitochondria and exosomes to other cells to convey messages. Astrocytes secrete extracellular matrix, which is a major component of the microenvironment. The processes of astrocytes can uptake neurotransmitters (e.g., glutamate, GABA) and buffer irons (e.g., Ca2+, K+) to maintain homeostasis of the microenvironment and influence synaptic plasticity. Despite secreting factors, there are calcium signals quickly propagating through gap junctions formed by connexins between astrocytes and other cells in order to coordinate cell functions.

The understanding of astrocytes has increased considerably over the past two decades owing to new technological advances in transcriptomics, in vivo imaging, optogenetics, and chemogenetics. The diversity and complexity of astrocytic contribution to health and disease are being unveiled, challenging the “neurocentric” dogma. Optogenetics is a useful technique; it allows noninvasive manipulation with high specificity and temporal precision on a millisecond scale [[11](#B11-life-12-00910)]. In general, channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2), calcium-translocating channelrhodopsin (CatCh), ChETA, and LiGluR are used for the depolarization of the membrane. Light-driven outward proton pumps such as archaerhodopsin (Arch) and chloride pumps such as halorhodopsin (NpHR) can induce hyperpolarization of the membrane after photostimulation [[12](#B12-life-12-00910)]. Optogenetics has been mainly used to manipulate neuronal activity to investigate neural circuits [[13](#B13-life-12-00910)]. Optogenetic approaches can also selectively manipulate astrocytic activity with specific promoters such as GFAP or Mlc1. Astrocyte-specific opsin expression in vivo is achieved by injecting an adeno-associated virus or lentivirus encoding an astrocyte-specific opsin into a target region. Alternatively, the opsin can be expressed using Cre/loxP and tetO-tTA systems in a genetically engineered mouse line [[14](#B14-life-12-00910)]. Thus, optogenetic targeting of astrocytes provides a robust experimental model to elucidate the role of astrocytes in brain functions.

Signals from optogenetically modulated astrocytes can drive neuronal activity and animal behavior. Glial photostimulation can lead to perturbation of motor behavior in the cerebellum. The underlying mechanism is that cerebellar astrocyte stimulation leads to glutamate release which then activates AMPA receptors on Purkinje cells and mGluR1 on synapses of parallel fibers to Purkinje cells. Then LTD is induced and motor behavior is changed. This finding indicates that astrocytic activity can modulate neuronal activity, synaptic plasticity, and behavioral response [[15](#B15-life-12-00910)]. Optogenetic stimulation of ChR2-expressing astrocytes in the brain stem chemoreceptor areas can trigger robust respiratory responses via ATP-dependent mechanism in vivo [[16](#B16-life-12-00910)]. Optogenetically activated astrocytes affect retrotrapezoid nucleus neurons via an ATP-dependent manner, while in the locus coeruleus, astrocytes activate NAergic neurons by releasing glutamate. So, there exists an area-specific and transmitter-dependent manner of astrocytic modulation of neuronal activity.

Optogenetic activation of astrocytes in the mouse posterior hypothalamus increases both rapid eye movement sleep (REM) and non–rapid eye movement sleep (NREM) during the active phase of sleep–wake regulation [[17](#B17-life-12-00910)]. Interestingly, selective photostimulation of astrocytes in the anterior cingulate cortex increased the wakefulness and disturbance of NREM under neuropathic pain condition [[18](#B18-life-12-00910)]. Thus, optogenetic manipulation of astrocytes in specific brain regions has different effects on sleep. This phenomenon may be due to astrocytic adenosine release and the different distribution of wake- and sleep-active neurons [[19](#B19-life-12-00910)]. Using electrophysiological recording and two-photon imaging, a study showed that astrocytes could trigger a switch of the cortical circuit to the slow-oscillation-dominated state in the neocortex, and this was due to transient glutamate release from activated astrocytes [[20](#B20-life-12-00910)]. This work not only directly demonstrated glutamate release by astrocytes after stimulation but also indicated that astrocytes could control the cortical synchronizations which were important for sleep and memory. Optogenetic stimulation of astrocytes localized in the medial basal hypothalamus could suppress food intake through increased extracellular levels of adenosine in a frequency-dependent manner, providing new insight into astrocytes in the control of energy states [[21](#B21-life-12-00910)].

Optogenetic manipulation of astrocytes provides direct evidence for the active role of astrocytes at the circuit level; the communication between astrocytes and neurons not only plays a role in regulating synaptic function but also plays a role in dominating the activity of the neural network [[22](#B22-life-12-00910)]. These studies can open up avenues for studying the role of astrocytes in higher-order brain functions and show that optogenetics is a good way of exploring astrocytic communication with other cell types.

## 2. Functions of Astrocytes in Ischemic Stroke

Stroke, of which approximately 87% is ischemic, is a leading cause of death and disability globally. Due to a lack of glucose and oxygen because of the loss of blood flow, neural tissue is biochemically and metabolically compromised, resulting in cell death after ischemic stroke. The role of astrocytes in ischemic stroke is complex; they work as versatile players in regulatory processes depending on context, region, and time.

### 2.1. Reactive Astrogliosis

Astrocytes undergo a dramatic morphology change which is commonly referred to as reactive astrogliosis after ischemic insult. Sofroniew gave a comprehensive and accurate definition of astrogliosis as “a finely gradated continuum of progressive changes in molecular expression, cellular hypertrophy, proliferation, and scar formation, which are subtly regulated by complex intercellular and intracellular signaling” [[23](#B23-life-12-00910)]. A consensus statement by various researchers recently defined reactive astrocytes as “astrocytes engage in molecularly defined programs involving changes in transcriptional regulation, as well as biochemical, morphological, metabolic, and physiological remodeling, which ultimately result in the gain of new function(s) or loss or upregulation of homeostatic ones in response to pathology” [[24](#B24-life-12-00910)].

After brain ischemia, astrocytes changed from the normally bushy form to a hypertrophic stellate shape and then to a highly polarized shape with long processes pointing to the ischemic core [[25](#B25-life-12-00910)]. Reactive astrocyte proliferation was increased, marked by upregulated GFAP in the acute phase (days 1–4 post-ischemia). Polarized astrocytes with elongated processes were steadily increased from the subacute phase (days 4–8 post-ischemia) and gradually formed a mature glial scar until the chronic phase (days 8–14 post-ischemia), also shown by high-resolution imaging in the ischemic cortex in vivo [[26](#B26-life-12-00910)]. Reactive astrocytes have heterogeneity in their sensitivity to ischemia, distance to the ischemic core, and subtypes [[27](#B27-life-12-00910)].

An acute increase in astrocytic Ca2+ signaling and subsequent glutamate and GABA release may represent the initial step after ischemia; Ca2+ can regulate many downstream signaling intermediates such as the phosphatase calcineurin, which will then activate NFAT or N-cadherin pathways [[28](#B28-life-12-00910)]. The STAT3, p38 MAPK, nuclear factor κB (NF-κB), and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) signaling pathways are involved in inducing the production of GFAP and transcription factors or retro-inhibitors of other pathways (e.g., SOCS3 for the JAK-STAT3 pathway or IκB for the NF-κB pathway) [[29](#B29-life-12-00910)]. The STAT3 pathway seems to play a prominent role in shaping the transcriptome of reactive astrocytes. Epidermal growth factor (EGF), fibroblast growth factor (FGF), endothelin-1, and ATP are reported to contribute to the proliferation of reactive astrocytes [[30](#B30-life-12-00910),[31](#B31-life-12-00910),[32](#B32-life-12-00910)]. The proliferation of reactive astrocytes is also regulated by Notch-1 in the peri-infarct region [[33](#B33-life-12-00910)]. In addition, class B scavenger receptor CD36 has recently been reported to be involved in astrocyte activation and glial scar formation in ischemic stroke patients [[34](#B34-life-12-00910)].

Reactive astrogliosis was traditionally considered to form glial scars that hamper neuronal repair. Nevertheless, increasing evidence indicated that reactive astrocytes could also exert beneficial functions. Transgenic ablation of reactive astrocytes after CNS injury markedly increased neuronal death and exacerbated tissue degeneration [[35](#B35-life-12-00910)]. There is a strong interest in better understanding this specific transformation of astrocytes in response to stroke.

### 2.2. Functions of Reactive Astrocytes in the Pathogenesis of Stroke

#### 2.2.1. Astrocyte-Neuron Interaction: Neuroprotection after Stroke

Metabolic support: Glycogen is predominantly stored in astrocytes and serves as the main energy reserve in the brain. During an energy crisis such as ischemia insult, glycogen can be broken down to glucose, metabolized to pyruvate via glycolysis, and eventually converted to lactate. Then, lactate is transported from astrocytes to neurons as an energy substrate through monocarboxylic acid transporters (MCTs) [[36](#B36-life-12-00910)]. Thus, reactive astrocytes can function as an energy source to supply neurons with substrates. Stroke stimulation induces astrocyte-specific MCT4 expression and enhances lactate production. Astrocyte-derived lactate may be critical for the survival of vulnerable neurons and contribute to stroke prevention. However, diminished lactate supply from astrocytes could facilitate stroke-induced neurodegeneration [[37](#B37-life-12-00910)]; further study will be needed to address this question.

Antiexcitatory effect: Ischemic injury caused by excess glutamate is a decisive factor in stroke outcome. Failure of astrocytes to remove this excess glutamate leads to excitotoxic damage. Excess glutamate in the ischemic brain causes hyperactivation of ionotropic glutamate receptors, which induces Ca2+ influx into the neurons and then triggers neuronal cell death [[38](#B38-life-12-00910)]. Astrocytes play an important role in glutamate regulation through involvement in the glutamate–glutamine cycle, namely by clearing synaptic glutamate and converting it into glutamine which will finally be transferred back into neurons. In this way, astrocytes have an antiexcitatory effect by uptaking glutamate with glutamate transporters EAAT1 (GLAST) and EAAT2 (GLT-1) [[39](#B39-life-12-00910)]. Upregulation of GLT-1 decreases infarct size and promotes behavioral recovery [[40](#B40-life-12-00910)]. Impairment of astrocyte activation decreased glutamate uptake and increased infarct volume in the GFAP−/−Vim−/− mouse model of stroke [[41](#B41-life-12-00910)]. The glutamate–glutamine cycle interfaces with several metabolic pathways such as the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and even lipid signaling [[42](#B42-life-12-00910)]. A recent study showed that synaptic lipid signaling can modulate glutamatergic transmission. The enzyme autotaxin in astrocytic presynaptic processes synthesizes lysophosphatidic acid 2 (LPA2) and influences glutamatergic transmission via presynaptic LPA2 receptors. Astrocyte-specific deletion of autotaxin reduces cortical excitability and subsequent negative stroke outcome [[43](#B43-life-12-00910)].

Antioxidant function: Astrocytes play a crucial role in antioxidant defense. Astrocytes contain the highest concentration of antioxidants and provide neighboring neurons with substrates for antioxidants such as glutathione [[44](#B44-life-12-00910)]. Glutathione is also involved in the glutamate–glutamine cycle and is increased in neurons after being co-cultured with astrocytes [[45](#B45-life-12-00910)]. Glutathione depletion exacerbated cortical infarction and edema after ischemia. Astrocytes from transgenic mice with low glutathione levels were ineffective at protecting neurons from apoptotic cell death [[46](#B46-life-12-00910)]. Thus, glutathione loss is involved in the development of infarction. Reactive astrocytes may also produce various free radicals in response to ischemia. The increased expression of S-100β and inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) led to oxidative stress [[47](#B47-life-12-00910),[48](#B48-life-12-00910)], which mediated neuronal death after stroke.

Mitochondria transfer: Mitochondria represents intracellular cores for energetics and cell viability; they can be released and transferred to other cells under certain conditions [[49](#B49-life-12-00910)]. For example, retinal neurons may transfer damaged mitochondria to astrocytes for disposal or recycling in wild-type mice [[50](#B50-life-12-00910)]. This prominent finding suggested that astrocytes may release mitochondrial particles that enter adjacent neurons after transient focal cerebral ischemia in mice. This transfer amplified cell survival signals mediated by CD38 and cyclic ADP ribose signaling in a calcium-dependent manner, and it eventually supported cell viability and functional recovery after stroke [[51](#B51-life-12-00910)]. Astrocytic “donation” of functional mitochondria to neurons is a novel endogenous neuroprotective and neuronal recovery mechanism after stroke and a potential mode of astrocyte–neuron crosstalk.

Exosomes: Recent studies also showed that astrocytes sent out exosomes, also called extracellular vesicles, which could transfer a large diversity of molecules such as lipids, nucleic acids, and proteins, serving as a new platform for complex intercellular communication [[52](#B52-life-12-00910),[53](#B53-life-12-00910)]. A previous study showed that astrocyte-derived exosomes could increase neuronal cell survival under ischemic conditions [[54](#B54-life-12-00910)]. The mechanisms have been revealed recently. Astrocytes also shuttle miR-190b through exosomes to inhibit neuronal apoptosis through modulating autophagy [[55](#B55-life-12-00910)]. Exosomes from ischemic preconditioned astrocytes shuttled miR-92b-3p to protect neurons against oxygen and glucose deprivation in vitro [[56](#B56-life-12-00910)]. Astrocytic exosome-conveyed microRNA-34c is neuroprotective via TLR7 and NF-κB/MAPK pathways against cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury in vivo [[57](#B57-life-12-00910)]. Astrocyte-derived exosomal miR-361, which downregulates the AMPK/mTOR signaling pathway by targeting CTSB, is neuroprotective both in vitro and in vivo [[58](#B58-life-12-00910)]. Besides conveying miRNAs, exosomes also transfer proteins. Extracellular vesicles secreted by astrocytes transport apolipoprotein to neurons and mediate neuronal survival upon oxidative stress [[59](#B59-life-12-00910)]. Astrocyte-derived exosomes treated with a semaphorin 3A inhibitor enhance stroke recovery via prostaglandin D2 synthase [[60](#B60-life-12-00910)]. However, this protective role of astrocytic exosomes exists under certain conditions; another study revealed that astrocytic exosomes in response to inflammatory stimulus interleukin-1β (IL-1β) contained cargo microRNAs and proteins that reduced neurite outgrowth and neuronal firing and promoted neuronal apoptosis [[61](#B61-life-12-00910)]. Activated human primary astrocyte-derived extracellular vesicles tested by label-free quantitative proteomic profiling revealed a notable upregulation of proteins including actin-associated molecules, integrins, and major histocompatibility complex in IL-1β-treated groups, they could be uptaken by neurons and thus negatively modulate neuronal uptake, differentiation, and firing [[62](#B62-life-12-00910)]. Identification of astrocyte-derived exosomes’ effects on both short- and long-distance targets and strategies may lead to the finding and development of new diagnostic and therapeutic methods.

Other mechanisms: Astrocytes can also release several neuroprotectants, including erythropoietin (EPO), VEGF, and glial-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF), all of which can reduce ischemic neuronal damage after stroke [[63](#B63-life-12-00910),[64](#B64-life-12-00910),[65](#B65-life-12-00910)]. Reactive astrocytes are known as an important source of steroids, especially estrogen. The expression of the enzyme aromatase and its production of 17β-estradiol in astrocytes is upregulated following brain ischemia. Knockout of aromatase in astrocytes in mice, leading to downregulation of estrogen and attenuated astrogliosis, displayed enhanced neuronal damage under ischemic conditions [[66](#B66-life-12-00910)]. Interestingly, neurons also secrete estrogen 17β-estradiol, which is also critical for astrocyte activation and release of neurotrophic factors in the ischemic brain [[67](#B67-life-12-00910)]. Despite releasing factors, a subset of reactive astrocytes within the ischemic penumbra region is found to be transformed into phagocytic cells. Phagocytic astrocytes upregulate ABCA1 and its downstream pathway molecules including MEGF10 and GULP1 to engulf large neuronal debris contributing to the remodeling of damaged tissues [[68](#B68-life-12-00910)].

#### 2.2.2. Astrocyte-Astrocyte Interaction: Functions of Gap Junctions after Stroke

Connexins (CXs), a kind of gap junction channel, allow for direct electrical and biochemical communication and support astrocytic key functions such as the spreading of metabolic substrates, spatial K+ buffering, and calcium waves [[69](#B69-life-12-00910)]. Hemichannels are precursors of gap junctions existing in the plasma and may open in response to triggers such as cell depolarization and calcium change; they may also function as gliotransmitter release channels [[70](#B70-life-12-00910),[71](#B71-life-12-00910)]. Hypoxia/reoxygenation and metabolic starvation lead to the opening of hemichannels in cultured astrocytes [[72](#B72-life-12-00910)]. Seven different CXs exist in different cell types: Cx43 is mainly expressed in astrocytes; Cx36 is the main neuronal connexin; and oligodendrocytes express Cx32, Cx47, and Cx29 [[73](#B73-life-12-00910),[74](#B74-life-12-00910)]. These channels have distinct functions in different cell types, and their expression can change dramatically under different conditions [[74](#B74-life-12-00910)].

The role of astrocytic gap junctions in stroke remains controversial. Astrocytic gap junctions remain open following ischemia in vivo and hypoxia in vitro [[75](#B75-life-12-00910),[76](#B76-life-12-00910)]; they could increase infarct volume by spreading proapoptotic factors, which caused delayed cell death in the penumbral region [[77](#B77-life-12-00910)]. ATP channeling, calcium wave spreading, and propagation of neuronal activity depression may also be implicated in the expansion of infarction [[78](#B78-life-12-00910)]. Studies showed that gap junction blockers reduced neuronal death and infarct volume in different experimental stroke models [[79](#B79-life-12-00910)]. Astrocytic Cx43 activation played a critical role in neuronal death by NMDA neurotoxicity during inflammation in neuron/astrocyte co-cultures. This excitotoxicity could be inhibited by a Cx43 blocker or Cx43 knockout in astrocytes [[80](#B80-life-12-00910)]. Inactivation of mGluR2 reduced the increased expression of Cx36 and neuronal death after ischemia. Genetic elimination of Cx36 also reduced neuronal death after ischemia [[81](#B81-life-12-00910)]. Thus, Cx36 is a critical component of glutamate-dependent neuronal death. Excessive opening of Cx43 hemichannels pathologically contributed to cell swelling and death by osmotic shifts as well as calcium overload [[82](#B82-life-12-00910)]. However, global heterozygous genetic ablation of Cx43 increased the infarct size and number of apoptotic cells in the penumbra area of ischemic mice with reduced astrogliosis [[83](#B83-life-12-00910)]. A similar outcome was obtained in a follow-up investigation using specific astrocyte Cx43 knockout mice [[84](#B84-life-12-00910)].

The reason for the controversy remains elusive. However, the different functions of gap junctions and their hemichannels should be taken into consideration; the blocking reagents and genetic modification have differences in targets, selectivity, mechanisms, and efficacy. Connexin mimetic peptides can block hemichannels without blocking gap junctions. Gap26/27, which mimics Cx43, was proved to be cardioprotective against infarction [[85](#B85-life-12-00910)]. The role of these mimics in ischemic brain injury needs to be investigated in the future. The phosphorylation of Cx43, which influences its internalization, degradation, and hemichannel activity, should not be overlooked [[86](#B86-life-12-00910)]. Moreover, CXs have both channel functions and nonchannel functions; many CXs can be anchored to scaffolding proteins via C-terminal (CT) interaction and influence gene expression [[87](#B87-life-12-00910)]. The impact of CT truncation of Cx43 includes increased infarct volume, reduced astrogliosis, and more microglial infiltration in the MCAO model [[88](#B88-life-12-00910)]. The nonchannel functions complicate its role after ischemic injury.

#### 2.2.3. Astrocyte and Microglia Crosstalk after Stroke: Inflammation after Stroke

Inflammation has long been regarded as a critical contributor to the pathophysiology of ischemic stroke [[89](#B89-life-12-00910)]. Both microglia and astrocytes are major components of the innate immune system in the brain and respond to damage-associated molecule patterns (DAMPs) after ischemic stroke; their bidirectional communication has recently been at the forefront of glial research. Microglia activation is the beginning of the inflammatory response, followed by infiltration of peripheral immune cells and astrocyte reactivity [[90](#B90-life-12-00910)]. Early transcriptome studies revealed two gene expression patterns for two subtypes of astrocytes: an A1 neurotoxic phenotype after exposure to specific cytokines including IL-1α, TNF-α, and the complement component subunit 1q (C1q) secreted by microglia that were exposed to lipopolysaccharide, and an A2 neuroprotective phenotype predominant at 72 h after ischemic stroke [[91](#B91-life-12-00910),[92](#B92-life-12-00910)]. These terminologies parallel the M1 and M2 types of activation in macrophages/microglia. A1 astrocytes show a compromised ability to induce synapse formation and phagocytose synapses which can induce neuronal apoptosis, and A2 astrocytes show upregulation of many neurotrophic factors and secrete proteins that promote CNS synaptogenesis, indicating neuroprotective and reparative functions [[91](#B91-life-12-00910)]. Activated microglia can release a series of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines. Microglia-derived cytokines can work as triggers and modulators of astrogliosis, because astrocytes express innate immune pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), such as toll-like receptors (TLRs), NOD-like receptors (NLRs), mannose receptors, scavenger receptors, and complement receptors [[93](#B93-life-12-00910)]. The release of IL-1α, TNF-α, and also fragmented and dysfunctional mitochondria from microglia trigger the A1 astrocytic response [[94](#B94-life-12-00910)]. C1q secreted by microglia also promotes A1 phenotype transformation, which is potentially mediated by scavenger receptor Megf10 expressed by astrocytes [[95](#B95-life-12-00910)]. Microinjection of the recombinant IL-1 into the neonatal brain could induce astrogliosis. The IL-6 or IL-1β knockout mice showed less astrogliosis after injury compared with the WT mice [[96](#B96-life-12-00910),[97](#B97-life-12-00910)]. Suppressing microglial proliferation with olomoucine could attenuate glial scar formation after injury in rats [[98](#B98-life-12-00910)]. Microglial TNF-a production promotes astrocyte glutamate release, which boosts neuron excitotoxicity, so microglia also modulate excitatory neurotransmission mediated by astrocytes [[99](#B99-life-12-00910)]. ATP derived from microglia could bind to P2Y1R located on the astrocyte membrane to amplify ATP release and increase excitatory postsynaptic currency frequency [[100](#B100-life-12-00910)].

The role of astrocytes in local immune reactivity and inflammation has long been overlooked. Reactive astrocytes can also release gliotransmitters; proinflammatory mediators such as IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1α, IL-1β, and IFN-γ; and free radicals, which act on the receptor expressed microglia to create a paracrine/autocrine feedback loop [[101](#B101-life-12-00910)]. A recent transcriptome analysis after stroke shows that markers of reactive astrocytes, Lcn2, GFAP, vimentin, and Timp1, were highly expressed and contributed to inflammation (e.g., Spp1, Cd52, Lcn2, and Ifi202b) [[92](#B92-life-12-00910)]. Astrocytes can induce the increased expression of MCP-1/CCR2 in microglia after ischemic stroke [[102](#B102-life-12-00910)]. TGF-β signaling is increased in reactive astrocytes and activates microglia after ischemic stroke [[103](#B103-life-12-00910)]. Galectin-9 serves as a communication signal of astrocyte–microglia crosstalk and promotes microglial TNF-α secretion in the co-culture system of astrocytes and microglia. Recombinant galectin-9 increased TNF-α and IL-6 secretion from microglia [[104](#B104-life-12-00910)]. Moreover, IL-10 released by microglia stimulates astrocytic TGF-β release, which in turn attenuates microglial activation as a feedback loop [[105](#B105-life-12-00910)]. ATP released from astrocytes after traumatic brain injury activates microglial cells, which could be inhibited by blockers of G protein-coupled purinergic receptors and connexin channels. Astrocytes secrete lipocalin protein orosomucoid-2 (ORM2) upon inflammatory stimulation, which modulates microglial activation. ORM2 can bind with microglial C-C chemokine receptor type 5 (CCR5) and block the chemokine C-X-C motif ligand (CXCL)-4–CCR5 interaction that is critical for microglial activation to exert anti-inflammatory effects during brain inflammation [[106](#B106-life-12-00910)]. A recent study revealed that specifically depleting astrocyte-derived estrogen after global cerebral ischemia led to upregulation of A2 astrocytes and less microglial activation, which can be rescued by exogenous 17β-estradiol administration [[66](#B66-life-12-00910)]. This implies that astrocytic steroids can modulate microglial function. Astrocytes also secrete high levels of another lipocalin protein, LCN2, revealed by recent transcriptome analyses one day after experimental ischemic stroke, whose receptor LCN2R, mainly expressed in microglia and neurons, opposes ORM2 functions and enhances microglial activity in vascular dementia animals [[107](#B107-life-12-00910)]. Astrocyte-derived exosomes conveying Cox2 small interfering RNA could restore microglial phagocytic activity after being uptaken by microglia in a neurodegenerative model [[108](#B108-life-12-00910)]. These results suggested that astrocytic molecule release and purinergic signaling are important modulators of inflammatory responses. Briefly, microglia- and astrocyte-derived factors can regulate each other. However, current studies on the microglia-astrocyte crosstalk are still mainly focused on CNS inflammatory diseases, and future research is still needed.

Recent findings suggested that astrocytes also interact with other infiltrating peripheral immune cells after stroke to modulate post-stroke neuroinflammation [[109](#B109-life-12-00910)]. The ablation of IκB in astrocytes reduced peripheral immune cell infiltration into the CNS in the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) model [[110](#B110-life-12-00910)]. These results indicated that reducing the astroglial NF-κB signaling pathway would attenuate proinflammatory cytokines produced by T cells during acute disease. Astrocytes enhanced lymphocyte toxicity after ischemic stroke by activating cytotoxic functions of natural killer cells (NKs) and CD8+ T lymphocytes mediated by IL-15/IL-15 receptor-α. IL-15 knockdown in astrocytes resulted in a decrease in tissue damage and better neurological outcomes after stroke [[111](#B111-life-12-00910)]. Astrocytes also act as a partial source of IL-17, which interacts with TNF-α and thus leads to neutrophil invasion and the expression of various proinflammatory molecules in vivo [[112](#B112-life-12-00910)]. Astrocytes increase IL-33 and CCL1 levels in response to stroke, and IL-33 is thought to promote the proliferation of Treg cells after stroke [[113](#B113-life-12-00910)].

These studies suggest that the global outcome is the result of intensive crosstalk between astrocytes, microglia, and infiltrating immune cells in CNS injury.

#### 2.2.4. Astrocyte and Endothelial Crosstalk: BBB Integrity and Edema after Stroke

The critical importance of astrocytes in the induction and maintenance of BBB structure and function has long been established. A recent study gives direct evidence by adopting a tamoxifen-inducible astrocyte ablation mouse model; leakage of fluorescently labeled cadaverine and blood plasma fibrinogen into the brain has been detected in adult mice [[114](#B114-life-12-00910)]. Conditional knockout of astrocytic Wnt release led to brain edema and increased vascular tracer leakage [[115](#B115-life-12-00910)]. Astrocytes could synthesize canonical tight junction proteins claudin 1, claudin 4, and junctional adhesion molecule-A [[116](#B116-life-12-00910)]. Treatment with extracellular vesicles from healthy astrocytes increased transendothelial electrical resistance and upregulated expression of tight junction proteins in monolayers of human brain endothelial cells in vitro [[117](#B117-life-12-00910)]. Astrocytes can also adjust the cerebrovascular tone to coordinate local blood supply with neuronal activity changes and local metabolic demands, forming a “neuroglia-vascular unit” [[118](#B118-life-12-00910)]. Optogenetic stimulation of cortical astrocytes elicits a widespread increase in cerebral blood flow [[119](#B119-life-12-00910)].

BBB breakdown leads to brain edema and hemorrhagic transformation, which are major complications during acute ischemic stroke. Astrocytes act as key regulators of brain edema, and their endfeet are estimated to ensheath more than 99% surface of blood vessels [[120](#B120-life-12-00910)]. The earliest and prominent astrocytic response to ischemia is astrocyte swelling which occurs at endfeet around capillaries due to ionic and osmotic dysfunction [[121](#B121-life-12-00910)]. Astrocytes play a major role in cytotoxic edema, particularly via water channel aquaporin 4 (AQP4), which is highly expressed on astrocyte endfeet. AQP4-depleted mice were observed to have enhanced neurologic outcomes and reduced brain edema after focal ischemia [[122](#B122-life-12-00910)]. Furthermore, AQP4 is also involved in astrocyte migration, glial scar formation, neuroinflammation, and extracellular K+ uptake [[123](#B123-life-12-00910)]. Loss of astrocyte–endothelial contacts resulted in the breakdown of BBB integrity leading to vasogenic edema during ischemia [[124](#B124-life-12-00910)]. Astrocyte-secreted MMPs and VEGF also increase blood vessel permeability and vasogenic edema after stroke [[125](#B125-life-12-00910)]. The increased expression of VEGF-A in reactive astrocytes led to disputed BBB integrity by downregulating claudin-5 and occludin in endothelial cells [[126](#B126-life-12-00910)]. Neutralization of IL-9 could downregulate astrocyte-derived VEFG-A to protect BBB integrity [[127](#B127-life-12-00910)]. However, reactive astrocyte-derived pentraxin-3 might support BBB integrity by regulating VEGF-related mechanisms in peri-infarct areas, which may comprise a compensatory mechanism [[128](#B128-life-12-00910)]. FGF2 also plays a dual role in the regulation of endothelial barrier function. Autocrine secretion of FGF2 is necessary for the establishment of a tight endothelial barrier, whereas exogenous FGF2 in concentrations higher than 4 ng/mL does harm, implying it regulates endothelial barrier function in a concentration-dependent manner [[129](#B129-life-12-00910)].

Pericytes are also important components of BBB and have receptors for a large number of vasoactive signaling molecules. Astrocytic laminin regulates pericyte differentiation and maintains BBB integrity [[130](#B130-life-12-00910)]. The pericyte conditioned medium promotes astrocyte proliferation after PDGFB treatment. GFAP knockdown mice showed higher pericyte/endothelial cell ratios than those observed in wild-type mice [[131](#B131-life-12-00910)]. However, direct evidence for astrocyte augmentation of pericyte coverage is lacking, and their communication under ischemic insult still needs further study.

#### 2.2.5. Astrocytic MicroRNAs in Stroke

MicroRNAs (miRNAs), 18–25 nucleotide-long noncoding RNAs, are potent post-transcriptional regulators of protein expression through interaction with specific mRNA targets [[132](#B132-life-12-00910)]. This post-transcriptional control is very complex because miRNAs can bind multiple mRNAs. Meanwhile, mRNAs can be bound by multiple miRNAs. Numerous miRNAs have a preferential cellular expression pattern. According to a recent microarray analysis of miRNA expression in major cell types of the CNS, miR-181, and miR-29 appeared to be more highly expressed in astrocytes [[133](#B133-life-12-00910)]. The miRNA profile changed after stroke, which suggested that miRNAs could contribute to ischemic injury by altering key signaling elements [[134](#B134-life-12-00910),[135](#B135-life-12-00910)]. The fast post-transcriptional effect and multitarget characteristics provide miRNAs with greater therapeutic potential for stroke. Here we will discuss several miRNAs enriched in astrocytes. miR-210 is significantly upregulated in astrocytes and activated by hypoxia-inducible factor-alpha (HIF-1a) during hypoxic injury [[136](#B136-life-12-00910)]. Our study found that blood miR-210 was significantly decreased in stroke patients for up to 14 days and correlated with clinical prognosis. The following animal study also confirmed the positive correlation between blood and brain after stroke. Thus, miR-210 acts as a novel sensitive biomarker in acute cerebral ischemia [[137](#B137-life-12-00910)]. miR-181a and miR-29a are miRNAs that coordinate mitochondrial homeostasis. The antagomir of miR-181a could reduce infarct lesions and CA1 neuronal loss after ischemia in vivo and protect primary cultured astrocytes but not neurons after OGD in vitro [[138](#B138-life-12-00910)].

miR-29a agomir upregulated PUMA, a member of the BCL2 family, to protect astrocyte and mitochondrial function [[139](#B139-life-12-00910)]. Controversial findings have been detected in vivo; upregulation of miR-29a protected neurons from apoptosis during cerebral ischemia [[140](#B140-life-12-00910)], while downregulation of miR-29 also rescued heart ischemia/reperfusion injury [[141](#B141-life-12-00910)]. This controversy may be due to the different targets of miR-29 in different cells, because luciferase assays indicated that the miR-29 family targets BCL2 family members, both proapoptotic (BAK and PUMA) and antiapoptotic (BCL-w and MCL1) [[142](#B142-life-12-00910)]. miR-29b is significantly downregulated and negatively associated with clinical severity in ischemic patients; a similar pattern is observed in mouse brains and blood. Dual-luciferase reporter system confirmed that AQP4 was the direct target of miR-29b. Overexpression of miR-29b decreased AQP4 expression, infarction volume and BBB disruption [[143](#B143-life-12-00910)]. miR-1

This is an open-access review article published in the journal *Life* (2022, Volume 12, Issue 6, article 910; DOI: 10.3390/life12060910) titled "Crosstalk of Astrocytes and Other Cells during Ischemic Stroke" by Tingting He, Guo-Yuan Yang, and Zhijun Zhang (affiliated with Shanghai Tenth People's Hospital, Tongji University, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University). The review examines the complex, bidirectional communication between reactive astrocytes and other brain cells during ischemic stroke, challenging the traditional "neurocentric" view of stroke pathology.

KEY CONTENT AREAS:

1. **Mechanisms of astrocyte crosstalk**: Astrocytes communicate through (a) fine processes contacting virtually all CNS parenchymal cells, (b) gap junction networks (homocellular/heterocellular), (c) receptors responding to neurotransmitters and other signals, and (d) release of "gliotransmitters" (glutamate, D-serine, ATP, GABA), growth factors, cytokines, chemokines, exosomes, and even mitochondria.

2. **Optogenetics in astrocyte research**: Recent studies use optogenetic manipulation (ChR2, CatCh, Arch, NpHR) with astrocyte-specific promoters (GFAP, Mlc1) to demonstrate that astrocytic activity modulates neuronal activity, synaptic plasticity, sleep-wake regulation, food intake, and behavioral responses.

3. **Reactive astrogliosis after ischemia**: Astrocytes transition from bushy to hypertrophic stellate to polarized morphology, forming glial scars by chronic phase (days 8-14 post-ischemia). Key signaling pathways include STAT3, p38 MAPK, NF-κB, TGF-β, and Notch-1.

4. **Neuroprotective functions of reactive astrocytes**: 
   - Metabolic support via glycogen breakdown and lactate transport through MCTs
   - Antiexcitatory effects via glutamate uptake (EAAT1/EAAT2 transporters, glutamate-glutamine cycle)
   - Antioxidant defense (highest glutathione concentrations in brain)
   - Mitochondrial transfer to neurons (CD38/cyclic ADP ribose signaling)
   - Exosome-mediated protection via miRNAs (miR-190b, miR-92b-3p, miR-34c, miR-361)
   - Release of neuroprotectants (EPO, VEGF, GDNF, estrogen/aromatase)
   - Phagocytic transformation to engulf neuronal debris (ABCA1, MEGF10, GULP1)

5. **Astrocyte-astrocyte gap junctions**: Controversial role of Cx43/Cx36 in stroke—gap junctions may spread proapoptotic factors (increasing infarct) but heterozygous Cx43 ablation also increases infarct size; connexin mimetic peptides (Gap26/27) may offer cardioprotection; non-channel functions of connexins complicate interpretation.

6. **Astrocyte-microglia crosstalk and inflammation**: Microglia release IL-1α, TNF-α, and C1q triggering neurotoxic A1 astrocyte phenotype, while A2 phenotype is neuroprotective (upregulated at 72h post-stroke). Bidirectional regulation involves galectin-9, ORM2/CCR5, LCN2, IL-10/TGF-β feedback loops, purinergic signaling, and astrocyte interactions with NK cells, CD8+ T cells (IL-15 pathway), IL-17, and Treg cells (IL-33).

7. **BBB integrity and edema**: Astrocyte endfeet ensheath >99% of blood vessel surface; AQP4 water channels mediate cytotoxic edema (AQP4-depleted mice show reduced edema and better outcomes); astrocyte-derived MMPs, VEGF-A downregulate tight junctions (claudin-5, occludin); pentraxin-3 and FGF2 have context-dependent protective effects.

8. **Astrocytic microRNAs**: miR-210 (biomarker in acute cerebral ischemia, elevated in stroke patients' blood for up to 14 days), miR-181a, miR-29a/b (targets AQP4, regulates mitochondrial homeostasis and apoptosis), with therapeutic potential for stroke.

CONCLUSION: The review argues that "neurocentric" strategies may be insufficient for neurological protection and recovery after ischemic stroke; future therapeutic strategies should target reactive astrocytes given their dual beneficial and detrimental roles in neuroprotection, neurorestoration, inflammation, and edema.
args.key_excerpts: "Reactive astrocytes provide neuroprotection through antioxidation and antiexcitatory effects and metabolic support; they also contribute to neurorestoration involving neurogenesis, synaptogenesis, angiogenesis, and oligodendrogenesis by crosstalk with stem cells and cell lineage. In the meantime, reactive astrocytes also play a vital role in neuroinflammation and brain edema."

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12407517)Abstract

Ischemic stroke, a frequently occurring form of stroke, is caused by obstruction of cerebral blood flow, which leads to ischemia, hypoxia, and necrosis of local brain tissue. After ischemic stroke, both astrocytes and the blood–brain barrier undergo morphological and functional transformations. However, the interplay between astrocytes and the blood–brain barrier has received less attention. This comprehensive review explores the physiological and pathological morphological and functional changes in astrocytes and the blood–brain barrier in ischemic stroke. Post-stroke, the structure of endothelial cells and peripheral cells undergoes alterations, causing disruption of the blood–brain barrier. This disruption allows various pro-inflammatory factors and chemokines to cross the blood–brain barrier. Simultaneously, astrocytes swell and primarily adopt two phenotypic states: A1 and A2, which exhibit different roles at different stages of ischemic stroke. During the acute phase, A1 reactive astrocytes secrete vascular endothelial growth factor, matrix metalloproteinases, lipid carrier protein-2, and other cytokines, exacerbating damage to endothelial cells and tight junctions. Conversely, A2 reactive astrocytes produce pentraxin 3, Sonic hedgehog, angiopoietin-1, and other protective factors for endothelial cells. Furthermore, astrocytes indirectly influence blood–brain barrier permeability through ferroptosis and exosomes. In the middle and late (recovery) stages of ischemic stroke, A1 and A2 astrocytes show different effects on glial scar formation. A1 astrocytes promote glial scar formation and inhibit axon growth via glial fibrillary acidic protein, chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans, and transforming growth factor-β. In contrast, A2 astrocytes facilitate axon growth through platelet-derived growth factor, playing a crucial role in vascular remodeling. Therefore, enhancing our understanding of the pathological changes and interactions between astrocytes and the blood–brain barrier is a vital therapeutic target for preventing further brain damage in acute stroke. These insights may pave the way for innovative therapeutic strategies for ischemic stroke.

**Keywords:**astrocytes, axon, blood–brain barrier, cytokines, endothelial cells, glial scar, ischemic stroke, phenotype, remodel, vascular

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12407517)Introduction

Ischemic stroke, also known as cerebral infarction, is a common cerebrovascular disease characterized by disruptions in brain blood supply, which result in localized ischemia, hypoxic necrosis, and subsequent neurological impairments (Walter, 2022; Liu et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025). Ischemic stroke poses a substantial global burden due to the high morbidity, disability, and fatality rates associated with it (Liu et al., 2025a; Zheng et al., 2025). The blood–brain barrier (BBB), a dynamic interface separating brain tissue from the circulating blood, plays a crucial role in maintaining brain homeostasis and normal neurological function. The BBB, which is composed primarily of brain microvascular endothelial cells, a basal membrane, pericytes, and astrocytes surrounding endothelial cells, strictly regulates the exchange of substances between the blood and the brain (Schulz et al., 2023).

The pathophysiological mechanism underlying ischemic stroke is complex, and BBB injury is a prominent pathological feature that substantially influences the course and progression of stroke. When a stroke occurs, secondary pathological changes such as inflammation and oxidative stress disrupt brain endothelial cells and impair vascular endothelial function. These changes directly or indirectly damage the structural and functional integrity of the BBB, disrupting the balance of the brain environment and normal central nervous system physiological function. The increased permeability of the BBB allows inflammatory cells, chemicals, and excess fluid from the blood to penetrate into brain tissue, disrupting water and ion homeostasis and leading to vasogenic brain edema and hemorrhagic transformation. This, in turn, activates microglia and astrocytes, exacerbating brain injury and neurological dysfunction and creating a vicious cycle (Jiang et al., 2018).

Astrocytes, as a key component of the BBB, play a major role in the various stages following ischemic stroke. In the early stages of ischemic stroke, astrocytes express aquaporin-4 (AQP4), which causes foot swelling and promotes the entry of pro-inflammatory factors that induce astrocyte activation. Although the BBB structure remains relatively intact at this stage, sodium transport can increase through transcellular transport, aggravating the formation of early edema (Chen et al., 2015). Subsequently, activated reactive astrocytes differentiate into two phenotypes (A1 and A2), secreting various cytokines such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), matrix metallopeptidases (MMPs), angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1), insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), and sonic hedgehog (Shh), which exhibit protective or destructive functions at different stages of cerebral ischemia. Reactive astrocytes can also affect the BBB through indirect pathways. Post-stroke inflammation significantly increases the content of adhesion junctions (AJs) in astrocytes, leading to neuronal iron imbalance (Donnini et al., 2006) by inducing the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and affecting BBB function through morphological changes in pericytes and endothelial cells. Furthermore, reactive astrocytes regulate brain-peripheral communication by secreting microRNA (miR)-rich exosomes, which affect BBB function (Wang et al., 2020a). In the middle and late stages of stroke, neurotoxic reactive astrocytes accumulate to form glial scars, preventing the spread of inflammation, while neuroprotective reactive astrocytes promote vascular remodeling.

This paper reviews the alterations in the BBB and the two distinct phenotypes of astrocytes across various stages following ischemic stroke, with a particular emphasis on the morphological and functional transformations. It elucidates the effects of reactive astrocytes on the BBB and vascular remodeling, which are mediated through various factors, brain iron imbalance, and exosomes. Furthermore, the review outlines the existing therapeutic agents that target the BBB and discusses the application of nanotechnology in this context. Enhancing the efficacy of drug delivery across the BBB and facilitating more precise targeting of cytokines are pivotal for developing therapeutic strategies aimed at mitigating BBB damage and improving the prognosis for patients with ischemic stroke (**[Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12407517#NRR.NRR-D-24-01417-F1)**).

Figure 1
[![Image 15: Figure 1](https://pmc-oa-opendata.s3.amazonaws.com/PMC12407517.1/NRR-21-1359-g001.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=12407517_NRR-21-1359-g001.jpg)

[Open in a new tab](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/figure/NRR.NRR-D-24-01417-F1/)

Changes in blood–brain barrier and astrocyte phenotypes following ischemic stroke.

After an ischemic stroke, the blood–brain barrier is damaged, leading to increased permeability that allows various pro-inflammatory factors and chemokines to infiltrate brain tissue. This infiltration promotes the polarization of astrocytes into predominantly A1 and A2 phenotypes, which exert opposing effects on the restoration of the blood–brain barrier. As the disease progresses, reactive astrocytes accumulate and migrate, forming glial scars. Within these scars, A1 astrocytes exhibit inhibitory effects on vascular reconstruction, while A2 astrocytes provide protective effects that support axon regeneration.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12407517)Search Strategy

For the purposes of this review, the literature was searched using a combination of the following terms: “Astrocytes” AND “ischemic stroke;” “blood–brain barrier” AND “ischemic stroke;” “blood–brain barrier” AND “astrocytes” OR “ischemic stroke;” “A1 astrocytes,” “blood–brain barrier,” AND “cytokines;” AND “A2 astrocytes,” “blood–brain barrier,” AND “cytokines.” The PubMed database was used to search for articles published between 2000 and 2025. This review includes studies addressing the structural alterations of the BBB at various stages after ischemic stroke, the structural and functional modifications in astrocytes, the cytokines secreted by A1 and A2 astrocytes, and the role of astrocytes in vascular remodeling.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12407517)Structure and Function of the Blood–Brain Barrier Under Physiological Conditions

The brain contains three crucial barrier layers that restrict and regulate the exchange of molecules between blood and nerve tissue: the BBB, the chorioid epithelium, and the arachnoid epithelium. Notably, the BBB plays a pivotal role in separating central and peripheral neurotransmitters and neuroactive substances, regulating the ionic microenvironment, and facilitating metabolic processes between brain cells and blood. It serves as a “physical barrier” within the brain (Abbott et al., 2006). The BBB is a protective layer primarily consisting of peripheral cells, endothelial cells (ECs), tight junctions (TJs), astrocytes, and a vascular basement membrane. It restricts and regulates the movement of molecules between the brain and blood, including the transport of nutrients (oxygen, glucose, and amino acids) and the maintenance of brain ion homeostasis (Jiang et al., 2018). Among its components, brain microvascular ECs are the most significant, forming the first effectively sealed “barrier” of the BBB alongside their intercellular junctions, known as TJs. TJs, which consist of transmembrane proteins, cytoplasmic attachment proteins (ZO1, ZO2, ZO3), and cytoskeletal proteins (actin), serve as the structural foundation for maintaining the permeability and integrity of the BBB. Perithelial cells are embedded within a basal membrane composed of a “mixed” extracellular matrix secreted by cerebral microvascular ECs, perithelial cells, and astrocytes, which collectively form the second “barrier” of the BBB. This basal membrane primarily consists of four proteins: type IV collagen, laminin, nestin, and heparan sulfate proteoglycan. Finally, astrocytes encapsulate brain microvascular ECs and pericytes, forming the third “barrier” of the BBB. The diverse cell populations constituting these three “barriers” are instrumental in safeguarding the integrity of the BBB and maintaining its normal physiological functions (**[Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12407517#NRR.NRR-D-24-01417-F2)**).

Figure 2
[![Image 16: Figure 2](https://pmc-oa-opendata.s3.amazonaws.com/PMC12407517.1/NRR-21-1359-g002.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=12407517_NRR-21-1359-g002.jpg)

[Open in a new tab](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/figure/NRR.NRR-D-24-01417-F2/)

Structure and function of the blood–brain barrier under physiological conditions.

The blood–brain barrier is primarily composed of pericytes, endothelial cells, tight junctions, astrocytes, and the vascular basement membrane. Endothelial cells are interconnected by tight junction proteins, including occludin, claudin, and ZO-1, while pericytes encircle these endothelial cells. Adhesion is facilitated by N-cadherin-mediated sporadic pitting. Astrocytes, which make up to 99% of the blood–brain barrier, have foot processes that directly envelop all brain capillaries, thereby regulating the transcription and expression of tight junction proteins in endothelial cells. ApoE: Apolipoprotein E; FGF-2: fibroblast growth factor 2; GDNF: glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor; Shh: sonic hedgehog; ZO: zonula occludens.

### Endothelial cells

The core of the BBB is formed by the cerebral vasculature composed of ECs (Obermeier et al., 2013), and its dysfunction is associated with the onset of neuroinflammation and brain edema (Chen et al., 2019). ECs play a crucial role in brain regulation and actively regulate cerebral blood flow through the production of various vasodilatory chemical mediators, including nitric oxide, arachidonic acid, and endothelin (Peterson et al., 2011). They are also involved in thrombus formation within the brain and help regulate hemostatic mechanisms (Fisher, 2013). The TJs between adjacent ECs create a barrier that is essential for selective transport of molecules. Specific transport systems on the luminal and abluminal membranes establish a “transport barrier” for transcellular traffic (Abbott et al., 2006). Studies have indicated that in the rat brain cortex, blood vessels begin to form around the 12 th day of embryonic development. ECs invade neural tissue through the surrounding vascular plexus and start expressing key proteins such as occludin, claudin, and zonula occludens (ZO)-1 (Daneman et al., 2010). ECs interact with one another through TJs and some AJs. TJs consist of a complex network of transmembrane proteins, including claudins, occludin, junction adhesion molecules, and cytoplasmic adhesion proteins, which actively resist the passage of potentially harmful substances into the central nervous system (Liebner et al., 2018). Under physiological conditions, adhesion molecules are expressed at low levels but play an important role in various neurological diseases. For instance, integrins, which are transmembrane glycoprotein receptors in the extracellular matrix, interact with basement membrane components such as collagen IV, fibronectin, and laminin. This interaction is essential for regulating BBB permeability and transport functions (Yang and Rosenberg, 2011).

### Pericytes

Pericytes, which are embedded in the basement membrane of microvessels, are an important component of capillaries that surround ECs and facilitate adhesion through N-cadherin-mediated sporadic pitted junctions (Campisi et al., 2018). They play an important role in regulating cerebral blood flow and capillary diameter, contributing to various vascular functions, including the formation and maintenance of the BBB as well as the regulation of vascular maturation, blood flow, and immune cell transport (Armulik et al., 2010). For instance, platelet-derived growth factor BB (PDGF-BB), which is secreted by ECs, binds to specific receptors on pericytes, inducing their recruitment, migration, and proliferation. This interaction is critical for maintaining BBB integrity and facilitating functional recovery following cerebral ischemia (Sweeney et al., 2016). The BBB becomes active around the 15 th day of embryonic development, and its integrity is closely linked to the coverage provided by pericytes. Pericytes enhance the compactness of ECs. Co-culture experiments have shown that pericytes can reduce angiopoietin-2 expression in ECs and limit endocytosis by inhibiting plasmalemma vesicle-associated protein. Thus, pericytes are essential for BBB formation and can significantly influence its permeability (Daneman et al., 2010).

### Astrocytes

Astrocytes are a pivotal type of glial cells, constituting the largest proportion of glial cells in the brain and spinal cord. They exhibit brain region specificity and high heterogeneity, playing crucial roles in maintaining brain tissue homeostasis and various metabolic processes (Verkhratsky and Nedergaard, 2018). As integral components of the neurovascular unit, the foot processes of astrocytes envelop all capillaries within the brain parenchyma. These astrocytes secrete laminin γ1, which induces the polarized formation of their own AQP4-positive foot processes and facilitates their connection with the outer basement membrane of the cerebrovascular system. Additionally, by producing laminin α1 and α2, astrocytes reinforce the basement membrane and stabilize pericytes (Xu et al., 2019). The secreted laminin α4 binds to integrin α3β1/α6β1 on the foot processes, promoting their adhesion to the basal membrane of the microvessel wall and regulating the structure and function of the BBB (Segarra et al., 2018). Moreover, astrocytes secrete various factors, including angiotensin, Shh, glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor, and fibroblast growth factor-2, to maintain BBB homeostasis. For instance, Ang derived from astrocytes binds to the angiotensin II type 1 receptor on ECs, promoting the formation and maintenance of tight endothelial cell connections (Obermeier et al., 2013). Shh acts on the receptor patched-1 (Ptc1) to activate the Hedgehog signaling pathway in ECs, inducing the expression of TJ proteins such as occludin and claudin-5 (Alvarez et al., 2011).

Connexin 43 (Cx43), a component of gap junctions and half-channels (Chen et al., 2018), not only protects astrocytes but also facilitates the export of toxic molecules (including Ca 2+, excess adenosine triphosphate [ATP], glutamate, nitric oxide, and ROS) from injured astrocytes. At the same time, it allows neuroprotective metabolites (such as Na+, K+, glutamine, antioxidants, and glucose) to enter ischemic astrocytes (Walz and Hertz, 1983; Goldberg et al., 1999). Additionally, Cx43 interacts with neurons, microglia, and oligodendrocytes, influencing their functional changes (Liang et al., 2020).

By secreting Wnt ligands, sphingosine-1-phosphate, apolipoprotein E, Shh, and other factors, astrocytes regulate the transcription and expression of endothelial TJ proteins, thereby enhancing intercellular connectivity. In summary, astrocytes play multifaceted roles in maintaining the structure and function of the BBB as well as protecting neuronal function (Alvarez et al., 2011; Obermeier et al., 2013; Prager et al., 2015).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12407517)Effects of Astrocytes on the Blood–Brain Barrier at Different Periods After Ischemic Stroke

Ischemic strokes progress through distinct stages: the hyperacute stage, which lasts up to 6 hours; the acute stage, spanning the first 3 days; the late acute stage, from 3 days to 1 week; and finally, the convalescent stage. A prominent pathological feature of the acute stage of ischemic stroke is the disruption of the BBB. The structural decomposition of the BBB can be delineated into four phases: endothelial swelling, endothelial membrane disruption, the breakdown of TJs between vascular cells and adjacent glial cells, and ultimately, complete vascular destruction (Krueger et al., 2015). The severity of ischemia is correlated with the onset of BBB dysfunction. Typically, during the initial stages of cerebral ischemia, the BBB remains intact temporarily. In clinical settings, increased BBB permeability usually manifests during the acute phase following ischemic stroke. However, in experimental models of ischemic stroke, BBB damage can be observed as early as 2 hours post-ischemia, with the degree of damage closely tied to the reperfusion timeline (Yang and Betz, 1994). Furthermore, an additional study has demonstrated that monophasic BBB leakage begins 25 minutes after ischemia-reperfusion and can persist for up to 5 weeks (Hu et al., 2017).

Conversely, BBB permeability exhibits a biphasic increase, peaking within hours of stroke onset and again 2 to 3 days post-stroke (Hu et al., 2017). When BBB function is compromised, the levels of claudin-5, occludin, matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-9, and VEGF in cerebrospinal fluid increase to varying degrees. The relatively straightforward method of detecting endogenous BBB injury markers is invaluable for rapidly assessing BBB damage and guiding early clinical treatment decisions (Bani-Sadr et al., 2023). Furthermore, human brain specimens collected during the acute phase of ischemic stroke from individuals with cerebral infarction revealed significant upregulation of Spp1, along with other signaling pathway components such as CD44, tissue inhibitor of MMP-1 (TIMP1), and MMP-12 across all neurovascular unit cell types. Among these, the upregulation of Spp1 was particularly prominent. Notably, administering an anti-osteopontin antibody helped preserve BBB function and decreased the likelihood of cerebral edema and hemorrhagic stroke (Spitzer et al., 2022).

### Changes in blood–brain barrier structure and function during acute ischemic stroke

The early post-ischemic period is characterized by cytoskeletal rearrangements and structural alterations within ECs. These cells contain numerous actin filaments, which are crucial for maintaining the morphological stability and the integrity of TJs. In response to specific stressors, the actin filaments undergo polymerization, forming linear stress fibers. This process triggers actomyosin contraction and increases cytoskeletal tension, ultimately leading to cellular morphological contraction and compromised junction-sealing efficiency. Consequently, this cytoskeletal rearrangement enhances permeability and results in BBB leakage (Hu et al., 2017). Within the first hour of ischemia-reperfusion, BBB damage is not associated with the activity of gelatinase B. Instead, the destruction of the BBB is primarily linked to the activation of the ROCK/myosin light chain (MLC) signaling pathway, sustained actin polymerization, and the breakdown of connexins in microvascular ECs (Shi et al., 2016). This study suggests that early cytoskeletal changes in ECs are the primary cause of early BBB disruption following stroke, contributing to inflammation and loss of nerve function. However, these changes also pave the way for subsequent BBB opening that is dependent on MMP activity.

#### Pericytes

Structural alterations in ECs and pericytes have long been recognized as key factors influencing early BBB permeability. As the initial responders to cerebral hypoxia within the BBB, pericytes are activated in response to vascular stimuli and migrate from microvessels by degrading the basement membrane, leading to BBB dysfunction. Studies have shown that pericytes undergo a transformation from a static, flat form to an amoeboid shape following ischemic stroke. They detach from the basal lamina within 1 hour of ischemia and migrate to areas of hypoperfusion (Gonul et al., 2002; Duz et al., 2007).

Moreover, under hypoxic conditions, pericytes demonstrate the ability to promote vascular repair and regeneration through paracrine signaling. For instance, exosomal miR-210 has been found to enhance mitochondrial function in ECs, inhibiting endothelial cell death and BBB damage caused by lipid peroxidation. Conversely, the exosomal inhibitor GW4869 can impair the improvement of barrier function (Gao et al., 2023b). These findings indicate the importance of protecting pericytes and maintaining BBB function in the early stages of stroke to effectively mitigate brain injury (Tsao et al., 2021).

#### Tight junction complexes

Alterations in the compact junction protein complex can compromise BBB integrity by increasing paracellular permeability. During the early stage of cerebral ischemia, TJ proteins, such as occludin, claudin-3, claudin-5, and ZO-1 undergo rapid downregulation. This downregulation facilitates the release of matrix MMPs, inflammatory cytokines, and other molecules (Fanning et al., 1998). Claudins are transmembrane proteins, with claudin-1, claudin-3, and claudin-5 predominantly expressed in ECs. Occludin, a membrane protein with four transmembrane segments, regulates paracellular permeability through phosphorylation. ZO-1, which serves as a marker indicative of BBB pathological changes (Nusrat et al., 2000), links claudins and occludin to the actin cytoskeleton (Fanning et al., 1998). A previous study indicated that within 24 hours of hypoxia, ZO-1 expression progressively declines, leading to vascular leakage and potentially exacerbating cerebral edema (Fischer et al., 2002). Vascular endothelial (VE)-cadherin promotes the phosphorylation of forkhead box protein O1 (FoxO1) and inhibits the nuclear translocation of β-catenin, thereby upregulating claudin-5 expression (Taddei et al., 2008). Notably, VE-cadherin expression at the BBB is reduced in mice with focal cerebral ischemia, suggesting that the disruption of adhesive junctions during stroke contributes to BBB dysfunction (Weinl et al., 2015). Additionally, junctional adhesion molecule-A, a membrane protein involved in maintaining tight adhesion integrity in brain ECs, exhibits significant downregulation at the lesion site 12 hours post-brain injury _in vivo_, which is accompanied by degradation of vascular fibronectin in the BBB (Yeung et al., 2008).

#### Regulation of transporters and endocytic transport mechanisms

The regulation of transporters and endocytic transport mechanisms plays a crucial role in altering BBB permeability. Vesicles, which are membrane microdomains formed within the cell membrane, serve as the primary organelles involved in endocytosis. Caveolin-1, the principal structural component of these vesicles, belongs to the caveolin-related protein family and has been implicated in vesicle transport and cellular signal transduction for substances such as transferrin, insulin, and cholesterol (Simionescu et al., 2009). In the early stages following ischemia, the postcapillary segment of cerebral microvessels in the compromised BBB exhibits multifocal distribution, indicative of vasogenic edema. As ischemic injury progresses, these multifocal areas expand and fuse. These changes are accompanied by an increase in the number of endothelial vesicles, which enhances endothelial endocytosis (Hoffmann et al., 2018). Within 6 hours after stroke onset, an elevation in the number of extracellular vesicles and the rate of endothelial cell endocytosis is observed. Two days later, severe structural defects emerge in endothelial TJs, impairing the BBB paracellular pathways (Knowland et al., 2014). Notably, significant increments in the expression of vesicular protein-1 and transendothelial vesicle precede disruptions in TJ and BBB integrity. Moreover, vesicles interact with TJ proteins, and a previous study has demonstrated that inhibiting caveolae-mediated endocytosis can effectively prevent the internalization of occludin under inflammatory stimulation (Shen and Turner, 2005). Substantial advancements have been made in the understanding of plasma membrane vesicles involved in endothelial cell endocytosis. As a result, these vesicles can be precisely guided through the cell to the target membrane through processes such as fission, docking, and fusion. They can either avoid or reach the lysosome, and through the physiological pathway of vesicle operation (Simionescu et al., 2009), enable accurate targeted drug delivery. This understanding holds great significance for the treatment of ischemic stroke.

### Influence of astrocytes on the blood–brain barrier during acute ischemic stroke

#### Structural and functional changes of astrocytes during acute ischemic stroke

Astrocytes constitute the largest cellular component in the brain and spinal cord, with their foot processes enveloping all capillaries within the brain parenchyma. As a result, astrocytes are the primary targets of ischemic injury during cerebral ischemia (Saito et al., 2011). _In vivo_ imaging studies have revealed changes in astrocytes following cerebral microinfarction. When the BBB is compromised, the influx of excitatory glutamate contributes to astrocyte swelling. This manifests as mild swelling of the astrocyte terminal foot and detachment of the endfoot membrane from the capillary basement membrane, while the overall morphology of the astrocyte remains relatively normal (He et al., 2010; Saito et al., 2011). Two to three days after cerebral microinfarction, localized edema, accompanied by astrocyte loss, decreased pericellular blood vessel coverage, and vascular extravasation—indicative of BBB dysfunction—become evident in the brain (Lee et al., 2022b). A previous study in adult Wistar rats subjected to middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) identified three types of astrocyte responses. In the preoptic area with small neuronal lesions, the cytoplasm was disaggregated, while swelling of the nucleus and cytoplasm primarily occurred in the caudate nucleus and cerebral cortex, with astrocyte terminal foot swelling appearing first. Meanwhile, neuronal changes were minimal, and the reactivity of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) in the surrounding brain tissue increased 4–6 hours later (Garcia et al., 1993). AQP4 plays a pivotal role in astrocyte swelling. Predominantly located in astrocyte terminal feet, AQP4, along with other channel proteins involved in bidirectional fluid exchange across the BBB, regulates water homeostasis in the central nervous system (Amiry-Moghaddam and Ottersen, 2003).

In the early stages of transient cerebral ischemia, AQP4 overexpression in the astrocytes in the ischemic region leads to water influx (Ribeiro et al., 2006), resulting in astrocyte swelling and increased hydrocephalus. This triggers the release of pro-inflammatory factors and chemokine adhesion molecules (Steiner et al., 2012), stimulating astrocyte polarization into reactive astrocytes and contributing to the inflammatory environment post-ischemia as well as BBB disruption. _In vitro_ experiments under oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD) conditions followed by reperfusion demonstrated a significant increase in C–C motif ligand 2 (CCL2) and CCL2 receptor secretion by astrocytes and neurons (Dimitrijevic et al., 2006; Ye et al., 2024). The application of an antisense oligonucleotide or neutralizing antibody reversed the enhanced BBB permeability and TJ protein redistribution. N-myc downstream regulatory gene 2 (NDRG2) promotes sodium transport and astrocyte polarization and inhibits brain edema. Through the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway, NDRG2 inhibits astrocyte glucose metabolism and promotes ferroptosis (Guo et al., 2021; Song et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2024).

Astrocyte functional changes are closely linked to inflammatory stimulation after ischemia (Munji et al., 2019). Early brain injury leads to BBB breakdown, allowing the entry of plasma heme into the brain parenchyma. This activates toll-like receptor (TLR) 2 on astrocytes, promoting the release of neurotoxic mediators such as free radicals, pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines (CCL2, chemokine (C–X–C motif) ligand 1 [CXCL1], and CXCL2), and nitric oxide (Gelderblom et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2024a). This exacerbates BBB disruption and secondary brain injury. Cx43 promotes astrocyte phenotypic transformation; inhibiting Cx43 degradation shifts astrocytes from a pro-inflammatory to an anti-inflammatory state, protecting them from ischemic stress-induced apoptosis (Wang et al., 2020b). However, Cx43 overexpression in astrocytes restores neurite growth (Wu et al., 2015). Neurotransmitter release from active neurons increases astrocyte Ca 2+ levels, leading to the release of arachidonic acid and subsequent prostaglandin conversion, with prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) being the most significant (Mishra et al., 2024). PGE2, which is mainly derived from inflammation- and immune response-activated astrocytes (Seregi, 1984), enhances inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) production through tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α and interferon (IFN)-γ (Hsiao et al., 2007).

In ischemic stroke, injured cells in the ischemic core and penumbra release cytokines, activating astrocytes and forming reactive astrocytes (Liu and Chopp, 2016). Recent studies have classified reactive astrocytes into A1 and A2 phenotypes on the basis of differences in gene expression. A1 reactive astrocytes exhibit neurotoxic effects, while A2 reactive astrocytes demonstrate neuroprotective effects (Liddelow and Barres, 2017; Liddelow et al., 2017; Clarke et al., 2018). A2 reactive astrocytes promote glial scar formation, phagocytosis, and BBB repair and inhibit inflammation through the secretion of interleukin (IL)-2, IL-10, transforming growth factor (TGF)-β, neurotrophic factors, neurogenic cytokines, and growth factors (Liddelow et al., 2017; Linnerbauer and Rothhammer, 2020; Price et al., 2021). They enhance phagocytosis via increased expression of ATP-binding cassette transporter A-1 (ABCA1) and its pathway molecules MEGF10 and GULP1, aiding tissue remodeling (Morizawa et al., 2017). ABCA1 depletion inhibits synapse growth and exacerbates BBB permeability and white matter lesions, worsening neurological deficits (Cui et al., 2015). Conversely, A1 reactive astrocytes lose normal astrocyte functions, such as promoting neuronal growth, maintaining synapses, and upregulating complement cascade genes. They secrete soluble neurotoxins, such as Serping1, H2-D1, Ggta1, Iigp1, Gbp2, and Fbln5, rapidly killing neurons and mature oligodendrocytes (Fan and Huo, 2021). Intraperitoneal injection of semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, can block the transformation of A1 astrocytes (Zhang et al., 2022a, b; **[Figure 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12407517#NRR.NRR-D-24-01417-F3)**).
