--- SOURCE 1: Frontiers | Insights gained from single-cell sequencing analysis of ischemic stroke ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cell-and-developmental-biology/articles/10.3389/fcell.2026.1784660/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article titled "Insights gained from single-cell sequencing analysis of ischemic stroke," published in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology (Vol 14, April 21, 2026). The authors (Yanqin Mei, Teng Guan, Longsheng Fu, Jiming Kong, and Yanni Lv from Nanchang University and University of Manitoba) systematically review over 50 scRNA-seq studies on ischemic stroke published since 2019.

KEY FINDINGS:
- 22 cell types were identified from brain tissues and 7 cell types from blood after ischemic stroke using scRNA-seq.
- 13 frequently reported cell types underwent extensive heterogeneity studies, including microglia, macrophages, oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, dendritic cells, T cells, monocytes, neutrophils, neurons, endothelial cells, vascular mural cells/pericytes, perivascular fibroblast-like cells, and vascular smooth muscle cells.
- The review details subcluster categorization, function-related subclusters, and newly discovered subclusters for each cell type.

CELL-SPECIFIC HIGHLIGHTS:
- Microglia: classified beyond traditional M0/M1/M2 into various subclusters (6-16 depending on study); identified pro-inflammatory vs homeostatic states; ischemic core vs penumbra differences; novel subclusters with antioxidant function via peroxiredoxin-1 and Itgb2+ microglia involved in energy metabolism.
- Macrophages: 6 subclusters at CNS borders; Foxp3+ macrophage subcluster distinct from M1/M2 enhancing efferocytosis; Tie2-expressing macrophages in patients associated with improved clinical prognosis.
- Oligodendrocytes: MCAO induces reactive Olig2+Edu+ subclusters aiding white matter repair; metabolic alterations early post-stroke; subcluster 4 (Sult1a1+) linked to apoptotic pathways.
- Astrocytes: classified into A1/A2 types; Nes and Ascl1 markers of A2-type neurotrophic function; Aldoc as reliable pan-astrocyte marker.
- T cells: Treg-derived osteopontin aids microglia-driven white matter repair; T cells migrate to brain 1-5 weeks post-stroke.
- Neutrophils: peak at 24h post-stroke; age-related changes lead to atypical neutrophils (CD62l low) exacerbating stroke.
- Endothelial cells: BBB-associated clusters show dysfunction; connexin 43 decreased in elderly; Wnt7a/Wnt7b engineered for BBB regulation.

IMMUNE RESPONSE AND CELL-CELL COMMUNICATION:
The review explores immune cell and non-immune cellular interactions and their regulatory influences, including the neurovascular unit (blood-brain barrier, neurons, pericytes, endothelial cells).

AGE-RELATED ISSUES:
Aging enhances apoptosis, disrupts endothelial circadian rhythms, and increases infiltration of peripheral macrophages; aged mice show higher Cxcl3 production by neutrophils linked to poorer reperfusion and outcomes.

METHODOLOGY:
Studies used various platforms including 10x Genomics, BD Biosciences, BD Rhapsody, Singleron GEXSCOPE, NovaSeq 6000, and Illumina HiSeq X. Models included MCAO (transient and permanent), four-vessel occlusion, and clinical patient samples from acute ischemic stroke.

FUTURE DIRECTIONS:
Anticipation for broader scRNA-seq application in ischemic stroke research, including cost reduction, integrated analysis, and biopharmaceutical development. scRNA-seq offers new insights into cellular heterogeneity, cell-cell interactions, novel therapeutic targets, and biomarkers.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Ischemic stroke represents a significant global health hazard, causing substantial morbidity, mortality, and long-term disability worldwide. The brain's complexity necessitates targeting ischemic stroke dysfunction syndrome. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) offers unbiased, high-resolution analysis of cell heterogeneity, revealing cellular markers and types."
</key_excerpts>



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


--- SOURCE 2: Single-cell transcriptomic analysis of the immune cell landscape in the aged mouse brain after ischemic stroke ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-022-02447-5

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article published in the Journal of Neuroinflammation (Volume 19, article number 83, published April 7, 2022) titled "Single-cell transcriptomic analysis of the immune cell landscape in the aged mouse brain after ischemic stroke." The open-access Brief Report was authored by Xuan Li, Jingjun Lyu, Ran Li, Vaibhav Jain, Yuntian Shen, Ángela del Águila, Ulrike Hoffmann, Huaxin Sheng, and Wei Yang, among others. It has received 108 citations and 15k accesses.

**Background:** Ischemic stroke primarily affects the elderly, and a complex immune response in the post-stroke brain is a key component of stroke pathophysiology. The study aimed to determine how stroke affects immune cell populations in the aged brain based on molecular profiles of individual cells.

**Methods:** The researchers used single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and developed a new transient ischemic stroke mouse model with late reperfusion — a modified transient transcranial MCAO (ttMCAO) model featuring a 6-hour ischemic duration. The right MCA trunk was ligated proximal to the cortical branch to the rhinal cortex, along with temporary ligation of the right common carotid artery (CCA). Reperfusion was verified using laser speckle contrasting imaging (LSCI), ink-gelatin vascular visualization, and lectin-labeling. All young mice survived the 6-h ttMCAO, though aged mice showed significantly worse neurologic outcomes than young mice. Flow cytometry revealed that infiltrated leukocytes peaked on post-stroke day 3.

**Results:** This study provided the first scRNA-seq dataset for immune cells in the stroke aged brain. Unsupervised clustering predicted 34 clusters, with 28 retained and annotated into 8 major cell types: 6 microglial clusters (MG1-6), 5 monocyte/macrophage clusters (MM1-5), 3 neutrophil clusters (Neut1-3), 4 dendritic cell clusters (DC1-4), 3 T-cell clusters (TC1-3), 3 B-cell clusters (BC1-3), 1 NK cluster, 1 ILC2 cluster, and 2 unknown clusters.

Key findings include:
- At least 6 transcriptionally distinct microglial subsets were identified; MG6 represents a novel stroke-specific microglial state with a unique "neutrophil-like" phenotype (expressing Cxcr2, S100a8, Il1b, and Mmp9).
- MM1 (dominant monocyte/macrophage cluster) increased from 0.5% to 14.9% after stroke and expressed potentially protective genes (Apoe, Arg1, Ym1, Cd93, Hmox1, Tgfbi, Hif1a).
- Neut1 (infiltrated mature neutrophils) increased from 0.3% to 18.7% after stroke and showed remarkably low Ly6g mRNA expression.
- A massive increase of DCs was observed, especially DC1 cells expressing high levels of MHC class II-related genes (H2-Aa, H2-Ab1, Cd74).
- Stroke profoundly altered the brain's immune landscape; Il1b was largely expressed in neutrophils, DCs, and macrophages (and MG6 microglia); neutrophils and MG6 microglia were major sources of Mmp9; Apoe was primarily expressed in monocyte/macrophages.
- CD11c (Itgax) was found in NKs and monocytes/macrophages, suggesting Flt3 as an alternative DC marker.

**Conclusions:** The study generated the first scRNA-seq dataset for immune cells in the stroke aged brain and offered novel insights into post-stroke immune cell heterogeneity, constituting an important step toward uncovering distinct immune subpopulations with unique functions in stroke pathophysiology.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We generated, for the first time, a composite picture of immune cell populations in the stroke aged brain at single-cell resolution. We discovered at least 6 microglial subsets in the stroke aged brain, including a potentially stroke-specific subtype."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Single-cell transcriptomic analysis of the immune cell landscape in the aged mouse brain after ischemic stroke | springermedizin.de ---
URL: https://www.springermedizin.de/single-cell-transcriptomic-analysis-of-the-immune-cell-landscape/20294138

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article (Brief Report) published on December 1, 2022, in the Journal of Neuroinflammation (Issue 1/2022), authored by Xuan Li, Jingjun Lyu, Ran Li, Vaibhav Jain, Yuntian Shen, Ángela del Águila, Ulrike Hoffmann, Huaxin Sheng, and Wei Yang. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1186/s12974-022-02447-5.

**Background:** Ischemic stroke primarily affects the elderly, and a complex immune response in the post-stroke brain is a key component of stroke pathophysiology. The study aimed to determine how stroke affects immune cell populations in the aged brain using single-cell molecular profiling.

**Methods:** The researchers used single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and developed a NEW transient ischemic stroke mouse model with late reperfusion—a modified transient transcranial MCAO (ttMCAO) model. Key features of the model: direct ligation of the right MCA trunk proximal to the cortical branch to the rhinal cortex (more proximal than existing distal MCAO models), temporary ligation of the right common carotid artery (CCA), and a long ischemic duration of 6 hours followed by reperfusion. This model causes damage to both cortex and striatum. All young and aged mice survived 6-h ttMCAO; aged mice showed significantly worse neurologic outcomes vs. young mice. Flow cytometry showed infiltrating leukocytes (especially monocytes/macrophages and neutrophils) increased from post-stroke day 1, peaking on day 3.

**scRNA-seq Results:** Deep scRNA-seq was performed on all CD45+ cells from aged brains on day 3 after sham or ttMCAO (cells pooled from 4 mice per sample, mechanically dissociated without enzymes, FACS-sorted viable CD45+ cells). Unsupervised clustering predicted 34 clusters; after quality control, 28 clusters were annotated into 8 major cell types: 6 microglial (MG1–6), 5 monocyte/macrophage (MM1–5), 3 neutrophil (Neut1–3), 4 DC (DC1–4), 3 T-cell (TC1–3), and 3 B-cell (BC1–3) clusters, plus one NK cluster, one ILC2 cluster, and 2 unknown clusters.

**Key findings:**
- **Microglia:** At least 6 transcriptionally distinct microglial subsets identified. MG1/MG2 are resting states (high P2ry12, Tmem119). MG5 is the predominant microglial subset after stroke, showing a highly proliferative state (upregulated Top2A, Stmn1, Mki67, Cdk1; downregulated homeostatic genes). MG6 is a NOVEL stroke-specific microglial state expressing high levels of Cxcr2, S100a8, Il1b, and Mmp9—a unique "neutrophil-like" phenotype.
- **Monocytes/macrophages:** MM1 increased from 0.5% (sham) to 14.9% (stroke), expressing potentially protective genes including Apoe, Arg1, Ym1 (Chil3), Cd93, Hmox1, Tgfbi, and Hif1a. MM2 expressed Cybb, Il1b, C3, and Hp.
- **Neutrophils:** Neut1 (infiltrated, mature neutrophils) increased from 0.3% to 18.7%, showing low Ly6g mRNA but upregulation of mitochondrial Complex I subunits (mt-Nd1–4), Aif1, Ly86, Il1b. Neut2 cells represent immature neutrophils (high Ltf, Camp, Ngp).
- **Dendritic cells:** DC1 cells (monocyte-origin) massively increased after stroke, highly expressing MHC class II-related genes (H2-Aa, H2-Ab1, Cd74), suggesting antigen-presenting contributions to stroke pathophysiology.
- **Gene expression mapping:** Il1b is largely expressed in neutrophils, DCs, and macrophages (only MG6 among microglia); Mmp9 primarily from neutrophils and MG6; Apoe mainly in monocyte/macrophages. Aif1 (Iba1) is expressed beyond microglia in subsets of monocytes/macrophages, neutrophils, and DCs. CD11c (Itgax) was found in NKs and monocytes/macrophages, suggesting Flt3 as an alternative DC marker.

**Conclusions:** This study provided the FIRST scRNA-seq data set for immune cells in the stroke aged brain, offering novel insights into post-stroke immune cell heterogeneity. It constitutes an important step toward uncovering distinct immune subpopulations with unique functions in stroke pathophysiology.

Ethics: Approved by Duke University Medical Center Animal Care and Use Committee. Open Access under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. Publisher: BioMed Central. Electronic ISSN: 1742-2094.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We generated, for the first time, a composite picture of immune cell populations in the stroke aged brain at single-cell resolution. We discovered at least 6 microglial subsets in the stroke aged brain, including a potentially stroke-specific subtype."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Characterizing stroke-related cellular changes in the surviving neurons of mouse ischemic stroke ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0197018625001597

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Neurochemistry International (Volume 191, December 2025, Article 106086) titled "Characterizing stroke-related cellular changes in the surviving neurons of mouse ischemic stroke." The study, led by Takeshi Ikegami and colleagues, investigated cellular and molecular alterations during acute and subacute phases of distal middle cerebral artery occlusion (dMCAO) in mice using single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq).

KEY FINDINGS:
- C57BL/6 mice were assigned to control, sham, dMCAO 3-day, and dMCAO 14-day groups.
- snRNA-seq identified diverse cell populations: neurons (glutamatergic and GABAergic), fibroblast-like cells, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, endothelial cells, and pericytes.
- Microglia transitioned from homeostatic states (marked by Siglech, P2ry12) to acute-phase (Lgals1, Top2a, Mki67) and disease-associated states, confirming the dataset captured stroke-related dynamics.
- Glutamatergic neurons declined on day 3 post-ischemia, while endothelial cells increased.
- Gene ontology analysis revealed neuronal death, autophagy, and cAMP biosynthesis pathways across all three glutamatergic subclusters.
- Elevated expression of Syngap1, Ikbkb, and Rock1 across glutamatergic subclusters suggested roles in cell death-related mechanisms and vulnerability to ischemic injury.
- Dissociation of SynGAP1 from PSD-95 after ischemia may enhance ERK1/2 phosphorylation, while ischemic preconditioning suppresses this dissociation and prevents ERK1/2 overactivation.
- Immunohistochemistry confirmed Syngap1 and CREB (cAMP response element-binding) pathway activation at 3 and 14 days post-ischemia.
- Suppressing CREB with pAAV-A-CREB reduced neuronal survival, underscoring its role in autophagy and neuroprotection.

CONCLUSION: The study identifies autophagy and cAMP pathways within the penumbra as promising therapeutic targets for ischemic stroke, providing mechanistic insight into stroke-induced molecular alterations. The article is open access under a Creative Commons license and has been cited 5 times. Keywords include: Autophagy, CREB pathway, Ischemic stroke, Microglial activation, SynGAP1, and Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"SnRNA-seq revealed stroke-induced cell state changes with efficient recovery of neurons. SnRNA-seq identified distinct cell types, including neurons, fibroblast-like cells, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, endothelial cells, and pericytes."
</key_excerpts>



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


--- SOURCE 5: Brain and blood single-cell transcriptomics in acute and subacute phases after experimental stroke ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10103945

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article (preprint from bioRxiv) titled "Brain and blood single-cell transcriptomics in acute and subacute phases after experimental stroke," authored by Lidia Garcia-Bonilla, Ziasmin Shahanoor, Rose Sciortino, Omina Nazarzoda, Gianfranco Racchumi, Costantino Iadecola, and Josef Anrather from the Feil Family Brain and Mind Research Institute at Weill Cornell Medicine (New York, NY). Published April 3, 2023 (PMID: 37066298, PMCID: PMC10103945).

STUDY OVERVIEW: The researchers conducted a longitudinal single-cell transcriptomic study of both brain cells and peripheral blood leukocytes in mice to characterize immune cell diversity during the acute (2 days) and subacute (14 days) phases after ischemic stroke. They used a transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) mouse model and droplet-based single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), analyzing 43,269 brain cells across 13 distinct major cell type clusters, plus purified blood leukocytes across 8 clusters.

KEY FINDINGS:
1. Microglia: Cerebral ischemia induced distinct transcriptomic states at day 2 vs day 14, with 8 microglia clusters identified. Homeostatic microglial genes (P2ry12, Tmem119) were downregulated after ischemia, while DAM (disease-associated microglia) genes (Apoe, Cst7, Clec7a, Lpl, Spp1) were upregulated. Pseudotime trajectory predicted Sham microglia progression to either day 2 or day 14 phenotypes, but no connection between day 2 and day 14 microglia. Proliferative microglia (expressing Top2A, Mki67) were found at the infarct border at day 2, suggesting repopulation of the ischemic territory by day 14. Cxcl10 and Igf1 were upregulated in microglia (Igf1 mainly at day 14).

2. Border-associated macrophages (BAM): Five BAM clusters identified; BAM4 was largely confined to day 2 with activation-linked genes (Spp1, Ccl8, Cstb, Lgals1). BAM showed altered transcriptomic signatures at day 2 but low divergence from sham by day 14.

3. Monocyte-derived cells (MdC): Six brain MdC populations identified. Trajectory analysis showed sequential transition of inflammatory blood monocytes (Mo1, Mo2) to brain MdC3 → MdC2 → MdC4 → MdC1 → final differentiation into MdC6. Patrolling monocytes were not a source of brain MdC. MdC1 and MdC6 expressed tissue-repair genes (Spp1, Gpnmb, Igf1).

4. Endothelial cells (EC): Nine EC subclusters identified, attributed to arteriovenous segments. Lrg1 was identified as a powerful marker of reactive venular EC early after ischemia, with strong upregulation in the ischemic hemisphere. IGF1-IGF1R signaling between BAM and EC was observed at Sham and day 2, while microglia and MdC6 contributed to this signaling at day 14.

5. Granulocytes/neutrophils: Six blood and six brain granulocyte clusters identified. In contrast to MdC, granulocytes were predicted to be continuously de-novo recruited from the blood rather than developing within the tissue. Brain granulocytes showed distinct transcriptomic patterns at early (Retnlg, Mmp8, Ly6g, Anxa1, Lcn2) vs late (Ccl3, Ccl4, Csf1, Gadd45b) phases.

6. Dendritic cells (DC): Nine brain DC subclusters identified (cDC1, cDC2, pDC, migDC, moDC). cDC2 was the largest population; DC1 (cDC2 with antigen presentation genes) was highest at day 14.

7. Lymphoid cells: Seven T cell clusters identified; T cell numbers increased at day 14 compared to Sham and day 2. One cluster (Tc6) was classified as type 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2).

8. Aging: Brain single-cell transcriptomics from aged mice did not show major changes compared to young mice, but aged and young brains differed in immune cell composition.

9. Blood vs. brain: Brain-infiltrating leukocytes displayed higher transcriptomic divergence than circulating counterparts, indicating that phenotypic diversification into cellular subsets occurs within the brain during early and recovery phases of ischemic stroke.

RESOURCE: The study provides a searchable online database called "StrokeVis" (https://anratherlab.shinyapps.io/strokevis/) that allows user-friendly access to the gene expression data at the gene and cell type level for endothelial and immune cell subsets from mouse brain and blood after stroke.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Cerebral ischemia triggers a powerful inflammatory reaction involving both peripheral leukocytes and brain resident cells. Recent evidence indicates that their differentiation into a variety of functional phenotypes contributes to both tissue injury and repair." (Abstract)
</key_excerpts>



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


--- SOURCE 6: Molecular Mediators of Angiogenesis and Neurogenesis after Ischemic Stroke - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12051358

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in Reviews in Neuroscience (Rev Neurosci, 2022; published in final form 2023 Jun 27) by researchers from UConn School of Medicine (Mitch R Paro, Arijit R Chakraborty, Sophia Angelo, Ketan R Bulsara, Rajkumar Verma) and University of Connecticut (Shyam Nambiar). The article, titled "Molecular Mediators of Angiogenesis and Neurogenesis after Ischemic Stroke," reviews the coupled processes of angiogenesis and neurogenesis after ischemic stroke and catalogs the molecular mediators and signaling pathways found in pre-clinical studies to upregulate both processes.

Key content:
- The article reviews the current understanding of cerebral angiogenesis (formation of new blood vessels to restore perfusion) and neurogenesis (formation of new neurons) after ischemic stroke, which are recognized as central mechanisms of post-stroke recovery and potential therapeutic targets.
- Angiogenesis is measured preclinically via increased microvascular density, increased cerebral blood flow (via laser Doppler or speckle flowmetry), endothelial cell proliferation (CD31/BrdU double-positive cells), and upregulation of angiogenesis-related mediators (VEGF, FGF, matrix metalloproteinases).
- Neurogenesis involves NSC proliferation in the subventricular zone (SVZ) and subgranular zone (SGZ), NSC migration to the injury site, translocation through the glial scar, differentiation into mature neurons, neurite outgrowth, and synaptogenesis. It is measured using markers including BrdU, doublecortin, nestin, and NeuN.
- Angiogenesis and neurogenesis are coupled processes: blood vessels provide oxygen, trophic factors, and physical scaffolds for NSC migration; new neurons produce factors promoting blood vessel survival. Key conceptual frameworks include the "angiogenic niche" (tissue level) and the "neurovascular unit" (NVU, cellular level).
- VEGF is highlighted as a central molecular mediator, promoting NSC proliferation via Flk-1 and Flt-1 receptors, with roles in both angiogenesis and neurogenesis.
- The article includes two comprehensive tables: Table 1 summarizes 50+ pre-clinical studies (interventions studied, methods, and associated mediators), and Table 2 organizes molecular mediators by mechanism (angiogenesis: increased microvessel density, endothelial proliferation, vascular tube formation, improved CBF; neurogenesis: NSC proliferation, migration, differentiation, synaptogenesis, neurite outgrowth; neuroprotection: reduced infarct size, improved cell survival; reduced gliosis; and mediator upregulation).
- Notable mediators identified include: eNOS, AMPK, EPO, VEGF, bFGF, BDNF, PKM2, HB-EGF, G-CSF, kallikrein, TGF-α, CXCL12, TRPV4, guanosine, HIF-1α, SHH, caveolin-1, ETB, leptin, GDNF, SDF-1, aFGF, HGF, PTH, DHA, NPD1, PTX3, ANGPTL4, microRNA-126/199/210, and others.
- Common signaling pathways discussed include AMPK, PI3K/Akt, ERK, HIF-1α, and NF-κB pathways.
- The authors note that the principal limitations of the current literature are the paucity of data demonstrating precise mechanistic connections between disparate mediators and the lack of a comprehensive framework for contextualizing diverse experimental findings. The review aims to provide a more unified understanding to guide development of novel therapeutic approaches for stroke survivors.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Angiogenesis and neurogenesis have emerged as central mechanisms of post-stroke recovery and potential targets for therapeutics."

**Key Background/Context:**

- Projected total direct medical cost for stroke in the US will reach $184.1 billion by 2030
- Over 90% of ischemic stroke patients cannot receive reperfusion therapy due to strict time windows (3.5–4.5 hours for thrombolysis, 6 hours for thrombectomy); even treated patients, >40% suffer long-term disabilities

- New blood vessels appear by day 3 and persist at least 90 days post-stroke
- VEGF-A significantly elevated post-stroke; interaction with VEGFR-2 drives endothelial cell proliferation and migration
- Key pro-inflammatory cytokines promoting angiogenesis include: MCP-1, TNF-α, TGF-β, G-CSF, FGF, IL-1β, IL-4, IL-6 (detailed in Table 1)

1. **Neutrophils:** First immune cells to infiltrate (peak at 1–3 days). Their functions (phagocytosis, respiratory burst, NET formation) cause neuronal/BBB injury. N2 phenotype (CD206+) skewing improves long-term recovery. Cathepsin secretion recruits endothelial progenitor cells via FPR2, promoting angiogenesis.

2. **Monocytes/Macrophages:** Infiltration peaks at 3 days; half shift to anti-inflammatory phenotype by day 7. Monocyte recruitment depends on CCR2; blocking CCR2 in the first week prevents long-term recovery. M2 macrophages (four subtypes: M2a, M2b, M2c, M2d) express IL-10 and TGF-β, contributing to inflammation resolution, efferocytosis, and angiogenesis (expressing GDF15, VEGF, FGF1, MMP-14). - Immune cells exhibit a biphasic regulatory mechanism post-stroke: damaging in acute phase, potentially protective in chronic recovery phase
- Anti-inflammatory interventions during acute phase may inadvertently harm long-term functional recovery
- Future therapies should target subtype transdifferentiation mechanisms (e.g., M1→M2, pro-inflammatory→anti-inflammatory) rather than simple immune cell depletion

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from R&D Systems provides an overview of neutrophil cell markers used to identify and classify neutrophils in both humans and mice, primarily for flow cytometry applications.

**Overview of Neutrophils:**
- Neutrophils are granule-containing, polymorphonuclear leukocytes that develop in the bone marrow from myeloid precursors.
- They play a central role in the innate immune response by destroying foreign particles intracellularly (in phagosomes) or extracellularly (via neutrophil extracellular traps/NETs) and promoting acute inflammation.
- In humans, neutrophils are the most abundant circulating leukocytes, accounting for 50-70% of white blood cells; in mice, they account for 10-25% of circulating leukocytes.

- Commonly identified by cell surface expression of Ly-6G and CD11b/Integrin alpha M.

**Human Neutrophil Markers:**
- Distinguished from eosinophils and monocytes by expression of both CD15 (antigen on immature neutrophil surfaces) and CD16/Fc gamma RIII, along with lack of CD14 expression.
- Additional common markers include CD66b/CEACAM-8, CD11b/Integrin alpha M, CD33, and the cytoplasmic marker myeloperoxidase.

**Data Examples:** The page includes flow cytometry data images for detecting Ly-6G (GR-1), CD11b, and CD45 in mouse cells, and CD15/Lewis X, L-Selectin/CD62, CD45, Integrin beta 2/CD18, and Siglec-3/CD33 in human cells.

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: Neutrophil extracellular traps and microglia/macrophages ... ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2026.1752471/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Frontiers in Immunology (Volume 17, February 3, 2026, DOI: 10.3389/fimmu.2026.1752471) titled "Neutrophil extracellular traps and microglia/macrophages interactions in stroke: from thromboinflammation to immunotherapy," authored by Nurittin Ardic (Med-International United Kingdom Health Agency Ltd., Nuneaton, UK) and Rasit Dinc (INVAMED Medical Innovation Institute, New York, NY, USA).

**Core Topic:** The bidirectional interaction between neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) and microglia/macrophages in ischemic stroke (IS), intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), and subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), and therapeutic strategies targeting this axis.

**Key Points:**

1. **Background:** Stroke is the second leading cause of death worldwide. IS accounts for ~80-85% of cases. Immune-mediated thromboinflammation is a central determinant of acute injury and secondary neurodegeneration. NETs are critical amplifiers of thromboinflammation, while microglia/macrophages regulate sterile inflammation.

2. **NET Formation & Structure:** NETs are chromatin-based structures containing decondensed DNA, histones (including citrullinated H3), neutrophil elastase (NE), myeloperoxidase (MPO), cathepsin G, MMP-9, LL-37, and tissue factor. Two formation pathways: suicidal NETosis (PAD4-dependent, hours) and vital NETosis (minutes, preserves viability, triggered by platelets, C5a, TLR2/TLR4). NETs promote immunothrombosis, activate factor XII, and resist fibrinolysis.

3. **NETs in Ischemic Stroke:** NETs form dense scaffolds in arterial thrombi, are mechanically stiffer and more resistant to thrombectomy and tPA. They cause microvascular obstruction and the "no-reflow" phenomenon, disrupt the BBB (via histone cytotoxicity, MMP-9 degradation of claudin-5/occludin), potentiate hemorrhagic transformation after thrombolysis, and impair neurovascular repair. NET content is higher in cardioembolic and large-artery atherosclerotic strokes. DNase I and PAD4 inhibitors reduce microvascular obstruction and infarct growth in animal models.

4. **NETs in Hemorrhagic Stroke:** Hemorrhage activates NETosis via hemoglobin, heme, iron, and thrombin. NETs stabilize hematomas, disrupt BBB, cause perihematomal edema, and impair hematoma clearance by physically blocking microglia/macrophage access to erythrocytes. In SAH, NETs contribute to vasospasm, microvascular dysfunction, delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI), and meningeal inflammation. Elevated plasma H3Cit-DNA correlates with early hematoma expansion.

5. **Bidirectional NET-Microglia Crosstalk:** NET components activate microglial pattern recognition receptors: TLR9 (dsDNA → NF-κB, type I IFN), cGAS-STING (cytosolic DNA → IFN-β), NLRP3 inflammasome (histones, oxidized mtDNA → IL-1β, IL-18, pyroptosis), AIM2 inflammasome, and TLR2/TLR4 (histone-mediated). In turn, activated microglia release IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-8/CXCL8, and ROS that promote further NETosis via the P2X7-NLRP3 pathway. ATP release from microglia activates neutrophil P2X7 receptors, driving Ca²⁺ influx and NLRP3-mediated NETosis. This creates a self-reinforcing feedforward inflammatory loop.

6. **Temporal Dynamics:** NET formation peaks early (6-24 hours post-stroke); microglial activation evolves over days to weeks. Spatial transcriptomic studies show NET-microglia interactions concentrated in peri-infarct microvessels ("hot spots") and along ICH hematoma edges.

7. **Therapeutic Strategies:** DNase I (enhances NET degradation), PAD4 inhibitors, NE/MPO inhibitors, histone neutralizing agents, NLRP3 inhibition, CSF1R modulation, and TREM2 agonism. Combination and temporally phased regimens are proposed. Biomarkers (H3Cit-DNA, MPO-DNA) and imaging approaches may enable personalized immunotherapy. NET-rich thrombi are associated with resistance to mechanical thrombectomy and decreased tPA response.

8. **Clinical Translation:** Higher plasma/thrombus H3Cit-DNA and MPO-DNA levels correlate with larger infarct volume, early neurological deterioration, hemorrhagic transformation, and poor functional outcomes. NET burden in thrombi is independently associated with lower recanalization success. No NET-targeted interventions have entered phase III trials for hemorrhagic stroke.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Stroke remains a leading cause of death and disability worldwide, and inflammation is increasingly recognized as a key driver of acute injury and secondary neurodegeneration."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Neutrophil extracellular traps and microglia/macrophages ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12909230

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in Frontiers in Immunology (2026 Feb 03;17:1752471, DOI: 10.3389/fimmu.2026.1752471) by Nurittin Ardic (Med-International United Kingdom Health Agency Ltd., Nuneaton, UK) and Rasit Dinc (INVAMED Medical Innovation Institute, New York, NY, USA). The article, titled "Neutrophil extracellular traps and microglia/macrophages interactions in stroke: from thromboinflammation to immunotherapy," provides a comprehensive analysis of the bidirectional interaction between neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) and microglia/macrophages in stroke.

KEY TOPICS AND FINDINGS:

1. **Background**: Stroke is the second leading cause of death worldwide. Ischemic stroke (IS) accounts for 80-85% of cases; intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) and subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) comprise the remainder. NETs are critical amplifiers of thromboinflammation and cerebrovascular injury, while microglia and infiltrating macrophages regulate sterile inflammation.

2. **NET formation and structure**: NETs are chromatin-based structures (first identified in 2004) composed of decondensed DNA, histones (H2A, H2B, H3, H4), neutrophil elastase (NE), myeloperoxidase (MPO), cathepsin G, MMP-9, and antimicrobial peptides. Two pathways exist: (a) Suicidal NETosis - canonical PAD4-dependent pathway, progresses over hours, and (b) Vital NETosis - rapid (minutes), preserves cell viability, triggered by platelets, complement (C5a), and TLR2/TLR4 activation.

3. **Bidirectional NET-microglia interaction**: NET-derived DNA, histones, and proteases activate microglial pattern recognition receptors including TLR9, cGAS-STING, TLR4, and NLRP3 inflammasome components, triggering cytokine release and pyroptosis. Activated microglia then promote neutrophil recruitment and NETosis via IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-8/CXCL8, ROS, and the P2X7-NLRP3 pathway, creating a self-reinforcing feedforward inflammatory cycle.

4. **NETs in ischemic stroke**: NETs contribute to thrombus formation and large vessel occlusion (NET-rich thrombi are stiffer, more resistant to fragmentation, and harder to remove via thrombectomy); resistance to thrombolysis (tPA); microvascular no-reflow phenomenon; BBB disruption via MMP-9-dependent degradation of claudin-5 and occludin; and hemorrhagic transformation after thrombolysis. Higher NET content is found in cardioembolic and large-artery atherosclerotic strokes. DNase I or PAD4 inhibitors reduce microvascular obstruction and infarct growth.

5. **NETs in hemorrhagic stroke**: NETs accumulate in hematomas and perihematomal vasculature, stabilizing hematomas and promoting expansion (elevated plasma H3Cit-DNA correlates with early hematoma expansion). NETs contribute to BBB disruption, perihematomal edema, microglial activation, and impair hematoma clearance by physically blocking phagocytosis. In SAH, NETs are associated with vasospasm and delayed cerebral ischemia.

6. **Microglia/macrophage roles**: Microglia transform from ramified surveillance cells to activated forms within minutes to hours after stroke. Peripheral monocytes infiltrate 12-24 hours post-stroke, peaking at days 3-5. Phenotypic plasticity extends beyond the M1/M2 paradigm, with disease-associated microglia (DAM), lipid droplet-accumulating, and heme-processing phenotypes identified by single-cell transcriptomics.

7. **Therapeutic strategies**: DNase I, PAD4 inhibitors, NE/MPO inhibitors, and histone neutralizing agents to reduce NET pathology; NLRP3 inhibition, CSF1R modulation, and TREM2 agonism for microglial modulation; combination and temporally phased regimens targeting both pathways. The article also discusses NET biomarkers (H3Cit-DNA, MPO-DNA), thrombus tissue analysis, and molecular imaging for patient stratification and personalized immunotherapy.

8. **Clinical relevance**: Elevated plasma or thrombus H3Cit-DNA and MPO-DNA levels are associated with larger infarct volume, early neurological deterioration, hemorrhagic transformation, poor recanalization, and worse functional outcomes. NET burden in resected thrombi independently predicts lower recanalization success and increased need for multiple device passes.

The review concludes that the NET-microglia/macrophage axis represents a promising immunomodulatory target in ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke, offering new avenues for precision therapy development. The article was received Nov 23, 2025; accepted Jan 19, 2026; published Feb 3, 2026.
</summary>

"Recent studies have highlighted a bidirectional interaction between NETs and microglia/macrophages that amplifies neuroinflammation and shapes stroke outcomes. NET-derived DNA, histones, and proteases can directly activate microglial receptors such as TLR9, cGAS–STING, TLR4, and NLRP3 inflammasome components, promoting cytokine release and pyroptotic responses."

--- SOURCE 3: Time-dependent dual effect of microglia in ischemic stroke ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0197018623001122

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in *Neurochemistry International* (Volume 169, October 2023, Article 105584) titled "Time-dependent dual effect of microglia in ischemic stroke" by Ping-long Fan, Sha-sha Wang, Shi-feng Chu, and Nai-hong Chen. The article reviews the dual (both protective and detrimental) role of microglia in ischemic stroke across acute, subacute, and chronic phases.

**Key Background Data:**
- Stroke is the third leading cause of death and disability worldwide; ~85% of strokes are ischemic.
- Global incidence of ischemic stroke was 7,630,800 cases in 2019, with an 87.55% increase from 1990 to 2019.
- Microglia constitute 5–20% of the total glial population and are resident macrophages of the CNS.
- Current first-line therapies are limited: intravenous thrombolysis has a 4.5-hour window; intravascular recanalization has a 16–24-hour window. Only 7.3% of acute ischemic stroke patients in developed European countries receive intravenous thrombolysis, and only 1.9% receive intravascular recanalization.

**Microglial Biology:**
- Microglia originate from erythro-myeloid progenitor cells in the embryonic yolk sac, emigrating to the CNS as early as embryonic day 8.5–10.5 in mice.
- Their survival depends on CSF-1R receptor signaling (via CSF-1 and IL-34 ligands).
- Resting microglia have a ramified morphology; upon activation they transform to amoeboid-like phagocytic phenotypes.
- Microglia are classified into M1 (pro-inflammatory/neurotoxic) and M2 (anti-inflammatory/neuroprotective) phenotypes, though this classification is increasingly viewed as oversimplified.

**Temporal Dynamics of Microglial Polarization:**
- M1-microglia upregulate markers (CD45, CD11b, Iba-1) within 0.5–1 hour after MCAO.
- M2-microglia appear as early as 12 hours after MCAO, increase at 1–3 days, peak at 3–5 days, and begin converting to M1-like microglia at 7 days, returning to pre-injury levels by day 14.
- Blood monocyte-derived macrophages infiltrate the CNS at day 3 post-stroke.

**Dual Effects Across Disease Phases:**

*Acute phase:*
- Activated microglia produce proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α) that exacerbate brain damage, but M2-microglia release anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-10, TGF-β) and neurotrophic factors (NGF, IGF-1, BDNF) that promote tissue repair and neuroprotection.
- Depletion of microglia using PLX5622 (CSF-1R inhibitor) increases infarct volume and neuronal injury, demonstrating their protective role.
- Microglia interact bidirectionally with astrocytes (inducing A1 detrimental or A2 beneficial reactive states), oligodendrocytes (participating in both myelin injury and remyelination), and brain microvascular endothelial cells (affecting BBB integrity).
- DAMPs (ATP, UTP, HMGB1, HSPs, peroxiredoxins, mitochondrial DNA) released by injured neurons activate microglia via TLRs and NLRP3 inflammasomes, initiating neuroinflammation.

*Subacute phase:*
- Microglia mediate infiltration of peripheral immune cells including neutrophils (infiltrating within 12h, peaking by day 3), monocyte-derived macrophages (peaking at 3–5 days), dendritic cells (24–72h), T cells (appearing at 24h, peaking within first week), and B cells (entering after 7 days).
- M1-microglia release chemokines promoting leukocyte recruitment; M2-microglia promote anti-inflammatory phenotypes in infiltrating cells.
- B cells play a protective role through IL-10 secretion; B cell-deficient mice develop larger infarcts and worse outcomes.
- Microglia serve as the main CNS source of CXCL13, regulating B cell migration.

*Chronic phase:*
- Post-stroke neuroinflammation contributes to long-term complications including depression, fatigue, dementia, and seizures.
- The review emphasizes that dynamic intervention of microglial subsets or functions is a promising therapeutic strategy.

**Conclusions:**
- Microglia play a time-dependent dual role in ischemic stroke, acting as both drivers of neuroinflammation and key mediators of tissue repair.
- Understanding the dynamic variation of microglial phenotypes at different stroke stages could aid in developing more effective therapeutic and diagnostic strategies.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The traditional concept that ischemic stroke is solely a vascular occlusion disorder has been expanded to include the dynamic interaction between microglia, astrocytes, neurons, vascular cells, and matrix components forming the 'neurovascular unit.'"
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Functions and mechanisms of microglia/macrophages in neuroinflammation and neurogenesis after stroke ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S030100821630003X

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Progress in Neurobiology (Volume 142, July 2016, Pages 23-44) by Xiao-Yi Xiong, Liang Liu, and Qing-Wu Yang, titled "Functions and mechanisms of microglia/macrophages in neuroinflammation and neurogenesis after stroke." DOI: 10.1016/j.pneurobio.2016.05.001. The article is highly cited (634 citations) and contains 302 references.

KEY FINDINGS AND ARGUMENTS:
- Microglia/macrophages are the major immune cells involved in defending the brain against damage following stroke (ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, and subarachnoid hemorrhage).
- Microglia and macrophages share the same origin (derived from primitive macrophages during brain development per fate mapping analysis by Ginhoux et al., 2010) and have similar biofunctions, but can play different roles in the injured brain due to different gene expression patterns.
- These cells have dual roles: normally they clear dead neural cells and restore neuronal function, but when excessively activated by damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) after stroke, they produce proinflammatory cytokines that disrupt neural cells and the blood-brain barrier and influence neurogenesis.
- The M1 microglia/macrophage phenotype (induced by LPS) is mainly destructive, while the M2 phenotype (induced by IL-4) is neuroprotective. In general, promoting M2 and inhibiting M1 phenotypes is beneficial to brain recovery after stroke.
- Microglia/macrophages are involved in each step of neurogenesis: they produce trophic factors that guide cell migration, but can also produce inflammatory cytokines that reduce the survival of new-born neurons.
- Neurogenesis occurs in two brain regions: the subgranular zone (SGZ) of the hippocampus and the subventricular zone (SVZ) of the lateral ventricles; neuroblasts must migrate to replenish lost neurons.

KEY RECOMMENDATIONS FOR FUTURE RESEARCH:
1. Future translational studies should target multiple key regulating molecules involved in microglia/macrophage activation and polarization, incorporating the concept of a "therapeutic time window" for sequential therapies.
2. Constructing new experimental stroke models should be considered (since successful approaches in experimental models have largely failed to translate to clinical trials, partly because stroke populations are predominantly elderly with comorbidities like hypertension).
3. Identifying new gene signatures for circulating immune cells when they enter the CNS should be considered.
4. Exploring endogenous neuroprotective mechanisms responsible for brain repair should be considered.

FUNDING: Supported by the National Natural Science Fund for Distinguished Young Scholars (81525008) and the National Basic Research Program of China (973 Program) (2014CB541605).

The article also covers: sterile inflammation as a critical element of stroke pathobiology, microglial activation mechanisms (including perivascular microglia engulfing endothelial cells via phagocytosis after reperfusion), microglia/macrophage polarization factors (e.g., CD14 deficiency, PPARgamma, PACAP, Ly6C(hi) monocytes), and promising therapeutic perspectives including targeting the NLRP3 inflammasome, Notch signaling, and various other molecules.
</summary>

"Microglia/macrophages are the major immune cells involved in the defence against brain damage. Their morphology and functional changes are correlated with the release of danger signals induced by stroke."

--- SOURCE 5: Therapeutic Role of Microglia/Macrophage Polarization in Intracerebral Hemorrhage ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2514-183X/9/1/4

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a peer-reviewed open-access review article published in *Clinical and Translational Neuroscience* (Volume 9, Issue 1, 2025) titled "Therapeutic Role of Microglia/Macrophage Polarization in Intracerebral Hemorrhage" by Rasit Dinc (INVAMED Medical Innovation Institute, New York, NY) and Nurittin Ardic (Med-International UK Health Agency Ltd., UK). DOI: 10.3390/ctn9010004. The article was submitted 15 November 2024, accepted 15 January 2025, and published 20 January 2025.

**Background and Significance:** Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is one of the most dangerous types of stroke, accounting for up to 20% of all stroke cases (over 2 million worldwide annually). It has a higher mortality rate than ischemic stroke or subarachnoid hemorrhage, with mortality rates reaching 54% after the index event, and more than half of fatal events occurring in the first 2 days. Only about 20% of survivors regain functional independence. In the US alone, ICH incurs an annual healthcare cost of USD 12.7 billion. Most patients are over 65 years of age.

**Pathophysiology:** ICH causes primary damage via mass effect from hematoma formation and secondary damage via inflammatory reactions. Disruption of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) allows uncontrolled flow of blood-borne cells and macromolecules into the brain, causing malignant brain edema. The inflammatory response involves both resident microglia proliferation and recruitment of circulating leukocytes (neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, lymphocytes). Immune cells secrete destructive substances including cytokines, reactive oxygen species (ROS), matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs-2, 3, and 9), and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs).

**Key Immune Cells in ICH:**
- **Microglia**: Largest population of brain immune cells, activated within minutes after injury (peripheral macrophages infiltrate 1-2 days later). Both microglia and macrophages are divided into M1 (pro-inflammatory/classically activated) and M2 (anti-inflammatory/alternatively activated) subtypes. M1 subtypes are active in early damage stages; M2 subtypes peak after day 7 in the resolution period.
- **M1 microglia** (induced by IFN-γ and LPS) produce TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β, IL-12, CC-2, NADPH oxidase, iNOS, MHC-II, and co-stimulatory molecules.
- **M2 microglia** (induced by IL-4 and IL-13) express IL-10, TGF-β, IGF-1, FGF, CSF-1, and neurotrophic growth factors, promoting phagocytosis, ECM repair, and neuron survival.
- **M2 subtypes** further divided into M2a (wound healing), M2b (immune-mediated), M2c (regulatory), and M2d (tumor-associated/proangiogenic).
- **Astrocytes**: Express PRRs and TLRs; A1 subtype increases pro-inflammatory cytokines, A2 produces IL-2, IL-10, TGF-β.
- **Neutrophils**: First responders, destructive role in BBB disruption; N1 subtype secretes ROS, cytokines, proteases, NETs; N2 subtype (induced by TGF-β) promotes resolution.
- **Monocytes/Macrophages**: Recruited via CCL2, CXCL12 and CCR2, CXCR2; M1 macrophages (CD14++CD16−) are pro-inflammatory; M2 macrophages (CD14+CD16++) are anti-inflammatory.
- **Lymphocytes**: CD4+ T cells predominant; Th17 cells disrupt BBB via IL-17/IL-22; Treg cells are anti-inflammatory (depletion increases brain damage, increasing them reduces ICH-induced inflammatory damage). Stroke-induced immunodepression (lymphopenia, spleen shrinkage) is a major cause of poststroke infections.

**Immune Cell Crosstalk:** Activated microglia induce astrocyte conversion to A1 type via IL-1α, TNF-α, and C1q. Astrocytes promote microglial pro-inflammatory polarization. M1 microglia accelerate Th1 polarization and inhibit Treg function. Th2 cells promote M2 macrophage polarization via IL-4 and IL-13. Treg cells promote microglial M2 polarization through IL-10. Microglia-derived LTB4 attracts neutrophils; microglia-derived IL-27 reduces hematoma and edema.

**Therapeutic Strategies (M2 Polarization):** The central role of microglia/macrophages in inflammation maintenance, their dual M1/M2 effects, and their plasticity make them prime therapeutic targets.
- **Minocycline**: Promotes M2 polarization by suppressing NLRP3 inflammasome, inhibits MMPs and microglial reactivity, reduces M1 markers (TNF-α, IL-1β), increases M2 markers (TGF-β, IL-10), stabilizes BBB.
- **Fingolimod (FTY720)**: S1PR agonist, crosses BBB, suppresses inflammation by modulating S1PR-positive cells, increases Treg cells, reduces NK cells, limits leukocyte adhesion.
- **IL-1Ra**: Reduces inflammatory biomarkers, safe and well-tolerated.
- **TLR4 blockade** (eritoran, MTS510, miR-1906, TAK-242): Reduces activated microglia, iNOS, ROS, and pro-inflammatory factors, protects BBB.
- **Chemokine manipulation**: Elevated serum CCL2 associated with poor outcomes; CX3CR1 deficiency improves functional recovery.
- **Deferoxamine and lactoferrin**: Iron chelation/support to reduce iron toxicity and promote hematoma resolution.

**Clinical Trials:** NCT01805895 (minocycline), NCT04088630 (fingolimod), NCT02175225 (deferoxamine), NCT03737344 (IL-1Ra).

**Delivery Strategies:** Target-decorated nanoparticles (NPs) allow localized, controlled delivery; magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) with targeting ligands can be localized to hemorrhage sites using external magnetic fields (EMF).

**Conclusions:** The pathophysiology of ICH is complex and multifaceted, with inflammation playing a dominant role in secondary injury. Cells involved in the inflammatory process have dual pro-inflammatory/destructive and anti-inflammatory/healing roles. Resident microglia are important therapeutic targets due to their role in the initiation phase and shaping immunity. Modulating microglia/macrophages to the M2 phenotype is considered a more appropriate therapeutic approach than general anti-inflammatory medications or M2-targeting alone. Although clinical results remain poor, experimental and clinical trial data show promise for deciphering ICH pathophysiology and providing treatment options.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Despite accounting for up to 20% of all stroke cases (over 2 million worldwide), ICH is associated with a higher mortality rate than ischemic stroke or subarachnoid hemorrhage, with mortality rates reaching 54% after the index event."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Experimental Neurology (Volume 400, June 2026, Article 115683) titled "Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in cerebrovascular disease mechanisms, detection, and therapeutic targeting." The article is authored by Zhinuo Li, Shao-Huang Wu, Xinyue Zhang, Tianrun Li, Mingyuan Xin, and Fangxi Liu (Li and Wu contributed equally). 

The review comprehensively examines the role of NETs in cerebrovascular diseases, particularly ischemic stroke. Key mechanisms covered include:
- During cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury, NETs enhance immunothrombi stability by forming DNA-histone scaffolds, conferring resistance to thrombolysis (particularly reducing effectiveness of tissue plasminogen activator/tPA).
- NETs exacerbate blood-brain barrier (BBB) damage by degrading tight junction proteins via inflammatory cascades.
- Persistent NET formation impedes vascular remodeling and neural repair, compromising long-term functional recovery.

The review discusses NET formation via two main pathways: suicidal NETosis (lytic, triggered by microbial pathogens or sterile stimuli through PRRs such as TLR4, TLR9, and CLEC5A, involving ROS signaling) and another distinct pathway. 

Detection and quantification methods are categorized into three groups: (1) Histology and in vivo imaging (co-localization of extracellular DNA with MPO, NE, or H3Cit), (2) Body fluid biomarkers (quantifying circulating complexes like MPO-DNA), and (3) additional methods.

The authors highlight that targeting NETs during the acute phase may enhance reperfusion efficiency and ameliorate neural injury, while modulating NETs during the repair phase can promote tissue regeneration. However, clinical translation faces significant obstacles including narrow therapeutic windows, limited intervention specificity, risk of infectious complications, and lack of biomarkers for patient stratification. Future research directions include elucidating NET heterogeneity, developing precise spatiotemporal modulation techniques, and advancing translational applications through multidisciplinary collaboration.

The article includes 91 references and has been cited by 3 subsequent publications (including related 2026 articles in Experimental Neurology, Brain Sciences, and Neurology International). The study was supported by the Liaoning Provincial Doctoral Scientific Research Start-up Fund Program and a China Medical University Undergraduate Training Program for Innovation and Entrepreneurship grant.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Neutrophil extracellular traps in ischemic stroke ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neurology/articles/10.3389/fneur.2025.1641985/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Frontiers in Neurology (12 September 2025, Vol. 16) titled "Neutrophil extracellular traps in ischemic stroke: mechanisms, clinical implications, and therapeutic potential" by Wenbo He, Zuoli Wu, Ying Liu, and Ziming Ye (from Guangxi Medical University-affiliated hospitals in Nanning, China).

## Main Topic
The review systematically examines the role of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs)—web-like structures of DNA and cytotoxic proteins released by activated neutrophils—in ischemic stroke pathophysiology, with focus on mechanisms, clinical implications, biomarkers, and therapeutic strategies.

## Key Findings

**NETs as Active Drivers of Stroke Pathology:**
- NETs promote three primary detrimental effects: (1) stable, lysis-resistant thrombi leading to poor clinical outcomes; (2) compromised blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity; and (3) amplified neuroinflammatory cascades.
- NETs are significantly elevated in acute ischemic stroke patients, particularly in those over 65 with atrial fibrillation or cardioembolic sources.
- NET formation peaks within 24 hours post-stroke and declines by 48 hours in murine models.

**Mechanistic Insights:**
- Upstream triggers include oxidative stress/ROS, DAMPs (e.g., HMGB1), and platelet activation.
- Two intracellular NETosis pathways: NADPH oxidase-dependent (classical lytic) and PAD4-dependent (histone citrullination leading to chromatin decondensation).
- Downstream effects include prothrombotic actions (DNA scaffold trapping platelets/RBCs, coagulation activation), BBB disruption (protease degradation of tight junctions, histone cytotoxicity to endothelial cells), and neuroinflammation amplification (NETs act as DAMPs activating microglia/astrocytes, perpetuating a vicious cycle).

**Clinical Implications:**
- High NET content in retrieved thrombi strongly predicts resistance to tPA, failed recanalization (mTICI <2b), and prolonged procedure times during mechanical thrombectomy.
- Older, more organized thrombi contain higher NET burdens; thrombus age is the sole independent predictor of NET content.
- Comorbidities (diabetes, obesity) "prime" neutrophils via gut dysbiosis, meta-inflammation, and metabolic reprogramming, leading to exaggerated NETotic responses.

**Biomarkers:**
- NLR (neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio) predicts poorer 90-day functional independence; H3Cit, cfDNA, NGAL, NHR, and MHR also explored as prognostic biomarkers.

**Therapeutic Strategies (Table 1):**
1. PAD4 inhibition (chloroquine and derivatives; tetrahydroisoquinolines)
2. NET degradation (DNase-I—though limited efficacy on fibrin-rich thrombi noted)
3. Physical removal (therapeutic apheresis)
4. EV-based indirect modulation (astrocyte/microglia-derived extracellular vesicles that cross the BBB)

**Research Trends:**
- China and the US lead research in this field (2025 bibliometric analysis).
- Key challenges: therapeutic specificity (risk of compromising innate immunity), defining optimal treatment window, and developing rapid clinical diagnostics for NET burden quantification.

## Conclusion
Targeting the thrombo-inflammatory functions of NETs represents a paradigm shift from a purely fibrin-centric view of stroke. Future research must address NET heterogeneity (pro-thrombotic vs. pro-inflammatory subtypes), potential reparative roles in subacute/chronic phases, and precise molecular mechanisms of NET-associated protease activity on BBB proteins. Funding was provided by Guangxi Natural Science Foundation, National Natural Science Foundation of China, and other grants.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"NETs are not mere bystanders but active drivers of stroke pathology... promoting stable, lysis-resistant thrombi, which directly contributes to poor clinical outcomes; compromising blood-brain barrier integrity; and amplifying the neuroinflammatory cascade."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Nature Communications (volume 11, article 2488, 2020) by Lijing Kang, Huilin Yu, Bing-Qiao Zhao, and colleagues, investigating how neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) impair revascularization and vascular remodeling after stroke. The study has 40,000 accesses and 532 citations.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Neutrophils accumulate in the peri-infarct cortex during all stages of ischemic stroke (peaking at 3 days and persisting to at least 14 days), with a 5.3-fold increase in myeloperoxidase (MPO) content at 3 days.
- Neutrophil-derived NETs (intravascular and intraparenchymal) peak at 3-5 days after stroke. NETs contain double-stranded DNA, histones, and granule proteins.
- Neutrophil depletion (via anti-Ly6G antibody) reduces blood-brain barrier (BBB) breakdown by 39.3% and enhances neovascularization by 29.8% at 14 days.
- Peptidylarginine deiminase 4 (PAD4), an enzyme essential for NET formation, is upregulated 29.3-fold in mRNA and 3.8-fold in protein expression in ischemic cortex at 3 days.
- PAD4 overexpression induces ~2.6-fold more NET formation, leading to reduced neovascularization, increased BBB damage, and worse neurological outcomes.
- Disruption of NETs by DNase 1 or inhibition of NET formation via PAD4 genetic ablation (PAD4−/− mice) or pharmacologic inhibition (Cl-amidine) increases neovascularization, vascular repair, and improves functional recovery.
- PAD inhibition reduces stroke-induced STING-mediated production of IFN-β; STING knockdown and IFN receptor-neutralizing antibody treatment reduce BBB breakdown and increase vascular plasticity.
- PAD4 deficiency or Cl-amidine treatment enhanced tight-junction proteins (ZO-1, claudin-5, occludin) and VE-cadherin in isolated brain microvessels, improving BBB integrity.
- Delayed treatment (starting 7 days after stroke) with anti-Ly6G antibody or DNase 1 still improved vascular remodeling and reduced BBB disruption at 14 days.

METHODOLOGY: The study used mouse models of cerebral ischemia, flow cytometry, in-vivo multiphoton microscopy, immunostaining, Western blotting, quantitative PCR, and behavioral tests (beam walking and forelimb force tests). NETs were identified by citrullinated histone H3 (H3Cit) staining, with 78.7% of H3Cit-positive cells being Ly6G-positive neutrophils.

CONCLUSION: NET release by neutrophils impairs vascular remodeling during stroke recovery, and targeting neutrophils/NETs represents a potential therapeutic strategy for promoting brain repair after stroke.
</summary>

"Neutrophils producing intravascular and intraparenchymal neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) peak at 3–5 days. Neutrophil depletion reduces blood-brain barrier (BBB) breakdown and enhances neovascularization at 14 days."

--- SOURCE 1: Frontiers | The role of astrocytes in ischemic stroke - mechanisms, functions and treatment ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cell-and-developmental-biology/articles/10.3389/fcell.2025.1700564/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## The Role of Astrocytes in Ischemic Stroke - Mechanisms, Functions and Treatment

**Publication Details:** This is a review article published in *Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology* (Section: Signaling), Volume 13, December 10, 2025 (DOI: 10.3389/fcell.2025.1700564). Authors: Yunlong Wang, Ding Wang, Dongyu Li, and Yuewen Ma (corresponding author) from the Department of Rehabilitation, The First Affiliated Hospital of China Medical University, Shenyang, China.

**Overview:** Ischemic stroke (IS) is the second leading cause of death worldwide after ischemic heart disease and the leading cause of death and disability in China since 2015, accounting for over 86.9% of all stroke cases. Despite thrombolytic therapy, mechanical thrombectomy, and bridging therapy, more than 80% of IS patients still experience functional impairment. Astrocytes—the most numerous glial cells in the brain—undergo activation after IS into "reactive astrocytes" with complex, dual roles (both harmful and protective) in stroke pathology.

**Intrinsic Molecular Mechanisms of Astrocyte Activation:**
1. **NF-κB Signaling Pathway:** TLR4 recognizes damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), activating NF-κB through TRIF/TRAF3/JNK and MyD88-dependent pathways. TREM-2 upregulation inhibits astrocyte activation. LMP2, PI3Kγ, and AGEs/RAGE interactions also promote NF-κB phosphorylation and astrocyte activation.
2. **STAT3 Signaling Pathway:** Increased STAT3 phosphorylation promotes inflammatory astrocyte activation. CRYAB and DRD2 inhibit activation by suppressing STAT3 phosphorylation. LCN2 upregulation activates the JAK2/STAT3 pathway. Neuron-derived 17β-estradiol (E2) promotes neuroprotective astrocyte activation, while FGF2 inhibits it. IL-6/sIL-6R complexes activate STAT3 via PI3Kγ.
3. **MAPK Signaling Pathway:** ERK, JNK, and p38 are all associated with cerebral ischemia. FasL promotes JNK phosphorylation, amplifying inflammatory responses. The ASK1–JNK axis can activate NF-κB, sustaining astrocyte responses.

**Non-Coding RNA Regulation:** miR-29c-5p and miR-210 promote astrocyte activation; miR-488-3p inhibits it (but lncRNA NEAT1 binds and neutralizes it); miR-137 loss increases Src expression activating MAPK; MSC-derived EVs deliver miR-125b-5p to inhibit TLR4/NF-κB; circHectd1 sponges MIR142 to elevate TIPARP and promote activation; circCDC14A from neutrophils also enhances activation.

**Other Regulatory Mechanisms:** Decreased PPARα impairs autophagic flux promoting activation; FUS protein inclusions induce excessive autophagy; AQP4 polarization impairs Aβ clearance and glymphatic function; thrombin binds PAR1 driving A2 reactive phenotype.

**Role of Reactive Astrocytes (Dual Functions):**
- **Harmful:** Secrete pro-inflammatory factors (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, CXCL10), disrupt BBB via decreased claudin-5/ZO-1 and increased P-gp/MMP9, promote permanent glial scar formation.
- **Protective:** Secrete IL-10, IL-1ra, Arg1, BDNF, IGF-1, GLT-1; promote VEGF and FGF2 for angiogenesis; maintain BBB integrity and promote vascular remodeling.

**Therapeutic Approaches:**

1. **Rehabilitation Therapies:**
   - **rTMS:** Preserves vasculature, reduces BBB hyperpermeability, downregulates C3/iNOS/IL-12, promotes S100A10/Arg1, enhances neuroprotection and cognitive recovery.
   - **Electroacupuncture (EA):** Activates CB1R, modulates glutamate, inhibits ROS, reduces BBB disruption, upregulates MCT1 for lactate shuttle.
   - **Hypothermia:** Reduces astrocyte death, downregulates MMP-2/MMP-9, protects BBB.
   - **Normobaric Hyperoxia (NBO):** Attenuates astrocyte activation, upregulates Cx43 and GPX4, reduces apoptosis.
   - **Exercise:** Promotes neuroprotective astrocyte phenotype, increases STAT3 and Gpc6, reduces infarct volume.

2. **Natural Bioactive Compounds:** Tetramethylpyrazine (TMP), Buyang Huanwu Decoction, Z-Guggulsterone (safe up to 1,600 mg/kg), Celastrol, Ginsenoside Rb1, Alpinia oxyphylla Miq extract, Storax, Ruta graveolens extract, Ginkgo biloba extract (EGB), Ginkgolide (GDL), and Cottonseed oil (CSO) all modulate astrocyte function through various mechanisms (NF-κB inhibition, JAK2/STAT3 suppression, anti-oxidant effects, neurotrophic factor promotion).

3. **Agonists and Small Molecules:** Sinomenine (DRD2 agonist), Oleoylethanolamide (PPARα agonist), Adjudin (Sirt3 activator, dual Sirt3/Foxo3a and Sirt3/Notch1 mechanisms), Afobazole (σ1/σ2 agonist, effective beyond acute phase), IL-33 (promotes M2 polarization), and intranasal C3a (binds C3aR on astrocytes, inhibits activation, upregulates IGF1 and Thbs4).

**Key Conclusions:** Most evidence remains preclinical. Future research should focus on large-scale multicenter randomized controlled trials, improving drug bioavailability and BBB permeability, developing targeted nanocarrier delivery systems, and standardizing rehabilitation protocols with personalized treatment strategies considering patient age, stroke severity, and genetic background.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Ischemic stroke, characterized by localized cerebral hypoperfusion due to various etiologies, exhibits high global incidence and mortality rates. Astrocytes, as key structural and functional components of the neurovascular unit, play a critical role in maintaining homeostasis in the central nervous system."
</key_excerpts>



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


--- SOURCE 2: Crosstalk of Astrocytes and Other Cells during Ischemic Stroke ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2075-1729/12/6/910

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access review article published in the journal *Life* (2022, Volume 12, Issue 6, article 910; DOI: 10.3390/life12060910) titled "Crosstalk of Astrocytes and Other Cells during Ischemic Stroke" by Tingting He, Guo-Yuan Yang, and Zhijun Zhang (affiliated with Shanghai Tenth People's Hospital, Tongji University, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University). The review examines the complex, bidirectional communication between reactive astrocytes and other brain cells during ischemic stroke, challenging the traditional "neurocentric" view of stroke pathology.

KEY CONTENT AREAS:

1. **Mechanisms of astrocyte crosstalk**: Astrocytes communicate through (a) fine processes contacting virtually all CNS parenchymal cells, (b) gap junction networks (homocellular/heterocellular), (c) receptors responding to neurotransmitters and other signals, and (d) release of "gliotransmitters" (glutamate, D-serine, ATP, GABA), growth factors, cytokines, chemokines, exosomes, and even mitochondria.

2. **Optogenetics in astrocyte research**: Recent studies use optogenetic manipulation (ChR2, CatCh, Arch, NpHR) with astrocyte-specific promoters (GFAP, Mlc1) to demonstrate that astrocytic activity modulates neuronal activity, synaptic plasticity, sleep-wake regulation, food intake, and behavioral responses.

3. **Reactive astrogliosis after ischemia**: Astrocytes transition from bushy to hypertrophic stellate to polarized morphology, forming glial scars by chronic phase (days 8-14 post-ischemia). Key signaling pathways include STAT3, p38 MAPK, NF-κB, TGF-β, and Notch-1.

4. **Neuroprotective functions of reactive astrocytes**: 
   - Metabolic support via glycogen breakdown and lactate transport through MCTs
   - Antiexcitatory effects via glutamate uptake (EAAT1/EAAT2 transporters, glutamate-glutamine cycle)
   - Antioxidant defense (highest glutathione concentrations in brain)
   - Mitochondrial transfer to neurons (CD38/cyclic ADP ribose signaling)
   - Exosome-mediated protection via miRNAs (miR-190b, miR-92b-3p, miR-34c, miR-361)
   - Release of neuroprotectants (EPO, VEGF, GDNF, estrogen/aromatase)
   - Phagocytic transformation to engulf neuronal debris (ABCA1, MEGF10, GULP1)

5. **Astrocyte-astrocyte gap junctions**: Controversial role of Cx43/Cx36 in stroke—gap junctions may spread proapoptotic factors (increasing infarct) but heterozygous Cx43 ablation also increases infarct size; connexin mimetic peptides (Gap26/27) may offer cardioprotection; non-channel functions of connexins complicate interpretation.

6. **Astrocyte-microglia crosstalk and inflammation**: Microglia release IL-1α, TNF-α, and C1q triggering neurotoxic A1 astrocyte phenotype, while A2 phenotype is neuroprotective (upregulated at 72h post-stroke). Bidirectional regulation involves galectin-9, ORM2/CCR5, LCN2, IL-10/TGF-β feedback loops, purinergic signaling, and astrocyte interactions with NK cells, CD8+ T cells (IL-15 pathway), IL-17, and Treg cells (IL-33).

7. **BBB integrity and edema**: Astrocyte endfeet ensheath >99% of blood vessel surface; AQP4 water channels mediate cytotoxic edema (AQP4-depleted mice show reduced edema and better outcomes); astrocyte-derived MMPs, VEGF-A downregulate tight junctions (claudin-5, occludin); pentraxin-3 and FGF2 have context-dependent protective effects.

8. **Astrocytic microRNAs**: miR-210 (biomarker in acute cerebral ischemia, elevated in stroke patients' blood for up to 14 days), miR-181a, miR-29a/b (targets AQP4, regulates mitochondrial homeostasis and apoptosis), with therapeutic potential for stroke.

CONCLUSION: The review argues that "neurocentric" strategies may be insufficient for neurological protection and recovery after ischemic stroke; future therapeutic strategies should target reactive astrocytes given their dual beneficial and detrimental roles in neuroprotection, neurorestoration, inflammation, and edema.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Reactive astrocytes provide neuroprotection through antioxidation and antiexcitatory effects and metabolic support; they also contribute to neurorestoration involving neurogenesis, synaptogenesis, angiogenesis, and oligodendrogenesis by crosstalk with stem cells and cell lineage. In the meantime, reactive astrocytes also play a vital role in neuroinflammation and brain edema."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Different roles of astrocytes in the blood–brain barrier during the acute and recovery phases of stroke ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12407517

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed review article published in Neural Regeneration Research (Neural Regen Res, 2025 Jun 19;21(4):1359, DOI: 10.4103/NRR.NRR-D-24-01417) from the College of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Beijing University of Chinese Medicine. The paper, titled "Different roles of astrocytes in the blood–brain barrier during the acute and recovery phases of stroke," reviews the pathological changes in the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and astrocyte phenotypes following ischemic stroke.

KEY FINDINGS:

**BBB Structure and Function:** The BBB is composed of three "barriers" — (1) brain microvascular endothelial cells with tight junctions (TJs) composed of occludin, claudins, and ZO proteins; (2) pericytes embedded in a basal membrane of type IV collagen, laminin, nestin, and heparan sulfate proteoglycan; and (3) astrocytes whose foot processes envelop all brain capillaries (astrocytes constitute up to 99% of the BBB). Astrocytes secrete factors including angiotensin, sonic hedgehog (Shh), glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor, and fibroblast growth factor-2 to maintain BBB homeostasis.

**Post-Stroke BBB Changes:** BBB damage follows four phases: endothelial swelling, endothelial membrane disruption, tight junction breakdown, and complete vascular destruction. BBB permeability increases biphasically — peaking within hours and again 2-3 days post-stroke. Pericytes transform from static flat cells to amoeboid shapes within 1 hour of ischemia, detaching from the basal lamina. TJ proteins (occludin, claudin-3/5, ZO-1) rapidly downregulate during early ischemia. Endothelial vesicle numbers and endocytosis increase within 6 hours post-stroke, with severe TJ defects appearing at 2 days.

**Astrocyte Phenotypes (A1 and A2):** Reactive astrocytes polarize into two phenotypes based on gene expression. A1 reactive astrocytes are neurotoxic, secreting vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), lipid carrier protein-2 (LCN-2), and glutamate, which exacerbate BBB damage by degrading tight junction proteins and increasing permeability. A2 reactive astrocytes are neuroprotective, secreting pentraxin 3 (PTX3), sonic hedgehog (Shh), angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1), and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), which maintain BBB stability and promote repair.

**Acute vs. Recovery Phases:** During the acute phase, A1 astrocytes promote BBB disruption through VEGF/MMP-9-mediated degradation of claudin-5 and occludin, while A2 astrocytes protect the BBB. In the middle and late (recovery) stages, A1 astrocytes promote glial scar formation and inhibit axon growth via GFAP, chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans, and transforming growth factor-β, whereas A2 astrocytes facilitate axon growth through platelet-derived growth factor and support vascular remodeling.

**Additional Mechanisms:** Astrocytes indirectly affect BBB function through ferroptosis (via NDRG2/Wnt/β-catenin signaling) and by secreting microRNA-rich exosomes. Connexin 43 (Cx43) promotes astrocyte phenotypic transformation and protects against ischemic stress-induced apoptosis. Semaglutide (a GLP-1 receptor agonist) can block A1 astrocyte transformation.

**Therapeutic Implications:** Understanding astrocyte-BBB interactions is a vital therapeutic target for preventing further brain damage in acute stroke. The review discusses existing therapeutic agents and nanotechnology applications for enhancing drug delivery across the BBB and enabling precise targeting of cytokines. The paper was received November 13, 2024, revised January 6, 2025, and accepted February 7, 2025.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"During the acute phase, A1 reactive astrocytes secrete vascular endothelial growth factor, matrix metalloproteinases, lipid carrier protein-2, and other cytokines, exacerbating damage to endothelial cells and tight junctions. Conversely, A2 reactive astrocytes produce pentraxin 3, Sonic hedgehog, angiopoietin-1, and other protective factors for endothelial cells."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Glial Cells: Role of the Immune Response in Ischemic Stroke ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7055422

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in Frontiers in Immunology (2020 Feb 26;11:294, doi: 10.3389/fimmu.2020.00294, PMC7055422, PMID 32174916) titled "Glial Cells: Role of the Immune Response in Ischemic Stroke" by Shenbin Xu, Jianan Lu, Anwen Shao (all from Hangzhou), John H. Zhang (Loma Linda, CA), and Jianmin Zhang (Hangzhou). The article is open-access under the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY).

KEY CONTENT:
- Ischemic stroke accounts for 75-80% of all strokes and is the predominant cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. The post-stroke immune response has emerged as a new breakthrough treatment target.
- Glial cells (microglia, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes) are the primary components of the peri-infarct environment in the CNS and exert both beneficial and detrimental effects during ischemic stroke.

MICROGLIA:
- Described by Santiago Ramón y Cajal in 1913 as the "third element" of the CNS; staining method developed by Pío Del Río-Hortega in 1918. Arise from embryonic yolk sac precursors; constitute 5-12% of glia in adult mouse brain and 0.5-16.6% of brain cells in adult human brain.
- First immune cells to sense ischemia, activated within 30 min to 1 h after middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO). Activation persists for several weeks.
- Polarization into M1 (proinflammatory) and M2 (anti-inflammatory/protective) phenotypes. iNOS is a marker for M1; arginase 1 for M2. LPS/IFNγ promote M1; IL-4 and IL-10 induce M2. There is a temporal shift from M2 to M1 phenotype within 7 days after ischemic injury.
- M1 microglia secrete TNF, IL-1β, IL-6 (acute phase, detrimental). M2 microglia produce neurotrophic factors like IGF1 and promote tissue repair (chronic phase).
- Microglia release MMPs (e.g., MMP-9) promoting BBB breakdown; perivascular microglia can phagocytize vascular endothelial cells.
- Activated by DAMPs including HMGB1, PRX family proteins, and galectin-3 via TLR4, P2X7/P2Y12 purinergic receptors, glutamate receptors, and TREM2.
- Microglial activation can induce A1 reactive astrocytes by releasing IL1α, TNFα, and C1q.
- Microglial VEGF-C stimulates OPC proliferation via VEGFR-3; M2 microglia drive oligodendrocyte differentiation during remyelination.

ASTROCYTES:
- Constitute 19-40% of glial cells. Reactive astrogliosis involves hypertrophy and GFAP overexpression. Form glial scar that walls off the lesion but hinders neuronal reconnection.
- A1 and A2 subtypes: A1 (induced by IL-1α, TNFα, C1q from activated microglia) contributes to neuronal/oligodendrocyte death; A2 (neuroprotective, upregulates neurotrophic factors). A2 transcripts were predominant at 72h after transient MCAO.
- Key signaling pathways in astrocyte-mediated neuroinflammation (Table 1): P2Y1 receptor (NF-κB pathway, proinflammatory cytokines), TLR2/TLR4 (JAK1/STAT1 and NF-κB pathways), CD36 (promotes GFAP expression, reduces infarct volume when knocked down), TGF-β (neuroprotective, reduces immune cell infiltration), STAT3 (suppresses proinflammatory cytokines, promotes neurogenesis), Notch1 (promotes reactive astrogliosis), NF-κB (promotes CD11b+ leukocyte infiltration), TWEAK/Fn14 (activates NF-κB), TIM3 (increases neutrophil infiltration and neuronal damage).

OLIGODENDROCYTES:
- Constitute 45-75% of glial cells. Highly vulnerable to ischemia; myelin disruption occurs after stroke. Myelin-associated antigens activate peripheral T cells causing autoimmune response.
- Inflammatory factors (TNF, MMP3, MMP9) from activated microglia impair oligodendrocytes/OPCs. Neuroinflammation affects demyelination and remyelination.
- Oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) can differentiate into oligodendrocytes following stroke and may result in functional recovery. Failure of OPC maturation into oligodendrocytes results in remyelination failure.

CONCLUSION: No effective treatment currently targets the immune response after ischemic stroke. Understanding the mechanisms of post-stroke immune regulation mediated by glial cells and their interactions with neurons is critical for developing future intervention targets. The roles of various glial cells differ at different stages of ischemic stroke, and future research should focus on these stage-specific functions and microglia-astrocyte-oligodendrocyte crosstalk.
</summary>
