Ischemia induces persistent pericyte constriction that does not restore even after complete recanalization of the occluded artery.[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr14-0271678X241237159) (a) Node-like discontinuities were noted along the course of microvessels in the ischemic hemisphere. (b) The DIC images illustrate frequent interruptions in the erythrocyte column in an ischemic capillary contrary to a continuous row of erythrocytes flowing through an intact capillary. (Green, c) Nodal constrictions on the ischemic capillaries colocalized with α-SMA-positive pericytes. These nodal constrictions might be brought on by pericytes. Indeed, when labeled pericytes with an antibody against α-smooth muscle actin (SMA), it suggested that the constricted microvessels segments colocalized with pericytes. Copyright 2009, Springer Nature.

Additionally, pericyte contraction can result from increased intracellular calcium ion concentration in cerebral ischemia.[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr14-0271678X241237159),[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr68-0271678X241237159),[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr69-0271678X241237159) Pericytes also contract during ischemia due to the uncontrolled rise in intracellular Ca 2+ resulting from energy loss triggered by acute cerebral ischemia that disrupts Ca 2+ homeostasis.[70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr70-0271678X241237159) This contraction may be mediated by α-smooth muscle actin (α-SAM).[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr71-0271678X241237159) In ischemia-reperfusion, intracellular pro-oxidant enzymes and mitochondria produce massive oxygen radicals with oxygen, resulting in an imbalance of oxidative and antioxidant functions in the body. In the reperfusion process, the significant accumulation of intracellular ROS, the paradox of oxygen, calcium, and pH change contribute to producing free radicals, developing oxidative stress, and other toxic factors. Among these changes, oxidative stress is a potent constriction inducer of pericytes. Oxygen and nitrogen radicals formed in the microvasculature during ischemia/reperfusion cause persistent pericyte constriction. Pericyte contraction occurred one hour after reperfusion in the MCAO model. It was proved that oxidative and nitrative radicals induced pericyte contraction to suppress oxidative and nitrative stress before reperfusion relieved pericyte contraction.[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr14-0271678X241237159) This study suggested the importance of pericyte contractility in ischemic stroke pathology.

Moreover, this study indicates that sustained contraction of pericytes might be the reason for the adverse outcome of thrombolysis therapy. The active contraction of pericytes may increase microcirculatory resistance than compression of the lumen by swollen end feet. Consequently, this mechanism may significantly contribute to microvascular clogging. Pericyte contractility may partially be involved in the microcirculation no-reflow.[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr14-0271678X241237159)

### Vasoconstriction

A research group performed a study with MCAO models, revealing that cerebral arteriole constrictions significantly reduce cerebral blood flow (CBF). These constrictions may induce inadequate reperfusion after ischemic stroke.[72](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr72-0271678X241237159) Multiple alternations are involved in this pathological constriction and vascular dysfunction, including increased arterial stiffness, diminished vascular reactivity, and decreased endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) phosphorylation.[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr73-0271678X241237159) Cerebral ischemia affects the vascular ECs, pericytes, and the entire NVU (including astrocytes, microglia, and neurons), leading to several restrictive layers and complicated interactions.[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr73-0271678X241237159) A research group conducted an experimental study to determine whether pericyte contraction affects blood flow recovery. They have verified that in pathological constriction of tiny distal vascular segments in ischemic stroke, vascular side branches are sensitive throughout the propagation of pressure gradients and nutrient supply.[74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr74-0271678X241237159) The changes within the extracellular potassium concentration in the brain during physiological events (e.g. neuronal activity) may be essential for regulating local cerebral blood flow.[75](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr75-0271678X241237159),[76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr76-0271678X241237159) High potassium concentrations in the extracellular fluid (<∼20mEq/L) cause a pronounced vascular smooth muscle contraction.[77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr77-0271678X241237159) –[81](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr81-0271678X241237159) Cerebrovascular resistance (CVR) changes were assessed by measuring the cerebral perfusion rate (CPR). Following 2 min of ischemia, CVR was decreased to the half control value, while significantly multiplied after 8 and 16 min of ischemia. Therefore, the no-reflow state was approached at 16 min of ischemia. Moreover, cerebral ischemia lasting 8 and 16 min in rats was amid a more significant increase in cis-cerebrospinal fluid potassium concentration and a subsequent increase in CVR.[82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr82-0271678X241237159) This study did not offer definitive proof for a causal relationship between the rise in the potassium concentration in brain extracellular fluid and the increase in CVR. However, due to the changes in the potassium concentration in cisternal cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which occur with a delay compared to the changes in brain extracellular fluid, it is necessary for the increase in potassium concentration within the brain interstitial fluid to be greater than the measurement observed in the cisternal CSF. The significant rise in potassium concentration in brain extracellular fluid alone may account for the observed changes in CVR.

## Risk factors and predictors for no-reflow

Merely relying on reopening large vessels is inadequate for effectively preventing and managing tissue damage progression. Identifying risk factors and predictors associated with no-reflow prevents its onset and enables timely intervention to improve the prognosis of patients with ischemic stroke.

Clinical risk factors include old age,[83](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr83-0271678X241237159) female sex, diabetes, hypertension, higher baseline National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score, lower Alberta stroke project early CT score (ASPECTS), poor collateral status, negative imaging performance, longer endovascular treatment delay, and increased biomarkers of inflammation and microcirculatory disorders.[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr84-0271678X241237159) Old age is consistently associated with poor neurological prognosis after stroke, possibly due to more comorbidities, higher complication rates and cardiogenic stroke incidence, and less recovery potential.[85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr85-0271678X241237159) –[87](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr87-0271678X241237159) Females are at an elevated risk of experiencing futile recanalization, primarily due to physiological disparities in coagulation, hormonal fluctuations, and immune responses during menopause.[88](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr88-0271678X241237159) Hypertension and hyperglycemia can increase BBB permeability,[89](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr89-0271678X241237159),[90](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr90-0271678X241237159) impair microvascular cerebrovascular reactivity,[91](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr91-0271678X241237159),[92](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr92-0271678X241237159) and exacerbate reperfusion injury.[93](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr93-0271678X241237159),[94](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr94-0271678X241237159) Multifactorial analysis showed that time from onset to endovascular treatment was an independent risk factor for ineffective recanalization.[95](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr95-0271678X241237159),[96](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr96-0271678X241237159)

The predictive factors associated with the occurrence of no-reflow primarily encompass four categories: individual health background and comorbidities, neurologic function scores, imaging manifestations and scores, and molecular markers: (1) Age >70 years, female sex, longer treatment delay and comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes, and atrial fibrillation) could be used as predictors of no-reflow.[83](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr83-0271678X241237159),[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr84-0271678X241237159) (2) Higher NIHSS score ≥10 is a significant predictor in a retrospective multifactorial analysis.[97](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr97-0271678X241237159),[98](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr98-0271678X241237159) (3) ASPECTS ≤5,[99](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr99-0271678X241237159) moderate-severe leukoaraiosis (van Swieten scale ≥2),[100](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr100-0271678X241237159) a large lesions in the deep white matter (DWM) on pretreatment diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI) which demonstrates a longitudinal hyperintense lesion in >80% of the DWM,[101](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr101-0271678X241237159) collateral score modified Rankin Scale (mRS) ≤ 2,[102](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr102-0271678X241237159) occlusion sites such as internal carotid artery occlusion, pre-stroke brain atrophy, and cerebral edema are shown to be predictors of no-reflow.[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr84-0271678X241237159),[103](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr103-0271678X241237159) (4) Molecular markers such as IL-6, IL-1,[104](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr104-0271678X241237159) the elevated peripheral blood neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR),[105](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr105-0271678X241237159) high sensitivity C-reactive protein, the increased levels of matrix metalloproteinase-9, tenascin-C, thioredoxin, decreased levels of a disintegrin and metalloproteinase with a thrombospondin type 1 motif, member13 and gelsolin,[106](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr106-0271678X241237159) and increased neutrophils count[107](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr107-0271678X241237159) are independent predictors of no-reflow.[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr84-0271678X241237159),[108](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr108-0271678X241237159) Due to the cost-effectiveness and ease of measuring biomarkers, the integration of these biomarkers with clinical imaging parameters to develop risk scoring systems has the potential to enhance early screening for no-reflow.

## Diagnosis of no-reflow

Clinical information on low/no-reflow is limited, and there is a lack of clear diagnostic indicators in the clinic. This is partly due to the challenges in accurately assessing vessel status in early studies without relying on invasive diagnostic angiography.[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr18-0271678X241237159) The clinical manifestations of no-reflow, observed in patients who have undergone successful restoration, lack distinct characteristics, thereby increasing the likelihood of oversight. In individuals, the proximal arteries of patients with ischemic stroke commonly exhibit a pathological condition characterized by the presence of atherosclerotic plaque and thrombus formation. Pro-inflammatory or pro-coagulant states such as diabetes and hyperlipidemia are common risk factors for stroke patients, which can increase the risk and intensity of the occurrence of no-reflow. The incidence of no-reflow also rises in patients with white matter hyperintensity burden, pre-stroke brain atrophy, cerebral edema, longer ischemia time, poorer neurologic recovery, and surge in interleukins and neutrophils.[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr84-0271678X241237159),[103](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr103-0271678X241237159),[109](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11318407#bibr109-0271678X241237159) Hence, further workup for no-reflow should be focused on patients presenting with the above conditions. args.summary:
This is a peer-reviewed review article published in the Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow & Metabolism (June 2024 issue, DOI: 10.1177/0271678X241237159) by authors from Hunan University of Chinese Medicine, China (Feiyue Sun, Jing Zhou, Xiangyu Chen, Tong Yang, Guozuo Wang, Jinwen Ge, Zhanwei Zhang, and Zhigang Mei). The article provides a comprehensive review of the "no-reflow" phenomenon after recanalization in ischemic stroke.

**Key Points:**

1. **Definition and Context**: No-reflow is the failure of microcirculatory reperfusion despite clot removal by thrombolysis or mechanical embolization. First described by Ames et al. in 1968 in rabbit brains. Up to 25% of ischemic strokes suffer from no-reflow, contributing to poor clinical outcomes.

2. **Clinical Significance**: Despite recanalization techniques achieving reperfusion in 70-80% of large-vessel occlusion cases, 30-68% of patients still show unfavorable outcomes ("futile recanalization"). IV rt-PA achieves recanalization in less than 20% of cases due to narrow therapeutic time windows. More than 50% of patients receiving rt-PA show no clinical improvement.

3. **Pathomechanisms** (5 main mechanisms described):
   - **Adhesion and aggregation of hematological components**: Erythrocyte aggregation, fibrin deposition, leukocyte accumulation via ICAM-1/VCAM-1/PECAM-1 upregulation, microthrombi formation, and embolic fragments blocking microcirculation.
   - **Capillary stalls with neutrophils**: Using two-photon imaging, studies showed 35% of capillaries in the ischemic core and 15% in the penumbra remained stalled after thrombolysis, predominantly due to neutrophil congestion rather than RBCs or platelets.
   - **Cellular and interstitial edema**: Cytotoxic edema (Na+ influx via cation channels, AQP4-mediated water transport, astrocyte end-foot swelling) and vasogenic edema (BBB breakdown leading to fluid accumulation and vessel compression).
   - **Pericyte contraction**: Pericytes cover ~80% of microvessels, and ischemia/reperfusion causes persistent pericyte constriction mediated by intracellular Ca2+ overload, oxidative stress, and α-SMA expression. Constriction worsens after reperfusion and doesn't reverse even after recanalization.
   - **Vasoconstriction**: Increased arterial stiffness, diminished vascular reactivity, decreased eNOS phosphorylation, and elevated extracellular potassium concentrations contribute to cerebral vasoconstriction and reduced CBF.

4. **Risk Factors and Predictors**: Old age (>70), female sex, diabetes, hypertension, higher NIHSS score (≥10), lower ASPECTS (≤5), poor collateral status, longer treatment delay, pre-stroke brain atrophy, and cerebral edema. Molecular markers include elevated IL-6, IL-1, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, matrix metalloproteinase-9, tenascin-C, thioredoxin, and decreased levels of ADAMTS13 and gelsolin.

5. **Diagnosis**: Detection rates vary widely (3%, 15%, 25%, and 42.5% in different studies) due to limited diagnostic means. Clinical manifestations lack distinct characteristics, increasing oversight risk. Diagnostic focus should be on patients with white matter hyperintensity burden, pre-stroke brain atrophy, cerebral edema, longer ischemia time, and elevated inflammatory markers.

6. **Therapeutic Strategies**: Targeted therapies include cilostazol, adhesion molecule blocking antibodies, PPARs activators, adenosine, pericyte regulators, plus adjunctive therapies such as extracorporeal counterpulsation, ischemic preconditioning, and complementary/alternative therapies. Neutrophil-depleting antibodies may restore capillary flow and improve prognosis.
args.key_excerpts: "No-reflow is a common phenomenon, which is defined as the failure of microcirculatory reperfusion despite clot removal by thrombolysis or mechanical embolization. It has been reported that up to 25% of ischemic strokes suffer from no-reflow, which strongly contributes to an increased risk of poor clinical outcomes."

## Highlights

*   •Reperfusion failure despite clot retrieval leads to unfavorable outcome in stroke 
*   •In the thrombin model of stroke, ≈30% capillaries remain occluded after thrombolysis 
*   •Capillaries are plugged by neutrophils, hindering blood flow 
*   •Neutrophil depletion facilitates capillary reperfusion and stroke recovery 

## Summary

Despite successful clot retrieval in large vessel occlusion stroke, ∼50% of patients have an unfavorable clinical outcome. The mechanisms underlying this functional reperfusion failure remain unknown, and therapeutic options are lacking. In the thrombin-model of middle cerebral artery (MCA) stroke in mice, we show that, despite successful thrombolytic recanalization of the proximal MCA, cortical blood flow does not fully recover. Using _in vivo_ two-photon imaging, we demonstrate that this is due to microvascular obstruction of ∼20%–30% of capillaries in the infarct core and penumbra by neutrophils adhering to distal capillary segments. Depletion of circulating neutrophils using an anti-Ly6G antibody restores microvascular perfusion without increasing the rate of hemorrhagic complications. Strikingly, infarct size and functional deficits are smaller in mice treated with anti-Ly6G. Thus, we propose neutrophil stalling of brain capillaries to contribute to reperfusion failure, which offers promising therapeutic avenues for ischemic stroke.

## Abstract

Prior studies have indicated that the neuroprotective effects of dexmedetomidine (DEX) in cerebral ischemia, yet its mechanisms remain elusive. Using multi-omics approaches (RNA-seq, metabolomics, and single-cell RNA-seq), we discovered that DEX pretreatment significantly reduced cerebral infarct volume and improved neurological function in middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) mice compared to PBS controls. Single-cell analysis revealed that DEX preserved microglial phagocytic function via metabolic regulation, leading to reduced microglial apoptosis and attenuated immune dysregulation—including decreased chemotactic neutrophils, B cells, and antigen-presenting fibroblasts. These cellular changes were corroborated by transcriptomic and metabolic profiles showing suppressed apoptosis and inflammation. Mechanistically, we identified HK2 (hexokinase 2) as a key regulator of microglial homeostasis, with its expression correlating with microglial migration, proliferation, and inflammation, findings validated in oxygen–glucose deprivation models. Collectively, our results demonstrate that DEX protects against cerebral ischemia–reperfusion injury by maintaining immune microenvironment homeostasis through microglial metabolic reprogramming mediated by HK2. This multi-omics study provides mechanistic insights supporting DEX’s translational potential in ischemic stroke therapy.

## Introduction

Stroke is a widespread and life-threatening condition globally [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR1 "Dal-Ré R (2011) Worldwide clinical interventional studies on leading causes of death: a descriptive analysis. Ann Epidemiol 21(10):727–731")], leading to significant rates of disability and mortality and imposing a substantial socioeconomic burden [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR2 "Bai B et al (2017) A randomised controlled multimodal intervention trial in patients with ischaemic stroke in Shandong, China: design and rationale. The Lancet 390:S13")]. Early-stage ischemic stroke is characterized by several key pathophysiological mechanisms, with disturbance of the blood‒brain barrier (BBB), microglia-mediated neuroinflammation, and oxidative stress considered prominent factors [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR3 "George PM, Steinberg GK (2015) Novel stroke therapeutics: unraveling stroke pathophysiology and its impact on clinical treatments. Neuron 87(2):297–309")].The BBB normally maintains central nervous system (CNS) homeostasis but becomes compromised during ischemia through vascular occlusion-induced hypoxia, triggering mitochondrial dysfunction and tight junction protein redistribution in brain microvascular endothelial cells [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR4 "Anderson CD et al (2013) Common variants within oxidative phosphorylation genes influence risk of ischemic stroke and intracerebral hemorrhage. Stroke 44(3):612–619"), [5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR5 "Bao Q et al (2018) Simultaneous blood-brain barrier crossing and protection for stroke treatment based on edaravone-loaded ceria nanoparticles. ACS Nano 12(7):6794–6805")]. This damage escalates during reperfusion via oxidative stress-mediated protein/lipid/DNA degradation [[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR6 "Sanderson TH et al (2013) Molecular mechanisms of ischemia–reperfusion injury in brain: pivotal role of the mitochondrial membrane potential in reactive oxygen species generation. Mol Neurobiol 47:9–23"), [7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR7 "Johri A, Beal MF (2012) Mitochondrial dysfunction in neurodegenerative diseases. J Pharmacol Exp Ther 342(3):619–630")]. Microglia, as the primary CNS responders, play dual roles in tissue repair and inflammatory exacerbation [[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR8 "Xiong X-Y, Liu L, Yang Q-W (2016) Functions and mechanisms of microglia/macrophages in neuroinflammation and neurogenesis after stroke. Prog Neurobiol 142:23–44"), [9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR9 "Zhang W et al (2021) Microglia-associated neuroinflammation is a potential therapeutic target for ischemic stroke. Neural Regen Res 16(1):6–11")]. Their overactivation promotes proinflammatory cytokine release and peripheral immune infiltration, establishing a vicious cycle of neurovascular injury.

DEX is a targeted alpha-2 agonist often utilized for its calming and anxiolytic effects during surgical procedures [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR10 "Keating GM (2015) Dexmedetomidine: a review of its use for sedation in the intensive care setting. Drugs 75(10):1119–1130")]. Its neuroprotective properties are closely linked to dual mechanisms: (1) sympathetic nervous system inhibition: By activating presynaptic α2-adrenergic receptors in the locus coeruleus, DEX suppresses norepinephrine release, thereby reducing sympathetic hyperactivity and stabilizing autonomic balance—a critical factor in mitigating post-stroke cerebral hypoperfusion and oxidative stress [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR11 "Fan S et al (2023) The α2 adrenoceptor agonist and sedative/anaesthetic dexmedetomidine excites diverse neuronal types in the ventrolateral preoptic area of male mice. ASN Neuro 15(1):17590914231191016")]; (2) anti-inflammatory regulation: DEX modulates neuroinflammation through NF-κB/NLRP3 pathway inhibition, attenuating microglial overactivation and subsequent proinflammatory cytokine release, while promoting anti-inflammatory mediators such as IL-10 [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR12 "Yang H et al (2024) Dexmedetomidine alleviates acute stress-induced acute kidney injury by attenuating inflammation and oxidative stress via inhibiting the P2X7R/NF-κB/NLRP3 pathway in rats. Inflammation 48(1):412–425")]. Emerging evidence implicates metabolic reprogramming in microglial phenotype regulation with HK2 serving as a pivotal metabolic-immune nexus—its mitochondrial binding regulates apoptosis while modulating NLRP3 inflammasome activity [[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR13 "Baik SH et al (2023) Hexokinase dissociation from mitochondria promotes oligomerization of VDAC that facilitates NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and activation. Sci Immunol 8(84):eade7652"), [14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR14 "von Herrmann KM et al (2018) NLRP3 expression in mesencephalic neurons and characterization of a rare NLRP3 polymorphism associated with decreased risk of Parkinson’s disease. NPJ Parkinson’s Dis 4(1):24")]. We hypothesize that DEX preserves microglial homeostasis through HK2-mediated metabolic adaptation, sustaining phagocytic function via oxidative phosphorylation while suppressing immune hyperactivation.

Although clinical studies associate DEX with reduced post-stroke complications [[15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR15 "Burlacu CC et al (2022) The role of miRNAs in dexmedetomidine’s neuroprotective effects against brain disorders. Int J Mol Sci 23(10):5452")], its precise mechanisms remain unclear beyond general anti-apoptotic/anti-inflammatory effects [[16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR16 "Zhou W et al (2021) Dexmedetomidine maintains blood-brain barrier integrity by inhibiting Drp1-related endothelial mitochondrial dysfunction in ischemic stroke. Acta Biochim Biophys Sin (Shanghai) 53(9):1177–1188")]. Crucially, the role of HK2 in mediating DEX’s metabolic-immune crosstalk has never been investigated, representing a critical knowledge gap.

To address this, we integrated bulk RNA-seq, scRNA-seq, and metabolomics in MCAO models to (1) determine whether DEX’s neuroprotection primarily arises from direct microglial metabolic reprogramming versus secondary immune modulation and (2) elucidate how HK2 coordinates metabolic adaptation with inflammatory resolution during DEX treatment.

## Materials and Methods

### Animal Information

Male C57BL/6 J mice (_n_ = 48, 6–8 weeks old, body weight 20–30 g) were purchased from Nanjing University Model Animal Research Center (Certificate No. SCXK 2022–0001). Animals were housed under specific pathogen-free (SPF) conditions with controlled temperature (22 ± 1°C), humidity (50 ± 10%), and a 12-h light/dark cycle, providing ad libitum access to standard chow and water. Mice were randomly assigned to three experimental groups using stratified randomization based on body weight: (1) control group (_n_ = 16), (2) MCAO group (_n_ = 16), and (3) DEX group (_n_ = 16). Sample size was determined by power analysis (_α_ = 0.05, power = 0.8) using historical effect size data from pilot studies. The use of male mice was based on the need to minimize confounding effects of hormonal fluctuations in females on neuroinflammatory responses and infarct variability, as estrogen is known to exert neuroprotective effects in cerebral ischemia models [[17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR17 "Suzuki S, Brown CM, Wise PM (2009) Neuroprotective effects of estrogens following ischemic stroke. Front Neuroendocrinol 30(2):201–211")]. While the exclusive use of male mice in this study enhances experimental consistency by eliminating confounding effects of female hormonal fluctuations on neuroinflammatory responses, we acknowledge this design limits generalizability to female stroke pathophysiology, which will be explicitly addressed in the “[Discussion](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Sec27)” section.

### MCAO Model Establishment and Drug Administration

The MCAO model was created as described earlier [[18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR18 "Luo C et al (2017) Dexmedetomidine protects mouse brain from ischemia-reperfusion injury via inhibiting neuronal autophagy through up-regulating HIF-1α. Front Cell Neurosci 11:197")]. Mice were anesthetized with isoflurane, initially given at 5% for induction and then kept at a level between 1.5% and 2.5%. An incision was made in the right external carotid artery to insert a 4–0 nylon monofilament coated with silicone rubber and advanced 9–11 mm into the internal carotid artery via the carotid bifurcation to occlude the MCA for 90 min. Cerebral blood flow in the MCA territory was monitored using transcranial laser Doppler flowmetry, with a successful occlusion defined as a 75% or greater reduction in regional cerebral blood flow. The rectal temperature was kept at 37 ± 0.5°C during the procedure with the help of a heating pad. After 90 min, the mice were reanesthetized for monofilament removal, followed by ligation of the incision. For DEX treatment, DEX was diluted or dissolved in 0.9% saline to a concentration of 10 µg/ml and then intraperitoneally injected into mice 0.5 h before surgery at a dosage of 0.1 µg/g. At the onset of ischemia, the DEX treatment group was administered DEX. Mice in the control and MCAO groups, which did not receive drug treatment, were administered an equivalent volume of 0.9% saline. The control group underwent the same procedural steps as the other groups, excluding the MCA occlusion. The study was conducted in compliance with the ARRIVE guidelines for animal research. Approval for the experimental procedures was granted by the Ethics Committee of Shanghai Tongren Hospital (No. A2023-021–01).

### Clinical Trial Number

Not applicable. This study involves animal models and in vitro experiments and does not constitute a clinical trial involving human participants.

### Infarct Size Measurements

One day following the MCAO, the infarct size was evaluated. After deep anesthesia, we swiftly extracted the brains after decapitating the mice and then divided them into coronal sections using a rodent brain matrix. Infarct volume was quantified using RadiAnt DICOM Viewer software. For each brain, three consecutive, equidistant coronal slices spanning the core of the MCA territory (typically centered around bregma and covering the region of maximal infarct extent) were selected for analysis. The MR images were loaded into the software, and the contrast/brightness was optimized to clearly depict the infarct boundaries. Then, the Freehand ROI drawing tool was used to manually outline the infarct area on each selected magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) slice. MRI was performed using a Bruker BioSpec 97/30 system with T2_TurboRARE sequence (TR = 4500 ms, TE = 33 ms; slice thickness = 0.7 mm; matrix = 256 × 256; FA = 90°; averages = 3). The software automatically measured the area of the drawn ROIs in square millimeters. The infarct area was calculated as the average infarct area across three consecutive slices showing the largest cross-sectional infarct region in the each group. This standardized approach enabled reliable quantification of the infarct size from the collected MRI data.

### Blood–Brain Barrier Permeability

Evans blue dye was administered intraperitoneally to evaluate the permeability of the BBB as a 4% solution in saline (100 µl), with slight modifications to previously established protocols [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR19 "Xie Z et al (2017) Netrin-1 preserves blood-brain barrier integrity through deleted in colorectal cancer/focal adhesion kinase/RhoA signaling pathway following subarachnoid hemorrhage in rats. J Am Heart Assoc 6(5):e005198")]. Following a 3-h circulation period, cold phosphate-buffered saline was used for transcardial perfusion of the mice. The brain was subsequently removed and divided into two hemispheres and promptly stored at − 80°C. The right hemisphere was homogenized in 1100 µl of PBS, subjected to sonication, and centrifuged at 13,000 × g for 30 min at 4°C. The collected supernatant was combined with an equal volume of trichloroacetic acid (TCA) and then incubated overnight at 4°C. Following a second centrifugation (13,000 × g, 30 min, 4°C), the concentration of Evans blue was quantified using a spectrophotometer at 610 nm.

### Single-Cell RNA Sequencing

Cerebral cortices and hippocampi from three biological replicates per group (control, MCAO, and DEX; _n_ = 1 mice per group) were meticulously collected and dissociated with the Miltenyi Adult Brain Dissociation Kit (130–107-677, Miltenyi), followed by lysis of red blood cells. After washing and resuspending, dissociated single cells were stained with Calcein-AM/PI and analyzed on a Countstar Fluorescence Cell Analyzer, yielding post-sorting cell viability > 85%. Dead cells were removed using the MACS Dead Cell Removal Kit (130–090-101, Miltenyi). Cells from the three biological replicates within each experimental group were pooled to ensure sufficient cell numbers for sequencing. A cell suspension (1000 cells/µl in PBS with 0.04% BSA) was loaded onto a 10 × Genomics Chromium Controller to generate single-cell gel beads-in-emulsions (GEMs). Reverse transcription reactions were performed in each GEM to amplify cDNA, followed by library construction according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Libraries were sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq platform with an average depth of 50,000 reads per cell. Cell quality control was performed using Seurat (v4.0) with the following thresholds: cells expressing < 200 genes were excluded as potential low-quality cells or ambient RNA-containing droplets, while those with > 5000 genes or > 15% mitochondrial reads were filtered to remove doublets and apoptotic cells. These thresholds were empirically determined based on scRNA-seq benchmarking studies demonstrating optimal signal-to-noise ratio preservation.

### Preprocessing of scRNA-Sequencing Data

The raw data were analyzed using the CellRanger workflow (version 4.0.0), with the mm10 genome serving as the reference for gene annotation. The Seurat pipeline (version 5.0.1) was employed to create a gene-barcode matrix within R software. Cells identified as low quality—defined as having fewer than 200 genes or more than 5% mitochondrial genes—were excluded prior to additional bioinformatic analysis.

### Cell Clustering Analysis, Annotation, and Visualization

PCA was used to detect batch effects. Cell clusters were established and displayed in UMAP using Seurat with proper resolutions. The FindMarkers and FindAllMarkers functions were used to identify cell markers that were unique or highly expressed in each cluster. For major clusters identified from total cells, unique and highly expressed genes or reported canonical cellular markers, as well as SingleR (1.4.1) and Msigdbr (7.4.1), were used to annotate the clusters. For reclustering of a cell type of interest, unique and highly expressed genes or reported canonical cellular markers were used to annotate these new subclusters.

### Functional Enrichment Analysis

GO and GSEA were performed using ClusterProfiler 4.0 [[20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR20 "Wu T et al (2021) clusterProfiler 4.0: a universal enrichment tool for interpreting omics data. The Innovation 2(3):100141")] based on gene sets in the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB) [[21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR21 "Liberzon A (2014) A description of the molecular signatures database (MSigDB) web site. Stem cell transcriptional networks. Springer, pp 153–160")]. _p.adjust_< 0.01 indicated statistical significance.

### Pseudotime Trajectory Analysis

Trajectory analysis of the microglial cell cluster was carried out with the Monocle 2 pipeline in R software [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR22 "Qiu X et al (2017) Single-cell mRNA quantification and differential analysis with Census. Nat Methods 14(3):309–315")]. The analysis utilized key parameters: num cells expressed ≥ 10, mean expression > 0.1, and qval < 0.001.

### Primary Cell Culture of Neurons and Microglia

Nine-day-old mice were sacrificed via the decapitation method, and the skin and scalp of each mouse were cut with scissors. The scalp was opened with tweezers, and the brain was carefully removed with the help of tweezers, lifting the brain without perforating it. The brain tissue was cut into pieces and digested with 0.25% trypsin. The cells were incubated at 37°C for 5–10 min in a culture chamber and gently mixed 2–3 times using a pipette. Cells dispersed from the tissue were then suspended in serum-containing medium and filtered through a 200-mesh filter. The cells were subsequently centrifuged at 1000 × g for 10 min and then transferred to a new flask. After 1 h, the suspension with unattached cells, including neurons and microglia, was transferred to another flask for another 4 h. The suspension containing neurons was then transferred to a new flask pretreated with polylysine for 12 h, which was then cultured in medium containing 1% B27 for further assays. Adhered microglia were cultured for 7–10 days and then collected by shaking at a speed of 200 r/min for approximately 2 h at 37°C. The microglia were subsequently washed with PBS, before being resuspended and centrifuged at 1000 × g for 3 min. A total of 2.5 × 10 5 neurons were cocultured with 5 × 10 5 microglia at 5% CO 2 and 37°C for 24 h for further treatment.

### Oxygen–Glucose Deprivation and Drug Treatment

The oxygen–glucose deprivation (OGD) model was established following a modified protocol [[18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR18 "Luo C et al (2017) Dexmedetomidine protects mouse brain from ischemia-reperfusion injury via inhibiting neuronal autophagy through up-regulating HIF-1α. Front Cell Neurosci 11:197")]. Primary neurons were co-cultured with microglia in Earle’s balanced salt solution during a standardized 24-h hypoxia phase (95% N₂, 5% CO₂, 37°C, 1% O₂) [[23](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR23 "Cheon SY et al (2016) Blockade of apoptosis signal-regulating kinase 1 attenuates matrix metalloproteinase 9 activity in brain endothelial cells and the subsequent apoptosis in neurons after ischemic injury. Front Cell Neurosci 10:213")]. Control groups were maintained in neurobasal medium under normoxic conditions (21% O₂). Following hypoxia exposure, all experimental groups underwent 4-h reoxygenation, with the DEX group receiving concurrent 1 µM dexmedetomidine (DEX) treatment [[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR24 "Dahmani S et al (2010) Characterization of the postconditioning effect of dexmedetomidine in mouse organotypic hippocampal slice cultures exposed to oxygen and glucose deprivation. J Am Soc Anesthesiol 112(2):373–383")]. This timeline was designed to evaluate DEX’s therapeutic effects during the acute I/R phase.

### Cell Apoptosis Assessment

Neurons were stained with Annexin V/PI according to the manufacturer’s guidelines. Briefly, they were stored in a light-protected setting at room temperature for 10 min while incubating with 10 µl of propidium iodide (PI) and 5 µl of FITC. Each sample, containing 1 × 10 5 cells, was analyzed using a flow cytometer.

### Western Blotting

Using a 10% SDS gel, 30 µg of protein was separated and then transferred to a PVDF membrane. The primary antibodies used included those against HK2 (1:200, ab209847, Abcam), MERTK (1:700, AF591, R&D), and β-actin (1:2000, 15,739, Invitrogen), incubated at 4°C overnight. After washing, HRP-conjugated anti-mouse or anti-rabbit IgG (1:5000, Invitrogen) was applied as a secondary antibody at room temperature for 1 h. The bands were semi-quantified using ImageJ software (NIH, Bethesda, MD).

### qPCR Analysis

To evaluate the expression levels of various genes, quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT‒PCR) was conducted. Using TRIzol reagent, extract Total RNA from cells and assess its purity with a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer. The RNA was then reverse transcribed into cDNA using the PrimeScript™ RT Reagent Kit. qRT–PCR was carried out using a SYBR Green PCR Mix Kit. Data were quantified using the ∆∆CT method, with β-actin as the reference control. The primers utilized in this research are listed below.

*   TNF-α: F-5′-CCCGAGTGACAAGCCTGTAG-3′

*   TNF-α: R-5′-GATGGCAGAGAGGAGGTTGAC-3′

*   IL1-β: F-5′-AGATGATAAGCCCACTCTAC-3′

*   IL-1β: R-5′- ACATTCAGCACAGGACTCTC-3′

*   IL-6: F-5′-ACAGCCACTCACCTCTTCAG-3′

*   IL-6: R-5′- CCATCTTTTTCAGCCATCTTT-3′

*   β-actin: F-5′-GTCGTACCACAGGCATTGTGTAGG-3′

*   β-actin: R-5′-GCAATGCCTGGGTACATGGTGG-3′

### RNA-Seq and Analysis

From the brains of mice in different groups, total RNA was isolated, and its integrity was analyzed using an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer. Samples with an RNA integrity number (RIN) of 7 or higher were chosen for further analysis. Libraries were constructed following the manufacturer’s guidelines using an mRNA LTSample Prep Kit. Sequencing of the libraries was performed on the Illumina platform, resulting in paired-end reads of either 125 bp or 150 bp. Transcriptome sequencing and differential expression gene (DEG) analysis were performed by OE Biotech, with a _p_ value < 0.05 and a |log2foldchange|> 1 established as the criteria for significant DEGs.

### Statistical Analysis

All data are presented as mean ± SEM. Between-group comparisons were analyzed by unpaired two-tailed Student’s _t_ tests for all possible pairwise combinations (Control vs MCAO, MCAO vs DEX, and Control vs DEX) using GraphPad Prism 9.0. Two-tailed _p_-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Outliers were identified using the ROUT method (Q = 1%) and excluded from analysis. To ensure objectivity, investigators performing infarct volume measurements (MRI analysis) and neurological assessments were blinded to group allocation throughout data collection and analysis.

## Results

### DEX Treatment Alleviated I/R Injury in the Mouse Brain

In our experimental plan, as illustrated in Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig1)A, we used a MCAO model to simulate brain I/R injury. To investigate the potential role of DEX in brain I/R injury, we administered DEX to mice 1 h prior to MCAO surgery, while the PBS-pretreated MCAO group served as the control group. Successful induction of the MCAO model was confirmed, as depicted in Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig1)B and C. Subsequently, we assessed the infarct size in the brain using MRI at 1 day post-MCAO. Notably, compared to the control group, pretreatment with DEX significantly reduced the infarct area (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig1)D). Statistical analysis using unpaired Student’s _t_-test indicated that the infarct area decreased by approximately 50% following DEX treatment (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig1)E). These findings demonstrate that, from a pathological standpoint, DEX plays a neuroprotective role in brain I/R injury. The experimental results support the notion that DEX treatment has potential therapeutic benefits in brain I/R injury.

### Transcriptional and Metabolic Changes Induced by DEX in Brain I/R Injury

To further explore the protective effects of DEX on brain I/R injury, we conducted RNA-seq and metabolomics analyses to assess transcriptional and metabolic changes. The RNA-seq results indicated that MCAO treatment, with or without pretreatment with DEX, led to the upregulation of genes associated with the immune response compared to the control group (Figure [S1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#MOESM1)). However, PCA of the DEGs revealed that pretreatment with DEX inhibited the transcriptional changes induced by MCAO surgery (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig2)A and B).

Furthermore, a comparison between the DEX and MCAO groups revealed notable differences in the upregulated DEGs. The DEGs upregulated in the DEX group were enriched in pathways related to neuron repair, such as synapse organization and axonogenesis. In contrast, the DEGs that were upregulated in the MCAO group were enriched in pathways related to the inflammatory response, including positive regulation of cell adhesion, cytokine production, and response to external stimuli (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig2)C–E).

The metabolomics analysis supported the findings from the RNA-seq assays, demonstrating significant disturbances in carbon and glycolysis metabolism in both the MCAO surgery group and the DEX pretreatment group (Figure [S2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#MOESM2)). However, when comparing the DEX group with the MCAO group, metabolomics analysis revealed enrichment of sphingolipid metabolism, apoptosis, and necroptosis pathways in the MCAO group. This further supports the notion that pretreatment with DEX acts as a protective factor against brain I/R injury (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig2)F and G).

Overall, the combined results from RNA-seq and metabolomics analyses provide insights into the transcriptional and metabolic changes associated with brain I/R injury and highlight the neuroprotective effects of DEX pretreatment in mitigating the inflammatory response and promoting neuron repair processes.

### Single-Cell RNA-Seq Cellular Distribution

To further investigate the changes in the immunological microenvironment, single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on mouse brain samples from the control, MCAO, and DEX groups 24 h after reperfusion. After quality control, a total of 20,239 cells from all four samples were retained for subsequent analysis. The control group contained 5465 cells, the DEX group contained 5070 cells, and the MCAO group contained 9704 cells. It is important to consider the total cell number when analyzing the distribution of certain cell clusters among different treatments.

Minimal batch effects in the scRNA-seq data were indicated by PCA, allowing direct merging of the total dataset without batch normalization (Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig3)A). The data were then clustered and annotated using marker genes, references from published manuscripts, and GSEA from the MSigDB C8 dataset (Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig3)B–D). Ten major cell clusters were identified in total, including microglia, neurons, transit amplifying cells, fibroblasts, NKT cells, neutrophil cells, immature neurons, endothelial cells, B cells, and neural stem cells. Among these clusters, microglia showed significant changes in distribution and quantity in the MCAO group. Neurons, transit amplifying cells, neutrophil cells, and B cells also exhibited distinct alterations. However, pretreatment with DEX partially attenuated these changes, indicating the significant role of DEX in the microenvironmental changes following I/R injury (Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig3)E and F).

Overall, scRNA-seq analysis, coupled with cell interaction analysis, provides insights into the changes in the immunological microenvironment in response to I/R injury and highlights the role of DEX in preserving microenvironmental stability.

### Effects of DEX on the Blood‒Brain Barrier

The BBB is known to be one of the first structures affected by impaired mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation during ischemic stroke due to the OGD. Therefore, we focused on examining endothelial and fibroblast clusters to investigate BBB-related changes. Upon reclustering the endothelial cells, seven subclusters were identified, with four clusters (cluster 0 to cluster 3) containing more than 93% of the cells. Compared to the control group, the DEX-treated MCAO group showed significantly reduced total cell numbers, particularly in endothelial cell populations (Figure [S3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#MOESM3)A-C). Additionally, compared to the control group, the DEX group exhibited an increased proportion of cells in cluster 2 (38.9% vs. 16.9%) and cluster 3 (14.7% vs. 0.1%), while the MCAO group exhibited an increased proportion in cluster 3 (28% vs. 0.1%) and a decreased proportion in cluster 2 (15.6% vs. 16.9%). Gene Ontology (GO) biological process (BP) analysis revealed that cluster 2 was enriched in pathways related to endothelial development, while cluster 3 was enriched in pathways related to oxidative phosphorylation (Figure [S4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#MOESM4)D). Gene expression analysis indicated that cluster 3 exhibited upregulated expression of genes such as Ndufa1, Sdhb, Uqcr11, Cox5b, Cox7b, and Mdh1, which are involved in the oxidative phosphorylation pathway (Figure [S4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#MOESM4)E). This suggests severe disturbances in mitochondrial function and oxidative phosphorylation [[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR25 "Au HC et al (1999) The NDUFA1 gene product (MWFE protein) is essential for activity of complex I in mammalian mitochondria. Proc Natl Acad Sci 96(8):4354–4359"),[26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR26 "Andrews KA et al (2018) Tumour risks and genotype-phenotype correlations associated with germline variants in succinate dehydrogenase subunit genes SDHB. SDHC SDHD J Med Genet 55(6):384–394"),[27](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR27 "Achreja A et al (2022) Metabolic collateral lethal target identification reveals MTHFD2 paralogue dependency in ovarian cancer. Nat Metab 4(9):1119–1137"),[28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR28 "Gao SP et al (2015) Loss of COX5B inhibits proliferation and promotes senescence via mitochondrial dysfunction in breast cancer. Oncotarget 6(41):43363–43374"),[29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR29 "Wang YP et al (2016) Arginine methylation of MDH1 by CARM1 inhibits glutamine metabolism and suppresses pancreatic cancer. Mol Cell 64(4):673–687")].

Similarly, for the fibroblasts, eight subclusters were identified, with the majority of cells enriched in subclusters 0–3 (Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig4)A–C). Both the MCAO and DEX groups showed a decreased proportion of cells in subcluster 0, which was functionally related to the BBB, as indicated by GO BP enrichment analysis (Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig4)C and D). Compared to the control group, the DEX group showed a slight increase in subcluster 1 (24% vs. 8%), while the MCAO group showed a significant accumulation of cells in subcluster 1 (35% vs. 8%) and subcluster 3 (13% vs. 6%) (Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig4)C). Functional analysis revealed that subcluster 1 was involved in antigen presentation, while subcluster 3 consisted of cells responding to oxidative stressors and participating in immune regulation (Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig4)D, G, and H). Trajectory analysis using Monocle 2 software revealed two distinct cell development pathways, with one pathway leading from subcluster 0 to subcluster 2 and the other pathway progressing from subcluster 0 to subcluster 1 and finally to subcluster 3 (Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig4)E and F). Analysis of DEGs along the pseudotime trajectory confirmed that fibroblasts upregulated genes involved in antigen presentation, immune response, and responses to oxidative stressors after MCAO treatment (Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig4)I and J). These findings suggest that DEX pretreatment protects the brain after I/R injury by alleviating oxidative stress and immune responses in endothelial and fibroblasts, thereby mitigating BBB damage.

**Fig.4**

[Full size image](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1/figures/4)

Effects of DEX on fibroblasts. **A** Major fibroblast clusters across all samples are displayed in a UMAP plot. **B** The each cluster markers are presented in a dot plot. **C** The distribution of each cluster within the samples is illustrated in a balloon plot. **D** Gene Ontology biological process enrichment across the clusters is shown in a dot plot. **E, F** The results of trajectory analysis are shown in a tree plot and are colored according to pseudotime and Seurat_clusters, respectively. **G, H** GSEA of the RECTOMEs of clusters 1 and 3, respectively. **I** Fifty genes differentially expressed along pseudotime. **J** Distinct genes are differentially expressed along pseudotime and colored according to Seurat_clusters

In summary, the examination of endothelial and fibroblast clusters revealed the protective effects of DEX on the BBB following I/R injury. DEX treatment alleviated oxidative stress and immune responses in endothelial and fibroblasts, thereby preserving BBB integrity.

### The Effects of DEX on Immune Cells in the Brain after I/R Injury

Microglia are known to be the first responders to BBB injury caused by ischemic stroke. They are crucial for maintaining tissue homeostasis by clearing cellular debris and recruiting and activating surrounding immune cells. Upon reclustering of the microglial cluster, seven subclusters were identified, and their distribution showed distinct patterns among the different groups (Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig3)E, Fig.[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig5)A–C). Distribution analysis revealed that the control group predominantly accumulated in subclusters 0 and 5, while the MCAO group exhibited a dramatic decrease in subclusters 0 and 5 and an increase in subclusters 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6. However, in the DEX group, these changes in the distribution induced by MCAO were inhibited, as indicated by decreases in subclusters 0 and increases in subclusters 1 and 3 (Fig.[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig5)D).

The effects of DEX on microglia. **A** Major clusters of microglial cells are displayed in a UMAP plot. **B** The distribution of microglial cells under various treatments is presented in another UMAP plot. **C** Cell markers for each cluster are shown in a heatmap. **D** The heatmap illustrates the distribution of microglial cell clusters, categorized from 0 to 7, across various experimental groups. **E** Gene Ontology biological process (GO BP) enrichment for each cluster is represented in a dot plot. **F, G** Distinct genes differentially expressed in each Seurat cluster according to the feature map and violin plot

GO functional analysis provided insights into the functions of each subcluster. Subcluster 0 represented M0-type microglia, subcluster 2 consisted of transcriptional regulatory cells, and subcluster 5 included antigen-presenting microglia under epigenetic regulation, which might have been induced by brain death during sample extraction surgery in the control group. Subcluster 1 represented activated microglia responsible for cellular debris clearance through phagocytosis. Subclusters 3 and 4 exhibited oxidative stress, with subcluster 4 experiencing greater oxidative disturbance and loss of phagocytic function. Subcluster 6 was an expanding cell cluster (Fig.[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#Fig5)C–E). Consistent with the GO analysis, subclusters 4 and 7 showed high expression of the proliferation marker Mki67, while subcluster 6 expressed the noncoding RNA Malat1 [[30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12035-025-05237-1#ref-CR30 "Zhang X et al (2017) Long noncoding RNA Malat1 regulates cerebrovascular pathologies in ischemic stroke. J Neurosci 37(7):1797–1806")]. This is an open-access research article published in Molecular Neurobiology (Volume 62, pages 16150–16167, published 01 August 2025) titled "Single-Cell RNA-Seq Revealed the Immune Microenvironment Reprogramming by Dexmedetomidine Treatment in Ischemic Stroke" by Wenyi Zhang, Xingyun Wang, Bing Zhang, Minjiang Yi, Yinzhong Lu, Shuyan Wang, Junfeng Zhang, and Guangming Zhang.

The study investigates the neuroprotective mechanisms of dexmedetomidine (DEX) in ischemic stroke using a middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) mouse model. Key findings:

**Study Design:** Male C57BL/6J mice (n=48, 6-8 weeks old) were divided into control, MCAO, and DEX groups. DEX (0.1 µg/g) was administered intraperitoneally 0.5h before surgery. Multi-omics approaches (bulk RNA-seq, metabolomics, and single-cell RNA-seq) were integrated.

**Key Results:**
- DEX pretreatment significantly reduced cerebral infarct volume by approximately 50% and improved neurological function in MCAO mice compared to PBS controls.
- Single-cell analysis (20,239 cells total) identified 10 major cell clusters including microglia, neurons, transit amplifying cells, fibroblasts, NKT cells, neutrophils, immature neurons, endothelial cells, B cells, and neural stem cells.
- DEX preserved microglial phagocytic function via metabolic regulation, reducing microglial apoptosis and attenuating immune dysregulation, including decreased chemotactic neutrophils, B cells, and antigen-presenting fibroblasts.
- RNA-seq and metabolomics confirmed suppressed apoptosis and inflammation with DEX treatment, while DEX-treated DEGs were enriched in neuron repair pathways (synapse organization, axonogenesis), whereas MCAO upregulated genes were enriched in inflammatory pathways.
- DEX protected the blood-brain barrier by alleviating oxidative stress and immune responses in endothelial cells and fibroblasts.
- HK2 (hexokinase 2) was identified as a key regulator of microglial homeostasis, with its expression correlating with microglial migration, proliferation, and inflammation. Findings were validated in oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD) models.

**Mechanistic Conclusion:** DEX protects against cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury by maintaining immune microenvironment homeostasis through microglial metabolic reprogramming mediated by HK2. This multi-omics study provides mechanistic insights supporting DEX's translational potential in ischemic stroke therapy.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991)Abstract

### Background

Ischemic stroke remains a leading cause of mortality and disability worldwide. Microglia, the resident immune cells of the central nervous system, perform critical roles in immune surveillance, debris clearance, and tissue repair. Analyzing the heterogeneity, activation trajectories, and metabolic states of microglia in ischemic stroke is essential for discovering therapeutic targets.

### Methods

We performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) on brains from ischemic and control rats and identified transcriptionally distinct microglial subpopulations. We conducted differential expression, pathway enrichment, pseudotime analysis, regulatory network inference, and cell-cell communication mapping to characterize functional states, key transcription factors, and intercellular crosstalk underlying microglial responses following cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury. We used Real-Time Quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), Western blot, and immunohistochemistry to measure relative RNA and protein expression levels.

### Results

We identified seven microglial subclusters with distinct transcriptional signatures. Ischemia-associated clusters exhibited strong activation of inflammatory pathways, increased glycolysis and lipid metabolism, and suppressed TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), reflecting a shift toward proinflammatory, energy-demanding phenotypes. Pseudotime analysis revealed transitions from homeostatic to pathological states, highlighting potential therapeutic windows. Regulatory network analysis identified activating transcription factor 3 (ATF3) as a central regulator controlling the expression of cholesterol 25-hydroxylase (CH25H) and secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1). Notably, ATF3 overexpression enhanced CH25H expression and selectively increased proinflammatory cytokine production, linking metabolic reprogramming to neuroinflammatory responses. Cell-cell communication analysis further revealed extensive remodeling of interactions with astrocytes, endothelial cells, and fibroblasts, potentially amplifying postischemic neuroinflammation.

### Conclusion

Our study demonstrates that cerebral ischemia induces transcriptionally and functionally distinct microglial subpopulations, characterized by metabolic reprogramming and proinflammatory activation. ATF3 serves as a central regulator linking CH25H-mediated metabolic changes to cytokine-driven neuroinflammation, highlighting potential therapeutic targets for modulating microglial responses and mitigating ischemia-induced brain injury.

**Keywords:**scRNA-seq, microglia, cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury, heterogeneity, functional states

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991)Introduction

Microglia are the resident immune cells of the brain and play a central role in maintaining cerebral homeostasis. As the first line of immune defense in the central nervous system (CNS), they rapidly sense and respond to changes in the brain microenvironment.[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#cit0001),[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#cit0002) Microglia not only maintain neural homeostasis and clear metabolic byproducts but also regulate neuroimmune processes as pivotal mediators of neuroinflammation.[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#cit0003),[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#cit0004) Growing evidence implicates microglia in the neuroinflammatory responses underlying a broad spectrum of neurological disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Parkinson’s disease (PD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, brain tumors, and stroke. In response to inflammatory stimuli, microglia undergo rapid phenotypic and functional transformations via complex signal transduction pathways, migrate to sites of injury, and orchestrate the initiation and progression of neuroinflammation through diverse immune mechanisms.[5–8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#cit0005)

Ischemic stroke is a major cause of permanent neurological impairment and death worldwide, yet effective therapeutic options remain limited.[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#cit0009) Previous studies have shown that following cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury, microglia are rapidly activated, initiating an early immune response. On the basis of different immune signals, microglia traditionally have been described as polarizing toward either a proinflammatory (M1) or an anti-inflammatory (M2) phenotype. The transition from M1 microglia to M2 microglia has been identified as an effective therapeutic strategy for ischemic stroke.[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#cit0010) However, recent advances in the origins and functions of microglia have challenged the traditional concepts of classical classification.[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#cit0011) In particular, it remains unclear how best to classify microglial subpopulations according to their heterogeneity and the distinct contributions of these subclusters following cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury. Activated microglia release proinflammatory cytokines that can directly exacerbate neuronal death and disrupt the blood-brain barrier. They also secrete complement components, recognize stressed neurons for removal, and phagocytose damaged cells.[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#cit0012),[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#cit0013) Importantly, microglia exhibit immune-metabolic flexibility. Recent studies have demonstrated that they express key genes involved in diverse metabolic pathways and, under different inflammatory conditions, display distinct metabolic signatures. Modulating the metabolic state of microglia not only reshapes their immune functions but also influences the course and outcome of neuroinflammatory diseases. These observations provide important insights into the mechanisms governing microglial behavior and point to potential therapeutic opportunities.[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#cit0014),[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#cit0015)

The advent of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has greatly expanded our understanding of microglial heterogeneity, uncovering disease-specific subpopulations,[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#cit0016),[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#cit0017) such as disease-associated microglia (DAM) in AD and microglia engaged in the clearance of oxidized phosphatidylcholine in multiple sclerosis.[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#cit0018),[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#cit0019) In this study, we used scRNA-seq to characterize both established and previously unrecognized markers of major brain cell types, thereby providing a more comprehensive view of the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury. Through distinct gene expression patterns, we identified ischemic stroke-associated microglia (ISAM) and further revealed their transcriptional dynamics and heterogeneity during post-stroke neuroinflammation. These stroke-associated microglial subpopulations, characterized by their signature genes, immune functions, metabolic states, and regulatory microenvironments, provide new insights into the pathogenesis of ischemic stroke. Accordingly, targeting these microglial populations may represent a highly promising therapeutic strategy for ischemic stroke.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991)Materials and Methods

### Animal

Healthy male Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats weighing 230–260 g were purchased from Liaoning Changsheng Biotechnology Company Limited. Rats were housed in a standard laboratory environment at 21–25 °C with a 12 h light/dark cycle and free access to food and water. All experiments adhered to the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Harbin Medical University.

### Rat Model of Cerebral Ischemia-Reperfusion

The rats were anesthetized via intraperitoneal injection of 3% pentobarbital sodium (40 mg/kg). They were placed on a temperature-controlled heating pad to maintain body temperature at 37 °C. The middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion (MCAO/R) model was established using the modified thread embolism method. The left common carotid artery, external carotid artery, and internal carotid artery were carefully separated by blunt dissection. The thread (Jialing Biotechnology, Cat. No. L3400, Guangzhou, China) was gradually inserted into the distal end of the external carotid artery after excision, and then was slowly advanced in the intracranial direction until resistance was felt, indicating occlusion of the middle cerebral artery. After 2 hours of ischemia, the filament was withdrawn to allow reperfusion for 1 day. The sham group underwent the same anesthesia and surgical procedures but without thread insertion. After full recovery from anesthesia, the success of the cerebral ischemia model was assessed using the modified Zea-Longa neurological deficit score.[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#cit0020)

The modified Zea-Longa neurological deficit score: 0, no neurological impairment; 1, inability to fully contract the contralateral forelimb upon tail elevation; 2, spontaneous circling behavior; 3, severe postural leaning; 4, absence of spontaneous locomotion and loss of consciousness. Rats scoring 2–3 were considered successfully modeled and were selected for further experiments.

### Single-Cell RNA Sequencing (scRNA-Seq)

The rats were allocated to sham and MCAO/R groups (n = 5 per group). Following perfusion with ice-cold phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), the brain hemispheres were rapidly isolated. The brain tissues were washed three times with Hank’s balanced salt solution (HBSS) and preserved in GEXSCOPE tissue preservation solution (Singleron Biotechnologies, Nanjing, China) until further processing. The brain tissues were diced into 1–2 mm 3 pieces, digested in GEXSCOPE tissue dissociation solution (Singleron Biotechnologies, Nanjing, China) at 37 °C for 15 minutes, and filtered through a 40 μm cell strainer (Bel-Art, Flowmi H13680-0040, New Jersey, USA). The cells were subsequently centrifuged, washed with PBS, resuspended in GEXSCOPE red blood cell lysis buffer (Singleron Biotechnologies, Nanjing, China), and incubated at room temperature for 10 minutes. The suspension was then centrifuged and washed with PBS again. The brain tissues from each group were pooled into single-cell suspensions for subsequent experiments.

Single-cell suspensions were loaded into a microfluidic device to capture individual cells and extract RNA, which was then reverse-transcribed into cDNA. The raw data were processed using CeleScope v1.5.2 (Singleron Biotechnologies, Nanjing, China) to generate gene expression profiles. Libraries were quantified using a Qubit 2.0 fluorometer and analyzed for insert size using an Agilent 2100/4200 Bioanalyzer. After ensuring the expected insert size, library concentrations were assessed via RT-qPCR for quality control. Sequencing was performed on an Illumina HiSeq X platform, and the data were stored in the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus database ([GSE199558](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/GSE199558)).

### Quality Control, Clustering, and Dimensionality Reduction

Quality control, dimensionality reduction, and clustering analyses were conducted using Scanpy v1.8.1 in a Python 3.7 environment. The data filtering criteria included the following: 1) removal of cells with fewer than 200 genes or within the top 2% for gene counts; 2) exclusion of cells in the top 2% for UMI counts; 3) elimination of cells with a mitochondrial content exceeding 20%; and 4) removal of genes expressed in fewer than 5 cells. The data were normalized on the basis of total counts per cell and log-transformed. The top 2000 highly variable genes were selected with the flavor = “seurat” parameter and analyzed via principal component analysis. The first 20 principal components were used for clustering with the Louvain algorithm and visualized with Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP).

### Differentially Expressed Gene Analysis

Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using Scanpy’s sc.tl.rank_genes_groups() function with the default Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Genes expressed in at least 10% of the cells in either group with |log2 fold change (FC)| > 1 were considered DEGs. The Benjamini-Hochberg correction was applied, and a corrected P < 0.05 was deemed statistically significant.

### Functional Enrichment Analysis

Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis of the DEGs were performed using the R package clusterProfiler v3.16.1. The GO pathway analysis included the biological process (BP), cellular component (CC), and molecular function (MF) categories. Pathways with adjusted P < 0.05 were considered significantly enriched and visualized via bar plots. For shared microglial subclusters between the two groups, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was used for pathway enrichment analysis.

### Pseudotime Trajectory Analysis

The cell differentiation trajectories of the microglial subtypes were reconstructed using Monocle2 v2.10.0. The top 2000 highly variable genes identified via FindVariableFeatures() in Seurat v3.1.2 were used for dimensionality reduction with DDRTree and trajectory construction. The plot_cell_trajectory() function in Monocle2 was used for visualization.

### Transcription Factor Regulatory Network Analysis

The transcription factor regulatory network was constructed using pySCENIC v0.11.0, which is based on single-cell RNA expression matrices and transcription factors from AnimalTFDB. GRNBoost2 was used to predict co-expression networks, CisTarget was applied to eliminate indirect targets and identify binding motifs, and AUCell was used to quantify transcription factor activity in each cell. Regulon activity scores (RASs) were calculated to quantify the activity of transcriptional regulators within individual cells and across clusters, which were visualized as heatmaps. Regulator specificity scores (RSSs) were computed to evaluate the specificity of each regulon across clusters, enabling the identification of cluster-specific transcriptional regulators.

### Cell-Cell Communication Analysis

CellPhoneDB v2.1.0 was used to predict ligand-receptor interactions between microglia and other cell types, with 1000 permutations for significance testing. Interaction significance was defined as P < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 1. The results were visualized using heatmap and dot plot representations.

### Immunofluorescence

Following euthanasia, the rats were perfused with cold PBS and then 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) to fix the brain tissues. The tissues were fixed in 4% PFA for 24 hours and dehydrated sequentially in 10%, 20%, and 30% sucrose gradients at 4 °C. Paraffin-embedded tissue sections (5 μm) were deparaffinized, subjected to antigen retrieval, and blocked with 3% hydrogen peroxide and 3% bovine serum albumin (BSA). The sections were stained with IBA1 (Cell Signaling Technology, Cat. No. 17198, Boston, MA, USA), ATF3 (Abcam, Cat. No. ab254268, Cambridge, MA, USA), CH25H (Abcam, Cat. No. ab214295, Cambridge, MA, USA), SPP1 (Proteintech, Cat. No. 22952-1-AP, Wuhan, China), and EGR1 (Proteintech, Cat. No. 22008-1-AP, Wuhan, China) antibodies. Multicolor staining was performed using TSA technology. DAPI was used for nuclear staining, and images were captured using a 3DHISTECH scanner.

### HAPI Cell Culture and Experimental Treatments

HAPI Cells (Yaji Biotechnology, Shanghai, China) were cultured in high-glucose DMEM containing 10% FBS and 1% antibiotics under standard conditions (37 °C, 5% CO 2, 95% relative humidity). For the oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R) model, the cells were washed with PBS, cultured in glucose-free medium (Gibco, Cat. No. 11966025, New York, USA), and incubated in a hypoxic environment (1% O 2, 95% N 2, 5% CO 2) at 37 °C for 8 hours. After replacing with the normal culture medium, continue the cultivation for 12 hours before sample collection. ATF3 overexpression plasmids, using PCDNA3.1 as the vector (Genechem), and siRNA were transfected into HAPI cells using Lipofectamine 2000 transfection reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat. No. 11668500, Waltham, MA, USA). After 48 h, the cells were harvested for RT-qPCR and Western blot analysis.

### Real Time Quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR)

Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol™ reagent (Invitrogen, Cat. No. 15596026, Carlsbad, California, USA) and quantified using a spectrophotometer. cDNA synthesis was performed using a reverse transcription kit (Takara, Cat. No. FSQ-101, Kyoto, Japan). Each RT-qPCR reaction (10 μL) contained cDNA, gene-specific primers, RNase-free water, and SYBR Green Master Mix (Roche, Cat. No. 4913914001, Basel, Switzerland). The reaction conditions included preincubation (95 °C for 30s), amplification cycles (95 °C for 5s, 60 °C for 30s) for 40 cycles, and a melting curve stage (95 °C for 15s, 60 °C for 60s). Actin was used as the reference gene.

### Western Blot

Proteins were extracted using RIPA lysis buffer (Beyotime, Cat. No. P0013B, Shanghai, China) containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors, and protein concentrations were measured using a BCA kit (Beyotime, Cat. No. P0010, Shanghai, China). Protein samples (20 μg) were separated via SDS-PAGE, transferred onto NC membranes, and blocked with 5% skim milk. The membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against β-actin (Abways, Cat. No. AB0035, Shanghai, China), SDHB (Proteintech, Cat. After secondary antibody incubation, protein bands were scanned with an Odyssey CLx Imaging System (LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, Nebraska, USA) and subsequently analyzed and processed using Image Studio software.

### Statistical Analysis

Data analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism 9.0. ANOVA (_F_-test) was used for multiple-group comparisons, whereas two-group comparisons were performed via two-tailed t tests. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. The data are presented as the means ± SDs (ns=no significant, *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991)Results

### Cell Type Identification

To comprehensively investigate the changes in major cell types in the ischemic hemisphere, we utilized scRNA-seq to analyze brain tissue from both the sham group and the MCAO/R group ([Figure 1A](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#f0001)). In total, 12,609 cells were profiled, including 5316 cells from the sham group and 8688 cells from the MCAO/R group ([Figure 1B](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#f0001)). Based on differential gene expression profiles, we conducted unsupervised clustering and cell-type annotation, assigning each cell to a distinct cluster. UMAP visualization revealed 14 major cell clusters ([Figure 1C](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#f0001)), encompassing astrocytes, capillary endothelial cells (CPECs), ependymal cells, oligodendrocytes, neuroblasts, endothelial cells (ECs), fibroblasts, pericytes, B lymphocytes (B Cells), T lymphocytes (T cells), neutrophils, macrophages (MPs), microglia, and plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs). The relative proportions of these cell clusters differed between the two groups ([Figure 1D](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12684991#f0001)).
