Contrasts included time after stroke, interaction of diagnosis x TP, and major risk factor categories (diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, and hypertension) with cutoffs for significance set to p < 0.02 and fold-change > |1.2| to create lists of genes. Fisher’s least significant difference (LSD) was used for individual contrasts [30].
Gene clustering Gene Expression Dynamics Inspector (GEDI) v2.1 [31] was used to create mosaic grids (tiles) of self-organizing maps for visualization of differentially expressed genes over time (https://​ github.​ com/​ midas-​ wyss/​ gedi). Two phases of training iteration were used (40 and 100) with linear initialization. Grid sizes were chosen depending on the total number of differentially expressed genes to analyze per sample type to keep a similar number of genes per tile in all mosaics (5×7, 7×8, and 4×6, for monocytes, neutrophils, and whole blood samples respectively). Tiles corresponding to gene clusters of like-behaving genes were formed based on Pearson’s correla-tion. Tiles are composed of the same genes across time points, and mosaics for monocytes, neutrophils, and whole blood have different tile composition.
Self-organizing maps (SOM) [32] were implemented in Partek Genomics Suite (alpha value set to 0.1, with ran-dom initialization, exponential decay function, Gaussian neighborhood, and rectangular topology). This was done to examine trajectories of gene expression over time. The input for SOM consisted of differentially expressed genes that are present in at least two of the studied time points. In total, 500,000 training iterations were performed. Map height and width were set to 4×4 (16 profiles) in monocytes, neutrophils, and whole blood in the analy-ses irrespective of IS cause. For SOM in DEGs analyzed per IS etiology, map height and width were set as follows: 2×2 (CE), 2×3 (LV), and 2×2 (SV) in monocytes; 2×2 (CE), 3×3 (LV), and 2×3 (SV) in neutrophils; 2×3 (CE), 2×2 (LV), and 2×2 (SV) in whole blood. Differentially expressed gene expression was standardized by shifting to a mean of 0 (standard deviation (SD) of 1). Profiles were summarized and represented with ± 1SD. Profiles with similar dynamics were merged (based on similar directionality in every time point) for gene ontology anal-yses and visualization.
Cell‑specific markers The presence or enrichment (p-value < 0.05 for significant enrichment) of gene lists with blood cell type-specific genes was assessed by comparing to previously described blood cell type-specific genes [33, 34]. Enrichment analy-ses were performed using hypergeometric probability testing (R function phyper).
Pathway and gene ontology analyses Pathway enrichment analyses were performed using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA, Ingenuity Systems®, QIAgen). For input, differentially expressed genes and their fold-changes from every time point and sample type, with a p < 0.05 and fold-change > |1.2|, were used. Pathways and predicted upstream regulators (Ingenuity Upstream Regulator analysis in IPA, white paper, Inge-nuity Systems®, QIAgen) with Fisher’s exact test p < 0.05 were considered statistically over-represented, and those that also have a Benjamini–Hochberg False Discov-ery Rate (FDR) correction for multiple comparisons are indicated in the figures. IPA also computes significant pathway activation or suppression (z ≥ 2.0 and z ≤ −2.0, respectively), by using the z-score—which is based on comparisons between input data and pathway patterns, causal relationships, and curated literature. Gene ontol-ogy (GO) enrichment was explored as implemented in Partek Genomics Suite in the Gene Set Analysis, using Fisher’s exact test and FDR correction for multiple com-parisons, with significance set at p<0.05.
Weighted gene co‑expression network construction and analysis Separate weighted gene co-expression networks were generated for isolated monocyte (MON network) and neutrophil (NEU network) data, as well as for whole blood (WB network). VRFC samples were excluded, and genes below a minimum of 40 counts in every sample were filtered out for MON and NEU, and below a total of 80 counts for WB. The MON network was generated using the 14,955 detected genes after filtering across 35 IS samples; the NEU network was generated using 13,921 genes across 31 IS samples; the WB network was gener-ated using 15,360 genes across 37 IS samples. Data were imported into R and checked for missing or zero-vari-ance counts using the function goodSamplesGenes.
Networks were generated with the Weighted Gene Co-Expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) package using a Pearson correlation to measure co-expression [24]. An approximate scale-free topology was depicted by the data. Soft thresholding powers (β) of 14, 8, and 16 were selected for the MON, NEU, and WB networks, respec-tively, to maximize strong correlations between genes while minimizing weak correlations [35]. A signed net-work was used to consider both positive and negative correlations [36]. The cutreeDynamic function (method = tree; deepsplit = 1; minimum module size = 50) was used to form modules due to its adaptability to complex dendrograms and ability to identify nested modules [36]. Hub genes were defined as the top 5% by interconnectiv-ity and may represent genes with important regulatory or molecular signaling roles [37, 38].

Ranked statistical tests were uti-lized to minimize the impact of outliers. Parameters were associated with the module eigengene, or first principal component of expression of genes within a module. Con-tinuous time since event and all clinical parameters (age, diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, hypertension, race, and sex) were examined on the complete datasets. A p-value < 0.05 was considered significant.
Hub gene analyses Functional modules were detected with HumanBase [39] in a tissue-specific manner, using all hub genes per sam-ple type as input (monocytes and whole blood). Briefly, this tool is based on shared k-nearest-neighbors and the Louvain community-finding algorithm. Gene ontology terms in the results are considered significant based on a corrected P-value < 0.05 (one-sided Fisher’s exact tests with a Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction for multiple comparison).
Results Cohort demographics Individuals were binned into time points (TPs) from stroke onset (TP1= 0–24 h, average ~15 h; TP2= 24–48 h, average ~32 h; and TP3= >48 h, average ~56 h), and vascular risk factor controls (VRFC) were assigned TP0 (Table 1). The cohort demographics and clinical charac-teristics per time point are presented in Table 1, as well as the total number of subjects per subgroup. The statis-tical analysis of variables showed that age, diabetes, and hypertension were not significantly different (p < 0.05) between TPs and controls in any of the sample types (monocytes, neutrophils, or whole blood). NIHSS at admission was significantly higher in subjects for samples at TP3 when comparing to VRFC in monocytes. Hyper-lipidemia was significantly different for TP1 in all sample types when comparing to VRFC, while sex is significantly different in whole blood at TP3. In this cohort, 5 out of 38 IS patients received thrombolytic therapy (recombi-nant tissue plasminogen activator, rtPA) within 4.5h of their stroke. None of the IS cases developed hemorrhagic transformation.
Gene expression dynamics in the acute and subacute post‑stroke phase The dynamic changes in differential gene expression across different time windows were assessed in mono-cytes (M, Additional file 1: Tables S1A-C), neutrophils (N, Additional file 1: Tables S1 D-F), and whole blood (WB, Additional file 1: Tables S1G-I) using a significance cutoff P<0.02 (Fig. 1). In monocytes, there were 290, 645, and 352 DEGs at 0–24 h (TP1), 24–48 h (TP2), and >48 h (TP3) compared to controls, respectively (Fig. 1). In neutrophils, 508 (TP1), 745 (TP2), and 547 (TP3) genes were differentially expressed compared to controls. A total of 610 (TP1), 260 (TP2), and 227 (TP3) DEGs were identified in whole blood compared to controls (Fig. 1 and Additional file 1: Table S1). Across the time points, the number of up- or downregulated DEGs in each sam-ple type showed distinct and dynamic trends. For exam-ple, in monocytes, most DEGs are downregulated, with the most at TP2 (Fig. 1A, right panel). Conversely, in neutrophils most genes are upregulated, peaking at TP2 (Fig. 1B, right panel). In whole blood, the highest upregu-lation occurs within the first 24 h (Fig. 1C, right panel). Biotypes of DEGs were relatively similar in monocytes and neutrophils, while in whole blood more lncRNAs and T-cell receptor genes were detected at >48 h post-stroke (Additional file 2: Fig. S1).
Pathway enrichment analyses also show distinctive shifts in molecular function and cellular roles of the DEGs over time per sample type. Most of the over-repre-sented pathways in monocytes are shared across at least two TPs (Fig. 2A) (average of 88.8% shared pathways) and most of these pathways are predicted to be signifi-cantly suppressed (Z ≤ −2.0), including chemokine, IL-8 signaling, and production of NO and ROS in monocytes/ macrophages (Additional file 1: Tables S2A-C and Addi-tional file 2: Fig. S2B and 2C). The only enriched path-ways with predicted activation are PTEN signaling (at 24–48 h and >48 h) and RhoGDI signaling (at 24–48 h) (Additional file 1: Tables S2B-C). Calcium signaling, CCR3, chemokine, CREB, and CXCR4 signaling were the top enriched pathways in monocytes at 0–24h (Fig. 2C). Actin, B cell receptor, ephrin, Erb, and ERK/MAK signal-ing were the top pathways over-represented in monocytes at 24–48 h (Fig. 2C). Similar pathways were regulated in monocytes at times >48 h in addition to estrogen, FLT3, GM-CSF, GNRH, and HIF signaling (Fig. 2C).
From the pathways exclusively regulated at a single TP, suppressed oxidative phosphorylation, suppressed Wnt/ Ca2+, heparan sulfate, and nNOS pathways top the list in the first 24 h (Fig. 2D, left panel). Ephrin B, Tec kinase, reelin, TGF-β, and IL-6 signaling are amongst the sup-pressed pathways at TP2 (Fig. 2D, middle panel), while tryptophan degradation and IL-15 signaling are sup-pressed at times over 48h (Fig. 2D, right panel).
In neutrophils, fewer enriched pathways were shared across at least two TPs (Fig. 3A, Additional file 1: Tables S2D-F) (average of 62.5% of shared pathways in TPs pairwise comparison). There were increased numbers of pathways at TP2 and TP3 compared to TP1 (Fig. 3A, C). Page 6 of 24 Carmona‑Mora et al. BMC Medicine (2023) 21:65 EIF2 signaling and leukocyte extravasation were over-represented at all TPs (Fig. 3B). CD40 and HIF pathways are over-represented at TP2 and TP3. Several interleukin pathways are enriched in the later TPs (Fig. 3C and Addi-tional file 1: Tables S2D-F). IL22 was expressed at TP2 and TP3 (Fig. 3C). IL-1, 4, 7, and 8 were exclusively over-represented in TP2, while IL-2, 10, and 15 pathways were only enriched after 48 h (Fig. 3D).
In contrast to the isolated cell samples, whole blood showed no shared pathways across all TPs (Fig. 4A). Most pathways were enriched at only one TP in whole blood (Fig. 4C and Additional file 1: Tables S2 G-I), and many of these were specific for 0–24 h including p53, AMPK and ATM signaling, and FXR/RXR activation (Fig. 4C).
Upstream regulators were computed to identify driv-ers of gene expression at specific TPs (Additional file 1: Table S3). Similar to what was seen with canonical path-way enrichment, there were more regulators shared across TPs for monocytes (Additional file 2: Fig. S2, Addi-tional file 1: Tables S3A-C) and neutrophils (Additional file 2: Fig. S3; Additional file 1: Tables S3 D-F) compared to whole blood (Additional file 2: Fig. S4; Additional file 1: Tables S3 G-I). Upstream regulators (both activators and suppressors) for monocytes included many molecules common to all time points: 15-LOX, ACKR3, BTNL2, CSF2, ERG, ERK, filgrastim, IKZF1, lipopolysaccha-ride, Msx3, OGA, PCYT2, PGR, PLA2R1, Progesterone, Rhox5, TNF, U18666A, and WAC (Additional file 2: Fig. S2; Additional file 1: Tables S3A-C). Upstream regulators for neutrophils predicted at all time points included the following: calcitriol, CIP2A, ciprofloxacin, CSF3, dexa-methasone, ESR1, filgrastim, FOXO3, FOXO4, interferon beta-1a, LARP1, MRTFB, MYCN, NUPR1, OSM, RPS15, RRP1B, torin1, TP53, and YAP1 (Additional file 2: Fig. S3; Additional file 1: Tables S3 D-F).
In contrast, the vast majority of upstream regulators are unique for every TP in whole blood (Additional file 2: Fig. S4; Additional file 1: Tables S3 G-I). In addition, there are more regulators in the first 24 h in whole blood (Additional file 2: Fig. S4; Additional file 1: Tables S3 G-I), Fig. 1 Differential expression across time points. Identification of time‑dependent DEG clustering profiles Tile mosaics based on self-organizing maps were con-structed for DEGs with GEDI to allow an overall view of gene clusters across time by correlated expression. These mosaics reveal the distinctive dynamics of gene expression changes across every time point in monocytes (Additional file 1: Table S4A), neutrophils (Additional file 1: Table S4B), and whole blood (Additional file 1: Table S4C) (Fig. 5). Every tile clusters a specific group of DEGs, and the tile mosaics for every time point show how that group of genes changes over time (Fig. 5 and Additional file 1: Table S4). Tracked at each coordinate, most tiles in the mosaic maps show evidence of dynamic changes at each time point (Fig. 5, 0 to >48 h).
To understand the trajectory of the DEG clus-ters over time following stroke and to identify key genes per time window, we analyzed expression pro-files using self-organizing maps (SOM) (Additional file 1: Table S5), where every cluster was plotted sepa-rately to obtain a profile. For each cell type including monocytes (Additional file 1: Table S5A), neutrophils (Additional file 1: Table S5B), and whole blood (Addi-tional file 1: Table S5C), there were different patterns of gene expression that included increases over time, decreases over time, peaks at 24–48 h, and valleys at 24–48 h (Fig. 6). Though comparable expression pat-terns between monocytes, neutrophils, and whole blood are seen over time, these were associated with unique functions (GO) in each cell type (Fig. 6, Addi-tional file 1: Tables S6A-L). Examples include neutro-phil degranulation which increases over time in whole blood, decreases of IL-1 secretion over time in mono-cytes, leukocyte migration peaking in neutrophils at 24 h, and a valley for regulation of platelet activation at 24–48 h in monocytes (Fig. 6).

BMC Medicine (2023) 21:65 Time‑dependent gene expression changes per stroke etiology To identify expression changes associated with IS causes, the same model and criteria for DEGs were used, but time points were considered as 0–24 h and over 24 h (>24 h) post-stroke in order to assure enough IS cases per etiology and time point. The cohort characteristics and analyses for the clinical variables after this re-strat-ification can be found in Additional file 1: Table S7. The cohort was split according to the main IS etiologies: car-dioembolic (CE, Additional file 1: Tables S8 A, B, G, H, M, N), large vessel (LV, Additional file 1: Tables S8 C, D, I, J, O, P), and small vessel (SV, Additional file 1: Tables S8 E, F, K, L, Q, R).
More DEGs were identified in all IS causes vs. VRFC in the >24 h period than in the first 24 h for monocytes and neutrophils (Fig. 7, Additional file 1: Table S8). In contrast, in whole blood the first day post-IS showed higher DEGs in CE and LV stroke, pointing to other criti-cal cell types in the response within this time window (Fig. 7 and Additional file 1: Table S8). Gene expression tended to be suppressed in monocytes following CE, LV, and SV strokes at all time points, whereas gene expres-sion was generally upregulated in neutrophils in all stroke etiologies at all time points (Fig. 7). Gene expression was increased in whole blood at 0–24 h in CV and LV strokes (Fig. 7). tPA treatment on 4–5 patients (depending on sample type) did not affect the gene expression changes identified. On PCA (principal component analysis), tPA subjects did not cluster specifically when assessing the DEGs in both 0–24h and >24 h (Additional file 2: Fig. S5).
Key DEG clusters per IS cause were identified using SOM for gene expression trajectories (Additional file 1: Table S9). Comparable expression trajectories over time are seen for CE, LV, and SV strokes in monocytes (Addi-tional file 1: Tables S9 A, B, C), neutrophils (Additional file 1: Tables S9 D, E, F), and whole blood (Additional file 1: Tables S9 G, H, I) (Fig. 8), although not all trajec-tory types are consistently present in every IS cause and in every sample type (Fig. 8).

Time‑associated gene expression networks/modules in monocytes, neutrophils, and whole blood To analyze the time-dependent changes that occur after IS from a genome-wide perspective, we used Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA). The gene expression counts for monocytes, neutrophils, and whole blood samples from IS patients were used to gen-erate three separate networks (Additional file 2: Fig. S6), and significant modules of co-expressed genes were iden-tified in relation to time (as continuous variable in hours post-IS) (Fig. 9A, Additional file 1: Table S11).
For monocytes, 36 modules of co-expressed genes and a module of unassigned genes (MON-Grey) were identified within this cell type network. Sixteen monocyte modules were found to be significant for time: MON-DarkRed, MON-MidnightBlue, MON-GreenYellow, MON-Sienna3, MON-Red, MON-Pink, MON-LightCyan, MON-Violet, MON-Yellow, MON-DarkMagenta, MON-SteelBlue, MON-Blue, MON-Grey60, MON-Tan, MON-PaleTurquoise, and MON-Magenta (Fig. 9A). The gene lists for each of these 16 modules are provided in Addi-tional file 1: Table S11A. Of these, MON-GreenYellow and MON-Blue were also significantly related to diabetes. In neutrophils, 48 modules of co-expressed genes and a module of unassigned genes (NEU-Grey) were identi-fied within the network (Fig. 9A). One neutrophil module (NEU-DarkSlateBlue) was significant for its relationship to time. The gene list associated with this one neutrophil module is provided in Additional file 1: Table S11B.
Within the whole blood network, 51 modules of co-expressed genes and a module (WB-Grey) of unassigned genes were identified. Ten of these whole blood mod-ules were significantly related to time: WB-Brown, WB-Grey60, WB-Tan, WB-Turquoise, WB-MidnightBlue, WB-SteelBlue, WB-DarkRed, WB-SaddleBrown, WB-Pink, and WB-MediumPurple3. Of these, WB-Tan and WB-DarkRed were also related to sex, while WB-Steel-Blue and WB-MediumPurple3 were also related to age. args.summary:
This is a peer-reviewed research article published in BMC Medicine (2023) by Carmona-Mora et al. from UC Davis and the University of Alberta, examining transcriptome dynamics in monocytes, neutrophils, and whole blood following ischemic stroke.

**Study Design & Methods:**
- 38 ischemic stroke patients (cardioembolic, large vessel, and small vessel/lacunar etiologies) and 18 vascular risk factor control (VRFC) subjects were recruited at UC Davis Medical Center
- RNA-seq transcriptomic profiling of peripheral monocytes (>93% purity via CD14 positive selection), neutrophils (>99% purity via negative selection), and whole blood
- Differential expression analyses performed at three time windows post-stroke: 0-24h (TP1), 24-48h (TP2), and >48h (TP3)
- Analytical approaches included differential expression analysis (ANCOVA model), self-organizing maps (SOM), GEDI tile mosaics, Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA), Gene Ontology enrichment, and Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA)
- 5 of 38 IS patients received thrombolytic therapy (rtPA); none developed hemorrhagic transformation

**Key Results:**
- Distinct temporal gene expression patterns were identified across cell types: 290/645/352 DEGs in monocytes, 508/745/547 DEGs in neutrophils, and 610/260/227 DEGs in whole blood at TP1/TP2/TP3 respectively
- Gene expression was generally UPREGULATED in neutrophils and DOWNREGULATED in monocytes across all time points for all stroke etiologies
- Monocyte pathways were largely suppressed (chemokine, IL-8 signaling, NO/ROS production), with PTEN and RhoGDI signaling predicted as activated
- Neutrophils showed enrichment of EIF2 signaling and leukocyte extravasation at all time points, with several interleukin pathways (IL-1, 4, 7, 8, 10, 15, 22) enriched at later time points
- Whole blood showed no shared pathways across all time points; most pathways were specific to 0-24h (p53, AMPK, ATM signaling, FXR/RXR activation)
- Interleukin signaling pathway enrichment differed by time point and stroke etiology
- More DEGs were found in >24h period for monocytes and neutrophils, while whole blood showed higher DEGs in the first 24h for cardioembolic and large vessel strokes
- WGCNA identified 36 monocyte modules (16 time-associated), 48 neutrophil modules (1 time-associated: NEU-DarkSlateBlue), and 51 whole blood modules (10 time-associated)
- Hub genes included SCAF11, JAK1, DICER1, CAPN2, UBC in monocytes and TNFRSF18, PCSK9, BCL2L1, VASP in whole blood
- Monocyte hub genes correlated with NIHSS on admission included MIER1, DICER1, FBXW5, SELPLG, TIA1, and BCKDK
- M1/M2 and N1/N2 polarization markers (CD14, CCR2, CSF1R, FCGR3A, CCL2, STAT3) were identified in time-associated monocyte modules; CCR2 presence suggests active monocyte recruitment to injury site
- Whole blood had more lncRNAs and T-cell receptor genes detected at >48h post-stroke
- tPA treatment did not affect gene expression changes identified (verified by PCA clustering)

**Conclusions:**
This is the first study to analyze transcriptional profiles of monocytes, neutrophils, and whole blood using RNA-seq at time points from 0 to >48h post-stroke. The study identifies potential time- and cell-specific biomarkers and treatment targets, and the identified genes/pathways are critical for understanding how immune and clotting systems change over time after stroke, which may assist with time-targeted, cell-specific therapy development.

## Abstract

Stroke is the third leading cause of death and long-term disability in the world. Considered largely a disease of aging, its global economic and healthcare burden is expected to rise as more people survive into advanced age. With recent advances in acute stroke management, including the expansion of time windows for treatment with intravenous thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy, we are likely to see an increase in survival rates. It is therefore critically important to understand the complete pathophysiology of ischemic stroke, both in the acute and subacute stages and during the chronic phase in the months and years following an ischemic event. One of the most clinically relevant aspects of the chronic sequelae of stroke is its extended negative effect on cognition. Cognitive impairment may be related to the deterioration and dysfunctional reorganization of white matter seen at later timepoints after stroke, as well as ongoing progressive neurodegeneration.The vasculature of the brain also undergoes significant insult and remodeling following stroke, undergoing changes which may further contribute to chronic stroke pathology. While inflammation and the immune response are well established drivers of acute stroke pathology, the chronicity and functional role of innate and adaptive immune responses in the post-ischemic brain and in the peripheral environment remain largely uncharacterized. In this review, we summarize the current literature on post-stroke injury progression, its chronic pathological features, and the putative secondary injury mechanisms underlying the development of cognitive impairment and dementia. We present findings from clinical and experimental studies and discuss the long-term effects of ischemic stroke on both brain anatomy and functional outcome. Identifying mechanisms that occur months to years after injury could lead to treatment strategies in the chronic phase of stroke to help mitigate stroke-associated cognitive decline in patients.

**Keywords:** Ischemic stroke, Chronic neurodegeneration, Microglia, Neuroinflammation, Cognition

## Introduction

Ischemic stroke is an acute cerebrovascular injury that occurs when there is an obstruction of blood supply to the brain, leading to long-term brain damage and neurological impairment. An estimated 87% of strokes are ischemic, due to either thrombosis or an embolism (Tsao et al. [2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR104)). Long-term functional and neurological impairments are common following stroke and can range from severe post-stroke dementia to minor deficits in motor function (Lawrence et al. [2001](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR54); Lo et al. [2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR61)). Furthermore, the incidence of chronic pathologic sequelae after stroke have been reported to be as high as 44% even over a decade after the stroke has occurred (Synhaeve et al. [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR98)). Not only do stroke survivors suffer from disability, but they are also burdened with treatment and rehabilitation expenses. The annual cost for stroke care has climbed to over $52 billion in the USA, with costs projected to nearly double by 2035 (Tsao et al. [2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR104)).

As an age-associated disease, the burden of stroke will continue to rise as the mean age of the population increases. This is evidenced by the 85% increase seen in the global rate of absolute stroke prevalence since 1990 (Collaborators [2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR19)). Furthermore, with the advent of increasingly effective acute interventions, more individuals are surviving for longer after stroke. In 2021, almost 70% of patients survived 3 or more years after stroke (Aked et al. [2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR2)). While this improved survival rate is heartening, clinical data indicate a significant subset of these patients suffer from progressive functional disability for months to years following stroke (Crichton et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR22)). Given stroke’s contribution to the expanding population of patients suffering from long-term neurological dysfunction and neurodegenerative disease (Stuckey [2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR95)), investigating secondary injury mechanisms driving chronic injury progression may hold great potential for gaining a better understanding of how to prevent and treat stroke’s chronic sequelae.

Despite the need to find novel therapies to intervene in the chronic pathology of stroke, most experimental stroke research primarily focuses on the acute aspects of stroke pathology. Due to considerations such as high mortality, housing costs, and practical limitations on experimental duration, studies implementing translational animal models of cerebral ischemia rarely progress beyond 30 days post-stroke. This leaves a critical gap in our understanding of stroke’s chronic impact on the brain (Sommer [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR91)). The paucity of data on the mechanisms underlying functional outcomes at chronic timepoints is present across the various domains of stroke pathology, including changes in immune activity, white matter integrity, neurovascular structure, and cerebral blood flow dynamics.

While there are considerably more studies reporting the chronic consequences of stroke in the clinical literature, these studies are limited in the degree to which they can investigate the causative mechanisms underlying chronic stroke progression. The purpose of this narrative review is to provide an overview of both clinical and pre-clinical literature investigating the chronic aspects of stroke pathophysiology in the areas of cognitive function, cerebrovascular function, and immunological activity at timepoints of at least one-month post-stroke in pre-clinical studies and six-month post-stroke in clinical studies.

### Chronic Post-stroke Cognitive Impairment

Chronic post-stroke cognitive impairment (cPSCI) is one of the most understudied clinically relevant sequelae of stroke (Chohan et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR17)). Broadly, cPSCI refers to any cognitive deficit or dysfunction resulting from stroke, which persist past the subacute phase of stroke. Over half of all stroke survivors experience some degree of long-term cognitive dysfunction following ischemic stroke (Mellon et al. [2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR65)) and these cognitive deficits have been shown to persist for as many as 15 years post-stroke (Schaapsmeerders et al. [2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR82)). While the precise cognitive dysfunction experienced by the individual is largely dependent on the location and size of the ischemic lesion, some of the most common domain-specific long-term cognitive impairments following stroke include deficits in processing speed, working memory, speech, visuospatial function, and attention (Corbetta et al. [2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR20); Dichgans and Leys [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR31); Douiri et al. [2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR32)). In addition to compromising domain-specific cognitive functions, stroke is also associated with multiple neurocognitive and mood disorders, the most prevalent of these being dementia and depression. Although cognitive dysfunction may be an effect of stroke’s chronic pathophysiology rather than a driver of it, understanding of these long-term effects provides valuable context to the content of this review. A brief look at the clinical impact of chronic cognitive impairment and mood disorder in stroke within the last 5 years can be found in Table[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#Tab1).

## Chronic Vascular Stroke Pathology

Stroke is foremost a vascular disease and therefore many of the fundamental changes related to its etiology are vascular in nature. While the acute cerebrovascular phenomena leading to the development of the infarct core and penumbra are well understood in ischemic stroke, the long-term dynamics of vascular growth and remodeling, as well as cerebral blood flow (CBF), following stroke require deeper investigation (Aam et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR1)). A key component to understanding the vascular-associated changes in the chronic phase of stroke is the impact on the blood–brain barrier (BBB).

### Blood–Brain Barrier Disruption

The BBB isolates the brain from neurotoxic molecules found in blood, while also facilitating the transport of essential nutrients to support parenchymal brain cells (Luca et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR26)). Disruption of the BBB in acute ischemic stroke is established in both human and animal models to occur within hours after ischemic insult (Aam et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR1)). Using MRI, BBB disruption has been demonstrated to occur for several weeks after stroke in animal models; however, human data on post-stroke BBB leakage thus far is limited to 7 days post-stroke (Bernardo-Castro et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR10)). BBB disruption is characterized by increased permeability resulting from cellular dysfunction and degradation of the extracellular matrix of cells making up the neurovascular unit (NVU), including endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, astrocytes, and pericytes. Under healthy conditions, these cells coordinate to maintain the integrity and proper function of blood vessels within the neurovascular compartment (Cai et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR12); Patabendige et al. [2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR71)). Comorbidities affecting the structural and functional dynamics of blood vessels play a major role in the degree of permeability occurring in the BBB following stroke. Hypertension, a well-known risk factor for stroke, causes a disruption of neurovascular coupling in the BBB which may continue to contribute to stroke pathology past the acute phase of ischemic injury (Cipolla et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR18)). Similarly, comorbidities affecting glycemia, such as diabetes mellitus and metabolic syndrome, are significant risk factors for worsened BBB permeability in the infarct region, as both hyper- and hypoglycemia have been shown to contribute to BBB dysfunction through the upregulation of matrix metalloprotease-2 and -9 and a decrease in tight junction proteins, including occludin and ZO-1 (Aam et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR1)).

Apart from the biphasic peaks in permeability shown to occur approximately 6 and 72–96 hours after an ischemic injury, clinical data on the evolution of BBB permeability past the subacute phase of stroke are limited (Bernardo-Castro et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR10)). Available literature on chronic stroke-induced BBB permeability in humans indicates a long-term elevation of vascular leakage in the brain after stroke. Blood vessels in the brains of human stroke patients, ranging from six months to two years post-stroke, exhibit differential expression of proteins involved in tight junction formation, including Claudin-1 and Claudin-5 (Sladojevic et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR90)). Chronically increased expression of Claudin-1 in place of Claudin-5 in the post-stroke brain is associated with increased vascular leakage in both humans and mice. Furthermore, inhibition of Claudin-1 in mice reduces endothelial barrier permeability and improves neurological recovery. Increased expression of tight junction proteins involved in immune recruitment, Junction Adhesion Molecule A (JAM-A), and Endothelial Cell Adhesion Molecule (ESAM) were also found in post-stroke brains (Sladojevic et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR90)).

A significant driver of BBB dysfunction is the inflammation induced by ischemic injury (Iadecola et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR43)). Mediated by upregulated ROS generation and NF-kB activation, the class B scavenger receptor, CD36, contributes to pro-inflammatory activity and BBB dysfunction for as long as three months after experimental stroke in mice. Deletion of CD36, which is widely expressed in immune and non-immune cells, results in significantly reduced IgG extravasation into the brain (Balkaya et al. [2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR7)**).** Additional evidence for chronic BBB permeability is seen in the investigation of minocycline as a treatment for stroke-induced BBB dysfunction in rats. In this study, researchers found that BBB hyperpermeability in the peri-infarct region persisted for a period of at least four weeks, concomitant with reduced tight junction protein expression (Yang et al. [2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR122)). Minocycline reduced this hyperpermeability by limiting the breakdown of the BBB through inhibition of matrix metalloproteases and pro-inflammatory microglial activity.

### Post-stroke Angiogenesis and Revascularization

The degree of collateral vascularization in the peri-infarct region, known as “collateral grade,” is a major determinant of infarct size in stroke patients (Liebeskind et al. [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR57)). Although the influence of collateral grade on stroke outcome in the acute phase of stroke is well established, more research is required to establish the role of collaterals in the chronic phase of stroke. In a rat model of cortical stroke, collateral surface vessels in the peri-infarct region experience growth in both length and diameter 30-days post-injury (Wei et al. [2001](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR114)). Interestingly, flow latency at the arteriocapillary junctions decreased at day 30 compared to immediately post-stroke, indicating that chronic collateral growth may not be functional and potentially contributes to chronic cerebral hypoperfusion. Although this study provides evidence that collateral vessel dynamics play a role in the chronic phase of stroke, the lack of precise temporal information on when collateral growth occurred is an important limitation to consider. Further indication of dysfunctional collateral involvement in the chronic phase of stroke is the increased incidence of capillary stalls in the peri-infarct cortex at four weeks after stroke in a photothrombotic mouse model (Williamson et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR117)). Collateral vessels have also been shown to exhibit significant remodeling and increased vascular perfusion in an middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAo) rat model at 30-day post-stroke (Tomita et al. [2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR102)). However, other recent experimental studies have reported that the period of vascular plasticity induced by stroke is limited to the two weeks following stroke, thus our understanding of the temporal dynamics of post-stroke angiogenesis remains ambiguous (Williamson et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR117)). Although increased collateral vessel density in the peri-infarct region is correlated with improved survival in stroke patients, to date there is very little data available on the time course of post-stroke angiogenesis in humans, other than that new vessels begin to form within 3–5 days post-stroke (Krupinski et al. [1994](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR52)). These results provide evidence for collateral angiogenesis in the chronic phase of stroke and indicate a need for further investigation into timepoints greater than one-month post-stroke to elucidate the mechanisms by which collateral revascularization in the peri-infarct region may contribute to chronic stroke recovery.

While acute induction of post-stroke angiogenesis may be problematic due to its potential to increase BBB permeability and exacerbate injury, several promising therapeutics for chronic post-stroke angiogenesis are being investigated. One such therapeutic involves administration of stem cell factor (SCF) in combination with granulocyte-colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF). This combinational therapy has been shown to induce blood vessel formation in the peri-infarct region, as well as improved long-term functional recovery when administered to rats (14 weeks post-stroke) and mice (17 weeks post-stroke) in the chronic phase of stroke (Cui et al. [2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR24); Zhao et al. [2007](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR127)). However, for this treatment and the others mentioned below, further studies evaluating the treatment’s safety and efficacy will be required prior to examining their therapeutic benefit in humans. Although the mechanisms by which these vascular changes occur are not well understood, evidence points to increased recruitment of bone marrow-derived stem cells and the transcription factor NF-κB as being key contributors in the process (Cui et al. [2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR24); Zhao et al. [2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR128)). Another promising combinational therapy for chronic stroke currently being investigated is sustained delivery of the angiogenic growth factors VEGF and Ang1. A recent study assessing the therapeutic potential of this combination in a photothrombotic rat model of ischemic stroke found that long-term delivery of VEGF/Ang1+, starting at 14 days post-stroke, prolonged the angiogenic window following ischemic injury and resulted in significantly increased vascularization in the ipsilesional cortex accompanied by improved recovery of sensorimotor function at 70 days after ischemic injury (Yanev et al. [2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR121)). Interestingly, resident macrophages are believed to be one of the primary mediators of VEGF-associated angiogenesis following acute ischemic injury (Ma et al. [2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR62)). Yet another therapeutic of interest for enhancing angiogenesis to improve chronic stroke recovery is the AMPK activator, metformin. While early exploration of the therapeutic potential of metformin for stroke recovery showed mixed results depending on the treatment window used (Li et al. [2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR56)), a follow-up study examining the effects of daily metformin treatment in mice for thirty days after stroke reports significant improvement of functional recovery coinciding with a marked enhancement of angiogenesis in the ischemic brain (Jin et al. [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR45)). Additionally, researchers found that the enhanced recovery and angiogenesis induced by metformin was dependent on significant long-term increases in myeloid cells with CD206+ phenotype and suppression of those with CD32+ phenotype. A consistent theme between the various angiogenic treatments discussed here is the mediating role of the central immune activity, suggesting that modulation of immune cell activity in the months following ischemic injury may hold potential as a therapeutic target for improving functional recovery in the chronic phase of stroke. Immune regulation of post-stroke angiogenesis has been reviewed elsewhere (Ma et al. [2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR62); Zhu et al. [2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR131)). However, given our currently limited understanding, further exploration of immune cell dynamics during the chronic phase of stroke is warranted to best realize this therapeutic potential (Fig. [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#Fig1)).

### The Role of Vascular Damage in cPSCI

One potential mechanism by which vascular damage may contribute to cognitive dysfunction is through disruption of white matter integrity throughout the brain and the subsequent development of white matter lesions (WMLs) (Haan et al. [2006](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR25); Hase et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR41); Kalaria et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR48)). Due to being the primary vascular supply for the white matter-rich subcortical regions of the brain, lacunar strokes are the subclass of ischemic stroke most strongly associated with injuries of this type (Gore et al. [2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR40)). Longitudinal clinical studies of cognitive recovery in stroke patients have shown that vascular cognitive impairment persists past six months in as many as 65% of patients, making it a major contributor to cPSCI (Ser et al. [2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR28)). The trajectory of cognitive function in the chronic phase of stroke is highly heterogeneous across individuals, as both spontaneous recovery and onset of dementia are exhibited at regular timepoints up to 24 months (Ser et al. [2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR28)). Additionally, in patients with post-stroke dementia, there is a 57% increased density of microcapillaries in the WM vasculature and WM vessels exhibit a 20–49% increase in width (Hase et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR41)). These vascular changes are hypothesized to be a compensatory mechanism for the WM dysfunction that arises following stroke. However, evidence for the role of vascular-related WM damage’s contribution to cognitive decline is mixed, with one clinical study finding that the degree of cognitive decline or improvement a patient experienced in the months following stroke was independent of their level of progressive vascular damage (Rasquin et al. [2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR77)). These clinical studies demonstrate that there is a dynamic nature to cognitive recovery in the chronic phase of stroke and highlight a need for further investigation into the non-vascular mechanisms which may be driving these differential outcomes in the months and years after stroke. In addition to vascular damage, another prospective source of long-term cognitive dysfunction in stroke is chronic brain inflammation and systemic immune dysfunction which are discussed below.

## Chronic Neuropathology of the Stroke Lesion

In mice, post-stroke macrophage infiltration into the stroke lesion persists for at least 1 month (Yan et al., 2020). Macrophage resorption of dead tissue eventually results in formation of a cystic cavity surrounded by a dense rim of fibrillary astrocytes that form a scaffold for glial scarring (Fig.[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#Fig2)). Activated microglia and macrophages with amoeboid or round morphology have been demonstrated to remain in the peri-lesional vascular connective tissue up to 6 years post-stroke in humans (Mena et al., 2004), indicating a chronic immune response that may persist for months to years after stroke (Liesz et al. [2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR58); Stanne et al. [2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR92)).

## Immune Activation Dynamics in the Chronic Phase of Stroke

A major driver of the inflammatory cascade following stroke is a class of cytotoxic molecules generated by ischemic injury, termed damage associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). A recruiter of immune cell infiltration, DAMPs are recognized by resident immune cells displaying pattern recognition receptors which, when bound, induce activation of a pro-inflammatory phenotype and a corresponding increase in the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Of particular interest to the discussion of chronic sequelae of stroke, secondary injury resulting from pathogenic immune activity begins within minutes after the primary injury occurs and can often persist for months and years (Shi et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR88)). See Fig.[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#Fig3) for a diagram summarizing this process.

The primary ischemic injury is inherently a traumatic, localized event that drives the initiation of a pro-inflammatory cascade that plays a role in both the acute and chronic phases of post-stroke recovery. Despite its importance to the evolution of stroke pathology in the chronic phase of the disease, the long-term patterns of immune activity are currently an area of relative neglect compared to our understanding of acute immune dynamics.

### Microglial Activation

Microglial involvement has an extended and dynamic role in stroke recovery. Rodent models demonstrate that inflammation shifts from the peri-lesional area to secondary sites of increased inflammation throughout the brain in the months following stroke (Walter et al. [2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR108)). Activated microglia populations at these sites exhibit inflammatory phagocytic activity even after one month post-stroke.

Microglia activation in response to DAMPs and reactive oxygen species (ROS) are both helpful and harmful to stroke recovery, in a temporally dependent manner. Acutely, microglia clean up cellular debris and other noxious particles within the stroke penumbra, protecting the surrounding tissue. However, inflammation caused by chronically activated microglia may contribute to chronic stroke sequelae. Increased production of tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) is proposed to contribute to neuronal loss via upregulated microglial phagocytosis (Neniskyte et al. [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR68)). Elevated TNF-α in the human brain has been shown to persist at least 15 months post-stroke, suggesting an influence on chronic neuroinflammation via microglial activation (Dziewulska and Mossakowski [2003](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR34)). Furthermore, microglia are the most transcriptionally active immune cell in mice at 84 days post-stroke (Cao et al. [2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR15)). In the chronic phase, these microglia show patterns of expression common to many neurodegenerative diseases, including the downregulation of _tmem119_ and _cx3cr1_ and upregulation of _apoe_, _axl_, _lpl_, _csf1_, and _cst7_. Further investigation into these diseases-associated microglial patterns of expression may be critical to understanding the immune contribution to strokes chronic neurocognitive sequelae.

## Peripheral Immune Cell Involvement

### Innate Immunity

Peripheral immune cell recruitment may also contribute stroke’s chronic sequelae. Acutely, stroke induces peripheral immune cell infiltration across the BBB into the brain parenchyma. The major effectors in this infiltration include macrophages, neutrophils, NK cells, T cells, and Tregs (Beuker et al. [2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR11); Chen et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR16); Selvaraj and Stowe [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR86)). Following the initial influx, peripheral immune involvement is seen in both humans and animals for at least 90 days, providing further evidence for the influence of immune activity in the chronic phase of stroke.

In adult MCAo mice, the infiltration of neutrophils into the brain peaks at 1–2 days post-stroke after which time numbers begin to recede (Cai et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR13)). Age has been shown to play a dynamic role in this infiltration, with aged mice experiencing increased neutrophil infiltration compared to young mice (Ritzel et al., 2018). In humans, the increase in neutrophils persists up to 90 days after stroke (Tsai et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR103)). Species differences in blood neutrophil frequencies may partially explain this discrepancy. However, at one year, there was no detectable difference in stroke patient neutrophil counts compared to the healthy control group. Neutrophils contribute to worsened stroke outcomes through the release neutrophil elastase, MMP-9, ROS, nitrogen species, and other pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and MIP-1α. These molecules promote disruption of the BBB and recruitment of other pro-inflammatory immune cells (Kasama et al. [2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR49); Romanic et al. [1998](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR80); Stowe et al. [2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR93)). The effects of normal aging on neutrophil function may exacerbate their impact in chronic stroke (Ritzel et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR79); Roy-O'Reilly et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR81)). Clinical data indicate that increased blood neutrophil counts raise the probability of post-stroke depression and the pro-inflammatory cytokines secreted by neutrophils are implicated in depressive pathology (Sun et al. [2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR97)). Indeed, reduction of infiltrated neutrophils within 24 hours of stroke is linked to a decreased infarct volume in both humans and mice (Cai et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR13)). A recent analysis on inflammatory correlates of post-stroke depression in the chronic phase of stroke provides additional evidence for the long-term involvement of neutrophils in stroke pathology. The analysis, conducted on 436 stroke patients over 1 year, found that neutrophil counts independently predicted post-stroke depression and played a mediating role in the relationship between stroke severity and post-stroke depression (Sun et al., 2022). These findings show neutrophils may be an especially important innate immune target for translational stroke research addressing stroke’s long-term cognitive impact.

Furthermore, monocyte infiltration of the stroke lesion core continually increases for as long as 28 days post-stroke (Garcia-Bonilla et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR38)). Inhibition of monocyte infiltration shows both positive and negative effects on stroke outcome. Beneficial effects of inhibiting monocyte infiltration include reduced infarct size and attenuated expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, while deleterious findings include reductions in angiogenesis, vascular density, and motor function (Berchtold et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR9)). In the initial stage of stroke-induced immune activation in mice, monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (MCP-1, also known as CCL2) recruits monocytes and macrophages to the injury site, increasing inflammation (Schilling et al. [2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR84)). The recruitment of blood-borne macrophages is also mediated by CX3C chemokine receptor 1 (CX3CR1) signaling, which promotes a neuroprotective phenotype (Tang et al. [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR100)). Peripheral macrophages appear in the ischemic region up to ten weeks post-stroke in mice (Weber et al. [2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR113)). The mechanisms underlying chronic peripheral monocyte involvement and whether their presence contributes to chronic sequelae remain unclear.

Recent evidence also points to increased immune cell trafficking due to stroke-induced gut leakage as another potential driver of cPSCI. In human-mouse fecal matter transplant (FMT) experiments, mice that received transplants from stroke patients with PSCI at 3 months post-stroke exhibited significantly increased post-stroke pathology compared to mice that received transplants from stroke patients without PSCI (Wang et al. [2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR112)). Effects of PSCI FMT found in this study include increases in circulating lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and markers of peripheral inflammation, reduced BBB integrity, and worsened cognitive decline. Interestingly, intraperitoneal injection of LPS elicited a similar effect as the PSCI FMT, indicating that TLR4 activation may be the leading culprit behind these changes.

### Adaptive Immunity

As part of the peripheral immune response, lymphocytes cross the BBB and migrate to the ischemic site. B lymphocyte infiltration is delayed compared to that of innate immune cells (Doyle et al. [2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR33)) and remains elevated for up to three months after ischemia in humans (Tsai et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR103)). B cells have been detected up to 12 weeks after stroke, appearing to form clusters with T cells in the peri-lesional area (Doyle et al. [2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR33)). These cells produce antibodies, such as IgG, IgM, and IgA, whose presence has shown to be dispersed throughout the injured area (Doyle et al. [2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR33); Zbesko et al. [2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR125)). Interestingly, B-cell-deficient mice perform better in cognitive tests, suggesting a role in development of cPSCI. Taken together, the above evidence suggests that B cells may be a target for delayed stroke treatment.

Associated with pro-inflammatory signaling and worsened outcomes in the chronic phase of stroke, T-cell activity persists dynamically into the chronic phase of stroke. Activated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells stay in the infarct site for up to one month post-stroke (Xie et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR118)). T cells can have a positive effect on stroke recovery through enhancement of post-stroke repair mechanisms, debris clearance, and attenuating inflammation (Selvaraj and Stowe [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR86); Peruzzotti-Jametti et al. [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR73)). In mice, T-cell density in the ipsilateral hemisphere at 28 days is negatively correlated with infarct volume (Vindegaard et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR106)). However, chronic peripheral T-cell secretion of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-1 is associated with poorer cognitive function and suppression of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 (Dzik et al. [1989](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR35); Yin and Li [2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR124)). Furthermore, it has been suggested that T cells may worsen functional deficits in patients exposed to infection in the chronic phase of stroke recovery (Learoyd et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR55)).

Similarly, Treg accumulation in the ipsilateral hemisphere continues for at least one-month post-stroke (Stubbe et al. [2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR94)). There is also a phenotypic shift toward IL-10 + Foxp3 + regulatory T cells in peripheral circulation up to six months following stroke (Kim et al. [2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR51)). Treg interaction with other T-cell subpopulations in the post-ischemic brain is still not well understood; however, the proportion of Tregs does not seem to have an impact on stroke severity (Yan et al. [2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11391890#CR120)). Further studies are required to elucidate the interactions between different T-cell populations and their effect at later stages of disease.

This is a scientific review article titled "Drivers of Chronic Pathology Following Ischemic Stroke: A Descriptive Review" published in Cellular and Molecular Neurobiology (Cell Mol Neurobiol, 2023 Dec 19;44:7, doi: 10.1007/s10571-023-01437-2). The authors are Grant W Goodman, Trang H Do, Chunfeng Tan, and Rodney M Ritzel (corresponding author) from the Department of Neurology, McGovern Medical School, The University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston. PMCID: PMC11391890, PMID: 38112809.

Key content and findings:

1. BACKGROUND: Stroke is the third leading cause of death and long-term disability worldwide, with 87% of strokes being ischemic. Annual stroke care costs exceed $52 billion in the USA, projected to nearly double by 2035. Global absolute stroke prevalence increased 85% since 1990. In 2021, almost 70% of patients survived 3+ years after stroke. Most experimental stroke research focuses on acute pathology, with animal models rarely progressing beyond 30 days post-stroke, creating a critical knowledge gap.

2. CHRONIC POST-STROKE COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT (cPSCI): Over half of all stroke survivors experience long-term cognitive dysfunction, persisting up to 15 years. Common deficits include processing speed, working memory, speech, visuospatial function, and attention. Key clinical data: 59% probability of PSCI at 3 and 18 months (Aam et al. 2020); MoCA scores averaging 21.9 in chronic stroke patients vs. healthy standard of 26 (Liu-Ambrose et al. 2022); post-stroke dementia incidence at 1 year was 34.4% in severe stroke, 8.2% in mild stroke (Pendlebury et al. 2019); pooled hazard ratio for previous stroke and dementia is 1.69 (Kuzma et al. 2018); dementia prevalence of 18.4% in stroke studies vs. 10% baseline in people 65+ (Craig et al. 2022). Post-stroke depression rates range from 32.2% to 63.75%.

3. CHRONIC VASCULAR PATHOLOGY: BBB disruption persists chronically after stroke. In humans, vascular leakage remains elevated 6 months to 2 years post-stroke with altered tight junction protein expression (Claudin-1 replacing Claudin-5). CD36 contributes to pro-inflammatory BBB dysfunction up to 3 months post-stroke in mice. BBB hyperpermeability persists at least 4 weeks in the peri-infarct region. Collateral vessels in the peri-infarct region grow in length and diameter 30 days post-injury but may not be functional, potentially contributing to chronic cerebral hypoperfusion. New vessels begin forming within 3-5 days post-stroke in humans.

4. ANGIOGENIC THERAPIES: Promising treatments include SCF+G-CSF combination (improved functional recovery at 14-17 weeks post-stroke in rats/mice), sustained VEGF/Ang1 delivery (improved vascularization and sensorimotor recovery at 70 days post-stroke), and metformin (enhanced angiogenesis and functional recovery with daily treatment for 30 days). Metformin's effects were dependent on increases in CD206+ myeloid cells and suppression of CD32+ phenotype.

5. CHRONIC NEUROPATHOLOGY: Macrophage infiltration persists at least 1 month in mice; activated microglia/macrophages remain in peri-lesional tissue up to 6 years post-stroke in humans. Old cystic infarcts form surrounded by reactive astrocytes (glial scarring).

6. IMMUNE ACTIVATION: DAMPs trigger pro-inflammatory cascades beginning within minutes and persisting months to years. Microglial activation shifts from peri-lesional to secondary sites throughout the brain. TNF-α elevation persists at least 15 months post-stroke in humans. At 84 days post-stroke, microglia are the most transcriptionally active immune cells, showing disease-associated expression patterns (downregulation of tmem119 and cx3cr1; upregulation of apoe, axl, lpl, csf1, cst7) similar to other neurodegenerative diseases.

7. INNATE IMMUNITY: Neutrophil infiltration peaks at 1-2 days post-stroke in mice, persisting up to 90 days in humans. Neutrophil counts independently predicted post-stroke depression in a study of 436 patients. Monocyte infiltration increases for up to 28 days post-stroke; peripheral macrophages appear up to 10 weeks post-stroke in mice. Stroke-induced gut leakage and PSCI fecal matter transplants increased LPS, reduced BBB integrity, and worsened cognitive decline in mice (likely via TLR4 activation).

8. ADAPTIVE IMMUNITY: B lymphocytes remain elevated up to 3 months after ischemia in humans and form clusters with T cells up to 12 weeks post-stroke. B-cell-deficient mice perform better in cognitive tests. Activated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells stay in the infarct site up to 1 month. Tregs accumulate in the ipsilateral hemisphere for at least 1 month, with a shift toward IL-10+ Foxp3+ regulatory T cells in circulation up to 6 months post-stroke.

CONCLUSION: The review emphasizes the critical need to understand mechanisms operating months to years after ischemic stroke to develop treatment strategies for the chronic phase that could mitigate stroke-associated cognitive decline. Most experimental research lacks data beyond 30 days post-stroke, and chronic immune, vascular, and white matter mechanisms remain largely uncharacterized.

## Abstract

Ischemic stroke recovery involves dynamic interactions between the central nervous system and infiltrating immune cells. Peripheral immune cells compete with resident microglia for spatial niches in the brain, but how modulating this balance affects recovery remains unclear. Here, we use PLX5622 to create spatial niches for peripheral immune cells, altering the competition between infiltrating immune cells and resident microglia in male mice following transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO). We find that early-phase microglia attenuation promotes long-term functional recovery. This intervention amplifies a subset of monocyte-derived macrophages (RAMf) with reparative properties, characterized by high expression of GPNMB and CD63, enhanced lipid metabolism, and pro-angiogenic activity. Transplantation of RAMf into stroke-affected mice improves white matter integrity and vascular repair. We identify Mafb as the transcription factor regulating the reparative phenotype of RAMf. These findings highlight strategies to optimize immune cell dynamics for post-stroke rehabilitation.

## Introduction

Ischemic stroke is a leading cause of mortality and permanent disability, with a rising prevalence worldwide[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR1 "Global, regional, and national burden of stroke and its risk factors, 1990-2019: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2019. Lancet. Neurol. 20, 795–820 (2021)."),[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR2 "Tsao, C. W. et al. Heart Disease and Stroke Statistics-2022 Update: A Report From the American Heart Association. Circulation 145, e153–e639 (2022)."). Following ischemia, the central nervous system undergoes an evolution from brain injury to neural repair, which is strongly influenced by both resident microglia and infiltrating immune cells[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR3 "Shichita, T., Ooboshi, H. & Yoshimura, A. Neuroimmune mechanisms and therapies mediating post-ischaemic brain injury and repair. Nat. Rev. Neurosci. 24, 299–312 (2023)."). In response to cerebral ischemia, neurons and glial cells in the infarct region rapidly undergo hypoxic cell death, releasing damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). These molecules activate microglia and trigger sterile inflammation. Once activated, microglia secrete inflammatory factors that contribute to secondary brain damage and the recruitment of peripheral immune cells[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR4 "Brown, G. C. & Neher, J. J. Microglial phagocytosis of live neurons. Nat. Rev. Neurosci. 15, 209–216 (2014)."). Peripheral immune cells, including neutrophils, macrophages, and lymphocytes, infiltrate ischemic brain tissues within 1 or 2 days following the activation of resident microglia[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR5 "Liesz, A. et al. The spectrum of systemic immune alterations after murine focal ischemia: immunodepression versus immunomodulation. Stroke 40, 2849–2858 (2009).") and further activate microglia through pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interferon-γ,IL-17, and IL-21[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR6 "Shichita, T. et al. Pivotal role of cerebral interleukin-17-producing gammadeltaT cells in the delayed phase of ischemic brain injury. Nat. Med 15, 946–950 (2009)."),[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR7 "Clarkson, B. D. et al. T cell-derived interleukin (IL)-21 promotes brain injury following stroke in mice. J. Exp. Med 211, 595–604 (2014)."). Sterile inflammation subsides approximately one to two weeks after ischemia. During this period, resident and infiltrating immune cells shift from a pro-inflammatory to a reparative phenotype. These immune cells produce neurotrophic factors and synaptic regulatory molecules around the injured brain, facilitating angiogenesis, axonal regeneration, synaptic modulation, and remyelination[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR3 "Shichita, T., Ooboshi, H. & Yoshimura, A. Neuroimmune mechanisms and therapies mediating post-ischaemic brain injury and repair. Nat. Rev. Neurosci. 24, 299–312 (2023)."),[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR8 "Garcia-Bonilla, L. et al. Spatio-temporal profile, phenotypic diversity, and fate of recruited monocytes into the post-ischemic brain. J. Neuroinflamm. 13, 285 (2016)."),[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR9 "Shi, L. et al. Treg cell-derived osteopontin promotes microglia-mediated white matter repair after ischemic stroke. Immunity 54, 1527–1542.e1528 (2021)."). Therefore, selectively inhibiting acute harmful inflammation while preserving subsequent reparative processes is considered a potential strategy for improving functional outcomes in patients with ischemic stroke.

Microglia, the most abundant immune cells in the brain, serve as the primary triggers of neuroinflammation in the central nervous system (CNS). However, overactivated microglia can hinder the transition of the immune environment to a repair state during ischemic stroke[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR10 "Unger, M. S., Schernthaner, P., Marschallinger, J., Mrowetz, H. & Aigner, L. Microglia prevent peripheral immune cell invasion and promote an anti-inflammatory environment in the brain of APP-PS1 transgenic mice. J. Neuroinflamm. 15, 274 (2018)."). Over-activated microglia may mistakenly identify and engulf healthy neurons, resulting in secondary brain damage[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR4 "Brown, G. C. & Neher, J. J. Microglial phagocytosis of live neurons. Nat. Rev. Neurosci. 15, 209–216 (2014)."). Additionally, they can attract CD8+ T cells, γδ T cells, and other cytotoxic cells into the brain[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR11 "Shi, Z. et al. Microglia drive transient insult-induced brain injury by chemotactic recruitment of CD8+ T lymphocytes. Neuron 111, 696–710.e699 (2023)."),[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR12 "Wang, Y.-R., Cui, W.-Q., Wu, H.-Y., Xu, X.-D. & Xu, X.-Q. The role of T cells in acute ischemic stroke. Brain Res. Bull. 196, 20–33 (2023)."), thereby exacerbating the inflammatory environment and hindering the subsequent repair process.

Colony stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R) inhibitors, such as PLX3397 and PLX5622, have been shown to selectively inhibit microglial proliferation and significantly reduce the number of microglia in the mouse brain[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR13 "Elmore, M. R. et al. Colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor signaling is necessary for microglia viability, unmasking a microglia progenitor cell in the adult brain. Neuron 82, 380–397 (2014)."). Multiple studies have highlighted the therapeutic potential of CSF1R inhibitors in treating a range of neurological disorders, including ischemic stroke[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR14 "Beuker, C. et al. Stroke induces disease-specific myeloid cells in the brain parenchyma and pia. Nat. Commun. 13, 945 (2022)."), neurodegenerative diseases[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR15 "Spangenberg, E. E. et al. Eliminating microglia in Alzheimer’s mice prevents neuronal loss without modulating amyloid-β pathology. Brain 139, 1265–1281 (2016)."), demyelinating diseases[16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR16 "Nissen, J. C., Thompson, K. K., West, B. L. & Tsirka, S. E. Csf1R inhibition attenuates experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis and promotes recovery. Exp. Neurol. 307, 24–36 (2018)."), CNS infections[17](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR17 "Spiteri, A. G. et al. PLX5622 Reduces Disease Severity in Lethal CNS Infection by Off-Target Inhibition of Peripheral Inflammatory Monocyte Production. Front Immunol. 13, 851556 (2022).") and brain injuries[18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR18 "Wang Y, et al. Early posttraumatic CSF1R inhibition via PLX3397 leads to time- and sex-dependent effects on inflammation and neuronal maintenance after traumatic brain injury in mice. Brain Behav Immun 106, 49–66 (2022)."). However, some research has indicated that the complete elimination of microglia can negate their protective effects and exacerbate brain injury following ischemic stroke[19](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR19 "Szalay, G. et al. Microglia protect against brain injury and their selective elimination dysregulates neuronal network activity after stroke. Nat. Commun. 7, 11499 (2016)."),[20](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR20 "Otxoa-de-Amezaga, A. et al. Microglial cell loss after ischemic stroke favors brain neutrophil accumulation. Acta Neuropathol. 137, 321–341 (2019)."),[21](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR21 "Marino Lee, S., Hudobenko, J., McCullough, L. D. & Chauhan, A. Microglia depletion increase brain injury after acute ischemic stroke in aged mice. Exp. Neurol. 336, 113530 (2021)."),[22](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR22 "Hamner, M. A. et al. Microglial depletion abolishes ischemic preconditioning in white matter. Glia 70, 661–674 (2022)."). These conflicting findings underscore the need for further investigation into the impact of CSF1R inhibitors on the immune microenvironment in neurological diseases, as well as the identification of optimal treatment strategies.

After the cessation of microglia depletion, the vacant microglial niche can be rapidly replenished, either by resident microglia or by monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) in the case of bone marrow chimeras[23](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR23 "Bruttger, J. et al. Genetic Cell Ablation Reveals Clusters of Local Self-Renewing Microglia in the Mammalian Central Nervous System. Immunity 43, 92–106 (2015)."). These cells typically exhibit enhanced repair capabilities during niche occupation, which is a key factor contributing to the neural repair-promoting effects of CSF1R inhibitors[24](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR24 "Willis, E. F. et al. Repopulating Microglia Promote Brain Repair in an IL-6-Dependent Manner. Cell 180, 833–846.e816 (2020)."). Accumulating evidence underscores immune niche competition between MDMs and microglia[25](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR25 "Guilliams, M. & Scott, C. L. Does niche competition determine the origin of tissue-resident macrophages? Nat. Rev. Immunol. 17, 451–460 (2017)."). Under physiological conditions, the niche vacated due to partial microglial loss is replenished by the proliferation of remaining microglia[26](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR26 "Huang, Y. et al. Repopulated microglia are solely derived from the proliferation of residual microglia after acute depletion. Nat. Neurosci. 21, 530–540 (2018)."). However, in irradiated mice, compromised blood-brain barrier integrity and inhibited microglial proliferation lead to predominant filling of the niche by recruited MDMs[23](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR23 "Bruttger, J. et al. Genetic Cell Ablation Reveals Clusters of Local Self-Renewing Microglia in the Mammalian Central Nervous System. Immunity 43, 92–106 (2015)."),[27](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR27 "Cronk, J. C. et al. Peripherally derived macrophages can engraft the brain independent of irradiation and maintain an identity distinct from microglia. J. Exp. Med. 215, 1627–1647 (2018)."). Notably, MDMs undergo a transformation into microglia-like cells after infiltrating CNS and can exist in the brain for a long time with retained monocyte characteristics[28](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR28 "Lund, H. et al. Competitive repopulation of an empty microglial niche yields functionally distinct subsets of microglia-like cells. Nat. Commun. 9, 4845 (2018)."). Recent studies indicate that MDMs exhibit stronger phagocytic capacity compared to microglia[29](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR29 "Park, K. W. et al. Delayed Infiltration of Peripheral Monocyte Contributes to Phagocytosis and Transneuronal Degeneration in Chronic Stroke. Stroke 53, 2377–2388 (2022)."), and early MDMs infiltration may be beneficial to stroke repair[30](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR30 "Ritzel, R. M. et al. Functional differences between microglia and monocytes after ischemic stroke. J. Neuroinflammation 12, 106 (2015)."). Nevertheless, it remains unclear whether and how microglia attenuation affects cerebral immune niches and contributes to long-term brain recovery in ischemic stroke remains unknown.

In this study, we modulated immune niche competition by employing early-phase microglia attenuation after ischemic stroke, leading to a significant expansion of repair-related macrophages (RAMf) in the ischemic brain. Our findings revealed that RAMf originate from CCR2+ monocytes and acquire the reparative phenotype upon entering the brain. Employing single-cell RNA sequencing, flow cytometry, and lipidomics, we demonstrated that RAMf significantly contribute to remyelination and angiogenesis following ischemic stroke. Furthermore, we identified Mafb as a key transcription factor regulating the reparative phenotype in RAMf, and enhancing RAMf differentiation through Mafb overexpression markedly improved white matter and vascular integrity after ischemic stroke. These findings offer perspectives on the cellular and molecular aspects of immune niche competition in the context of ischemic stroke, paving the way for potential therapeutic strategies.

## Results

### Early-phase microglia attenuation alters the immune niche in ischemic stroke and promotes long-term stroke recovery

Numerous peripheral immune cells swiftly infiltrate into the brain following ischemic injury and play significant roles at different stages. Emerging evidence increasingly implicates a competition for the immune niche between peripheral immune cells and resident microglia[25](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#ref-CR25 "Guilliams, M. & Scott, C. L. Does niche competition determine the origin of tissue-resident macrophages? Nat. Rev. Immunol. 17, 451–460 (2017)."). Understanding this delicate balance in the context of ischemic stroke may yield valuable insights for novel therapeutic approaches.

In this study, we aim to resolve the changes of immune cell composition in the brain following inhibited microglial proliferation. A transient (60 min) middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) model was established in CCR2-GFP mice, which were then fed either with a CSF1R inhibitor PLX5622 chow or a control diet consecutively for 5 days (Fig.[1A](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#Fig1)). No significant difference in infarct volume was observed between the two groups of mice. Subsequently, we employed multiplex immunohistochemistry (mIHC) to identify immune cells, which demonstrated decreased Tmem119+ cells and accumulated CCR2+ cells in stroke mice treated with PLX5622 (Figs.[1B, C](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#Fig1), [S1A](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#MOESM1)). Flow cytometry analysis further confirmed that treatment with PLX5622 for 5 days reduced the number of CD45 low CD11b+ Ly6G- microglia by approximately 70% and increased the infiltration of macrophages at 5 days post-injury (dpi) (Fig.[S1B, C](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58254-y#MOESM1)).
