## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133)Abstract

Stroke is a leading cause of severe disability and mortality worldwide. Glial cells in the central nervous system (CNS) not only provide nutritional support but also play crucial roles in the inflammatory response. Microglia and astrocytes, integral components of the innate immune system, are involved in all stages of stroke and are active participants in inducing post-stroke neuroinflammation. Recent studies have increasingly focused on the potential crosstalk between microglia and astrocytes, identifying it as a promising area for understanding the pathogenesis and therapeutic mechanisms of CNS inflammatory diseases. These cells not only undergo dynamic phenotypic changes but also establish an intimate two-way dialogue by releasing various signaling molecules. This review paper elucidates the spatiotemporal dynamics of microglia and astrocytes in post-stroke neuroinflammation and highlights interaction pathways and potential therapeutic strategies for stroke.

**Keywords:**Ischemic stroke, hemorrhagic stroke, microglia, astrocytes, crosstalk, neuroinflammation, spatiotemporal dynamics, glia

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133)INTRODUCTION

1
Stroke is an acute cerebrovascular disease that significantly threatens human health and quality of life worldwide. It ranks as the second leading cause of death globally, following ischemic heart disease, and is the third leading cause of death and disability [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r1)]. In 2019, the incidence of stroke in China reached 276.7 cases per 100,000 population [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r2)]. Stroke is categorized into hemorrhagic stroke (HS, including intracerebral hemorrhage and subarachnoid hemorrhage) and ischemic stroke (IS). IS is the most common type of stroke, accounting for 87% of all stroke cases and 62.4% of global new cases in 2019 [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r2)].

Primary brain injury occurs immediately after stroke, essentially referring to mechanical brain damage, but it triggers a series of complex pathophysiological events, including cellular toxicity, neurotoxicity, oxidative and nitrosative stress, apoptosis, and inflammatory responses, leading to secondary brain injury (SBI) and further exacerbation [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r3)]. Neuroinflammation is a crucial process during stroke, involving a cascade immune response mediated by cellular and molecular components. This includes the activation of microglia, astrocytes, and endothelial cells, as well as infiltration of peripheral immune cells and the release of inflammatory factors [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r4), [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r5)]. Damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) are molecules released by stressed or damaged cells, recognized by pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) as danger signals. This recognition triggers innate immune responses and initiates inflammatory cascades [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r6)].

In HS, DAMPs originate from blood components in the subarachnoid space and/or brain parenchyma and by-products of plasma proteins (thrombin, fibrinolytic enzymes, _etc_.). In IS, DAMPs arise from dead and degenerated neurons due to the microvascular system and the blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r7), [8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r8)]. DAMPs activate innate and non-immune cells, release cytokines and chemokines, and recruit more inflammatory cells. These cells, in turn, upregulate and actively secrete more DAMPs, forming a positive feedback loop that amplifies the inflammatory response. Ultimately, this cascade leads to brain edema, secondary brain ischemia, ischemic-to-hemorrhagic transformation, neuronal apoptosis, and various forms of irreversible brain damage, resulting in serious adverse outcomes (Fig. **[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#F1)**) [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r9)-[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r11)].

Microglia and astrocytes play extensive and critical roles in the development of the CNS. Under physiological conditions, they maintain highly bidirectional communication, crucially regulating aspects such as cell numbers, synaptic transmission, and vascular development [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r12), [13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r13)]. Microglia can regulate the proliferation of astrocytes, influence astrocytic control over neuronal dependence, and affect neurotransmission [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r14), [15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r15)]. Astrocytes, in turn, recruit microglia and promote physiological functions of microglia associated with synapses and neural circuits [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r16)]. After stroke, microglia and astrocytes, as two major groups of reactive glial cells, become activated and polarized, exhibiting close interaction in neuroinflammation. Although previous studies have shown interactions and cascading amplification between microglia and astrocytes in neuroinflammation [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r17), [18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r18)], the mechanisms of crosstalk between them in post-stroke neuroinflammation require further elucidation. In this review, we discuss the pathophysiological changes of microglia and astrocytes after stroke, emphasizing the complex communication between these two cells in neuroinflammation and potential therapeutic strategies related to their crosstalk, providing valuable insights and targets for the pathological research and clinical treatment of stroke.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133)MICROGLIA AND POST-STROKE NEUROINFLAMMATION

2
### Physiological Function of Microglia

2.1
Microglia originate from primitive myeloid progenitor cells within the yolk sac and migrate to the CNS during development, constituting 10-15% of neuroglial cells [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r19)]. They maintain homeostasis of the CNS, phagocytize dead cells or cellular debris, participate in synaptic remodeling and pruning, regulate neuronal connections, and repair damage [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r20)].

As regulatory cells in neuroimmune responses, microglia participate in inflammatory reactions and respond rapidly, acting as scavengers. In the resting state, microglia are inactive, with stationary cell bodies and highly branched processes that establish direct communication with other nerve cells and blood vessels for immune surveillance. However, when confronted with pathological stimuli, microglia become activated and respond swiftly to perform inflammatory functions. They transition from a highly branched morphology to amoeboid cells to cope with various challenges [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r21)].

### The Pathophysiology of Microglia in Post-Stroke Neuroinflammation

2.2
The response of microglia to different stages of stroke can be characterized by changes in their morphological function and polarization. Polarization is a phenotypic change in microglia induced by pathological stimulation, mainly including the “classically activated” M1 phenotype or the “selectively activated” M2 phenotype, which plays a dual role in the pro-inflammatory/anti-inflammatory and injury/repair processes [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r22)]. Activation of M1 microglia promotes inflammatory response and leads to neurotoxicity, usually induced by lipopolysaccharide (LPS), Toll-like receptors (TLRs), and interferon-γ [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r23), [24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r24)]. Conversely, M2 microglia exhibit anti-inflammatory effects, participating in debris clearance and tissue repair after injury, and are usually induced by IL-4, IL-13, and TGF-β [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r25)]. Apart from stroke, they are also well-represented in a wide range of neurodegenerative and neurotrauma-induced pathologies. Recent research has found that in addition to the classical pro- and anti-inflammatory phenotypes, there are more complex activation states, including dynamically balanced microglia expressing _Tmem 119_ and _Hexb_, as well as other subtypes related to neural repair and stroke-associated microglia (SAM) with antioxidant properties [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r26), [27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r27)]. Although this binary classification is too simplistic due to the overlapping functional states and complex, evolved phenotypes of microglia, we continue to use the M1/M2 phenotype in this article for ease of understanding.

After stroke, microglia undergo temporal and spatial changes and can be activated and change their cellular morphology within minutes [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r28), [29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r29)]. During acute phases (<1 day), activation of microglia in the ischemic region first appeared around the lesion and correlated closely with the extent of neuronal damage. Thirty minutes after the onset of permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion (pMCAO), activated microglia were observed at the periphery of the ischemic lesion, characterized by enlarged cell bodies and thickened processes. Over time, microglia spread more widely and gradually extended into the cortex, peaking at 48 h [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r30)]. Activation of microglia could be observed 3.5 h after MCAO reperfusion, whereas microglia in the ischemic core appear 12 h later [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r31)].

In subacute and chronic phases, microglia undergo dynamic phenotypic changes. Perego _et al._ [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r32)] observed in pMCAO that microglia showed different morphologies and functions at different time intervals. 24 h after ischemic injury, microglia were activated, showing a branched morphology in the peri-infarct region and an amoeboid morphology in the ischemic core. The rounded microglia were widespread in the ischemic area, likely corresponding to recruited peripheral immune cells. CD68 microglia were initially present at the border area and infiltrated the core area by 7 days, displaying characteristics of phagocytic cells that phagocyte neurons. Markers of M2 microglia (Ym1 and CD206) appeared abundantly in the ischemic core as early as 24 h after injury, with their protective effects persisting for at least 7 days before declining. In MCAO mice, researchers observed consistent expression levels of M1 microglial markers CD32 and pro-inflammatory cytokines (such as IL-1β and TNF-α), significantly increased by day 3, peaked at day 14, followed by a decrease and maintaining stability in the ischemic border area; whereas CD206 and Ym1/2 peaked at day 7 and declined rapidly thereafter [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r33)]. Similarly, Hu _et al._ [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r34)] found that in transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) mice, the gene expression level of M2 microglia was detected at 1-3 days after ischemia, peaked at 3-5 days, decreased at 7 days, and returned to the pre-injury level by day 14. In contrast, the gene expression of M1 microglia was initially low, starting to rise by day 3 and persisting until 14 days after ischemia. Shu _et al._ [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r35)] also showed that microglia tended to be polarized into M2 phenotype 3 days after tMCAO.

However, in HS, microglia appear to exhibit an opposite polarization trend as in IS. During acute phases, the activation of microglia first occurred at 1 h after collagenase injection [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r36)] and 4 h after autologous blood injection [[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r37)]. Activated microglia participate in hematoma phagocytosis. _In vitro_ experiments indicate that a single microglial cell can phagocytize multiple red blood cells in a very short time, and with the increase of microglial density, multinucleated giant microglia/macrophages may appear around the hematoma and the surrounding area [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r38), [39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r39)]. In a collagenase-induced ICH model, Yang _et al._ [[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r40)] found that amoeboid microglia at the hemorrhagic center exhibited an M1 phenotype and selectively secreted IL-1β. Wan _et al._ [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r41)] discovered that in ICH constructed by autologous blood injection, M1 microglia were activated early, appeared at 4 h, persistently highly expressed for 1-3 days, and declined after 7 days. In a collagenase-induced ICH model, Lan _et al._ [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r42)] observed a significant increase in M1 (CD16/32+) microglia from 24 to 72 h, albeit with a reduced proportion due to a substantial increase in M2 (Ym-1+) microglia. In subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), Zheng _et al._ [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r43)] observed a dynamic polarization process of microglia from M1 to M2 phenotypes, with morphological changes from ramified (1-3 days, M1) to spindle-shaped (bipolar microglia expressing both M1 and M2 markers) and finally to amoeboid shape (5-10 days, M2). Gris _et al._ [[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r44)] found in their study that IL-6 levels rapidly increased in both SAH patients and experimental SAH models.

In summary, the ratio of M1/M2 changes dynamically. Microglia transition from the dominant state of M2 to M1 in IS and M1 to M2 in HS (Fig. **[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#F2)**). This also reflects the difference between HS and IS in neuroinflammation, that is, in the early stage inflammatory response is heavier in HS, while ischemia and hypoxia is heavier in IS. Although there is an inflammatory response in IS, the main role may be to promote repair and neuroprotection. With the increase of time and the accumulation of inflammatory factors, neuroinflammation will further aggravate. However, to date, the exact timing and triggers of the phenotypic changes remain unknown. Different models of stroke, the degree of bleeding/infarction, and the size of the lesion are all factors affecting M1 and M2 polarization. In addition, aging gender has also been shown to influence phenotypic changes [[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r45), [46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r46)]. Therefore, it is important to assess the time course of M1 and M2 polarization after stroke to further investigate the timing of the most efficient transition to phenotypes, in order to select the optimal temporal switch to reduce inflammation and improve neurological outcomes.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133)ASTROCYTES AND POST-STROKE NEUROINFLAMMATION

3
### Physiological Function of Astrocytes

3.1
Astrocytes originate from glial cells of neural precursors and are the most abundant in the CNS, accounting for approximately 20-40% of glial cells [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r47)]. In the past, astrocytes were considered as a “glue-” like function, providing structural and nutritional support for neurons. In recent years, more and more functions have been elucidated. Astrocytes are the main cells in the neurovascular unit and are essential for the formation and growth of cerebrovascular beds and the maintenance of neurovascular function [[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r48)]. Astrocytes regulate the release of active molecules such as glutamate (Glu) and adenosine and modulate the excitability and synaptic transmission of neurons. They also control the strength and plasticity of synapses through gap junctions and provide cellular connections between neuronal circuits and blood vessels, which are helpful in regulating local blood flow, maintaining the dynamic balance of extracellular fluid, responding to neuronal activities, and coordinating glucose metabolism [[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r49)].

### The Pathophysiology of Astrocytes in Post-Stroke Neuroinflammation

3.2
After stroke, under the stimulation of microglia and inflammatory factors, astrocytes are activated and then rapidly proliferate and become hypertrophic, leading to reactive astrocytosis. This is a graded reaction characterized by the increased expression of intermediate filament proteins, including glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), vimentin, and nestin [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r50)]. GFAP is a structural protein, and its expression changes are associated with the proliferation intensity of reactive astrocytes. Within the time window of 2-6 h after stroke, GFAP levels can distinguish between IS and early ICH [[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r51)]. In the early stages of IS, aquaporins (AQPs) regulate the rapid membrane expansion and transport of water, causing astrocytes to swell, which leads to the increase of intracranial pressure and the decrease of cerebral blood flow [[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r52)]. After HS, blood extravasation activates the coagulation cascade to produce thrombin, which not only leads to the formation of perihematoma edema but also triggers the sustained activation of protease-activated receptor PAR1 in astrocytes. This activation induces rapid remodeling of astrocyte processes adjacent to glutamatergic synapses, including contraction, flattening, proliferation, and foot processes away from excitatory glutamatergic synapses, potentially affecting long-term neuroplasticity and exacerbating brain injury [[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r53)].

Reactive astrocytes play a dual role at different stages of stroke. On one hand, they release a large number of inflammatory factors, MMPs, and chemokines to aggravate inflammation and induce neuronal death; on the other hand, they release trophic factors, lipoxins A4 and B4, excitatory amino acids to inhibit neuroinflammation, and regulate the production of microglial inflammatory mediators to promote neuroprotection, exert anti-inflammatory effects and promote synaptic formation and neuronal survival [[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r54), [55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r55)]. After stroke, reactive astrocytes usually present two subtypes: the pro-inflammatory A1 phenotype and the anti-inflammatory A2 phenotype. With the deepening of research, the phenotypes of astrocytes are gradually enriched, and according to their differences in gene expression, they can present a variety of activation states from pro-inflammatory to anti-inflammatory rather than simple A1 and A2 polarized phenotypes [[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r56)]. Therefore, we used a pro-inflammatory/anti-inflammatory description in place of the A1/A2 phenotype.

After stroke, astrocytes preferentially differentiate into a “pro-inflammatory” phenotype rather than an “anti-inflammatory” phenotype. In the tMCAO mice, within 14 days, the number of perifocal regions C3d+/GFAP+ cells in the marginal area of ischemic focus increased gradually, and the expression of inflammatory factors such as TNF and IL-6 increased. On day 3 after the stroke, a large number of pro-inflammatory astrocytes were wrapped around the blood vessel wall and destroyed the integrity of the BBB [[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r57)]. In MCAO, the number of pro-inflammatory astrocytes in the penumbra of cerebral ischemia increased continuously to the peak on day 14, and the appearance of anti-inflammatory astrocytes was delayed, peaked on day 7, and decreased on day 14 [[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r58)]. In the tMCAO model, researchers found that after 72 h, the anti-inflammatory-related transcription predominated over the pro-inflammatory-specific transcripts, suggesting neuroprotective effects [[59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r59)]. After ICH, the pro-inflammatory astrocyte marker C3 was active and peaked on day 3 [[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r60)]. After experimental SAH, the continuous increase of C3 level indicated that astrocytes preferentially differentiated into a pro-inflammatory phenotype [[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r61), [62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r62)]. Obviously, the trend of morphology and phenotype of astrocytes after HS and IS is consistent in time and space, but the transformation and peak time of pro-inflammatory/anti-inflammatory phenotype may be affected by different models and disease severity.

Within days after injury, around the lesion, activated astrocytes further form glial scar by secreting extracellular matrix molecules to participate in the regulation of neuroinflammation. Glial scar is a network formed by glial cell processes and thin filament proteins in plasma, whose formation is highly dependent on hypertrophy, proliferation, and cellular overlap of microglia and astrocytes [[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r63)]. Finally, abundant proliferating astrocytes form glial scars between damaged areas and healthy tissue. In the early stages, it reduces excitotoxicity by siphoning K+ and Glu uptake. By forming physical and functional walls around the lesion, the glial scar closes the injured site, regulates the plasticity of nerves, and controls the local immune response in space and time to inhibit the spread of inflammation [[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r64)]. However, in the late stages, the uncontrolled proliferation of glial scars releases pro-inflammatory factors and expresses a series of molecules that inhibit neuronal migration and axonal regeneration, such as chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPGs), which is not conducive to nerve regeneration [[65](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r65)]. Therefore, the heterogeneity of phenotype and function of reactive astrocytes after stroke affects the progress of inflammation.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133)MICROGLIA-ASTROCYTE CROSSTALK PROMOTES POST-STROKE NEUROINFLAMMATION

4
### Microglia Activate Pro-Inflammatory Astrocytes

4.1
Microglia are more sensitive to pathogens/damage, whereas astrocyte responses are usually delayed and cannot be fully activated in the absence of microglia [[66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r66)]. After a stroke, microglia preferentially respond to pathological stimuli and secrete IL-1α, TNF-α, and C1q after activation, triggering reactive signals of astrocytes through soluble and membrane-bound signaling molecules, inducing their transformation into pro-inflammatory astrocytes. This leads to neuronal and oligodendrocyte death and forms a neuroinflammatory cascade [[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r54), [67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r67), [68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r68)]. Whether through acute CNS injury or systemic LPS injection, microglial activation induces pure pro-inflammatory astrocytes both _in vitro_ and _in vivo_ [[67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r67)]. C1q is one of the initiating molecules of the classical complement activation pathway, which produces chemotactic C3a and C5a through the complement cascade. On one hand, this attracts neutrophils and monocytes to migrate to the lesion and activates cells to release more inflammatory mediators. On the other hand, it activates astrocytes toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype and contributes to synaptic toxicity [[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r69), [70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r70)]. Astrocytes express the class F scavenger receptor Megf10, a receptor for C1q, and can clear apoptotic neurons through the Megf10/C1q pathway [[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r71)]. However, under pathological conditions, C1q levels rise sharply, temporarily increasing ROS and NO levels, promoting pro-inflammatory cytokines, and leading to neuronal death [[72](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r72)]. Additionally, astrocytes release C3a, which binds to the C3a receptors (C3aR) on microglia, thereby triggering microglial secretion of more C1q and pro-inflammatory factors [[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r73)]. Deleting C1q in microglia not only prevents the deposition of C3a on astrocytes but also reduces the upregulation of TLR4 in microglia [[74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r74)]. Activated microglia also release interleukin, monocyte chemotaxis protein-1 (MCP-1), and macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF), which is crucial in the initial triggering and regulation of astrocytes during acute phases [[75](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r75)].

TNF-α and IL-1 not only act as inflammatory factors to trigger reactive astrogliosis but also act as a pro-inflammatory signal amplifier in microglia-astrocytes crosstalk, amplified by the unique physiological structure of astrocytes. In experimental stroke models, TNF-α and IL-1 were overexpressed as early as 2 h after ICH and 24 h after IS [[76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r76), [77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r77)]. Astrocytes express IL-1β receptor (IL-1R) [[78](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r78)], and IL-1 stimulates the expression of GFAP and hypertrophy of astrocytes, indicating its important role in mediating astrocyte activation [[79](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r79)]. TNF-α receptors exist in astrocytes, and their activation can inhibit the excitatory amino acid transporter (EAAT) on astrocytes, causing increased extracellular Glu concentrations and neurotoxicity, promoting calcium influx and cellular overload. Simultaneously, they activate microglial-mGluR2, promote further release of TNF-α, and exacerbate inflammatory response [[80](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r80), [81](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r81)].

SDF-1α, also known as CXC chemokine ligand 12 (CXCL12), and its receptor CXCR4 have been reported to be upregulated in cerebral ischemic penumbra tissue, which attracts inflammatory cells to release pro-inflammatory factors and aggravate brain injury [[82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r82), [83](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r83)]. SDF-1α is a known stimulator of astrocyte proliferation [[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r84)]. Studies have confirmed that astrocytes are involved in SDF-1α/CXCR4 autocrine/paracrine signaling [[85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r85)]. After a stroke, TNF-α amplifies the Glu release cascade through SDF-1α/CXCR4, increases neuronal excitotoxicity, promotes the continuous release of pro-inflammatory mediators (TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6) from microglia and astrocytes, and positively feedback regulates the neuroinflammatory microenvironment [[86](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r86), [87](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r87)]. The release of TNF-α stimulates microglia to express high levels of HMGB1 and TLR4, increases inflammatory cytokines and NF-κB activity, and promotes the response of astrocytes [[88](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r88)].

In addition to pro-inflammatory cytokines, mitochondria may become a new mechanism of glial cell interactions in neuroinflammation. Mitochondrial fission and fusion, as the basis of mitochondrial quality control, regulate the activity and function of glial cells, ensuring the dynamic equilibrium state of mitochondria in response to changes in stress conditions [[89](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r89)]. After the stroke, excessive mitochondrial fission triggers apoptosis, which is mediated by dynamin-associated protein 1 (Drp1). The key process is the phosphorylation of Drp1 and its subsequent relocalization to the outer mitochondrial membrane and binding to the Fis1 receptor, which subsequently promotes microglia-induced neuroinflammation [[90](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r90), [91](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r91)]. Mitochondrial morphology becomes discontinuous after accelerated fission, leading to mitochondrial fragmentation, and these microglial extracellular mitochondria activated by DAMPs are a driving force for the progression of secondary neuronal damage, participating in communication with astrocytes [[92](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r92)]. Recent research showed that under pathological conditions, DAMPs and neurotoxic proteins further activated microglia, induced excessive mitochondrial fission mediated by Drp1/fis1, and mitochondrial dysfunction. This released fragmented extracellular mitochondria and generated diffusion signals to astrocytes into a neurotoxic phenotype, exacerbating pathogenic inflammation [[93](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r93)]. Liu _et al._ [[94](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r94)] found that in tMCAO, M1 microglia released damaged and unhealthy mitochondrial debris, transferred to neurons, and fused with neuronal mitochondria, deteriorating neurological prognosis. To date, the potential interaction of intercellular mitochondrial transmission in glia-glia and glia-neuron after stroke remains unclear and warrants further investigation.

### Activated Astrocytes Induce M1 Microglia

4.2
Astrocytes activated by microglia lose many physiological functions and release inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, ATP, and specific proteins that act on microglia, thus forming a paracrine feedback loop that aggravates neuroinflammation.

#### IL-17A/IL-17RA

4.2.1
IL-17A and its receptor IL-17RA are involved in post-stroke inflammation and disruption of the BBB. IL-17A belongs to the IL-17 family (IL-17A~IL-17F), which is a major inflammatory mediator and can induce the expression of inflammatory genes [[95](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r95)]. Astrocytes are the main source of IL-17A production. During acute phases of stroke, IL-17A is involved in microglial activation and neuroinflammation, promoting the expression of TNF-α, IL-1β, and other inflammatory factors and downstream signaling molecule NF-κB p65 [[96](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r96), [97](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r97)]. IL-17A also induces chemokines CXCL1 and CXCL2 to participate in the expansion and recruitment of neutrophils, which aggravates neuroinflammation [[98](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r98), [99](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r99)]. IL-17RA exists on the surface of microglia and is the main target of the IL-17 signaling pathway [[100](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r100), [101](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r101)]. Studies have shown that the knockdown of IL-17A significantly reduces the activation of microglia and promotes their transformation to the M2 phenotype [[102](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r102)]. Therefore, the IL-17A/IL-17RA pathway induces the formation of M1 microglia after stroke.

#### IL-15/IL-15R

4.2.2
IL-15 is a cytokine that regulates the proliferation, chemotaxis, and survival of immune cells. In the inflammatory CNS, IL-15 is mainly derived from astrocytes [[103](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r103), [104](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r104)]. IL-15 is a factor specifically upregulated after stroke and acts as an immune enhancement regulator. Studies have shown that astrocyte-derived IL-15 in the ischemic brain promotes the migration of T cells to inflammatory tissues, affects the activation and effector function of CD8+ T cells and NK cells, aggravates brain damage, and knockdown of IL-15 improves the immune response of the damaged brain [[103](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r103), [105](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r105), [106](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r106)]. In addition, IL-15 can enhance the Th1 response after acute cerebral ischemia, which is manifested by an increase in the number of CD4+ T cells [[105](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r105)]. The IL-15 receptor (IL-15R) is a heterotrimeric receptor composed of three chains: IL-15Rα, IL-2/IL15Rβ, and γc [[107](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r107)]. Intracellular IL-15 transmits signals through a “trans-presentation” mode, binding to high-affinity IL-15Rα to form a complex, triggering signal transduction through IL-15Rβ and γc on neighboring cells [[108](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r108)]. Microglia express IL-15R and thus could be receptive to IL-15 from astrocytes to form crosstalk [[109](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r109)]. Recent studies have shown that IL-15 plays a mediator in microglia-astrocyte crosstalk after ICH, increasing the expression of CD86, IL-1β, and TNF-α from microglia and skewing microglia toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype. Astrocyte-derived IL-15 mainly affects the response of microglia. After the elimination of microglia, the aggravation of brain injury caused by IL-15 is attenuated [[110](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r110)].

#### CCL2/CCR2

4.2.3
Chemokine ligand 2 (CCL2), also known as MCP-1, is the main endogenous agonist of CCR2 and is involved in the inflammatory response after CNS injury. In neuroinflammation, CCL2 is mainly derived from astrocytes and can bind to CCR2 to induce microglial activation [[111](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r111), [112](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r112)]. After stroke, CCL2/CCR2 induces microglial recruitment, increases leukocyte infiltration and the expression of inflammatory mediators, further aggravates damage to the BBB, and leads to brain edema and neuronal death [[113](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r113), [114](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r114)]. Microglia express CCR2 [[115](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r115)]. In _in vitro_ cell culture experiments, TNF-α stimulation causes astrocytes to release a large amount of CCL2, which enhances the ability of microglia to migrate to the site of injury through the CCL2/CCR2 pathway and induces their polarization to the M1 phenotype. The above phenomenon is inhibited after CCL2 siRNA or the use of CCR2 inhibitors [[116](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r116)].

#### GM-CSF/GM-CSFR

4.2.4
Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) is mainly produced by astrocytes, which is a potent activator of microglia and participates in the pro-inflammatory process [[111](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r111), [117](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r117)]. GM-CSF exerts its biological function by binding to the GM-CSF receptor complex. GM-CSFR is highly expressed in microglia in the CNS [[118](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r118)]. GM-CSF can cross the BBB and may mediate the pathogenic effects of neuroinflammation [[119](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r119)]. Although GM-CSF itself can not induce the secretion of classic inflammatory cytokines like IL-1β or TNF-α, it can be achieved by acting directly or indirectly on microglia. GM-CSF promotes microglial migration through the upregulation of cathepsin, MMP-9, -11, and -12, thereby triggering excessive inflammatory responses [[120](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r120)]. Studies have shown that GM-CSF increases the expression of TLR4 and CD14 in microglia by activating ERK1/2 and p38 and promotes neuroinflammation by increasing the production of LPS-induced inflammatory mediators (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, NO) [[118](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r118)]. In a microglia-astrocyte co-culture system, GM-CSF stimulates the proliferation of microglia _in vitro_ and induces polarization of M1 microglia [[121](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r121)].

#### S100B Protein

4.2.5
S100B, a member of the S100 protein family, is predominantly expressed in astrocytes in the brain. It is an alarm protein released during brain injury and acts as an intracellular regulator and extracellular signal and participates in various cellular processes such as cell proliferation, differentiation, apoptosis, inflammation and metabolism [[122](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r122), [123](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r123)]. Under physiological conditions, S100B has trophic effects on neurons and promotes Glu uptake. However, it increases after stroke, inducing migration and morphological changes of microglia, upregulating the expression of pro-inflammatory transcription factors, and stimulating the release of MMP-9 and NO, leading to cytotoxic effects and SBI [[124](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r124)]. Extracellular S100B may upregulate chemokine expression through RAGE and stimulate microglial migration, thus participating in the dissemination of inflammation in the brain [[125](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r125)]. Zhou _et al._ [[126](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r126)] showed that in MCAO, S100B induced excessive production of INOS and high-level release of NO, activated NF-κB, promoted the polarization and migration of M1 microglia, and aggravated inflammatory damage after cerebral ischemia. The study found that the administration of Arundic Acid (AA) to inhibit S100B could prevent the increase in microglial activation after injury [[127](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r127)].

#### Connectin 43

4.2.6
Connexin 43 (Cx43), composed of gap junction and hemichannel functional units, is one of the main gap junction proteins in astrocytes, involved in maintaining cellular and tissue homeostasis [[128](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r128)]. In the early stages of stroke, Cx43 is involved in indirect interactions between astrocytes and microglia, mediated through a vicious cycle involving Cx43 hemichannel activation. On one hand, activated microglia release pro-inflammatory factors (such as TNF-α and IL-1β), increasing the permeability of astrocytic Cx43 hemichannels, leading to the release of ATP, Ca 2+, and Glu, and regulating downstream signaling intermediates (including STAT3, p38 MAPK, NF-κB), thereby enhancing the proliferation of reactive astrocytes and activation of M1 microglia, intensifying pro-inflammatory activity [[129](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r129), [130](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r130)]. On the other hand, ATP can activate purinergic receptors, known as P2 receptors, to enable the continuous activity of the inflammasome in various brain cell types, including microglia, promote the spread of ischemic brain injury, and aggravate neuroinflammatory injury [[131](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r131)]. After a stroke, P2X7 receptors on microglia are activated by ATP, triggering the release of IL-1β, IL-18, and TNF-α, promoting apoptosis and contributing to deep ion imbalance during neuronal death [[132](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r132), [133](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r133)]. Recently, researchers have developed genetically encoded fluorescent sensors for monitoring the spatiotemporal dynamics of ATP _in vivo_. Results indicated functional specialization and coordination between astrocytes and microglia, with astrocytes sensing damage and encoding injury information and microglia subsequently decoding this information to adapt to various stimuli and drive changes in their activation states [[134](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r134)].

#### PRDX6-iPLA2

4.2.7
Peroxiredoxin 6 (PRDX6) is the sole 1-Cys member of the peroxiredoxin family, functioning as a dual enzyme with glutathione peroxidase and Ca 2+-independent phospholipase A2 (iPLA2) activities. Increasing evidence suggests that PRDX6 is predominantly expressed in astrocytes [[135](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r135), [136](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r136)]. In primary cultured astrocytes, the iPLA2 activity of PRDX6 induces its own proliferation and increases pro-inflammatory factors [[137](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r137)]. Shanshan _et al._ [[138](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r138)] observed in OGD/R co-cultures of microglia/neurons and in the MCAO model that PRDX6-iPLA2 is associated with the secretion of neurotoxic inflammatory mediators in microglia, potentially regulating neuroinflammation _via_ TLR2/4. Downregulation of PRDX6-iPLA2 significantly mitigates neuronal damage in co-cultures. Recently, Peng _et al._ [[139](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r139)] found that after cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury, PRDX6-iPLA2 activity is significantly upregulated in astrocytes, inducing ROS production and further promoting M1 microglial polarization, revealing the mechanisms of astrocyte-microglia crosstalk and oxidative stress-neuroinflammation crosstalk. Future research should explore how PRDX6 serves as a multifaceted communicator between astrocytes, neurons, microglia, and other brain cells.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133)MICROGLIA-ASTROCYTE CROSSTALK REPAIRS POST-STROKE NEUROINFLAMMATION

5
The inhibition of inflammation between microglia and astrocytes can be achieved through cytokines, transcription factors, specific proteins, extracellular vesicles, and mitochondria.

### Microglia Regulate Astrocytes

5.1
#### IL-10/IL-10R

5.1.1
IL-10 is a key anti-inflammatory cytokine, produced not only by Th2 cells or Treg cells but also acts as a feedback modulator of various immune responses [[140](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r140)]. In IS, IL-10 is produced by regulatory T cells, macrophages, and microglia [[141](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r141)]. In ICH, microglia-derived IL-10 can trigger a series of intracellular signal transduction events, activating signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3)-dependent pathway to accelerate hematoma clearance and inhibit the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines [[142](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r142), [143](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r143)]. Clinical trials have shown that IL-10 can serve as an independent predictor for stroke-related infections and may predict the prognosis in patients with acute IS [[144](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645133#r144), [145](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1

This is a review article published in Current Neuropharmacology (April 25, 2025) titled "Microglia-Astrocyte Crosstalk in Post-Stroke Neuroinflammation: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Strategies" by Tong Shang, Binglin Kuang, Yaxin Shang, and Wei Zou (corresponding author) from the First Affiliated Hospital of Heilongjiang University of Chinese Medicine, Harbin, China. The paper is open access under CC BY 4.0 (PMCID: PMC12645133, PMID: 40289984).

KEY FINDINGS:

1. Stroke Epidemiology: Stroke is the second leading cause of death globally and third leading cause of death and disability. In 2019, China's stroke incidence was 276.7 cases per 100,000. Ischemic stroke (IS) accounts for 87% of all stroke cases and 62.4% of global new cases in 2019. Stroke is categorized into hemorrhagic (HS, including intracerebral hemorrhage and subarachnoid hemorrhage) and ischemic types.

2. Microglia in Post-Stroke Neuroinflammation: Microglia originate from primitive myeloid progenitors in the yolk sac, constituting 10-15% of neuroglial cells. They polarize into M1 (pro-inflammatory, induced by LPS, TLRs, IFN-γ) and M2 (anti-inflammatory, induced by IL-4, IL-13, TGF-β) phenotypes. After ischemic stroke, microglia transition from M2 to M1 dominance; in hemorrhagic stroke, the opposite occurs (M1 to M2). Activation occurs within minutes after stroke (30 min after pMCAO onset; 3.5 h after MCAO reperfusion). M1 markers (CD32, IL-1β, TNF-α) significantly increase by day 3 and peak at day 14; M2 markers (CD206, Ym1/2) peak at day 7 and decline rapidly. In HS, microglial activation occurs at 1 h (collagenase injection) or 4 h (autologous blood injection). Other subtypes include Tmem119/Hexb-expressing microglia and stroke-associated microglia (SAM).

3. Astrocytes in Post-Stroke Neuroinflammation: Astrocytes are the most abundant CNS glial cells (20-40% of glial cells). After stroke, they undergo reactive astrocytosis with increased GFAP, vimentin, and nestin expression. GFAP levels within 2-6 h can distinguish IS from early ICH. They polarize into pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory phenotypes (formerly A1/A2). Pro-inflammatory astrocyte marker C3 peaked on day 3 after ICH. Reactive astrocytes form glial scars, which initially reduce excitotoxicity but later inhibit neuronal migration and axonal regeneration via CSPGs.

4. Crosstalk Mechanisms Promoting Neuroinflammation (Microglia→Astrocytes): Microglia secrete IL-1α, TNF-α, and C1q to induce pro-inflammatory astrocyte transformation. C1q activates the complement pathway (C3a/C5a), attracting neutrophils/monocytes and promoting synaptic toxicity. Astrocytes express Megf10 (C1q receptor). TNF-α and IL-1 act as signal amplifiers, overexpressed as early as 2 h after ICH and 24 h after IS. SDF-1α/CXCR4 signaling amplifies Glu release cascades and inflammatory mediators. Mitochondrial fragmentation via Drp1/Fis1-mediated fission releases extracellular mitochondria that activate neurotoxic astrocyte phenotypes.

5. Crosstalk Mechanisms Promoting Neuroinflammation (Astrocytes→Microglia): Several pathways induce M1 microglial polarization:
- IL-17A/IL-17RA: Astrocytes are the main source of IL-17A; knockdown reduces microglial activation and promotes M2 transformation.
- IL-15/IL-15R: Astrocyte-derived IL-15 promotes T cell migration, CD8+ T cell/NK activation; mediates microglia-astrocyte crosstalk in ICH, skewing microglia toward pro-inflammatory phenotype.
- CCL2/CCR2 (MCP-1): TNF-α stimulation causes astrocytic CCL2 release, enhancing microglial migration and M1 polarization; inhibited by CCL2 siRNA or CCR2 inhibitors.
- GM-CSF/GM-CSFR: Astrocyte-derived GM-CSF promotes microglial migration and M1 polarization via ERK1/2 and p38 pathways, upregulating TLR4 and CD14.
- S100B: Increases after stroke, induces microglial migration, M1 polarization, and NO release via NF-κB; Arundic Acid (AA) inhibits this.
- Connexin 43 (Cx43): Hemichannel activation releases ATP, Ca2+, and Glu, enhancing reactive astrocyte proliferation and M1 microglial activation.
- PRDX6-iPLA2: Predominantly expressed in astrocytes; activity upregulated after ischemia-reperfusion, inducing ROS production and M1 microglial polarization.

6. Crosstalk Mechanisms for Repair (Anti-inflammatory): IL-10/IL-10R signaling is key. Microglia-derived IL-10 activates STAT3-dependent pathways to accelerate hematoma clearance and inhibit pro-inflammatory cytokine production. IL-10 can serve as an independent predictor for stroke-related infections and prognosis in acute IS patients.

CONCLUSION: Understanding the spatiotemporal dynamics and bidirectional crosstalk between microglia and astrocytes in post-stroke neuroinflammation provides valuable therapeutic targets for stroke treatment. The review emphasizes the need to assess M1/M2 polarization timing to select optimal temporal switches for reducing inflammation and improving neurological outcomes. Factors affecting polarization include stroke model, bleeding/infarction degree, lesion size, aging, and gender.

"IS is the most common type of stroke, accounting for 87% of all stroke cases and 62.4% of global new cases in 2019." "Microglia transition from the dominant state of M2 to M1 in IS and M1 to M2 in HS." "After a stroke, microglia preferentially respond to pathological stimuli and secrete IL-1α, TNF-α, and C1q after activation, triggering reactive signals of astrocytes through soluble and membrane-bound signaling molecules, inducing their transformation into pro-inflammatory astrocytes." "Clinical trials have shown that IL-10 can serve as an independent predictor for stroke-related infections and may predict the prognosis in patients with acute IS."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific research article published in Stroke (2015, Vol. 46, Issue 10, pages 2916–2925) examining the role of neutrophils in exacerbating ischemic brain injury in hyperlipidemic mice. The study was conducted by researchers from the University Hospital Essen (Germany), the University of Utah School of Medicine, and the University Duisburg-Essen.

--- SOURCE 14: Neutrophil extracellular traps in ischemic stroke - PMC - NIH ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12463598

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Frontiers in Neurology (September 12, 2025, Vol 16, article 1641985) examining the role of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in ischemic stroke. Authors Wenbo He, Zuoli Wu, Ying Liu, and Ziming Ye (from Nanning, China) review the mechanisms, clinical implications, and therapeutic potential of NETs in stroke pathology.

Key findings from the review:

**What are NETs?** NETs are web-like structures composed of decondensed DNA, histones, and granular enzymes released by activated neutrophils. While essential for host defense, their dysregulated formation in the cerebral microvasculature drives a vicious cycle of tissue injury.

**Core detrimental effects in stroke:**
1. **Promoting stable, lysis-resistant thrombi** - The dense DNA/histone/enzyme scaffold creates physically robust thrombi resistant to fibrin-centric lytic agents like recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (r-tPA). High NET content in retrieved thrombi is significantly associated with unsuccessful recanalization (mTICI <2b) and prolonged procedure times during mechanical thrombectomy.
2. **Compromising blood-brain barrier integrity** - NET-associated proteases (neutrophil elastase, matrix metalloproteinases) degrade tight junction proteins and basement membrane; NET histones are directly cytotoxic to endothelial cells.
3. **Amplifying neuroinflammation** - NET DNA and histones act as DAMPs, activating microglia and astrocytes, triggering a cytokine storm that recruits more neutrophils, perpetuating a vicious cycle.

**Mechanisms of NETosis:**
- Upstream triggers: ROS burst from ischemia-reperfusion, DAMPs (especially HMGB1), and platelet-neutrophil interactions
- Two pathways: (1) NADPH oxidase-dependent classical lytic pathway; (2) PAD4-dependent pathway involving histone citrullination and chromatin decondensation

**Clinical evidence:**
- NET levels are significantly elevated in acute ischemic stroke patients, particularly those over 65 with atrial fibrillation or cardioembolic sources
- NET formation peaks within 24h post-stroke, declining by 48h in murine models
- Older, more organized thrombi contain higher NET burdens; thrombus age was the sole independent predictor of NET content
- Systemic comorbidities (diabetes, obesity) "prime" circulating neutrophils, making them hyper-responsive and predisposed to exaggerated NETosis upon stroke onset via gut dysbiosis and meta-inflammation mechanisms

**Therapeutic strategies (Table 1):**
1. Inhibiting NET formation - PAD4 inhibitors (e.g., chloroquine), tetrahydroisoquinolines
2. Degrading existing NETs - DNase I (but limited efficacy in fibrin-rich thrombi as monotherapy)
3. Physical removal - therapeutic apheresis for circulating NETs
4. EV-based indirect modulation - astrocyte/microglia-derived extracellular vesicles that can cross the BBB

**Biomarkers:** NET markers (H3Cit, cfDNA, NE-DNA, MPO-DNA), NLR (neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio), NHR (neutrophil-to-HDL ratio), and MHR (monocyte-to-HDL ratio) show prognostic utility in stroke.

**Future directions:** Research led by China and the US; key controversies include the potential "double-edged sword" nature of NETs - whether they may have reparative roles in subacute/chronic recovery phases. Major translational challenges include ensuring therapeutic specificity and defining the optimal treatment window.

The review concludes that targeting the thrombo-inflammatory functions of NETs represents a paradigm shift from a purely fibrin-centric view of stroke, opening new avenues for more effective therapies.
</summary>

"NETs are not mere bystanders but active drivers of stroke pathology... targeting the thrombo-inflammatory functions of NETs represents a paradigm shift from a purely fibrin-centric view of stroke, opening new avenues for developing more effective therapies."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Ligand-specific binding forces of LFA-1 and Mac-1 in neutrophil adhesion and crawling ---
URL: https://www.molbiolcell.org/doi/10.1091/mbc.E16-12-0827

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Molecular Biology of the Cell (Vol. 29, No. 4) titled "Ligand-specific binding forces of LFA-1 and Mac-1 in neutrophil adhesion and crawling" by Ning Li, Hao Yang, Manliu Wang, Shouqin Lü, Yan Zhang, and Mian Long (corresponding author) from the Center of Biomechanics and Bioengineering, Institute of Mechanics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China. The article was published online on December 27, 2017 (DOI: 10.1091/mbc.E16-12-0827) and monitored by editor Alex Mogilner.

The study investigates the mechanical forces of β2 integrin-ligand bonds (LFA-1 and Mac-1) with their endothelial counterreceptors (ICAM-1, ICAM-2, RAGE, JAM-A, JAM-C) during polymorphonuclear leukocyte (neutrophil, PMN) recruitment.

METHODS: The researchers used single-molecule atomic force microscopy (AFM) to measure dynamic force spectra for various LFA-1/Mac-1–ligand bonds. They tested low-affinity conformations (using TS1/18 mAb) and high-affinity conformations (using Mn²⁺ activation) of the integrins, across loading rates ranging from 3,171–114,852 pN/s. They also performed parallel flow chamber tests using mouse bone marrow-derived PMNs to assess adhesion, spreading, polarization, and crawling on different ligands.

KEY RESULTS:
- LFA-1–ICAM-1 and LFA-1/Mac-1–JAM-C bonds exhibited the highest mechanical strength (rupture forces), especially after Mn²⁺ activation.
- Mn²⁺ activation increased bond strength by 56.1 ± 4.1, 37.7 ± 2.0, 17.7 ± 3.1, 37.4 ± 4.3, and 34.0 ± 5.9 pN for LFA-1–ICAM-1, –ICAM-2, –RAGE, –JAM-A, and –JAM-C bonds, respectively; and 18.0 ± 2.6, 20.0 ± 0.8, 25.2 ± 4.2, 11.5 ± 1.4, and 32.0 ± 2.8 pN for Mac-1–ICAM-1, –ICAM-2, –RAGE, –JAM-A, and –JAM-C complexes.
- LFA-1 dominates PMN adhesion on ICAM-1 and ICAM-2, while Mac-1 mediates PMN adhesion on RAGE, JAM-A, and JAM-C, consistent with their bond strengths.
- All ligands can trigger PMN spreading and polarization; Mac-1 induces outside-in signaling more effectively than LFA-1.
- LFA-1–ICAM-1 and LFA-1/Mac-1–JAM-C bonds can accelerate PMN crawling under high shear stress, presumably due to their high mechanical strength.
- Higher bond rupture forces correspond to longer bond lifetimes.
- RAGE exhibited extremely high binding activity but low bond strength, resulting in unstable adhesion.
- JAM-A had the lowest ability to mediate PMN adhesion among all ligands tested.
- Mouse LFA-1–ICAM-1 bonds showed similar strength patterns to human, supporting cross-species relevance.

CONCLUSION: The work provides new insight into the basic molecular mechanisms of physiological ligands of β2 integrins in PMN recruitment, showing that ligand-specific binding functions of LFA-1 and Mac-1 correlate directly with their mechanical bond strengths.
</summary>

"LFA-1 dominates PMN adhesion on ICAM-1 and ICAM-2, while Mac-1 mediates PMN adhesion on RAGE, JAM-A, and JAM-C, which is consistent with their bond strength."

--- SOURCE 3: Intercellular Adhesion Molecule 1: More than a Leukocyte Adhesion Molecule ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2079-7737/12/5/743

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a review article published in the journal *Biology* (Volume 12, Issue 5, Article 743) titled "Intercellular Adhesion Molecule 1: More than a Leukocyte Adhesion Molecule" by Cameron D. Haydinger, Liam M. Ashander, Alwin Chun Rong Tan, and Justine R. Smith from the College of Medicine and Public Health, Flinders University, Adelaide, Australia. It was published on 19 May 2023 (DOI: 10.3390/biology12050743).

**Key Content:**

**Overview:** ICAM-1 is a transmembrane protein in the immunoglobulin superfamily expressed on multiple cell types (endothelial cells, epithelial cells, fibroblasts, leukocytes) and upregulated by inflammatory stimuli including TNF-α, IL-1β, IFN-γ, IL-6, reactive oxygen species, high glucose, and shear stress. It mediates cellular adhesive interactions by binding to β2 integrins MAC-1 and LFA-1, as well as hyaluronan, fibrinogen, major group rhinoviruses, and proteins from Plasmodium falciparum and Toxoplasma gondii.

**ICAM1 Gene:** Located on the short arm of chromosome 19 (19p13.2) in an 80 kb cluster with ICAM3, ICAM4, and ICAM5; ICAM2 maps to chromosome 17. The gene comprises seven exons and six introns. Key promoter elements include binding sites for NF-κB, AP-1, SP1, IRF1, IRF3, and ETS1. TNF-α-driven upregulation is primarily via NF-κB, though JAK/STAT pathways may maintain chronic inflammatory states. IFN-γ upregulation involves STAT1 homodimers; IL-6 involves STAT3. Alternative splicing generates multiple isoforms; the authors describe a previously unpublished human alternative transcript (exons 2-4 splicing, 303 amino acids, inducible by TNF-α and IL-1β). Post-transcriptional regulation involves mRNA stabilization via MAPKAPK2/HuR and microRNAs (miR-17-3p, miR-126-3p, miR-150-5p, miR-223, miR-148b-3p, and ICAM-1 related lncRNA).

**ICAM-1 Protein:** Type I transmembrane protein, 55 kDa peptide core, heavily glycosylated (76–114 kDa). Composed of five extracellular Ig domains (D1–D5), a transmembrane domain, and a short cytoplasmic tail. Binds LFA-1 via Glu34 in D1; binds MAC-1 via Asp229 and Glu254 in D3. Forms homodimers through D3–D5 interactions. Undergoes N-glycosylation at eight sites. Soluble ICAM-1 (sICAM-1) is generated by proteolytic cleavage (via ADAM17, ADAM10, MMP-9) or alternative splicing, and elevated levels are found in sepsis, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, severe COVID-19, cancers, atherosclerosis, and systemic inflammatory diseases.

**Roles in Immune Function:** ICAM-1 mediates leukocyte trafficking (slow rolling, arrest, firm adhesion, crawling, diapedesis), including signaling through Rho GTPases, actin cytoskeleton remodeling, and PIEZO1 mechanosensitive calcium channels. It is involved in immune synapse formation between lymphocytes and antigen-presenting cells. Emerging roles include wound healing and efferocytosis (phagocytosis of apoptotic cells).

**Disease Involvement:** ICAM-1 is implicated in cardiovascular diseases, autoimmune disorders, certain infections, sepsis, and cancer—where it can both promote or protect against cancer depending on type and cell populations. It has long been a therapeutic target, though few therapeutics have been successful to date.
</summary>

"Intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1) is a transmembrane protein in the immunoglobulin superfamily expressed on the surface of multiple cell populations and upregulated by inflammatory stimuli."

--- SOURCE 4: Frontiers | The Inflammatory Response After Ischemic Stroke: Targeting β2 and β1 Integrins ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2019.00540/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Frontiers in Neuroscience (May 28, 2019) by Danielle N. Edwards and Gregory J. Bix from the University of Kentucky, examining the inflammatory response after ischemic stroke with a focus on targeting β2 and β1 integrins. The article was published in the journal's Neurodegeneration section as part of a research topic on CNS protection and repair, and was edited by Xin Qi (Case Western Reserve University).

KEY POINTS:

**Background:** Ischemic stroke is a leading cause of death and disability with limited therapeutic options (t-PA and endovascular mechanical thrombectomy). These interventions restore blood flow but do not address the inflammatory, necrotic, and blood-brain barrier (BBB) mechanisms that follow. Post-reperfusion inflammation involves cytokine activation, calcium influx, and leukocytic infiltration to the ischemic area.

**Leukocyte recruitment and infiltration:** The initial endothelial response upregulates selectins (P-selectin at 15 min, E-selectin at 2 h post-ischemia), which facilitate leukocyte recruitment. Neutrophils arrive within 30 min to a few hours after reperfusion, peaking at 1-3 days. Mononuclear leukocytes (monocytes/lymphocytes) dominate from 24 h to 7 days post-reperfusion. T-lymphocytes (not B-cells) are the dominant damage-inducing lymphocytes and have been detected up to 60 days post-stroke in patients. High neutrophilic infiltration is associated with damaged cerebrovasculature; depletion reduces infarct volume.

**Integrin overview:** Integrins are heterodimers composed of 18 α and β subunits creating 24 combinations, grouped into RGD, laminin, collagen, and leukocyte-specific receptors. They undergo conformational changes ("inside-out" signaling from chemokines, then "outside-in" signaling upon ligand binding) to permit leukocyte rolling and transmigration. Both β1 and β2 integrins must be inhibited to achieve complete leukocyte arrest.

**β2 integrins (leukocyte-specific, most highly expressed on circulating leukocytes):**
- **αLβ2 (CD11a/CD18, LFA-1):** Expressed on all leukocytes, highest on T-lymphocytes. Preferentially binds ICAM-1. Inhibition in transient (but not permanent) middle cerebral artery occlusion models reduces infarct volume, edema, and mortality. ICAM-1 antibody Enlimomab was tested clinically but halted early due to increased infection, infarct volumes, neurological scores, and mortality.
- **αMβ2 (CD11b/CD18, Mac-1):** Expressed on all leukocytes; binds ICAMs, JAMs, fibrinogen, complement C3bi, and others. Antibodies against CD11b/CD18 reduce infarct volume and restore cerebral blood flow. Recombinant neutrophil inhibitory factor (rNIF) also shows benefit. Effective in transient but not permanent occlusion models. UK279276 (rNIF) and Hu23F2G (Leukarrest) reached Phase II trials but were halted due to no observed efficacy.

**β1 integrins:**
- **α4β1 (CD49d/CD29, VLA-4):** Localized primarily to leukocytes and microglia; preferentially binds VCAM-1. Preclinical results are contradictory—some studies show reduced inflammation but no improvement in infarct volume or function; a multi-center randomized trial showed efficacy only in small infarcts. Natalizumab (anti-α4 antibody), successful in MS and Crohn's disease, showed no improvement in a Phase II ischemic stroke trial (ACTION), and two of 79 patients died from serious infections.
- **α5β1 (CD49e/CD29, VLA-5):** Comprises ~50% of β1 integrins on neutrophils and monocytes; primarily binds fibronectin. Inhibited by small peptide ATN-161, which prevented CD45+ leukocyte infiltration, reduced BBB permeability, functional deficits, edema, and infarct volume in experimental models. α5β1 is highly sensitive to calcium and induced by TNFα.

**Clinical implications:** No clinical stroke trials have targeted the αL subunit. Efalizumab showed promise in psoriasis. Clinical translation has been disappointing overall due to: inadequate rodent models (single species, sex, age), poor understanding of post-stroke changes, and patient variability (time to ER, stroke location, collaterals, co-morbidities). Human ischemic stroke patients do not show the same αMβ2 upregulation seen in rodent models.

**Future directions:** The authors advocate for continued preclinical research to understand how integrin expression and function change after stroke, potentially identifying stroke-dependent integrin changes that could serve as viable therapeutic targets without off-target effects. They emphasize that integrins' diversity and complexity present both challenges and opportunities for targeted stroke therapies.
</summary>

"Integrins have been shown to be necessary for leukocyte adhesion and migration, and thus are of immediate interest in many inflammatory diseases, including ischemic stroke."

SUMMARY:

- 71.7% of patients had poor functional outcome at 3 months, including 36.6% who died.

**Abstract/Key Findings:**
The study investigated the temporal dynamics of neutrophils after ischemic stroke using both patient data and an animal (mouse) model of transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO). Key findings include:
- Neutrophil counts in peripheral blood increased soon after stroke onset in patients, with higher counts indicating detrimental outcomes
- In mice, neutrophil counts peaked at 12h after cerebral ischemia in blood, followed by a 1-2 day spike in brain lesions
- Neutrophil clearance peaked at 2 days after stroke; extracellular traps (NETs) were mostly detected at 2-3 days after stroke
- Expression of the N2 marker CD206 on infiltrated neutrophils was relatively stable

- Skewing neutrophils toward the N2 phenotype (via TGFβ) before stroke reduced infarct volumes at 1 day after tMCAO
- Conditioned medium from ischemic neurons drove neutrophils away from the protective N2 phenotype and increased extracellular trap formation

- 225 Chinese (Han ethnicity) patients with acute ischemic stroke admitted within 24h of symptom onset (Jan 2014–Aug 2018) and 56 healthy controls were analyzed
- 58 patients had infections (respiratory or urinary); 167 did not

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific review article published in Current Neuropharmacology (2023 Mar 8;21(3):621, DOI: 10.2174/1570159X20666220706115957) by Meizhen Xie, Yulei Hao, Liangshu Feng, Tian Wang, Mengyue Yao, Hui Li, Di Ma, and Jiachun Feng from the Department of Neurology and Neuroscience Center, The First Hospital of Jilin University, Changchun, China. The article reviews neutrophil heterogeneity and its roles in the inflammatory network after ischemic stroke (PMCID: PMC10207908, PMID: 35794770; received 2022 Mar 29, accepted 2022 Jun 13; licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0).

KEY FINDINGS AND CONTENT:

1. **Neutrophils in Ischemic Stroke**: Neutrophils are the first peripheral immune cells to enter the brain after ischemic stroke, crossing the blood-brain barrier (BBB) to reach the ischemic parenchyma. They are mobilized from peripheral immune organs (bone marrow and spleen) and participate in stroke-related neuroinflammation. Traditionally, neutrophils were believed to aggravate brain injury through release of proteases, reactive oxygen species (ROS), pro-inflammatory factors, and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs).

2. **Clinical Trial Failures and Heterogeneity**: Clinical trials targeting neutrophils for cerebral infarction treatment have failed, partly because only a subgroup of neutrophils ("harmful neutrophils") may cause damage. This has led to recognition of neutrophil heterogeneity.

3. **N1 and N2 Neutrophil Phenotypes**: Analogous to M1/M2 macrophages, neutrophils polarize into two functional phenotypes after ischemic stroke. N1 neutrophils (dominant during acute phase, within 3 days) promote inflammation and damage neural structures via proteases, ROS, and NETs. N2 neutrophils (increasing in later phases) are neuroprotective, releasing anti-inflammatory factors and neuroprotective mediators. N1 and N2 phenotypes are highly plastic and can transform into each other under certain conditions, making them promising therapeutic targets.

4. **Neutrophil Origins**: Bone marrow produces ~10^7 neutrophils/day in mice and ~10^11 in humans. Differentiation progresses through five stages (promyelocytic cells, bone marrow cells, mesenchymal cells, band neutrophils, segmented neutrophils) regulated by transcription factors (C/EBP α/β/ε, PU.1, Gfi-1) and G-CSF. Release from bone marrow is regulated by the CXCR4/CXCR2 balance (CXCR4 retains, CXCR2 promotes release via CXCL1/CXCL2). Extramedullary reservoirs exist in spleen, lung, and liver.

5. **Neutrophil Lifespan and Heterogeneity**: Historically considered short-lived (7-9 hour half-life), newer research shows human circulating neutrophils live ~5-5.4 days (18 hours in mice). Neutrophil aging (characterized by decreased CD62L, increased CXCR4) follows circadian rhythms, is regulated by microbiota, and involves the IL-23/IL-17/G-CSF axis. Neutrophil heterogeneity is confirmed by morphological characteristics (density gradients: HDD, NDN, LDN), surface markers, and single-cell transcriptomics.

6. **Single-Cell Sequencing**: Neutrophils form a single transcriptional continuum called "neutrotime" across tissues (bone marrow = immature end; spleen and blood = mature end). Unbiased clustering divides them into 8 clusters (G0-4 from bone marrow, G5a-c from peripheral blood). In cancer, human neutrophils resolve into 5 subsets (hN1-5) and mouse into 6 (mN1-6). Future research should characterize phenotypic, transcriptional, and functional profiles of neutrophils in stroke. The concept of "brain cytoprotection" (rather than "neuroprotection") is proposed in the era of highly effective reperfusion. Neutrophil-targeted therapies may serve as adjunctive treatments to reperfusion therapy, given that nearly half of thrombectomy patients do not experience clinical improvement.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Ischemic stroke triggers the brain to release a variety of neuronal 'help me' signals, such as ATP, high mobility group box 1 (HMGB1), hypoxia‐inducible factor 1α (HIF‐1α), S100β, and brain‐derived antigens, thereby activating immune cells both within the CNS and in the periphery."; "Among the diverse types of immune cells associated with the innate immune response after stroke, neutrophils are first responders infiltrating into the ischemic brain and contributing to acute post-ischemic brain injury."; "By releasing matrix metalloproteinase‐9 (MMP‐9), neutrophils may cause the disintegration of the BBB and lead to the exacerbation of neuroinflammation."; "The failure of the trial and preclinical data suggests that only animals with permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion and relatively small lesions benefit from the intervention... Hence, the clinical population did not match the profile of the animals in which the therapy was effective."; "Given the highly successful rate of thrombectomy in patients with large vessel occlusions nowadays, however, nearly half of the patients do not experience clinical improvement."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 12: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in cerebrovascular disease mechanisms, detection, and therapeutic targeting ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0014488626000464

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a review article published in the journal Experimental Neurology (Volume 400, June 2026, Article 115683) titled "Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in cerebrovascular disease mechanisms, detection, and therapeutic targeting." The article is authored by Zhinuo Li, Shao-Huang Wu, Xinyue Zhang, Tianrun Li, Mingyuan Xin, and Fangxi Liu, and is available via DOI: 10.1016/j.expneurol.2026.115683.

KEY CONTENT:
The review comprehensively examines the role of Neutrophil Extracellular Traps (NETs) in cerebrovascular diseases, particularly ischemic stroke. NETs comprise decondensed DNA scaffolds and granular proteins including histones, myeloperoxidase (MPO), and neutrophil elastase (NE).

MAIN FINDINGS:
1. NETs play a vital role in cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury by enhancing the stability of immunothrombi through DNA-histone scaffolds, conferring resistance to thrombolysis.
2. NETs exacerbate blood-brain barrier (BBB) damage by degrading tight junction proteins via inflammatory cascades.
3. Persistent NET formation impedes vascular remodeling and neural repair, compromising long-term functional recovery.
4. NET interactions with coagulation networks within thrombi are associated with reduced effectiveness of tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) in thrombolytic therapy.
5. NETs form via two distinct pathways: suicidal NETosis (lytic process triggered by microbial pathogens or sterile stimuli via PRRs such as TLR4, TLR9, and CLEC5A) and a second pathway.

DETECTION METHODS (three categories):
- Histology and in vivo imaging (co-localization of extracellular DNA with MPO, NE, or H3Cit)
- Body fluid biomarkers (quantifying circulating complexes such as MPO-DNA)
- A third category of current methodologies

THERAPEUTIC STRATEGIES:
- Targeting NETs during the acute phase may enhance reperfusion efficiency and ameliorate neural injury
- Modulating NETs during the repair phase can promote tissue regeneration

CHALLENGES TO CLINICAL TRANSLATION:
- Narrow therapeutic windows
- Limited intervention specificity
- Risk of infectious complications
- Lack of biomarkers for patient stratification

The authors note NETs exhibit pathological duality: protective in the acute phase (sequestering pathogens and clearing necrotic debris) but harmful when excessive or persistent. The review has 91 references and has been cited 3 times. The article was supported by the Liaoning Provincial Doctoral Scientific Research Start-up Fund Program and China Medical University Undergraduate Training Program for Innovation and Entrepreneurship.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"During cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury, NETs enhance the stability of immunothrombi by forming DNA-histone scaffolds, thereby conferring resistance to thrombolysis. They also exacerbate damage to the blood-brain barrier (BBB) by degrading tight junction proteins via activation of inflammatory cascades."
</key_excerpts>

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: Frontiers | Insights gained from single-cell sequencing analysis of ischemic stroke ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cell-and-developmental-biology/articles/10.3389/fcell.2026.1784660/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article titled "Insights gained from single-cell sequencing analysis of ischemic stroke," published in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology (Vol 14, April 21, 2026). The authors (Yanqin Mei, Teng Guan, Longsheng Fu, Jiming Kong, and Yanni Lv from Nanchang University and University of Manitoba) systematically review over 50 scRNA-seq studies on ischemic stroke published since 2019.

KEY FINDINGS:
- 22 cell types were identified from brain tissues and 7 cell types from blood after ischemic stroke using scRNA-seq.
- 13 frequently reported cell types underwent extensive heterogeneity studies, including microglia, macrophages, oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, dendritic cells, T cells, monocytes, neutrophils, neurons, endothelial cells, vascular mural cells/pericytes, perivascular fibroblast-like cells, and vascular smooth muscle cells.
- The review details subcluster categorization, function-related subclusters, and newly discovered subclusters for each cell type.

CELL-SPECIFIC HIGHLIGHTS:
- Microglia: classified beyond traditional M0/M1/M2 into various subclusters (6-16 depending on study); identified pro-inflammatory vs homeostatic states; ischemic core vs penumbra differences; novel subclusters with antioxidant function via peroxiredoxin-1 and Itgb2+ microglia involved in energy metabolism.
- Macrophages: 6 subclusters at CNS borders; Foxp3+ macrophage subcluster distinct from M1/M2 enhancing efferocytosis; Tie2-expressing macrophages in patients associated with improved clinical prognosis.
- Oligodendrocytes: MCAO induces reactive Olig2+Edu+ subclusters aiding white matter repair; metabolic alterations early post-stroke; subcluster 4 (Sult1a1+) linked to apoptotic pathways.
- Astrocytes: classified into A1/A2 types; Nes and Ascl1 markers of A2-type neurotrophic function; Aldoc as reliable pan-astrocyte marker.
- T cells: Treg-derived osteopontin aids microglia-driven white matter repair; T cells migrate to brain 1-5 weeks post-stroke.
- Neutrophils: peak at 24h post-stroke; age-related changes lead to atypical neutrophils (CD62l low) exacerbating stroke.
- Endothelial cells: BBB-associated clusters show dysfunction; connexin 43 decreased in elderly; Wnt7a/Wnt7b engineered for BBB regulation.

IMMUNE RESPONSE AND CELL-CELL COMMUNICATION:
The review explores immune cell and non-immune cellular interactions and their regulatory influences, including the neurovascular unit (blood-brain barrier, neurons, pericytes, endothelial cells).

AGE-RELATED ISSUES:
Aging enhances apoptosis, disrupts endothelial circadian rhythms, and increases infiltration of peripheral macrophages; aged mice show higher Cxcl3 production by neutrophils linked to poorer reperfusion and outcomes.

METHODOLOGY:
Studies used various platforms including 10x Genomics, BD Biosciences, BD Rhapsody, Singleron GEXSCOPE, NovaSeq 6000, and Illumina HiSeq X. Models included MCAO (transient and permanent), four-vessel occlusion, and clinical patient samples from acute ischemic stroke.

FUTURE DIRECTIONS:
Anticipation for broader scRNA-seq application in ischemic stroke research, including cost reduction, integrated analysis, and biopharmaceutical development. scRNA-seq offers new insights into cellular heterogeneity, cell-cell interactions, novel therapeutic targets, and biomarkers.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Ischemic stroke represents a significant global health hazard, causing substantial morbidity, mortality, and long-term disability worldwide. The brain's complexity necessitates targeting ischemic stroke dysfunction syndrome. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) offers unbiased, high-resolution analysis of cell heterogeneity, revealing cellular markers and types."
</key_excerpts>
