Results and discussion Natalizumab treatment does not improve post-stroke recovery and neuronal plasticity To model the clinical study design of Natalizumab treatment for stroke from the two clinical trials in an animal model, we used a photothrombotic stroke (PT) model resulting in equal lesion volumes and behavioral deficits in both treatment groups at the acute phase, corresponding to the equal characteristics of the study populations with Natalizumab or control treatment in the clinical trials. Mice of mixed sex then received anti-CD49d or an isotype control antibody i.p. 2 h after stroke, followed by injections every second week over a period of 3 mo, based on previous reports and the pharmacokinetic analyses of cellular anti-CD49d saturation (Fig. S1, A–D). We used a panel of in vivo imaging techniques for cortical plasticity, behavior tests, the assessment of lesion size and synaptic plasticity, which were proven to sensitively detect therapeutic effects on chronic post-stroke recovery (Cramer et al., 2019b; Cser´ ep et al., 2020; Sadler et al., 2020). Anti-CD49d treatment did not improve long-term lesion involution based on in vivo widefield imaging (Fig. 1, A and B; and Fig. S1 D) and also had no effect on histologically quantified lesion volumes after PT as well as in an independent stroke model of distal middle cerebral artery occlusion (dMCAo) used in the majority of previous reports on the effects in the acute post-stroke phase (Fig. 1 C and Fig. S1 E). Moreover, re-covery of behavior deficits using a well-established multipa-rameter neuroscore (Llovera et al., 2015) and cylinder test (Llovera et al., 2014) also did not differ between treatment groups throughout the observation period of 3 mo after stroke (Fig. 1 D). Additionally, we examined functional neuronal con-nectivity using in vivo widefield calcium imaging. We observed equal network disturbances in pairwise comparisons of func-tional cortical areas in both treatment groups after stroke (Fig. 1 E). Moreover, we did not detect anti-CD49d-associated im-provement in neuronal network connectivity after stroke nei-ther within the ischemic hemisphere nor across homotopic areas of both brain hemispheres (Fig. 1 F). Correspondingly, quanti-fication of synaptic spine density as a marker of synaptic plas-ticity at 3 mo after stroke did not reveal a difference between treatment groups, which were both returned to baseline levels (naive). These results clearly indicate a lack of efficacy for anti-CD49d to improve functional recovery in the chronic post-stroke phase in two preclinical stroke models, which is comparable to the outcome of the clinical trials testing the efficacy of Natali-zumab in stroke patients (Elkind et al., 2020; Elkins et al., 2017; Liesz et al., 2011; Llovera et al., 2015).
Anti-CD49d only transiently reduces cerebral lymphocyte counts after stroke Therefore, we next aimed to analyze the biological efficacy of anti-CD49d treatment in reducing long-term lymphocyte inva-sion to the injured brain, which could not be studied in the clinical trials. To this end, we performed quantitative flow cy-tometric analyses at acute and chronic time points after stroke.
Corresponding to previous studies by us and others, anti-CD49d significantly decreased cerebral lymphocyte invasion at the acute phase in male and female animals (Fig. 2 A and Fig. S3 A).
In contrast, no difference in cerebral leukocyte count was de-tectable between treatment groups at 1 mo after stroke for any of the T cell subtypes, which we quantified in a multidimensional flow cytometric analysis (Fig. 2, B and C). Interestingly, we found T cells among leukocyte populations to specifically accu-mulate in the chronic phase after stroke (Fig. S2). Next, we performed immunofluorescence labeling of CD3+ T cells to an-alyze the spatial distribution of T cells after stroke. Consistent with our flow cytometric results and a previous report (Doyle et al., 2015), we found dense T cell accumulation within the chronic lesion but did not detect a difference in intralesional T cell density between control or anti-CD49d–treated groups at 28 d after stroke (Fig. 2 D). We analyzed the spatial clustering of T cells by calculating the Clark–Evans agglomeration index (R index), which indicates cell clustering for an R < 1 (Fig. 2 E).
Interestingly, the R index ranged between 0.3 and 0.7 for both acute (day 7) as well as for chronic (day 28) time points, re-gardless of treatment groups. Additionally, chronic T cell accu-mulation and their local clustering was confirmed in the dMCAo stroke model for both treatment groups (Fig. S3 B). Thus, the chronic accumulation of T cells in the post-ischemic brain as-sociates with local clustering of T cells likely due to local, in-tracerebral proliferation. This finding could potentially explain the difference in treatment efficacy of anti-CD49d between the acute stroke outcome (with transiently reduced cerebral T cell invasion) and long-term recovery. Taken together, our approach to monitor the treatment efficacy of anti-CD49d for chronic recovery in two independent stroke models could have pre-dicted the inefficacy of Natalizumab in clinical stroke trials.
Moreover, this first-ever analysis of long-term effects of anti-CD49d treatment on the cerebral lymphocyte pool provides a mechanistic rationale for the futile treatment effects in the chronic post-stroke phase.
T cells proliferate intracerebrally after stroke We next aimed to distinguish chronic recruitment versus local proliferation as the potential cause of the chronic lymphocyte accumulation in the post-stroke brain. This document is the doctoral dissertation of Alessio Ricci, submitted in January 2024 at Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München (Graduate School of Systemic Neurosciences), under the supervision of Prof. Dr. Arthur Liesz at the Institute for Stroke and Dementia Research. The dissertation examines the role of T cells in the chronic phase after stroke.

**Core Topic:** The research focuses on how T cells behave in the chronic phase (weeks to months) after ischemic stroke, and whether targeting T cell infiltration is an effective therapeutic strategy for stroke recovery.

**Key Background:**
- Stroke is the second leading cause of death worldwide; ischemic strokes account for 62.4% of cases
- Recanalization therapies (thrombolysis, thrombectomy) are limited by narrow time windows
- Chronic stroke treatment is limited to physical rehabilitation; no pharmacological treatments exist
- T cells play a mostly detrimental role in the acute phase after stroke
- Anti-CD49d (Natalizumab) treatment showed strong efficacy in preclinical studies of acute stroke but failed in clinical trials (ACTION and ACTION-II) when chronic outcomes (90 days) were assessed

**Study 1 (Published in J Exp Med, 2021; Heindl, Ricci et al.):** 
- Demonstrated that T cells can proliferate locally within the brain after stroke, evading Natalizumab's effects
- Anti-CD49d treatment significantly reduces T cell numbers in the acute phase but their numbers increase in the chronic phase via local (intracerebral) proliferation
- This local proliferation was confirmed in both mice and human autopsy samples
- Anti-CD49d treatment failed to improve functional recovery, neuronal plasticity, lesion involution, or functional connectivity in the chronic phase across two stroke models (photothrombotic and dMCAo)
- Chronic T cell accumulation showed local clustering (Clark-Evans agglomeration index 0.3-0.7), consistent with local proliferation
- This provides a mechanistic explanation for the discrepancy between preclinical and clinical results

**Study 2:**
- Demonstrated that post-stroke T cells acquire a tissue-resident memory (TRM) phenotype
- Post-stroke T cells express typical TRM markers (CD69, low CD62L/S1PR1/CCR7)
- TRM maintenance relies on MHC class I and chemokine signaling (notably CXCR3 and CXCR6)
- Lymphocytes play a crucial role in restoring functional connectivity after stroke, likely via microglia-dependent mechanisms
- This was assessed using inducible knockout mouse models, adoptive T cell transfer in lymphocyte-deficient (Rag1−/−) mice, high-parametric flow cytometry, and single-cell mRNA sequencing

**Key Conclusions:**
- Chronic neuroinflammation persists for months after stroke, contrary to earlier assumptions that it resolves within weeks
- Local T cell proliferation in the brain, rather than continued invasion from blood, maintains chronic T cell populations
- A deep mechanistic understanding of pathophysiological processes is critical when translating preclinical findings to patients
- The molecular mechanisms identified (tissue-residency, chemokine signaling) open new avenues for immunomodulatory strategies to promote stroke recovery
- The glial scar acts as a permeable barrier (up to 70 kDa) allowing lymphocyte-secreted mediators to influence neurons
- Regulatory T cells (Treg) play protective roles in chronic recovery via IL-10, amphiregulin (AREG), and osteopontin (OPN) secretion, promoting remyelination, suppressing astrogliosis, and shifting microglia toward pro-reparative phenotypes
args.key_excerpts: "Our results stress how a deep mechanistic understanding of pathophysiological processes is of pivotal importance when translating preclinical findings to patients. Furthermore, we described local proliferation as a central mechanism that maintains T cells in the post-stroke brain."

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410)Abstract

Neutrophils are classically considered as cells pivotal for the first line of defense against invading pathogens. In recent years, evidence has accumulated that they are also important in the orchestration of adaptive immunity. Neutrophils rapidly migrate in high numbers to sites of inflammation (e.g., infection, tissue damage, and cancer) and are subsequently able to migrate to draining lymph nodes (LNs). Both at the site of inflammation as well as in the LNs, neutrophils can engage with lymphocytes and antigen-presenting cells. This crosstalk occurs either directly via cell–cell contact or via mediators, such as proteases, cytokines, and radical oxygen species. In this review, we will discuss the current knowledge regarding locations and mechanisms of interaction between neutrophils and lymphocytes in the context of homeostasis and various pathological conditions. In addition, we will highlight the complexity of the microenvironment that is involved in the generation of suppressive or stimulatory neutrophil phenotypes.

**Keywords:**inflammation, immune-regulation, neutrophil, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, immune-paralysis, neutrophil phenotypes, T-cells

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410)Introduction

Neutrophils are particularly known for their potent anti-microbial functions ([1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B1)). This notion is enforced by various congenital neutrophil deficiencies, which show marked clinical phenotypes characterized by enhanced susceptibility to bacterial and fungal infections ([2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B2), [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B3)). Infections, sterile inflammation, and other non-chronic challenges to the immune system are characterized by a rapid influx of neutrophils into the affected tissue ([4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B4)). These neutrophils respond to chemo-attractants and adhesion molecules expressed on endothelial cells, and their main function is to clear infections and/or debris. In addition, they influence inflammatory responses through interactions with various cells of the immune system, such as antigen-presenting cells (APCs) and lymphocytes ([5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B5), [6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B6)). This has been observed in both murine models and in _ex vivo_ studies with isolated cells from humans. Although neutrophils have long been considered to be composed of a homogenous population, an increasing body of literature supports the presence of multiple neutrophil phenotypes in cancer and inflammation ([7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B7)–[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B10)). This heterogeneity can be induced by specific differentiation programs in the bone marrow or orchestrated by extracellular signals derived from inflammatory tissue (e.g., cytokines, bioactive lipids, or chemokines) ([11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B11), [12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B12)). The contribution of distinct neutrophil populations to immune suppression has not been resolved. In addition, in murine models and some human studies, clear distinctions were suggested between neutrophils and granulocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells (G-MDSCs). These issues have been reviewed in detail ([13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B13), [14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B14)). This review will focus on the location and relevant diseases in which both (suppressive) neutrophils and G-MDSCs modulate adaptive immune responses and the mechanisms behind this process.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410)Location of the Interaction between Neutrophils and Lymphocytes

### Site of inflammation – bystander response

The early phase of infection is characterized by an influx of neutrophils and monocytes, which precedes the development of an antigen-specific response. Simultaneously, small numbers of T-cells are recruited into the infected tissue. Some of these T-cells can be activated and proliferate ‘‘in situ’’ in response to antigen presentation by myeloid cells ([15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B15)). In addition, inflammatory cytokines cause proliferation and activation of non-specific T-cells in the profoundly pro-inflammatory microenvironment. This process has been coined the ‘‘bystander response’’ and was first seen in viral infections ([16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B16)). It has recently been suggested that this bystander response contributes to early pathogen control in mice by enabling bystander memory T-cells to recognize and eliminate micro-organisms, such as _Listeria monocytogenes_ infected cells in a NKG2D-dependent manner ([17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B17)).

It is conceivable that a large and uncontrolled bystander response might predispose for auto-immunity and self-reactivity through the proliferation of self-reactive T-cells ([18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B18)). It is tempting to speculate that neutrophils are involved to limit and control this bystander T-cell response as the timing of massive neutrophil tissue infiltration and the bystander response coincide.

### Lymph nodes and primary lymphatic tissue

Neutrophils are found both in LNs and spleen particularly under inflammatory conditions ([19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B19)–[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B24)). Dynamic imaging studies have shown that neutrophils are recruited to and form swarms in infected LNs in mice ([25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B25), [26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B26)). In addition, neutrophil migration to afferent LNs in response to tissue inflammation has been shown in various murine models ([19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B19)–[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B24)).

There are two possible routes for neutrophils to enter LNs, via blood vessels or via afferent lymphatics (Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#F1)). The first route requires exiting the circulation via high endothelial venules (HEVs). This mechanism is controversial, as human neutrophils seem to lack the expression of CCR7, a receptor for CCL21 and required for lymphocyte exiting through HEVs ([27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B27)). Nonetheless, it has been shown in a murine model of ovalbumin-induced inflammation that neutrophil homing to LNs via the HEV takes place and requires integrins αMβ2 (MAC-1), αLβ2 (LFA-1), and l- and P-selectin ([19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B19)). In LN-draining inflammatory tissue, additional chemokines and cytokines could orchestrate the attraction of neutrophils via HEVs. This has also been shown in tumor-draining LNs, when the tumor was subjected to photodynamic therapy. This treatment induces additional sterile inflammation. In this model, neutrophils are recruited to tumor-draining LNs via the HEV in an IL-17-dependent manner ([20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B20)).

Neutrophil migration to LNs via afferent lymphatics has been observed in various murine models of infections, vaccinations, and cancer and seems to depend on MAC-1 and CXCR4 expression on neutrophils ([19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B19), [22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B22)) (see Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#F1)). The area in the LN that is occupied by neutrophils will determine which cells they encounter, and how they can influence subsequent immune responses. Neutrophils have been reported to occupy the medullary region and interfollicular zone ([23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B23)). Neutrophils migrate to these areas in the LN during infection with _Staphylococcus aureus_. There they exhibit short- and long-term interactions with B-cells, thereby inhibiting production of antibodies, and thus humoral responses ([23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B23)). Furthermore, neutrophil B-cell interactions have also been observed in primary lymphoid organs in various mouse models. In the marginal zone of the spleen, neutrophils were observed to contribute to antibody production and class switching by activating B-cells by producing BAFF, APRIL, and IL-21 ([24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B24)). In this study, evidence was provided for the existence of a similar population of neutrophils that modulate B-cell responses in humans. However, this remains controversial as in a subsequent study, no splenic neutrophil–B cell interactions could be observed in humans ([28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B28)). It seems firmly established, at least in various murine models that neutrophils enter primary and secondary lymphatic sites during the immune response evoked by various inflammatory stimuli. Apart from regulating immunity in inflamed tissue, they may play a role in regulating immune responses at these privileged immune sites (see below).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410)The Role of Neutrophils in Controlling Immune Responses Evoked by Bacterial and Viral Infections, Sterile Inflammation and Cancer

### Viral infections

Acute viral infections, such as influenza, are ideal models to study cellular kinetics during the immune responses and the putative modulating effects of neutrophils hereon. Influenza and RSV infections are characterized by an early large influx of neutrophils in the lung tissue followed several days later by a virus specific CD8+ T-cell response ([29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B29)–[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B31)). Neutrophils might facilitate the development of this antigen-specific response as they are able to serve as APCs in influenza infection in mice ([31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B31), [32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B32)). Such antigen presentation by influenza-infected neutrophils has been demonstrated and was found to be mediated by MHC-I and co-stimulatory molecules CD80 and CD86, which leads to induction and activation of anti-viral responses of CD8+ T-cells ([32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B32)). On the other hand, it is tempting to speculate that neutrophils may also inhibit T-cell responses in viral infections by inhibiting T-cell proliferation and inducing T-cell apoptosis. The mechanisms of this suppression will be discussed below and involve reactive oxygen species (ROS), arginase-I (ARG), and PD-L1. This has also been found in other inflammatory scenarios ([33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B33)–[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B35)). The role of immune suppression by neutrophils _in vivo_ in murine models of viral infections has not been adequately experimentally verified, but may be deduced from the fact that pathology in mice is T-cell dependent and that depleting neutrophils often results in an exaggerated response and pathology ([31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B31), [36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B36)). In chronic viral infections, such as human hepatitis B virus (HBV), it has recently been shown that recruitment of neutrophils to the liver limits immune pathology through inhibiting bystander and HBV specific T-cells in an arginase-dependent way, thus protecting the host from immune-mediated damage ([37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B37)). These neutrophils were isolated from the PBMC fraction and were termed G-MDSC ([13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B13)).

### Bacterial infections

As in viral infections, bacterial infections are associated with a large recruitment of neutrophils. The pivotal difference with viral infections is that phagocytosis and killing of bacterial targets by phagocytes is the principle mechanism of pathogen eradication ([1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B1)). Ineffective killing of phagocytosed bacteria results in intracellular (phagosomal) survival and can lead to pathogen shuttling to distant sites and LNs ([38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B38), [39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B39)). Recently, it has been shown that neutrophils from mice infected with _S. aureus_ migrated to the draining LNs and limited humoral responses through direct cellular interactions with B-cells. These direct cellular interactions were also found for neutrophil–T-cell interactions in humans ([40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B40)). Kamenyeva et al. suggested that suppression of antibody production by neutrophils _ex vivo_ was dependent on TGF-β ([23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B23)). However, the contribution of the reduced humoral response to pathogen load was not assessed.

As mentioned above, in the early course of infection, large numbers of neutrophils are recruited to the affected tissue where modulation of T-cell responses most likely occurs with early recruited T-cells. These early lymphocytes mainly belong to the family of γδ-T-cells ([41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B41)). These γδ-T-cells are thought to play a role in early pathogen clearance through production of cytokines and their crosstalk with innate immune cells ([41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B41)). Neutrophils play an important role in the initiation of these γδ-T-cell responses. Phagocytosis of bacteria enables neutrophils to activate γδ-T-cells and induce their proliferation ([42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B42)). This is dependent on (1) the microbial metabolite (E)-4-hydroxy-3-methyl-but-2-enyl pyrophosphate (HMB-PP), which neutrophils release after phagocytosis of bacteria and (2) the presence of monocytes for cellular contact-induced activation ([42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B42)). However, other human studies have revealed the ability of neutrophils to suppress γδ-T-cells activation, possibly providing a negative-feedback mechanism ([43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B43), [44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B44)).

The early instruction of γδ-T-cells in humans by neutrophils parallels the role of these innate immune cells in the early instruction of T-cell responses in mice. In a murine model of _Legionella pneumophila_, neutrophils from pulmonary tissue are pivotal for the development of a TH1 response. In this model which resembles human disease, neutrophils were depleted by neutrophil-specific antibody Ly-6G, and this led to more TH2 skewing and more disease ([45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B45)).

T-cell instruction, activation, and proliferation mostly require antigen-presenting cells, such as dendritic cells, B-cells, and macrophages. Neutrophils have been shown to both negatively and positively affect antigen presentation by these APCs under different conditions. This has extensively been reviewed previously ([46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B46), [47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B47)). Neutrophils may simply affect the amount of available antigen by phagocytosis, and thus limit antigen presentation by professional APCs ([48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B48)). Alternatively, neutrophils might function as APCs themselves ([49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B49), [50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B50)). This possibility is supported by several studies showing the expression of MHCII and co-stimulatory molecules on neutrophils under different clinical conditions ([51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B51)–[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B53)).

### Disseminated bacterial infections (sepsis)

Severe bacterial infections can result in systemic dissemination of bacteria that can lead to severe clinical conditions, such as sepsis and septic shock. These conditions are characterized by severe systemic inflammation, which can result in severe inflammatory damage to the host when not properly controlled. Immune inhibitory mechanisms have evolved in order to prevent this exaggerated inflammatory response ([54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B54)). The specific role of neutrophils in this immune suppression has not been adequately studied. This is a challenging research question as depletion or inhibition of neutrophil functions with the purpose of studying their anti-inflammatory role has profound impact on bacterial clearance. Identification of suppressive mechanisms that do not influence pathogen clearance and neutrophil-specific murine knockout models may aid in answering this question.

In humans, evidence has accumulated that neutrophils might contribute to the immune suppression seen in sepsis. Neutrophils in septic-shock patients express ARG and suppress T-cell functions, probably through depletion of l-arginine as detailed below ([55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B55)). Immune suppression in sepsis can be at least in part attributed to the PD-1/PD-L1 axis that is involved in control of apoptosis in T-cells ([56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B56)). Interestingly, expression of PD-L1 on tissue neutrophils has also been shown during chronic inflammation ([57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B57)). The expression of PD-L1 on human neutrophils was found to be induced by the TH1 cytokine, interferon-γ, _in vitro_ ([35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B35)).

### Sterile inflammation/vaccination

Neutrophils also play a role in the fine tuning of inflammation under sterile conditions. Many studies have been performed in ovalbumine (OVA)-induced immune responses in murine models. The OVA models are used as vaccination and allergy models and are useful to study the development of adaptive immune responses. The role of neutrophils in the OVA model follows the above-described findings in microbial models. The cells seem to effectively cross-prime CD8+ T-cells in an MHCI-dependent manner ([58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B58)). They function as APCs or influence the capacity to present antigens by professional APCs ([59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B59), [60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B60)). For instance, dendritic cells have been shown to take up antigens acquired from phagocytosed apoptotic neutrophils ([61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B61)).

These examples show that neutrophils can increase antigen presentation as APC or by delivering antigen to APCs. On the other hand, there are reports that neutrophils decrease the level of antigen presentation by APCs through an unknown mechanism during brief cellular interactions ([48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B48)). These findings show that it is difficult to predict in which circumstances neutrophils stimulate or suppress antigen presentation even when very similar and well-controlled models are used.

### Cancer

There is a large body of literature, which shows a heterogeneous population of myeloid cells characterized by their potential to inhibit adaptive immunity, and thus anti-tumor immune responses ([14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B14)). These myeloid-derived suppressor cells consist of mononuclear cells and neutrophils in different stages of maturation. G-MDSCs facilitate tumor growth in various murine models through suppression of CD8+ responses and production of cytokines ([62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B62)–[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B64)). In addition, in human cancer patients, G-MDSCs and suppressive neutrophils are isolated from the peripheral blood ([65](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B65), [66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B66)). Although the distinction between neutrophils and G-MDSCs is not clear, the modulating role of these cells in the immune responses induced by tumors has become an accepted paradigm, and is extensively reviewed elsewhere ([13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B13), [67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B67)). Neutrophils are involved in both pro- or anti-tumor immune responses. Importantly, they have recently been shown to promote metastasis ([7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B7), [68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B68)). Their anti-tumor effects are mediated by their direct antibody-dependent cytotoxicity and their production of pro-inflammatory cytokines near and inside the tumor ([69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B69)). These properties will not be discussed in this short review.

The pro-tumor effects of neutrophils are mediated by different mechanisms. First, neutrophils play an essential role in angiogenesis through expression of matrix metallo-proteases, such as MMP9 ([70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B70), [71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B71)). Second, in multiple murine models they inhibit anti-tumor CD8+ T-cell responses through mechanisms described below. The suppression of anti-tumor T-cell responses by neutrophils was recently shown to be pivotal in tumor metastasis in a murine model of breast cancer ([7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B7)). In this study, γδ-T-cells facilitated neutrophil recruitment to the tumor via an IL-17 and G-CSF mediated pathway. The microenvironmental cues for the switch in neutrophil phenotype from pro- to ­anti-tumor are slowly being unraveled. In a model of lung cancer, TGF-β induces or recruits neutrophils with a pro-tumor phenotype (termed N1), whereas blocking TGF-β induces an anti-tumor neutrophil phenotype (termed N2) ([11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B11)).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410)Mechanisms of T-Cell Suppression by Neutrophils and G-MDSCs

Despite the evidence that neutrophils can stimulate T-cell responses, most studies point toward a direct suppressive role of these cells on different T-cell responses in various disease models as described above. The mechanisms of suppression have been reviewed in detail elsewhere and are summarized in Figure [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#F2) ([13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B13)). Most of the mechanisms that neutrophils employ to suppress T-cell functions are closely related to their anti-microbial functions, i.e., the same or similar mediators are used. Two of the most frequently reported mechanisms are via ARG and ROS.

The serine proteases elastase and cathepsin G inactivate T-cell stimulating cytokines, IL-2 and IL-6, and catalyze shedding of cytokine receptors for IL-2 and IL-6 on T-cells ([72](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B72), [73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B73)). (2) Production of ROS and release of arginase. Both agents can result in downregulation of TCRζ on T-cells, thereby arresting the cell in the G0-G1 phase ([40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B40), [74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B74)–[78](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B78)). (3) Expression of PD-L1. Upregulation of this ligand is associated with interferon-dependent PD1-mediated T-cell apoptosis ([35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B35), [56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B56)). T-cell activation by neutrophils is attained by (4) indirect antigen presentation. Dendritic cells take up antigens from apoptotic neutrophils and serve as APC for T-cells ([61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B61)). (5) Direct antigen presentation. Neutrophils posses the capacity to cross-prime CD8+ T-cells directly in a MHCI-dependent manner ([32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B32)). (6) Release of microbial metabolites (HMB-PP). Neutrophils release bacterial products after ingestion to activate γδ-T-cells ([42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B42)).

ARG is found in the gelatinase containing granules of neutrophils and is thought to contribute to antifungal immunity trough depletion of l-arginine ([79](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B79), [80](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B80)). Depletion of l-arginine also results in a cell cycle arrest in activated T-cells in the G0-G1 phase, which limits T-cell proliferation ([74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B74)). This is thought to occur through downregulation of TCRζ ([75](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B75), [76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B76)). It seems that the expression of TCRζ requires l-arginine for adequate expression and functionality ([81](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B81)). In addition, l-arginine is required for dephosphorylation of cofilin. Cofilin is pivotal for the stability of the immunological synapse. Therefore, depletion of l-arginine by ARG impairs the formation and stability of an immunological synapse, which is required for T-cell activation and proliferation ([82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B82), [83](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B83)).

ROS are an intricate part of neutrophil anti-microbial defense and the lack of ability to produce ROS as, seen in chronic granulomatous disease, is characterized by severe infections ([84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B84)–[86](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B86)). One of the products of NADPH oxidase activation is hydrogenperoxide (H 2 O 2). H 2 O 2 can suppress T-cell proliferation and activation through various mechanisms. It induces apoptosis, decreases Nf-κB activation, and downregulates TCRζ ([77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B77), [78](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B78)). In addition, T-cell suppression by ROS is also accompanied by the oxidation of cofilin ([77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B77), [87](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B87)). Cofilin can, therefore, be influenced by both ARG and ROS: both mechanisms being employed by neutrophils. Therefore, the T-cell suppression by disruption of cofilin might prove to be a useful therapeutic target.

Interestingly, regulatory T-cells are resistant to oxidative stress ([88](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B88)). This suggests that regulatory T-cells are less sensitive to suppression than other T-cells, thus enhancing the overall suppressive effect of H 2 O 2.

Suppression of T-cell activation and proliferation requires high concentrations of H 2 O 2 ([33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B33), [87](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B87)). This amount of ROS might only be reached in inflammatory tissue with massive neutrophil influx. A more elegant way of suppression via H 2 O 2 is through cell-cell contact between neutrophils and T-cells. Such a direct mechanism for delivery of ROS in an immunological synapse has been identified ([29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B29)). Here, neutrophil-T-cell contacts were mediated by MAC-1.

Another important suppressive pathway requires similar cell-cell contacts: inhibition via T-cell PD-1 by PD-L1, a potent inducer of apoptosis in T-cells 1, expressed on neutrophils during sepsis ([25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B25)). The underlying mechanism of PD-L1 expression is an interferon dependent process ([35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B35)). The PD-1/PD-L1 axis is thought to be an important mechanism in the immune suppression found in sepsis patients by inducing lymphocyte apoptosis and monocyte dysfunction ([56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B56)). Blocking this axis after the induction of sepsis by administering a PD-1 blocking antibody improves survival in mice by increasing pathogen clearance ([89](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B89)). This suppressive mechanism might be protective in tissues with severe inflammatory infiltrates, but may be detrimental as immune suppression aggravates sepsis. At this moment, one can only speculate regarding the role of PD-L1 on neutrophils in this immune suppressed state.

Finally, neutrophils can modulate T-cells by degranulating granular constituents, such as neutrophil elastase. These proteases are able to cleave and inactivate essential cytokines, such as IL-2 and receptors, such as the IL-2 and IL-6 receptor on T-cells ([72](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B72), [73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B73)).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410)Conclusion

The studies mentioned in this review have led to the consensus that neutrophils are capable of modulating adaptive immune responses through interactions with T- and B-cells and possibly APCs. The mechanistic studies in mice have been corroborated with human _ex vivo_ data. These studies show that neutrophils are capable of directly interacting with lymphocytes and modulating their responses at local sites of inflammation as well as in draining LNs. One of the key remaining issues is the question whether human neutrophils show functional plasticity as has been suggested by us and others ([13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B13), [90](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B90)). This plasticity can occur at different levels: (1) the existence of functional subsets, which are intrinsically different or (2) the transdifferentiation into suppressive neutrophils or even into an APC type of hybrid cell ([90](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B90)–[92](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B92)). The microenvironmental cues mediating the switch from classical neutrophils to suppressive neutrophils have barely been studied although TGF-β seems to play an important role in microbial and tumor models ([11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B11), [23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B23)).

In conclusion, murine and human studies to date show that neutrophils are potent modulators of immunity. The first step of establishing a strategy to target immune modulatory neutrophils without influencing their essential anti-microbial functions is finding relevant human diseases in which this modulation plays a pivotal role ([93](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4568410#B93)). The unraveling of microenvironmental cues mediating the recruitment of and/or “switching” into suppressive neutrophils in such diseases is essential in understanding and targeting of this pathway.

args.summary:
This is a scientific review article published in Frontiers in Immunology (2015, doi: 10.3389/fimmu.2015.00471) by Pieter H. C. Leliefeld, Leo Koenderman, and Janesh Pillay (University Medical Center Utrecht, Netherlands) titled "How Neutrophils Shape Adaptive Immune Responses." The review examines the emerging role of neutrophils beyond their classical first-line antimicrobial defense, focusing on how they modulate adaptive immunity.

Key topics covered:
- Neutrophils migrate in high numbers to sites of inflammation (infection, tissue damage, cancer) and can subsequently migrate to draining lymph nodes (LNs), where they interact with lymphocytes and antigen-presenting cells (APCs) via direct cell-cell contact or through mediators like proteases, cytokines, and reactive oxygen species (ROS).
- Two routes for neutrophil entry into LNs: via high endothelial venules (HEVs) requiring integrins αMβ2 (MAC-1), αLβ2 (LFA-1), and selectins, or via afferent lymphatics depending on MAC-1 and CXCR4. In LNs, neutrophils occupy the medullary region and interfollicular zone, where they can inhibit humoral (antibody) responses by interacting with B-cells (via TGF-β), or in the spleen's marginal zone, contribute to antibody production and class switching via BAFF, APRIL, and IL-21.
- In viral infections (influenza, RSV, HBV), neutrophils can act as APCs (presenting antigen via MHC-I and co-stimulatory molecules CD80/CD86 to activate CD8+ T-cells) or suppress T-cell responses. In chronic HBV, neutrophils (termed G-MDSCs) limit immune pathology by inhibiting T-cells via arginase.
- In bacterial infections, neutrophils activate γδ-T-cells through the microbial metabolite HMB-PP released after phagocytosis, and are pivotal for TH1 responses (e.g., in Legionella pneumophila models). Neutrophils can also negatively or positively affect antigen presentation by professional APCs.
- In sepsis, neutrophils contribute to immune suppression via arginase (depleting L-arginine), the PD-1/PD-L1 axis (inducing T-cell apoptosis, interferon-dependent), and other mechanisms. Blocking PD-1 improved survival in mice by increasing pathogen clearance.
- In cancer, granulocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells (G-MDSCs) and suppressive neutrophils promote tumor growth by suppressing CD8+ T-cell responses. TGF-β induces pro-tumor (N1) phenotype while blocking TGF-β induces anti-tumor (N2) phenotype. Neutrophils promote metastasis, angiogenesis (via MMP9), and can be recruited to tumors by IL-17 and G-CSF pathways involving γδ-T-cells.
- Mechanisms of T-cell suppression by neutrophils include: (1) degranulation of elastase and cathepsin G, which inactivate IL-2/IL-6 and shed their receptors; (2) production of ROS (H2O2) and release of arginase, which downregulate TCRζ and arrest cells in G0-G1 phase and disrupt cofilin (important for the immunological synapse); (3) PD-L1 expression causing PD-1-mediated T-cell apoptosis. Regulatory T-cells are resistant to oxidative stress.
- T-cell activation mechanisms include indirect antigen presentation (dendritic cells take up antigens from apoptotic neutrophils), direct antigen presentation (cross-priming CD8+ T-cells in an MHCI-dependent manner), and release of microbial metabolites (HMB-PP) to activate γδ-T-cells.
- A key remaining question is whether human neutrophils exhibit functional plasticity through functional subsets or transdifferentiation into suppressive neutrophils or APC-type hybrid cells. The microenvironmental cues (especially TGF-β) mediating the switch from classical to suppressive neutrophils are poorly understood.

The review concludes that targeting immune-modulatory neutrophils without affecting their essential antimicrobial functions requires identifying relevant human diseases where this modulation plays a pivotal role.
args.key_excerpts: "Neutrophils are classically considered as cells pivotal for the first line of defense against invading pathogens. In recent years, evidence has accumulated that they are also important in the orchestration of adaptive immunity."

## Abstract

### Objective

Non-canonical myeloid cell populations are increasingly recognized as critical regulators of inflammation in neuroimmunological disease. Here, we investigate the role of alternatively activated neutrophils (aaN) in limiting encephalitogenic T cell responses during experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), a widely used model of multiple sclerosis.

### Methods

Arginase-1–expressing aaN were identified and characterized within central nervous system (CNS) infiltrates during EAE using flow cytometry, single-cell RNA sequencing, and fluorescent in situ hybridization (RNAscope) combined with immunohistochemistry. The immunomodulatory properties of aaN were evaluated in vitro using CD4⁺ T cell suppression assays and in vivo by adoptive transfer of ex vivo–generated aaN during the preclinical phase following encephalitogenic T-cell injection.

### Results

aaN were consistently detected within the CNS throughout EAE and spatially co-localized with encephalitogenic T cells. Transcriptomic profiling of aaN revealed enrichment of pathways associated with regulation of T cell activation and immune suppression. CNS-derived aaN potently inhibited CD4⁺ T cell proliferation in vitro. Therapeutic augmentation of this population, via adoptive transfer of ex vivo–generated aaN into mice following the injection of encephalitogenic T cells, delayed clinical EAE onset, markedly reduced the accumulation of pathogenic T cells within CNS lesions, and significantly enhanced neuronal survival. Mechanistically, ex vivo–generated aaN suppressed T cell responses through a contact-dependent, PD-L1–independent pathway, indicating a previously unrecognized mode of neutrophil-mediated immunoregulation.

### Interpretation

These findings identify aaN as a previously underappreciated immunoregulatory population within the inflamed CNS that restrains pathogenic T cell responses and limits neuroinflammation during EAE. Collectively, our data support the therapeutic potential of strategies that augment aaN activity, including autologous aaN-based cell therapy or interventions that promote CNS homing, polarization, and persistence of endogenous aaN, as novel approaches for disease modification in multiple sclerosis.

## Background

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a multifocal, inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system (CNS) and the leading cause of non-traumatic neurological disability among young adults in the Western Hemisphere [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR1 "Attfield KE, Jensen LT, Kaufmann M, Friese MA, Fugger L. The immunology of multiple sclerosis. Nat Rev Immunol. 2022;22(12):734–50.")]. Experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), a widely used murine model of MS, can be induced by adoptive transfer of myelin-specific, Th17-polarized CD4⁺ T cells into naïve recipients [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR2 "Carbajal KS, Mironova Y, Ulrich-Lewis JT, Kulkarni D, Grifka-Walk HM, Huber AK, et al. Th Cell Diversity in Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis and Multiple Sclerosis. J Immunol. 2015;195(6):2552–9."), [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR3 "Segal BM. The diversity of encephalitogenic CD4+ T cells in multiple sclerosis and its animal models. J Clin Med. 2019. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm8010120
                  
                .")]. Upon reactivation within the CNS, these encephalitogenic T cells recruit peripheral myeloid cells —particularly neutrophils and monocytes —that contribute to demyelination and axonal injury. Neutrophils have been implicated in blood–brain barrier disruption and amplification of neuroinflammation during early EAE lesion development [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR4 "Carlson T, Kroenke M, Rao P, Lane TE, Segal B. The Th17-ELR+ CXC chemokine pathway is essential for the development of central nervous system autoimmune disease. J Exp Med. 2008;205(4):811–23."),[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR5 "Kroenke MA, Chensue SW, Segal BM. EAE mediated by a non-IFN-gamma/non-IL-17 pathway. Eur J Immunol. 2010;40(8):2340–8. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1002/eji.201040489
                  
                ."),[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR6 "Rumble JM, Huber AK, Krishnamoorthy G, Srinivasan A, Giles DA, Zhang X, et al. Neutrophil-related factors as biomarkers in EAE and MS. J Exp Med. 2015;212(1):23–35."),[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR7 "McColl SR, Staykova MA, Wozniak A, Fordham S, Bruce J, Willenborg DO. Treatment with anti-granulocyte antibodies inhibits the effector phase of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis. J Immunol. 1998;161(11):6421–6."),[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR8 "Pierson ER, Wagner CA, Goverman JM. The contribution of neutrophils to CNS autoimmunity. Clin Immunol. 2018;189:23–8.")], while monocyte-derived macrophages and dendritic cells exacerbate pathology via release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, reactive oxygen species, and matrix-degrading enzymes, as well as antigen presentation [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR9 "Segal BM. CNS chemokines, cytokines, and dendritic cells in autoimmune demyelination. J Neurol Sci. 2005;228(2):210–4."), [10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR10 "King IL, Dickendesher TL, Segal BM. Circulating Ly-6C+ myeloid precursors migrate to the CNS and play a pathogenic role during autoimmune demyelinating disease. Blood. 2009;113(14):3190–7.")].

Traditionally, monocyte derived cells and neutrophils have been portrayed as uniformly pro-inflammatory effector cells with limited phenotypic variability. However, advances in single-cell and spatial transcriptomic profiling reveal considerable heterogeneity and plasticity within these myeloid lineages [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR11 "Jordao MJC, Sankowski R, Brendecke SM, Sagar, Locatelli G, Tai YH, et al. Single-cell profiling identifies myeloid cell subsets with distinct fates during neuroinflammation. Science. 2019;363(6425)."),[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR12 "Ng LG, Ostuni R, Hidalgo A. Heterogeneity of neutrophils. Nat Rev Immunol. 2019;19(4):255–65."),[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR13 "Dong Y, Kang Z, Zhang Z, Zhang Y, Zhou H, Liu Y, et al. Single-cell profile reveals the landscape of cardiac immunity and identifies a cardio-protective Ym-1(hi) neutrophil in myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury. Sci Bull (Beijing). 2024;69(7):949–67.")]. For example, subsets of monocytes/macrophages, as well as macrophage-like cells such as microglia, can undergo alternative activation in response to specific environmental cues, acquiring an arginase-1 (Arg1)/mannose receptor (Mrc1/CD206) expressing phenotype associated with immunoregulatory and reparative properties [[14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR14 "Wynn TA, Vannella KM. Macrophages in tissue repair, regeneration, and fibrosis. Immunity. 2016;44(3):450–62.")]. There is growing evidence that alternatively activated macrophages and microglia can suppress destructive neuroinflammation and limit tissue damage in the nervous system, thereby promoting functional recovery [[15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR15 "Shechter R, Miller O, Yovel G, Rosenzweig N, London A, Ruckh J, et al. Recruitment of beneficial M2 macrophages to injured spinal cord is orchestrated by remote brain choroid plexus. Immunity. 2013;38(3):555–69."),[16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR16 "Pedragosa J, Miro-Mur F, Otxoa-de-Amezaga A, Justicia C, Ruiz-Jaen F, Ponsaerts P, et al. CCR2 deficiency in monocytes impairs angiogenesis and functional recovery after ischemic stroke in mice. J Cereb Blood Flow Metab. 2020;40(1_suppl):S98–116."),[17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR17 "Ahrends T, Aydin B, Matheis F, Classon CH, Marchildon F, Furtado GC, et al. Enteric pathogens induce tissue tolerance and prevent neuronal loss from subsequent infections. Cell. 2021;184(23):5715-27 e12.")]. These insights have stimulated efforts to develop therapeutic strategies that enhance the recruitment or induction of reparative myeloid populations, as well as ex vivo–engineered autologous myeloid cell therapies [[18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR18 "Yang J, Xie Y, Xia Z, Ji S, Yang X, Yue D, et al. HucMSC-Exo Induced N2 Polarization of Neutrophils: Implications for Angiogenesis and Tissue Restoration in Wound Healing. Int J Nanomedicine. 2024;19:3555–75.")].

To date, most studies of alternatively activated myeloid cells in in EAE, MS, or spinal cord injury have focused on monocyte-derived cells and microglia [[15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR15 "Shechter R, Miller O, Yovel G, Rosenzweig N, London A, Ruckh J, et al. Recruitment of beneficial M2 macrophages to injured spinal cord is orchestrated by remote brain choroid plexus. Immunity. 2013;38(3):555–69."), [19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR19 "Miron VE, Boyd A, Zhao JW, Yuen TJ, Ruckh JM, Shadrach JL, et al. M2 microglia and macrophages drive oligodendrocyte differentiation during CNS remyelination. Nat Neurosci. 2013;16(9):1211–8."), [20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR20 "Giles DA, Washnock-Schmid JM, Duncker PC, Dahlawi S, Ponath G, Pitt D, et al. Myeloid cell plasticity in the evolution of central nervous system autoimmunity. Ann Neurol. 2018;83(1):131–41.")]. In contrast, far less is known about the potential for neutrophils—typically regarded as short-lived and cytotoxic—to adopt immunoregulatory phenotypes or actively promote CNS repair. Recent evidence indicates that, under specific conditions, neutrophil lineage cells can also adopt non-canonical states [[21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR21 "Cuartero MI, Ballesteros I, Moraga A, Nombela F, Vivancos J, Hamilton JA, et al. N2 Neutrophils, Novel Players in Brain Inflammation After Stroke Modulation by the PPAR gamma Agonist Rosiglitazone. Stroke. 2013;44(12):3498–508."),[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR22 "Fridlender ZG, Sun J, Kim S, Kapoor V, Cheng G, Ling L, et al. Polarization of tumor-associated neutrophil phenotype by TGF-beta: “N1” versus “N2” TAN. Cancer Cell. 2009;16(3):183–94."),[23](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR23 "Hou Y, Yang D, Xiang R, Wang H, Wang X, Zhang H, et al. N2 neutrophils may participate in spontaneous recovery after transient cerebral ischemia by inhibiting ischemic neuron injury in rats. Int Immunopharmacol. 2019;77:105970."),[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR24 "Cartwright JA, Potey PMD, Livingstone E, Campana L, Starkey Lewis PJ, Oremek MEM, et al. Temporal dichotomy of neutrophil function in acute liver injury and repair. JHEP Rep. 2025;7(7):101417."),[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR25 "Ogawa K, Asano K, Yotsumoto S, Yamane T, Arita M, Hayashi Y, et al. Beyond host defense and tissue injury: the emerging role of neutrophils in tissue repair. Am J Physiol Cell Physiol. 2024;326(3):C661–83.")]. For example, the granulocytic myeloid derived suppressor cells (G-MDSCs) and so-called “N2” neutrophils that accumulate in tumor microenvironments actively inhibit T cell responses [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR22 "Fridlender ZG, Sun J, Kim S, Kapoor V, Cheng G, Ling L, et al. Polarization of tumor-associated neutrophil phenotype by TGF-beta: “N1” versus “N2” TAN. Cancer Cell. 2009;16(3):183–94."), [27](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR27 "Antuamwine BB, Bosnjakovic R, Hofmann-Vega F, Wang X, Theodosiou T, Iliopoulos I, et al. N1 versus N2 and PMN-MDSC: a critical appraisal of current concepts on tumor-associated neutrophils and new directions for human oncology. Immunol Rev. 2023;314(1):250–79."), [28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR28 "Veglia F, Sanseviero E, Gabrilovich DI. Myeloid-derived suppressor cells in the era of increasing myeloid cell diversity. Nat Rev Immunol. 2021;21(8):485–98.")]. In addition, we previously identified a distinct population of immature, alternatively activated neutrophils (aaN) that promote neuronal survival and axon regeneration following optic nerve and spinal cord injury, mediated in part through secretion of neurotrophic factors and modulation of the lesion microenvironment [[29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR29 "Jerome AD, Sas AR, Wang Y, Hammond LA, Wen J, Atkinson JR, et al. Cytokine polarized, alternatively activated bone marrow neutrophils drive axon regeneration. Nat Immunol. 2024;25(6):957–68."), [30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR30 "Sas AR, Carbajal KS, Jerome AD, Menon R, Yoon C, Kalinski AL, et al. A new neutrophil subset promotes CNS neuron survival and axon regeneration. Nat Immunol. 2020;21(12):1496–505.")]. Whether similar populations arise spontaneously during autoimmune demyelination and influence disease course is unknown.

Here, we report that Arg1-expressing aaN spontaneously emerge within EAE inflammatory lesions where they co-localize with pathogenic T cells and display potent immunosuppressive properties. Augmenting this population via adoptive transfer of ex vivo–generated aaN delayed clinical EAE onset, reduced the accumulation of encephalitogenic T cells within CNS infiltrates and enhanced neuron survival. Mechanistically, aaN suppressed myelin-reactive T cell proliferation in a contact-dependent manner, revealing a previously unrecognized immunomodulatory role for neutrophils in CNS autoimmunity.

## Methods

### Mice

Wild-type C57Bl/6 (strain #027) and congenic Ly5.1 (strain #564) mice were obtained from Charles River Laboratories (Wilmington, MA) at 8–12 weeks of age. Arg1 YFP reporter mice (strain #015857) and 2D2 T cell receptor (TCR) transgenic mice (strain #006912) were obtained from Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME). All mice were housed under specific pathogen-free conditions in microisolator cages.

### Induction and assessment of EAE

EAE was induced as previously described [[31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR31 "Duncker PC, Stoolman JS, Huber AK, Segal BM. GM-CSF promotes chronic disability in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis by altering the composition of central nervous system-infiltrating cells, but is dispensable for disease induction. J Immunol. 2018;200(3):966–73.")]. Briefly, donor mice were immunized with MOG 35–55 peptide (100 μg; MEVGWYRSP-FSRVVHLYRNGK; Biosynthesis) emulsified in CFA (Sigma, F5881), at four sites over the flanks. Inguinal, axial, and brachial lymph nodes and spleens were harvested 10–14 days later, homogenized, and passed through a 70 μm strainer to achieve a single-cell suspension. The dissociated cells were cultured with MOG 35–55 peptide (50 μg/mL; Biosynthesis) under Th17-polarizing conditions (8 ng/mL recombinant murine IL-23 (R&D), 10 ng/mL recombinant murine IL-1α (Peprotech), and 10 μg/mL anti–IFNγ monoclonal antibody (Bio X Cell)), in RPMI (Gibco, 21,870,084) supplemented with HEPES buffer (Gibco, 15,630,080), MEM non-essential amino acids (Gibco, 11,140,076), sodium pyruvate (Gibco, 1,360,070), β-mercaptoethanol (Gibco, 21,985,023), L-glutamine (Gibco, 25,030,081), Pen Strep (Gibco, 15,140,122), and 10% FBS (Gemini Bio-products, 100–106)). After 96 h of culture, CD4+ T cells were purified using L3T4 magnetic bead sorting (Miltenyi Biotec) and injected into naïve syngeneic recipients (5.0 × 10 6 CD4+ T cells per mouse i.p.). EAE mice were intravenously injected on days 4 and 6 post- CD4+ T cell transfer with either purified bone-marrow neutrophils (5.0 × 10 6 cells/injection), zymosan-modulated intraperitoneal neutrophils (5.0 × 10 6 cells/injection), or PBS alone. Recipient mice were observed daily for signs of EAE by an examiner blinded to the experimental groups. Mice were scored using a 5-point scale, as previously reported [[32](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR32 "Kroenke MA, Segal BM. Th17 and Th1 responses directed against the immunizing epitope, as opposed to secondary epitopes, dominate the autoimmune repertoire during relapses of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis. J Neurosci Res. 2007;85(8):1685–93.")]: 0 = no abnormality, 0.5 = distal limp tail, 1 = complete limp tail, 1.5 = difficulty righting from supine position, 2 = inability to right from a supine position, 2.5 = overt gait abnormality, 3 = difficulty elevating body while walking, 3.5 = unilateral hind limb paralysis, 4 = bilateral complete hind limb paralysis, 4.5 = moribund, 5 = death.

### Flow cytometry

Cells were washed and resuspended in FACS buffer containing a fixable viability dye (eFluor506 or eFluor780; eBioscience), and Fc Block (anti-CD16/32, clone 2.4G2; 100 ng/mL), and incubated at 4°C for 15 min. Cells were then washed with FACS buffer and incubated with fluorochrome-labeled monoclonal antibodies specific for individual surface markers at 4°C for 25 min. Following a third wash, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA). For intracellular staining, the BD Biosciences’ Cytofix/Cytoperm™ Fixation/Permeabilization Kit was used according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Data were acquired on a FACS Symphony flow cytometer (BD Biosciences) or FACSMelody flow cytometer (BD Biosciences) and analyzed using FlowJo software (Tree Star).

The following flow cytometry antibodies were obtained from BD Biosciences: CD4 (GK1.5; BUV395), CD11b (M1/70; BV786), CD11c (HL3; BUV737), CD14 (rmC5-3; BV650), CD45 (30-F11; BUV805), CD62L (MEL-14; APC), CD84 (mCD84.7rMAb; BV711), CD279 (RMP1-30; BUV737), F4/80 (T45-2342; PE-CF594), and Ly6G (1A8; BUV563). The following antibodies were obtained from eBioscience: CD44 (IM7, APC) and Ki67 (SolA15; PE-Cy7). The following antibodies were obtained from Invitrogen: CD4 (RM4-5; APC), CD11b (M1/70; APC-Cy7), CD44 (IM7; PE-Cy7), CD45 (30-F11, eFluor 450), CD45.1 (A20; FITC), CD101 (Moushi101; PE-Cy7), and CD206 (MR6F3; Alexa Fluor 700). Arginase-1 (PE) was obtained from R&D systems.

### RNAscope and immunohistochemistry

Spinal cords were harvested from mice following transcardial perfusion with 10 mL of 1 × PBS, followed by 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) Thoracoumbar spinal cord segments, where inflammatory lesions are most prominent in EAE, were dissected for analysis. Tissues were post-fixed overnight in 4% PFA, washed in 1 × PBS, and cryoprotected in 30% sucrose at 4°C. Tissues were then embedded in optimal cutting temperature (O.C.T.) compound (Fisher Scientific, Cat. No. 23–730-571), rapidly frozen on dry ice, and stored at − 80°C until cryosectioning at − 20°C on a Leica CM1950 cryostat. Sections(10–12 µm) were collected on Superfrost Plus slides for subsequent RNAscope and immunofluorescence analyses.

RNAscope Multiplex Fluorescent assays were performed according to the manufacturer’s protocol with minor modifications. Cryosections were warmed at 60°C for 15 min, post-fixed in 4% PFA at room temperature for 5 min followed by antigen retrieval at 99°C for 10 min. Sections were washed twice in distilled water, and dehydrated through graded ethanol for 5 min each. Slides were incubated with hydrogen peroxide at room temperature for 10 min, followed by dehydration and air-drying. After ethanol removal, sections were air-dried for 5 min and loaded into ACD slide holders. Protease III was applied, and sections were incubated at 40°C for 30 min. Following washes with distilled water, sections were hybridized with the _Cxcr2_ probe for 2 h at 40°C. Signal amplification was performed through three amplification steps at 40°C, and fluorescent signals were developed using TSA Vivid dyes according to the manufacturer’s protocol.

For immunofluorescence co-detection, sections were incubated overnight at room temperature with an antibody cocktail prepared in ACD co-detection antibody diluent (Cat. No. 323160) containing αArg1 (1:100; R&D Systems, Cat. No. IC5868F), αCD3ε (1:100; Novus Biologicals, Cat. No. NB600-1441), and αLy6G (1:200; eBioscience, Cat. No. 16–9668-82). Corresponding secondary antibodies were applied the following day and the slides were incubated for 2 h at room temperature. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI, and tissue autofluorescence was quenched using 0.5 × TrueBlack solution in 70% ethanol for 10 min. Coverslips were mounted using Fluoromount-G mounting medium.

Negative controls included RNAscope negative control probes (ACD) and sections processed without primary antibodies to assess nonspecific secondary antibody staining. In addition, fluorescence minus one (FMO) controls were used when appropriate to establish signal thresholds. Spinal cords from n = 6 mice were analyzed (biological replicates), and 1–2 sections per mouse were examined (technical replicates). Imaging and quantification were performed by investigators blinded to experimental group identity.

For retinal whole-mount staining and retinal ganglion cell (RGC) quantification, mice were transcardially perfused with 1 × PBS, eyes were enucleated, and tissues were fixed in PFA for 2 h. Retinas were dissected under a stereomicroscope, permeabilized with 3% Triton X-100, blocked with 5% normal donkey serum, and incubated with rabbit anti-mouse Brn3a antibody (Synaptic Systems, 411 003) at 4°C for 72 h, followed by Alexa Fluor 594–conjugated donkey anti-rabbit secondary antibody (Invitrogen, A-21207) overnight. Whole mounts were washed, mounted on Superfrost Plus slides, and imaged using an Olympus IX71 inverted microscope with an Olympus DP72 camera. Brn3a⁺ RGCs were quantified using Imaris software across eight fields per retina, sampled from all quadrants at predefined distances from the optic nerve head.

### Spinning disk confocal imaging

Tissue sections were imaged using a Yokogawa SoRa-W1 spinning disk confocal unit mounted on a Nikon Ti2 inverted microscope controlled with NIS-Elements. Images were acquired using a 60 × 1.4 NA Plan Apo oil-immersion objective and a Hamamatsu ORCA-Fusion BT sCMOS camera, yielding a pixel size of 108 nm and a z-step size of 150 nm. Laser lines at 405, 488, 577, 639, and 748 nm were used to sequentially excite the respective probes, with matched bandpass emission filters. Images shown in Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#Fig2) were further processed using the 3D blind deconvolution algorithm with 25 iterations and low-noise parameters in the NIS Elements.

### Single-cell RNA-Seq analysis

Single-cell libraries were generated using the10X Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 5’ kit (PN-1000263). Approximately 18,000 live cells (targeting 10,000 cells) were loaded onto Chromium chip to create thousands of gel bead-in-emulsion (GEMs). Single-cell RNA sequencing data were analyzed using Seurat v4.4.0. Feature barcode matrices, generated by Cell Ranger from four blood and four spinal cord samples, were imported into a Seurat object (_min.cells_ = 3). Quality control filtering was applied to remove low-quality cells using the following criteria: mitochondrial gene percentage < 10%, ribosomal gene percentage < 40%, nFeature_RNA > 200 and < 4000, and nCount_RNA < 10,000.

Datasets were normalized and integrated using the SCTransform workflow with glmGamPoi to account for sample-to-sample variation, followed by dimensional reduction using principal component analysis (PCA) with the top 20 principal components. Cells were clustered using graph-based clustering at a resolution of 0.1 and visualized using UMAP. Clusters were initially generated by unsupervised clustering. Neutrophil populations were subsequently identified based on expression of canonical granulocytic lineage markers, including Csf3r, Ly6g, and Cxcr2. These markers were selectively enriched in a subset of clusters within the master object and were not broadly expressed across other myeloid populations**.** Clusters enriched for these markers (clusters 0, 6, 8, and 12; Fig. S1) were annotated as neutrophils and extracted for downstream analysis. The neutrophil subset was then reclustered using 20 principal components at a resolution of 0.5, yielding several groups that were consolidated into three major neutrophil subclusters.

Cluster marker genes were identified using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test implemented in Seurat’s FindAllMarkers function. Marker genes were defined as those showing higher expression in one cluster relative to the others and meeting the criteria of adjusted _p_< 0.05 and log₂ fold change > 0.25. The genes Mpo and Mrc1 were also included in heatmap visualizations based on their biological relevance. Differential gene expression between spinal cord and blood neutrophils was determined using the FindMarkers function with a Wilcoxon test, with significance defined as adjusted _p_< 0.05 after multiple testing correction. Gene ontology enrichment analysis of cluster marker genes was performed using clusterProfiler.

Visualization of gene expression patterns was performed using ComplexHeatmap. Heatmaps display scaled expression values, with scaling performed across all tissues and clusters; however, only spinal cord and blood cells from Cluster 1 were shown in the final plots. Violin plots were used to display the distribution of Arg1 expression across individual cell barcodes. Dimplot visualizations split by tissue were generated using merged UMAP cluster assignments for color shading. Pie charts were used to visualize the relative distribution of cells from different disease stages within neutrophil subclusters. Because these plots summarize pooled single-cell counts from the integrated dataset, they are presented for descriptive purposes and were not subjected to statistical testing**.**

### Intraperitoneal (i.p.) lavage and neutrophil isolation

Naïve C57BL/6 adult mice were injected i.p. with 500 μL of zymosan (2 μg/μL in 1XPBS) and euthanized 36–48 h later by CO 2 fixation. The peritoneal cavity was lavaged with 10 mL of sterile ice-cold PBS, which was recovered after a 5 min. dwelling time. Neutrophils were isolated from the lavage fluid using anti-Ly6G magnetic beads (MACS; Miltenyi Biotec) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Cell purity (95–99%) was confirmed via flow cytometry.

### Bone-marrow neutrophil isolation

Naïve C57BL/6 adult mice were euthanized by CO 2 fixation. Femurs, tibias, and humeri were dissected and cleared of surrounding muscle. Bone marrow cells were flushed out with MACS buffer (1XPBS supplemented with 0.5% BSA and 2 mM EDTA). Neutrophils were isolated from total bone marrow cells using anti-Ly6G magnetic beads (MACS; Miltenyi Biotec), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Cell purity (95–99%) was routinely confirmed by flow cytometry.

### CNS mononuclear cell isolation

Mice were anesthetized with isoflurane and transcardially perfused with 10 mL of 1 × PBS. Spinal cords were isolated by hydraulic extrusion through the spinal canal using 5 mL of FACS buffer. Brain and spinal cord parenchyma were mechanically dissociated in HBSS supplemented with collagenase A (1 mg/mL; Roche) and DNase I (1 mg/mL; MilliporeSigma) using an 18-gauge needle, followed by enzymatic digestion at 37°C for 20 min. Mononuclear cells were enriched by centrifugation in 27% Percoll (GE Healthcare) for 5 min at 800 × g and 4°C. The myelin and debris layer was removed, and the resulting cell pellet was collected for flow cytometric analysis (see _Flow Cytometry_).

Following dissection of the brain and spinal cord, meninges were carefully peeled from the skull cap and spinal column respectively. Brain and spinal cord meninges were processed separately and digested in HBSS containing collagenase A (1 mg/mL) and DNase I (1 mg/mL) at 37°C for 20 min and passed through a 70-µm cell strainer. Meningeal cells were collected for flow cytometric analysis.

### Preparation of CD4 T cell-depleted splenocytes

Spleens were mechanically dissociated through a 70-µm cell strainer. Red blood cells were lysed using ACK lysis buffer (Quality Biologicals), and the reaction was quenched with FACS buffer. CD4 cells were depleted from the dissociated cell preparation using MACS CD4⁺ magnetic beads (L3T4; Miltenyi Biotec) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

### T cell suppression assay

CD4⁺ T cells were isolated from pooled lymph nodes and spleens of naïve C57BL/6 mice by positive selection using anti-CD4⁺ magnetic beads (L3T4; MACS, Miltenyi Biotec) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Purified CD4⁺ T cells were labeled with CFSE using the CellTrace™ CFSE Proliferation Kit (Invitrogen). Arg1⁺ neutrophils (CD45⁺ CD11b⁺ Ly6G⁺ YFP⁺) and Arg1⁻ neutrophils (CD45⁺ CD11b⁺ Ly6G⁺ YFP⁻) were FACS-sorted from CNS mononuclear cells isolated from Arg1 YFP reporter mice during EAE (Fig. S2A). The purity of CD4⁺ T cells and neutrophil populations was routinely confirmed by flow cytometry (95–99%).

Unless otherwise indicated, suppression assays were performed at a 1:1 T cell to neutrophil ratio. For polyclonal stimulation, CFSE-labeled CD4⁺ T cells (0.3 or 1.5 × 10 5 per well) were cultured in 200 µl of media in 96-well round-bottom plates coated with anti-CD3ε monoclonal antibody (1 µg/mL; eBioscience, clone 145-2C11) and supplemented with soluble anti-CD28 monoclonal antibody (1 µg/mL; eBioscience, Cat. No. 16–0281-82). For antigen-specific stimulation, CFSE-labeled 2D2 CD4⁺ T cells (5.0 × 10 5 cells per well) were co-cultured with CD4⁻ splenocytes (5.0 × 10 5 cells per well) pulsed with MOG 35–55 peptide (50 µg/mL). In selected experiments, blocking monoclonal antibodies were added at 10 µg/mL including PD-L1 (Invitrogen, Cat. No. 16–5982-85), GPNMB (Invitrogen, Cat. No. PA5-47,301), Galectin-9 (Bio X Cell, Cat. No. BE0218), PD-L2 (Bio X Cell, Cat. No. BE0112), and ICAM-1 (Invitrogen, Cat. No. MA5407). Cells were cultured for 96 h at 37°C in 5% CO₂, harvested and analyzed by flow cytometry.

Transwell assays were conducted using 24-well Transwell plates fitted with 5.0-µm pore size inserts (Corning Costar). CFSE-labeled CD4⁺ T cells (0.5 × 10⁶ cells/mL) were seeded in the lower chamber with plate-bound anti-CD3ε monoclonal antibody and soluble anti-CD28 monoclonal antibody, as described above, while neutrophils (0.5 × 10⁶ cells/mL) were placed in the upper insert.

### Statistics

Comparisons between two groups were conducted using paired or unpaired two-tailed Student’s _t_ tests, as appropriate. Comparisons involving multiple groups were analyzed by one-way or two-way ANOVA with correction for multiple comparisons, as specified in the figure legends. Disease severity curves were compared using unpaired two-tailed Student’s _t_ tests with Welch’s correction at individual time points where indicated, as well as by analysis of the area under the curve (AUC) for individual mice. In addition, overall disease course was assessed using a mixed-effects model. Differences in disease incidence were analyzed using a log-rank (Mantel–Cox) test. Outliers were identified using ROUT analysis and excluded when appropriate. Statistical significance was defined as _P_< 0.05 (*) with _P_< 0.01 (**), _P_< 0.001 (***), and _P_< 0.0001 (****). Statistical methods employed for RNA-seq analysis are described in the preceding subsection.

### Schematic design

All figure schematics were created with BioRender.com.

### Study approval

All animal experiments were performed in accordance with an IACUC-approved protocol at The Ohio State University.

## Results

### Alternatively activated neutrophils accumulate in the inflamed CNS during EAE

To identify aaN within the CNS during EAE, CD45.1⁺ encephalitogenic Th17 cells were adoptively transferred into CD45.2 + Arg1 YFP reporter mice. On day 7 post-transfer (p.t.), spinal cord immune cells and peripheral blood mononuclear cells were harvested and analyzed by multiparameter flow cytometry. T-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (tSNE) of pooled CD45⁺CD11b⁺Ly6G⁺ cells revealed discrete clustering that clearly distinguished CNS-infiltrating neutrophils from circulating neutrophils (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#Fig1)A). Each cluster contained cells derived from multiple animals, indicating that the observed populations were consistently present across mice. Peripheral blood neutrophils (red) exhibited a conventional mature phenotype– Ly6G hi CXCR2 hi—and lacked expression of Arg1-YFP and other alternative activation markers (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#Fig1)A, B). In contrast, spinal cord-infiltrating neutrophils segregated into two populations: one resembling conventional neutrophils (purple; Ly6G hi CXCR2 int F4/80−Arg1-YFP−), and the other expressing features consistent with immaturity (blue; Ly6G low CXCR2 low F4/80+) and alternative activation (Arg1-YFP+CD84+). Notably, the cells in the latter cluster aberrantly expressed CD14, a marker typically associated with monocytes and monocyte-derived cells. We have previously observed a similar CD14⁺ aaN subset with neuroprotective properties in the peritoneum and vitreal fluid following local injection of the fungal cell wall extract, zymosan [[29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR29 "Jerome AD, Sas AR, Wang Y, Hammond LA, Wen J, Atkinson JR, et al. Cytokine polarized, alternatively activated bone marrow neutrophils drive axon regeneration. Nat Immunol. 2024;25(6):957–68.")]. Importantly, the relative abundance of aaN in the spinal cord inversely correlated with clinical EAE severity at the time of euthanasia (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#Fig1)C), suggesting a potential immunoregulatory or neuroprotective role.

**Fig.1**
