[Full size image](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9/figures/1)

An endogenous population of alternatively activated immature neutrophils emerges in the CNS during EAE. Spinal cord immune cells and peripheral blood mononuclear cells were harvested on day 7 post-transfer (p.t.) of encephalitogenic CD4 + T cells. **A-C** Cells pooled from 3 mice were analyzed by multiparameter flow cytometry. **A** t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (tSNE) of pooled neutrophils, identified as viable Ly6G+ CD11b+ CD45+ cells. Spinal cord clusters were manually delineated based on their spatial segregation within the t-SNE map. **B** Representative histograms showing mean fluorescent intensity (MFI) of the indicated markers across the three identified neutrophil clusters. Gray histograms indicate fluorescence minus one (FMO) controls used to define gating thresholds. **C** Linear regression analysis depicting the correlation between the total number of Arg1+ neutrophils per spinal cord at peak EAE against the area under the clinical disease score curve (AUC) for individual mice. **D**-**G** Spinal cord immune cells and peripheral blood mononuclear cells were isolated from EAE mice at four stages (preclinical, onset, peak, and late) and analyzed by single-cell RNA sequencing (RNAseq). **D** UMAP visualization of blood-derived (left) and spinal cord-derived (right) neutrophils pooled across all time points. **E** Heatmap of selected differentially express genes (scaled log2) across the three neutrophil clusters, highlighting markers of neutrophil maturation and alternative activation. **F** Gene Ontology Biological Process (GO BP) enrichment analysis of Cluster 3 marker genes. **G** Pie charts showing the relative proportions of circulating (left) and spinal cord-infiltrating (right) neutrophils within each cluster across different stages. **H** Heatmap of differentially expressed genes comparing blood- and spinal cord- derived neutrophils within cluster 3. **I** Violin plots comparing _Arg1_ expression blood- versus spinal cord- derived neutrophils within cluster 3. Data are from 1 experiment representative of two independent experiments with n = 3–5 mice per time point per experiment

To further characterize the diversity of CNS-infiltrating neutrophils, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was performed on CD45⁺ cells FACS-isolated from spinal cord mononuclear cell preparations of EAE mice. Cells identified as neutrophils (Fig. S1) were subset for further analysis. UMAP analysis revealed a distinct neutrophil cluster (Cluster 3; green) enriched for transcripts associated with alternative activation, namely _Arg1_, _Mrc1_, _Cd14_, _Ccl5_, and _Tgfb1_, while being relatively depleted of terminal maturation markers such as _S100a8_, _S100a9_, _Cd101_, _Sell_ and _Cxcr2_ (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#Fig1)D, E). This scRNA-seq–defined aaN cluster resembled the aaN subset identified by flow cytometry, and similarly exhibited elevated CD14 expression. In contrast, Cluster 2 (red) displayed a transcriptional program consistent with mature circulating neutrophils (_Cxcr2_, _Sell_, _Csf3r_, _Cd101_) and was enriched in blood samples, whereas Cluster 1 (blue) exhibited features of inflammatory tissue neutrophils (_Mpo_, _S100a8_, _S100a9_) and was enriched in the spinal cord. Although _Cd101_ has been proposed as a marker distinguishing immature from mature neutrophils, its expression can be heterogeneous in neutrophils that have entered inflamed tissues [[33](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#ref-CR33 "Saqib M, Das S, Nafiz TN, McDonough E, Sankar P, Mishra LK, et al. Pathogenic role for CD101-negative neutrophils in the type I interferon-mediated immunopathogenesis of tuberculosis. Cell Rep. 2025;44(1):115072.")]. Accordingly, cluster identity was assigned based on the overall transcriptional program rather than _Cd101_ expression alone.

Gene Ontology Biological Process (GO BP) enrichment analysis of Cluster 3 marker genes revealed significant enrichment of pathways involved in regulation of T cell activation, regulation of immune effector and inflammatory responses, negative regulation of T cell activation, regulation of neuron apoptotic processes, wound healing, myelination, response to IL-4, and neuron projection regeneration (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9#Fig1)F). ## Scientific Article Summary: Alternatively Activated Neutrophils Limit T Cell–Driven Neuroinflammation

**Publication Details:**
- Published: 27 March 2026 in the *Journal of Neuroinflammation* (Volume 23, article number 151, 2026)
- Open access article, DOI: 10.1186/s12974-026-03780-9
- 1186 accesses at time of page retrieval

**Authors:** Jeffrey R. Atkinson, Calli Bellinger, Andrew D. Jerome, Ashley Munie Gardner, Hayley K. Groover, Shuo Chen, Arnetta McVey Moffatt, Jesse A. Sepeda, Amy Dokiburra, Luke A. Hammond, Tom Liu, Amy Webb, Andrew R. Sas, and Benjamin M. Segal (lead corresponding author).

**Objective:**
The study investigates the role of alternatively activated neutrophils (aaN) in limiting encephalitogenic T cell responses during experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), a widely used mouse model of multiple sclerosis (MS).

**Key Background Context:**
- Multiple sclerosis is the leading cause of non-traumatic neurological disability among young adults in the Western Hemisphere.
- EAE is induced by adoptive transfer of myelin-specific, Th17-polarized CD4⁺ T cells into naïve recipients.
- Traditionally, neutrophils and monocyte-derived cells were viewed as uniformly pro-inflammatory; however, recent advances in single-cell and spatial transcriptomics reveal considerable heterogeneity and plasticity within these myeloid lineages.
- Prior work from this group identified aaN populations that promote neuronal survival and axon regeneration following optic nerve and spinal cord injury.

**Methods:**
1. **Animals:** C57BL/6, congenic Ly5.1, Arg1 YFP reporter mice, and 2D2 TCR transgenic mice.
2. **EAE induction:** MOG 35–55 peptide immunization in CFA, followed by Th17-polarized CD4⁺ T cell adoptive transfer (5.0 × 10⁶ cells/mouse i.p.).
3. **Identification of aaN:** Flow cytometry, single-cell RNA sequencing (10X Chromium), and RNAscope fluorescent in situ hybridization combined with immunohistochemistry.
4. **Functional assays:** In vitro CD4⁺ T cell suppression assays (CFSE-based), transwell assays for contact-dependence, and in vivo adoptive transfer of ex vivo–generated aaN during the preclinical phase.
5. **Disease scoring:** Standard 5-point EAE clinical scale (0 = no abnormality to 5 = death), with blinded assessment.

**Key Results:**
1. **aaN accumulate in inflamed CNS during EAE:** A distinct population of immature, alternatively activated neutrophils (Arg1⁺, Ly6G^low, CXCR2^low, F4/80⁺, CD14⁺, CD84⁺) emerged spontaneously within spinal cord EAE lesions and co-localized with pathogenic T cells. The relative abundance of aaN in the spinal cord inversely correlated with clinical EAE severity.

2. **Transcriptomic profiling:** scRNA-seq identified a distinct neutrophil cluster (Cluster 3) enriched for alternative activation transcripts including *Arg1*, *Mrc1*, *Cd14*, *Ccl5*, *Tgfb1*, *Cd274* (PD-L1), and *Icam1*, while depleted of terminal maturation markers (*S100a8*, *S100a9*, *Cd101*, *Sell*, *Cxcr2*). Gene Ontology enrichment revealed pathways involved in regulation of T cell activation, negative regulation of T cell activation, regulation of neuron apoptotic processes, wound healing, myelination, and neuron projection regeneration.

3. **Functional immunosuppression:** CNS-derived aaN potently inhibited CD4⁺ T cell proliferation in vitro. Adoptive transfer of ex vivo–generated aaN into mice following encephalitogenic T cell injection:
   - Delayed clinical EAE onset
   - Markedly reduced accumulation of pathogenic T cells within CNS lesions
   - Significantly enhanced neuronal survival

4. **Mechanism:** aaN suppressed T cell responses through a contact-dependent, PD-L1–independent pathway, revealing a previously unrecognized mode of neutrophil-mediated immunoregulation. Blocking experiments tested PD-L1, GPNMB, Galectin-9, PD-L2, and ICAM-1 antibodies.

5. **Tissue-adapted reprogramming:** *Arg1*, *Tgfb1*, *Cd274*, *Cd14*, and *Icam1* transcripts were significantly upregulated in spinal cord-derived neutrophils within Cluster 3 compared with blood-derived counterparts, suggesting transcriptional reprogramming within the CNS microenvironment.

**Conclusion/Interpretation:**
The findings identify aaN as a previously underappreciated immunoregulatory population within the inflamed CNS that restrains pathogenic T cell responses and limits neuroinflammation during EAE. The data support therapeutic potential for strategies that augment aaN activity, including autologous aaN-based cell therapy or interventions promoting CNS homing, polarization, and persistence of endogenous aaN, as novel disease-modifying approaches for multiple sclerosis.

**Study Details:**
- All animal experiments performed per IACUC-approved protocol at The Ohio State University.
- Statistics: Student's t-tests, one/two-way ANOVA, mixed-effects models, log-rank (Mantel-Cox) tests; significance at P<0.05.
args.key_excerpts: "Alternatively activated neutrophils (aaN) were consistently detected within the CNS throughout EAE and spatially co-localized with encephalitogenic T cells. Transcriptomic profiling of aaN revealed enrichment of pathways associated with regulation of T cell activation and immune suppression."

## Abstract

Stroke is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, and consists of two types, ischemic and hemorrhagic. Currently, there is no effective treatment to increase the survival rate or improve the quality of life after ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke in the subacute to chronic phases. Therefore, it is necessary to establish therapeutic strategies to facilitate functional recovery in patients with stroke during both phases. Cell-based therapies, using microglia and monocytes/macrophages preconditioned by optimal stimuli and/or any therapies targeting these cells, might be an ideal therapeutic strategy for managing stroke. Microglia and monocytes/macrophages polarize to the classic pro-inflammatory type (M1-like) or alternative protective type (M2-like) by optimal condition. Cell-based therapies using M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages might be protective therapeutic strategies against stroke for three reasons. First, M2-like microglia and monocytes/monocytes secrete protective remodeling factors, thus prompting neuronal network recovery via tissue (including neuronal) and vascular remodeling. Second, these cells could migrate to the injured hemisphere through the blood–brain barrier or choroid–plexus. Third, these cells could mitigate the extent of inflammation-induced injuries by suitable timing of therapeutic intervention. Although future translational studies are required, M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages therapies are attractive for managing stroke based on their protective functions.

## 1. Introduction

Stroke is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, and is categorized into two types, ischemic and hemorrhagic. The majority (70–80%) of stroke cases is ischemic, while intracerebral hemorrhage accounts only for 10–20% of all stroke cases [[1](#B1-ijms-18-02135)]. Recently, several therapeutic strategies, such as thrombolytic treatments for acute ischemic stroke, were identified [[2](#B2-ijms-18-02135)]. However, the patients who are eligible for the treatments are still between 3.4% and 5.2% of all patients with acute ischemic stroke because of the very narrow therapeutic time window [[3](#B3-ijms-18-02135)]. To date, there is still no effective treatment that increases the survival rate or improves the quality of life after ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke [[4](#B4-ijms-18-02135),[5](#B5-ijms-18-02135),[6](#B6-ijms-18-02135)] in the subacute to chronic phases. Currently, physical rehabilitation is considered the only effective therapeutic option to prompt functional recovery after stroke [[7](#B7-ijms-18-02135)]. Therefore, it is necessary to establish other therapeutic strategies to facilitate the functional recovery in patients with stroke in the subacute and chronic phases.

“Single-target” therapies may be insufficient because ischemic and hemorrhagic cerebral injury involves several mechanisms. It has been proposed that therapeutic approaches should target multiple cell types to promote protection and recovery [[8](#B8-ijms-18-02135)]. Cell-based therapies using bone marrow mononuclear cells or bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem/stromal cells may be an effective “multi-target” therapeutic strategy to facilitate functional recovery in patients with stroke during the subacute and chronic phases through pleiotropic mechanisms [[8](#B8-ijms-18-02135),[9](#B9-ijms-18-02135)]. One such mechanism observed in cell-based therapies, using neural progenitor cells and mesenchymal stem cells, was the induction of axonal outgrowth and angiogenesis through the secretion of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) or brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) [[10](#B10-ijms-18-02135),[11](#B11-ijms-18-02135),[12](#B12-ijms-18-02135),[13](#B13-ijms-18-02135)]. In addition, although it is not known whether the recovery environment modulated by cell-based therapies is a direct effect of the administered/transplanted cells themselves, peripheral immune cells may also alter the cytokines released from the periphery into the brain parenchyma [[14](#B14-ijms-18-02135)]. For example, human umbilical cord-blood cell therapy might induce alternations, increasing the production of anti-inflammatory interleukin-10 (IL-10), and decreasing the production of pro-inflammatory interferon-γ (INF-γ) from splenocytes [[15](#B15-ijms-18-02135)]. Although cell-based therapies against stroke are attractive, there remain several clinical concerns, including the distinct therapeutic mechanism and efficiency with which bone marrow-derived cells cross the blood–brain barrier (BBB) [[16](#B16-ijms-18-02135)].

Cell-based therapies using microglia and monocytes/macrophages, and any strategies targeting these cells, might be a promising therapeutic strategy because these cells are the main source of the above-mentioned growth factors in the central nervous system (CNS) [[8](#B8-ijms-18-02135),[17](#B17-ijms-18-02135)]. Although several studies have demonstrated that microglia and monocytes/macrophages might deteriorate the outcome after stroke in the acute phase [[4](#B4-ijms-18-02135),[18](#B18-ijms-18-02135),[19](#B19-ijms-18-02135),[20](#B20-ijms-18-02135)], these cells are known to play protective roles through tissue and vascular remodeling after stroke, during both the subacute and chronic phases [[20](#B20-ijms-18-02135),[21](#B21-ijms-18-02135),[22](#B22-ijms-18-02135)]. The protective M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages exert their effect through the secretion of remodeling factors, such as VEGF, BDNF, and matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9) [[23](#B23-ijms-18-02135),[24](#B24-ijms-18-02135),[25](#B25-ijms-18-02135)], in addition to protective cytokines, such as transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) and IL-10 [[26](#B26-ijms-18-02135),[27](#B27-ijms-18-02135)], which may facilitate anti-inflammation, axonal outgrowth, and angiogenesis after ischemic [[20](#B20-ijms-18-02135),[21](#B21-ijms-18-02135),[27](#B27-ijms-18-02135),[28](#B28-ijms-18-02135)] and hemorrhagic stroke [[22](#B22-ijms-18-02135),[29](#B29-ijms-18-02135),[30](#B30-ijms-18-02135)]. Furthermore, microglia and infiltrating macrophages constitute the predominant phagocytes removing dead cells and tissue debris for remodeling after stroke [[31](#B31-ijms-18-02135)]. In addition, administrated microglia and monocytes/macrophages can cross the BBB, particularly in the pathological condition [[32](#B32-ijms-18-02135),[33](#B33-ijms-18-02135),[34](#B34-ijms-18-02135)]. Therefore, cell-based therapies using microglia and monocytes/macrophages preconditioned by optimal condition and/or any therapies targeting these cells might be an ideal therapeutic strategy for stroke.

In this review, we describe the pathophysiological roles of microglia and monocytes/macrophages after stroke. In addition, we briefly outline the therapeutic mechanisms of using microglia and monocytes/macrophages polarization for prompting neuronal network and angiogenesis, attenuating inflammation, and improving the therapeutic outcomes of patients with stroke.

## 2. The Differences and Similarities between Microglia and Monocytes/Macrophages

Microglia and monocytes/macrophages have distinct cellular origins. Microglia originate from yolk sac progenitors in the neuroepithelium, and express, in the adult brain, high levels of CX3C chemokine receptor 1 (CX3CR1), cluster of differentiation 11b (CD11b), and F4/80, low levels of CD45, and no C-C chemokine receptor type 2 (CCR2) [[35](#B35-ijms-18-02135)]. In contrast, monocytes/macrophages originate from hematopoietic stem cells. The inflammatory monocytes/macrophages express CCR2, CD11b, Ly6C, and low levels of CX3CR1 [[36](#B36-ijms-18-02135)]. After stroke, the release of nucleotides (ATP, UTP) from injured cells, including neurons, activates purinergic receptors on microglia and monocytes/macrophages, and leads to the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines [[17](#B17-ijms-18-02135)]. Recently, the purinergic receptor P2Y12 (P2Y12R) has been identified as a specific marker for microglia in rodents, thus enabling their distinction from monocytes/macrophages [[37](#B37-ijms-18-02135)]. Thus, the expression of P2Y12R might be specific for microglia, including human microglia [[38](#B38-ijms-18-02135),[39](#B39-ijms-18-02135)]. However, both microglia and monocytes/macrophages express the same extent of cell surface markers (e.g., CD11b, F4/80, Iba-1) and share similar functions [[40](#B40-ijms-18-02135)], including fundamental functions, such as phagocytosis and modulation of inflammation.

## 3. Microglia and Monocytes/Macrophages Act as Double-Edged Sword after Stroke

The function of microglia and monocytes/macrophages changes according to the different polarization states. Previously, several studies have demonstrated that microglia and monocytes/macrophages might play harmful roles in the acute phase of ischemic [[18](#B18-ijms-18-02135),[19](#B19-ijms-18-02135),[20](#B20-ijms-18-02135),[41](#B41-ijms-18-02135)] and hemorrhagic stroke [[42](#B42-ijms-18-02135)]. This was evidenced by in vitro experiments using microglial cultures stimulated with pro-inflammatory factors, such as lipopolysaccharide (LPS), IFN-γ, or tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α, which demonstrated the death of cultured neurons in the presence of the activated microglia (or the resulting supernatant) [[43](#B43-ijms-18-02135),[44](#B44-ijms-18-02135)]. Therefore, microglia and monocytes/macrophages were thought to accelerate inflammation. However, they have also been demonstrated to exert a protective role in processes involved in neurological recovery, including neurogenesis, axonal outgrowth, synaptogenesis, angiogenesis, oligodendrogenesis, and remyelination in several CNS diseases [[45](#B45-ijms-18-02135),[46](#B46-ijms-18-02135)]. Based on these findings, microglia and monocytes/macrophages act as a double-edged sword, by playing essential roles in clearing debris, inflammation, causing tissue damage, and promoting tissue healing (remodeling) [[22](#B22-ijms-18-02135),[27](#B27-ijms-18-02135),[47](#B47-ijms-18-02135),[48](#B48-ijms-18-02135)].

## 4. Phenotypic Polarization of Microglia and Monocytes/Macrophages after Stroke

The activated microglia and monocytes/macrophages have been defined as either classic (pro-inflammatory; M1-like) or alternative (anti-inflammatory or protective; M2-like) under pathophysiological conditions. More precisely, M1-like microglia secrete pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-12, IL-23, and nitrogen monoxide (NO), and exacerbate inflammation and tissue injury. In contrast, M2-like microglia secrete anti-inflammatory cytokines, such as TGF-β, IL-4, IL-10, Il-13, and growth factors such as VEGF, BDNF, platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), and progranulin, suppress inflammation, and promote tissue recovery [[49](#B49-ijms-18-02135),[50](#B50-ijms-18-02135),[51](#B51-ijms-18-02135),[52](#B52-ijms-18-02135),[53](#B53-ijms-18-02135)] ([Figure 1](#fig_body_display_ijms-18-02135-f001)a,b). Critical for the regulation of the immune response, the initial M1-like response is typically followed by a secondary M2-like activation that is important for wound healing and suppression of inflammation. This ideal concept is based on findings suggesting that IL-4 induced inflammatory macrophages adopt an alternative activation phenotype and reduce pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion in vitro [[54](#B54-ijms-18-02135)]. Similar to macrophages, microglia also polarize to M1- or M2-like phenotypes [[20](#B20-ijms-18-02135),[21](#B21-ijms-18-02135),[27](#B27-ijms-18-02135)]. In response to interferons (IFNs) from helper T cells [[55](#B55-ijms-18-02135)], LPS or damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) stimulation through Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) [[56](#B56-ijms-18-02135),[57](#B57-ijms-18-02135)], or IL-4/IL-13 signaling, the microglia and monocytes/macrophages undergo M1- or M2-like activations. The activation of the triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) stimulates the phagocytic activity in microglia and downregulates the expression of TNF-α and inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) [[58](#B58-ijms-18-02135)]. Opposing effects were obtained by TREM2 overexpression, while TREM2 deficiency attenuated the phagocytic activities of microglia and exacerbated the ischemic damage in experimental stroke [[31](#B31-ijms-18-02135)] ([Figure 1](#fig_body_display_ijms-18-02135-f001)b). Thus, TREM2 is an anti-inflammatory receptor that simultaneously promotes a phagocytic activity. These results indicated that TREM2 might be an important player in controlling microglial M1/M2-like phenotypes. Moreover, recent studies have shown that exposure of classically activated macrophages (M1-like) to apoptotic cells causes a switch towards an alternatively activated M2-like phenotype of activated phagocytosis (the so-called “dead cell clearance hypothesis”) [[59](#B59-ijms-18-02135),[60](#B60-ijms-18-02135)]. This concept, which is based on the functional skewing of mononuclear phagocytes, and occurs in vivo under physiological and pathological conditions, is likely truer for macrophages than for microglia, in which mixed phenotypes have been observed [[61](#B61-ijms-18-02135)].

## 5. Influence of Age and Sex on the Polarized Activation of Microglia and Monocytes/Macrophages

Age and sex have been reported to affect polarization. Aged microglia derived from aged mice exhibit increased basal expression of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 [[62](#B62-ijms-18-02135)]. These results indicated that the M1-like polarization was accelerated by aging. Moreover, in female mouse brains, ischemia-induced microglial activation enhanced the production of IL-6 via estrogen receptor signaling [[63](#B63-ijms-18-02135)]. This result showed that the M1-like or M2-like polarization was modulated by sex hormones. Based on these observations, it becomes imperative to evaluate the effect of age and sex on microglia and monocytes/macrophages.

## 6. Polarized Activation of Microglia and Monocytes/Macrophages for Providing Therapeutic Strategies

Microglia are highly plastic cells that may rapidly transit between different states. Indeed, microglia have been shown to express both M1- and M2-like markers at the same time [[23](#B23-ijms-18-02135),[40](#B40-ijms-18-02135),[64](#B64-ijms-18-02135)]. In addition, microglia and monocytes/macrophages might be categorized into four main states, namely the (1) classically activated M1-microglia with cytotoxic properties, (2) M2a-microglia with an alternate activation, which is involved in repair and regeneration, (3) M2b-microglia with an immunoregulatory phenotype, and (4) M2c-microglia with an acquired-deactivating phenotype [[65](#B65-ijms-18-02135)]. Generally, M1-like microglia predominate at the injury site at the end stage of disease, when the immunoresolution and repair process of M2-like microglia are dampened. Although the polarization of M1/M2-like microglia during amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) may induce motoneuron degeneration or neuroprotection [[66](#B66-ijms-18-02135)], isolated microglia from mutant superoxide dismutase 1-ALS mice revealed a microglial subpopulation between M1-like and M2-like phenotypes by transcriptome analysis [[67](#B67-ijms-18-02135)]. In brain tissues from patients with Alzheimer’s disease, cluster analysis revealed that the frontal cortex of early Alzheimer’s disease samples was polarized to either the M1 or M2a neuroinflammatory phenotype, but not the M2-like phenotype [[68](#B68-ijms-18-02135)]. In addition, tumor-associated microglia and monocytes/macrophages are also divided to several subpopulations [[35](#B35-ijms-18-02135),[69](#B69-ijms-18-02135)]. The terminology and concept of the M1- and M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages might be complicated and disagreeable [[70](#B70-ijms-18-02135),[71](#B71-ijms-18-02135)], and they might thus be oversimplified. However, several studies using rodents demonstrated that M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages improved the disease outcomes after therapeutic interventions, as described below. Thus, the polarized activation (M1- or M2-like phenotype) is a simple and desirable approach for providing therapeutic strategies in vivo.

## 7. Dynamic Polarized Changes of Microglia and Monocytes/Macrophages after Stroke

Resident microglia are major inflammatory cells in the brain, and are among the first cells to respond to brain injury [[72](#B72-ijms-18-02135),[73](#B73-ijms-18-02135)]. Post-ischemic proliferation of microglia and monocytes/macrophages peaks at 48–72 h after focal cerebral ischemia and may last for several weeks after initial injury [[19](#B19-ijms-18-02135),[21](#B21-ijms-18-02135),[53](#B53-ijms-18-02135)]. Temporal analyses of microglial phenotypes in ischemic animals demonstrated that M2-like microglia were detectable from 12 h, temporally increased at 1 to 3 days, and decreased several days after cerebral ischemia [[20](#B20-ijms-18-02135),[21](#B21-ijms-18-02135)] ([Figure 2](#fig_body_display_ijms-18-02135-f002)a). On the other hand, M1-like microglia increased in the first 14 days after ischemic stroke.

![Ijms 18 02135 g002](/ijms/ijms-18-02135/article_deploy/html/images/ijms-18-02135-g002-550.jpg "Ijms 18 02135 g002")

**Figure 2.**
Dynamic polarized changes of microglia and monocytes/macrophages after stroke. (**a**) Temporal polarization changing by microglia and monocytes/macrophages after ischemic stroke by cell markers. The M1-like response exhibits an increasing trend in the first 14 days. The M2-like response exhibits a transient increasing trend in the first 1 to 2 days. Subsequently, the M2-like response exhibits a decreasing trend. However, it is unknown whether the M2-like response exhibits an increasing trend over the first 14 days. The balance of evidence supports an M2 to M1-like phenotype switch in the first 2 to 3 days. (**b**) Temporal polarization changing by microglia and monocytes/macrophages after hemorrhagic stroke. The M1-like response occurs as early as 6 h after hemorrhage, while the M2-like response starts to increase on day 1 after hemorrhage. Although a mixed M1- and M2-like microglial phenotype is evident during days 1 to 3, the balance of evidence supports an M1 to M2 phenotype switch in the first 7 days. The levels of most pro-inflammatory cytokines return to baseline on day 14. Abbreviations: mΦ, macrophage.

Moreover, very little is known about the microglial and monocytic polarization after hemorrhagic stroke. Post-hemorrhagic temporal analysis of microglial phenotypes demonstrated that M1-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages increased acutely as early as 6 h after hemorrhagic stroke, and exhibited a decreasing trend in the first 14 days after hemorrhagic stroke [[22](#B22-ijms-18-02135),[74](#B74-ijms-18-02135)]. In contrast, the microglial M2-like response increased on day 1 and exhibited an increasing trend in the first 14 days ([Figure 2](#fig_body_display_ijms-18-02135-f002)b). Although a mixed M1-like and M2-like microglial phenotype was evident on days 1 to 3, there is evidence that supports an M1- to M2-like phenotype switch during the first 7 days [[30](#B30-ijms-18-02135)]. However, these results were obtained from animal models, and evidence of microglial and monocytes/macrophages polarization in human brains and blood samples after stroke is still lacking. Nevertheless, M1- to M2-like phenotype transition in the brain and blood may occur in patients after stroke. The results of the temporal change of cellular polarization demonstrated that increasing M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages during the acute phase would be an effective therapeutic strategy after both ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke.

## 8. Therapeutic Potential of M2-Like Microglia and Monocytes/Macrophages against Ischemic Stroke

Cell-based therapies using M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages might be protective therapeutic strategies against ischemic stroke based on three reasons ([Figure 3](#fig_body_display_ijms-18-02135-f003)).

![Ijms 18 02135 g003](/ijms/ijms-18-02135/article_deploy/html/images/ijms-18-02135-g003-550.jpg "Ijms 18 02135 g003")

**Figure 3.**
Illustration of the therapeutic effects of M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages. Abbreviations: BBB, blood-brain barrier.

### 8.1. Tissue and Vascular Remodeling by M2-Like Microglia and Monocytes/Macrophages

Because M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages secrete protective remodeling factors after ischemia, including VEGF, BDNF, progranulin, and TGF-β [[10](#B10-ijms-18-02135),[24](#B24-ijms-18-02135),[28](#B28-ijms-18-02135),[53](#B53-ijms-18-02135)], they may facilitate axonal outgrowth and angiogenesis after ischemic stroke. There is direct evidence supporting a recovery-promoting effect of M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages following focal cerebral ischemia [[28](#B28-ijms-18-02135),[75](#B75-ijms-18-02135)]. Indeed, M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages expressed VEGF, TGF-β, and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) in the injury lesions, and were shown to enhance axonal growth of corticospinal motor neurons [[28](#B28-ijms-18-02135),[76](#B76-ijms-18-02135)]. Additionally, non-primed, not M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages had no effect on the recovery of sensorimotor function at 4 weeks or 3 months post-insult [[28](#B28-ijms-18-02135),[75](#B75-ijms-18-02135)]. These data indicated that the M2-like state of microglia and monocytes/macrophages is essential for the recovery promoting effect. This is in agreement with previous findings reported following the depletion of infiltrating monocytes/macrophages after ischemic stroke abolished long-term behavioral recovery and drastically decreased tissue expression of anti-inflammatory genes, including TGF-β and CD163 [[34](#B34-ijms-18-02135)]. In addition, axonal outgrowth was observed to exert active effects on the surrounding angiogenesis. After the administration of M2-like microglia, remodeling factors such as VEGF, TGF-β, and MMP-9 are secreted in the brain parenchyma, thus resulting in angiogenesis [[28](#B28-ijms-18-02135)]. It has been also demonstrated that metformin treatment may induce M2-like polarization and result in angiogenesis following stroke [[77](#B77-ijms-18-02135)]. Therefore, the recovery-promoting effect is most likely due to secreted factors from M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages that can promote tissue remodeling (axonal outgrowth and angiogenesis).

Although the administration of M2-like monocytes/macrophages prompted functional recovery, the infarct volume was not reduced by the cell therapy [[75](#B75-ijms-18-02135)]. The release of IL-10 by M2-like microglia enhanced dendritic spine formation and synaptogenesis in cultured neurons [[78](#B78-ijms-18-02135)]. Furthermore, microglia have been reported to release TNF-α, which increased in turn, spine density [[79](#B79-ijms-18-02135)]. Interestingly, microglial contact directly induced synapse formation in the developing cortex [[80](#B80-ijms-18-02135)]. Thus, microglial P2Y12R might be necessary for synaptogenesis following brain injury [[81](#B81-ijms-18-02135)]. These changes may be behind the M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages enhanced functional synaptogenesis in the remaining neurons. In normal adult brain, chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan, a component of the extracellular matrix, has been reported to inhibit axonal outgrowth [[82](#B82-ijms-18-02135)], and is shown to be cleaved and degraded by MMP-9 [[83](#B83-ijms-18-02135)]. Microglia is the main source of MMP-9 [[84](#B84-ijms-18-02135)] and cathepsin L after ischemia [[85](#B85-ijms-18-02135)]. These proteinases might degrade the extracellular matrix and prompt axonal outgrowth. Recently, it was reported that growth factor progranulin knockout microglia reduced synaptic formation [[86](#B86-ijms-18-02135)]. We also reported microglial secretion of progranulin after ischemia [[53](#B53-ijms-18-02135)]. These results support the notion that secretion of growth factors, cytokines, and proteinases by microglia and monocytes/macrophages directly enhances neuronal repair. Thus, M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages would prompt neuronal network recovery through tissue remodeling (including neuronal tissue) by growth factors, cytokines, and proteinases.

### 8.2. Infiltrating Properties of M2-Like Microglia and Monocytes/Macrophages

The ideal characteristics of cell-based therapies and any medication is the possibility of crossing the BBB and reaching the injured brain parenchyma, which is a feature of M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages. The accumulation of microglia and infiltration of monocytes/macrophages into the brain after ischemic stroke has been demonstrated by translocator protein (TSPO) as a biomarker of positron emission tomography (PET) [[87](#B87-ijms-18-02135)], and ultrasmall superparamagnetic particles of iron oxide (USPIO) as a biomarker of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) [[88](#B88-ijms-18-02135)]. Pathophysiologically, the adhesion receptor macrophage-1 antigen (Mac-1) mediates the adhesion of microglia and monocytes/macrophages to the endothelial surface. This effect might be important for the infiltration of microglia and monocytes/macrophages into the affected brain parenchyma [[89](#B89-ijms-18-02135),[90](#B90-ijms-18-02135)]. Moreover, the upregulation of Mac-1 following the preconditioning of M2-like microglia to oxygen-glucose deprivation enabled the microglia to cross the BBB and reach the injured brain parenchyma [[28](#B28-ijms-18-02135)]. Several studies have demonstrated that the chemokine stromal-derived factor-1 (SDF-1, also known as CXCL12) plays a role in the homing of microglia and monocytes/macrophages, as well as stem cells, to the areas of ischemic injury [[91](#B91-ijms-18-02135),[92](#B92-ijms-18-02135),[93](#B93-ijms-18-02135)]. In addition, M2-like monocytes/macrophages could infiltrate the ischemic hemisphere via the choroid plexus–cerebrospinal fluid route [[75](#B75-ijms-18-02135)]. Interestingly, M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages, but not the non-primed or non-M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages, could migrate into the ischemic hemisphere through the BBB [[28](#B28-ijms-18-02135)] or choroid–plexus [[75](#B75-ijms-18-02135)]. This ability of the M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages is crucial for the success of cell-based therapies.

### 8.3. The Anti-Inflammation Effect of M2-Like Microglia and Monocytes/Macrophages

Both M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages can suppress inflammation. Neuroinflammation occurs several days after ischemic stroke and within 7 days after hemorrhagic stroke, which may be the consequence of increased M1-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages [[18](#B18-ijms-18-02135),[19](#B19-ijms-18-02135),[20](#B20-ijms-18-02135),[21](#B21-ijms-18-02135)]. Administration of M2-like microglia and M2-like polarization by IL-4 may suppress inflammation and enhance functional recovery after ischemic stroke [[28](#B28-ijms-18-02135),[94](#B94-ijms-18-02135)]. Therefore, M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages could suppress the extent of inflammation-induced injuries by therapeutic intervention. Thus, interventions by M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages are ideal approaches for suppressing inflammation.

## 9. Previous Reports on the Effects of M2-Like Microglia and Monocyte/Macrophage against Ischemic Stroke

Studies on direct administration of primary microglia, cell-line microglia, and monocytes/macrophages against ischemic stroke have been reported [[24](#B24-ijms-18-02135),[28](#B28-ijms-18-02135),[34](#B34-ijms-18-02135),[95](#B95-ijms-18-02135),[96](#B96-ijms-18-02135),[97](#B97-ijms-18-02135),[98](#B98-ijms-18-02135)]. Although some reports demonstrated the suppression of neuronal cell death and/or improvement of functions [[24](#B24-ijms-18-02135),[28](#B28-ijms-18-02135),[34](#B34-ijms-18-02135),[95](#B95-ijms-18-02135),[96](#B96-ijms-18-02135),[97](#B97-ijms-18-02135)], other studies reported no effect [[98](#B98-ijms-18-02135)] ([Table 1](#table_body_display_ijms-18-02135-t001)).

**Table 1.**
The list of cell therapies using microglia and monocytes/macrophages for ischemic stroke.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

However, most previous evaluations did not take M1/M2-like cellular polarization into consideration, although we reported intravascular administration of M2-like microglia preconditioned by optimal oxygen-glucose deprivation directly improved functional outcome after ischemic stroke [[28](#B28-ijms-18-02135)]. Additionally, subcutaneous [[99](#B99-ijms-18-02135)] or intraventricular [[94](#B94-ijms-18-02135)] administration of IL-4 induced the polarization of endogenous microglia and monocytes/macrophages to M2-like characteristics. The results improved functional outcomes after ischemic stroke. On the other hand, intravenous administration of IL-4 induced neutrophilic hyperresponse and allergic reaction [[100](#B100-ijms-18-02135)]. Recently, it was reported that selective and unselective monocyte/macrophage depletion and M1- and M2-like macrophage transfer did not influence tissue damage and functional outcomes within 42 days after cerebral ischemia [[101](#B101-ijms-18-02135)].

In addition, several clinical trials using mononuclear cells and stem cells similar to monocytes/macrophages, have been undertaken to test their safety and preliminary efficacy in patients with ischemic stroke ([Table 2](#table_body_display_ijms-18-02135-t002)). According to the ClinicalTrials. gov trial registry (<https://clinicaltrials.gov/>), four trials were completed [[102](#B102-ijms-18-02135),[103](#B103-ijms-18-02135)]. However, they did not use polarized cells. Additionally, other open trials using mononuclear cells and mesenchymal stem cells have been conducted. However, only one prior trial using blood mononuclear cells and M2-like macrophages has been conducted [[102](#B102-ijms-18-02135),[103](#B103-ijms-18-02135),[104](#B104-ijms-18-02135),[105](#B105-ijms-18-02135),[106](#B106-ijms-18-02135),[107](#B107-ijms-18-02135)]. Further studies are warranted for therapeutic strategies using microglia and monocytes/macrophages against ischemic stroke, to evaluate the optimal timing of the interventions, compare microglia or monocytes/macrophages therapies, and determine how to stimulate cells and polarize their status.

**Table 2.**
The list of clinical trials using mononuclear cells for ischemic stroke.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

## 10. Therapeutic Potential of M2-Like Microglia and Monocytes against Hemorrhagic Stroke

Microglia and monocytes/macrophages act as phagocytes to scavenge debris in the CNS. The M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages, which play an important role in hematoma clearance, healing, and neuroprotection, might be a reasonable candidate therapy for the recovery from hemorrhagic stroke [[29](#B29-ijms-18-02135),[74](#B74-ijms-18-02135)]. The scavenger receptor CD36 contributes to the increasing phagocytic ability of microglia and monocytes/macrophages [[108](#B108-ijms-18-02135)]. Furthermore, CD36 deficiency might lead to TLR4 upregulation and IL-10 secretion. The TLR4-mediated phagocytosis might contribute to microglial polarization (polarized to M1-like) and function. Although both M1-like and M2-like microglia and macrophages express phagocytic receptors, M2-like microglia and macrophages may present a stronger phagocytic ability to remove dead neurons than the M1-like phenotype [[109](#B109-ijms-18-02135),[110](#B110-ijms-18-02135)]. On the other hand, the M1-like phenotypes may cause neuronal loss by increasing phagocytosis of viable neurons, because of producing high levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) [[49](#B49-ijms-18-02135),[111](#B111-ijms-18-02135),[112](#B112-ijms-18-02135),[113](#B113-ijms-18-02135)]. In contrast, the M2-like phenotypes trigger anti-oxidative responses after stroke by suppressing the levels of ROS. Moreover, M2-like phenotypes induced anti-oxidative responses by increasing the levels of glutathione-SH (GSH) and heme oxygenase-1 [[114](#B114-ijms-18-02135),[115](#B115-ijms-18-02135),[116](#B116-ijms-18-02135),[117](#B117-ijms-18-02135)]. Thus, phagocytosis mediated by M2-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages may be neuroprotective, whereas that mediated by M1-like microglia and monocytes/macrophages may result in neuronal damage. However, whether modulating this polarization might resolve hematoma and improve functional recovery remains to be elucidated.

Currently, several medications are undergoing clinical trials (reviewed by Lan et al. [[22](#B22-ijms-18-02135)]). These medications are reported to either prompt decreasing levels of M1-like microglia (e.g., fingolimod, deferoxamine) [[118](#B118-ijms-18-02135),[119](#B119-ijms-18-02135)] or increasing levels of M2-like microglia (e.g., Chinese medicine sinomenine) [[120](#B120-ijms-18-02135)]. However, cell therapies using microglia and monocytes/macrophages have yet to be investigated.

## 11. Conclusions

In a recent report, microglia-like cells have been derived from cultured human embryonic stem (ES) and induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells, and a robust and efficient protocol for the rapid production of microglia-like cells was established [[121](#B121-ijms-18-02135)]. Microglia/monocytes from iPS cells might be a potential candidate for therapeutic applications in stroke, provided that the tumorigenesis issue in cells derived from iPS cells is resolved. Cryopreservation negatively affects the cellular viability of cells. Both fresh and frozen monocytes/macrophages have similar beneficial effects in a rodent ischemic stroke [[122](#B122-ijms-18-02135)]. The use of both autologous and allogenic cells raises the possibility that mononuclear cells (monocytes/macrophages) could potentially be stored as a banked source for possible therapeutic use when the need arises. Microglia and monocytes/macrophages are thought to potential cell therapies for several CNS diseases, psychiatric diseases [[123](#B123-ijms-18-02135)], Alzheimer’s disease [[124](#B124-ijms-18-02135)], and traumatic brain injury [[125](#B125-ijms-18-02135)]. Although future translational studies are required, microglia and monocytes/macrophages therapies are attractive targets to manage stroke based upon their protective functions.

args.summary:
This is a scientific review article published in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences (Int. J. Mol. Sci. 2017, 18(10), 2135) by Masato Kanazawa, Itaru Ninomiya, Masahiro Hatakeyama, Tetsuya Takahashi, and Takayoshi Shimohata, examining the therapeutic potential of microglia and monocytes/macrophages polarization for stroke treatment. The article belongs to the Special Issue on "Microglia in Aging and Neurodegenerative Disease" and was published on October 13, 2017.

KEY CONTENT:

1. **Background**: Stroke is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, with 70-80% being ischemic and 10-20% hemorrhagic. Only 3.4-5.2% of acute ischemic stroke patients are eligible for thrombolytic treatment due to narrow therapeutic windows. No effective treatment exists for the subacute-to-chronic phases of stroke.

2. **Microglia vs. Monocytes/Macrophages**: Microglia originate from yolk sac progenitors and express high levels of CX3CR1, CD11b, and F4/80, with P2Y12R as a specific marker. Monocytes/macrophages originate from hematopoietic stem cells and express CCR2 and Ly6C. Both share phagocytic functions.

3. **Double-Edged Sword**: These cells play harmful roles in the acute phase (accelerating inflammation) but protective roles in neurogenesis, axonal outgrowth, synaptogenesis, angiogenesis, and remyelination during recovery phases.

4. **Polarization**: M1-like cells (pro-inflammatory) secrete TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-12, IL-23, and NO, exacerbating tissue injury. M2-like cells (anti-inflammatory/protective) secrete TGF-β, IL-4, IL-10, IL-13, VEGF, BDNF, PDGF, and progranulin, suppressing inflammation and promoting tissue recovery. TREM2 activation stimulates phagocytic activity while downregulating TNF-α and iNOS.

5. **Temporal Dynamics**: After ischemic stroke, M2-like cells increase at 12h, peak at 1-3 days, then decrease; M1-like cells increase over 14 days. After hemorrhagic stroke, M1-like cells increase at 6h; M2-like cells increase from day 1, with an M1-to-M2 switch in the first 7 days.

6. **Therapeutic Mechanisms**: M2-like microglia/monocytes/macrophages are protective because: (a) they secrete remodeling factors (VEGF, TGF-β, MMP-9) promoting axonal growth and angiogenesis; (b) they can cross the BBB and migrate to injured hemispheres (via Mac-1 upregulation, SDF-1/CXCL12 homing, and choroid-plexus routes); (c) they suppress inflammation when administered at appropriate timing.

7. **Preclinical Evidence**: Intravascular administration of M2-like microglia preconditioned by oxygen-glucose deprivation improved functional outcomes after ischemic stroke. IL-4 administration (subcutaneous or intraventricular) induced endogenous M2 polarization with improved outcomes. Depletion of monocytes/macrophages abolished long-term behavioral recovery.

8. **Hemorrhagic Stroke**: M2-like cells play important roles in hematoma clearance via CD36-mediated phagocytosis and anti-oxidative responses (increasing GSH and heme oxygenase-1). Medications like fingolimod and deferoxamine reduce M1-like cells; sinomenine increases M2-like cells.

9. **Future Directions**: Microglia-like cells derived from human ES/iPS cells are potential therapeutic candidates. Both fresh and frozen monocytes/macrophages show similar beneficial effects. Cell-based therapies remain attractive but require translational studies to evaluate optimal timing, cell type comparison, and stimulation/polarization methods.

First, M2-like microglia and monocytes/monocytes secrete protective remodeling factors, thus prompting neuronal network recovery via tissue (including neuronal) and vascular remodeling. Second, these cells could migrate to the injured hemisphere through the blood–brain barrier or choroid–plexus. Third, these cells could mitigate the extent of inflammation-induced injuries by suitable timing of therapeutic intervention."

--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] Role of Neutrophils in Exacerbation of Brain Injury After Focal ... - UC Irvine ---
URL: https://escholarship.org/content/qt5b10w3m8/qt5b10w3m8.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific research article published in Stroke (2015, Vol. 46, Issue 10, pages 2916–2925) examining the role of neutrophils in exacerbating ischemic brain injury in hyperlipidemic mice. The study was conducted by researchers from the University Hospital Essen (Germany), the University of Utah School of Medicine, and the University Duisburg-Essen.

**Background & Purpose:** The study builds on prior findings that hyperlipidemia exacerbates ischemic brain injury and is associated with elevated granulocyte numbers. The authors sought to establish the causal link between neutrophils and exacerbated brain damage in hyperlipidemia.

**Methods:** Male wildtype (C57BL/6J) mice fed normal chow and ApoE knockout (ApoE−/−) mice fed a high-cholesterol Western diet were subjected to 20-minute middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO). Key interventions included: (1) CXCR2 blockade using the selective antagonist SB225002 (2 mg/kg) or neutralizing CXCR2 antiserum, and (2) neutrophil depletion using anti-Ly6G antibody. Analysis at 72 hours post-ischemia included immunohistochemistry, flow cytometry, and real-time PCR. Functional outcomes were assessed via rota rod and tight rope tests at 4, 7, and 14 days post-ischemia. A total of 352 male mice were examined.

**Key Results:**
1. CXCR2 antagonization significantly reduced neurological deficits and infarct volumes that were exacerbated in hyperlipidemic ApoE−/− mice.
2. Neutrophil depletion mimicked the neuroprotective effects of CXCR2 blockade, and adding CXCR2 antagonist to neutrophil-depleted mice provided no additional benefit, confirming the effect was neutrophil-specific.
3. Cerebral neutrophil infiltration and peripheral neutrophilia, both increased by ischemia in hyperlipidemia, were attenuated by CXCR2 antagonization.
4. CXCR2 blockade increased neutrophil apoptosis and reduced CXCR2, iNOS, and NOX2 expression on bone marrow neutrophils.
5. CXCR2 antagonization reduced oxidative DNA damage (8-oxo-dG) in ischemic brains of hyperlipidemic mice.
6. CXCR2 inhibition did not affect ischemic brain injury in normolipidemic wildtype mice, indicating that the protective effect is specific to hyperlipidemic conditions.

**Conclusion:** The data demonstrate a causal role of neutrophils in the exacerbation of ischemic brain injury induced by hyperlipidemia. CXCR2 blockade, which prevents neutrophil recruitment into the brain and reduces peripheral neutrophilia, may be an effective therapeutic option for stroke treatment in patients with hyperlipidemia. The authors emphasize that pre-clinical and clinical stroke studies should carefully consider inflammation-associated co-morbidities like hyperlipidemia, which can alter the responsiveness of ischemic brain tissue to therapy.

**Funding:** German Research Council (HE3173/2-1 and HE3173/2-2), Mercator Research Center Ruhr (AN-2011-0081), and NIH (R01NS041249).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Our data demonstrate a role of neutrophils in the exacerbation of ischemic brain injury induced by hyperlipidemia. Accordingly, CXCR2 blockade, which prevents neutrophil recruitment into the brain, might be an effective option for stroke treatment in patients suffering from hyperlipidemia."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: New Insight Into Neutrophils: A Potential Therapeutic Target for ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8317226

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in Frontiers in Immunology (2021 Jul 14;12:692061, doi: 10.3389/fimmu.2021.692061) titled "New Insight Into Neutrophils: A Potential Therapeutic Target for Cerebral Ischemia." The paper is authored by Ran Chen, Xu Zhang (co-first authors), Lijuan Gu, Hua Zhu, Yi Zhong, Yingze Ye, Xiaoxing Xiong (corresponding), and Zhihong Jian (corresponding), all from Wuhan, China. PMID: 34335600, PMCID: PMC8317226.

KEY FINDINGS:

1. **Background**: Ischemic stroke is a leading cause of permanent disability and death worldwide. After stroke, immune cell infiltration into the brain can both mediate neuronal apoptosis (aggravating injury) and promote neuronal repair/differentiation/regeneration.

2. **Neutrophils as first responders**: Neutrophils are the first immune cells to enter the brain from the periphery after ischemic stroke, accumulating within minutes to a few hours after injury. They are followed by monocytes (which peak 3-7 days post-ischemia).

3. **Dual role of neutrophils**: Neutrophils can be harmful (releasing proinflammatory factors, ROS, proteases, MMPs that damage the BBB and cause secondary injury) but also beneficial (participating in angiogenesis and tissue repair via FPR2 activation, VEGF, and EGF).

4. **Mechanisms of injury**: Neutrophils aggravate ischemic injury through several mechanisms: (a) adhering to endothelial cells and blocking microvascular blood flow (no-reflow phenomenon), (b) producing proteases, MMPs, and ROS that damage vascular endothelium and increase BBB permeability, (c) producing vasoconstrictive substances (leukotrienes, prostaglandins, platelet-activating factors), and (d) releasing neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) that directly damage neurons or induce thrombosis.

5. **Temporal/spatial distribution**: Enzmann et al. showed PMNs are mainly confined to the lumen surface or perivascular space of neurovascular units rather than entering the brain parenchyma. Neutrophil numbers in the ischemic brain peak on days 1-3 and gradually decrease. At 48-96 hours post-ischemia, more neutrophils are found in brain parenchyma than at 14 hours. VLA-4-mediated neutrophil entry into the brain is a key factor in behavioral injury after ischemia.

6. **N1 vs N2 neutrophil phenotypes**: Similar to M1/M2 macrophages, N2 neutrophils promote inflammation reduction by releasing anti-inflammatory mediators and have neuroprotective effects. N2 polarization is induced by IL-10, TGF-β, IL-13, and IL-4, while N1 polarization is facilitated by IFN-β, IFN-γ, and IL-12. PPAR-γ agonist rosiglitazone promotes N2 phenotype switching, which alleviates cerebral infarction.

7. **TLR4 role**: TLR4 deficiency increases the number of N2 neutrophils and is associated with neuroprotection after stroke. Notably, neutrophil depletion combined with TLR4 deletion actually exacerbates brain injury, suggesting TLR4 deletion's neuroprotective effect requires neutrophils.

8. **Neutrophil production**: Normal adults produce 1-2 × 10^11 neutrophils per day. G-CSF regulates neutrophil production (though not absolutely necessary—G-CSF knockout mice still produce ~25% of normal granulocytes). The IL-23–IL-17–G-CSF axis is the main physiological feedback circuit regulating neutrophil homeostasis.

9. **Bone marrow release**: CXCR4 retains neutrophils in bone marrow; CXCR2, G-CSF receptor, or TLR signaling affect release. Disruption of CXCR4 signaling may be a common mechanism for cytokine/chemokine-induced neutrophil release.

10. **Therapeutic implication**: The authors propose a new therapeutic strategy involving local targeting of neutrophils at the onset of cerebral ischemia rather than nonselective overall inhibition of neutrophil function. VLA-4 blockade, CD39 expression, and regulation of neutrophil polarization (toward N2 phenotype) represent promising targeted interventions.

11. **Key molecular players**: DAMPs (including HMGB1), TLR2/4, NADPH oxidase, ROS, MMP-9, MMP-8 (from neutrophils), MPO, ICAM-1, selectins, CXCR2/CXCL1, CXCL12/CXCR4, IL-8, oncostatin M, and GPR30 are all involved in the neutrophil-mediated inflammatory cascade after cerebral ischemia.

12. **T cell comparison**: T cells contribute minimally to early behavioral dysfunction after stroke but reduce infarct volume and play important roles in chronic recovery (e.g., Treg-derived osteopontin promotes microglial repair activity, oligodendrocyte formation, and myelin regeneration).

The article includes detailed figures illustrating the inflammatory response after cerebral ischemia and the role of NADPH oxidase in ROS production and neutrophil activation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Neutrophils are the first group of immune cells to enter the brain from the periphery after ischemic stroke, and their exact role in cerebral ischemia remains to be further explored."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Frontiers | Neutrophil extracellular traps and microglia/macrophages interactions in stroke: from thromboinflammation to immunotherapy ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2026.1752471/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Frontiers in Immunology (Vol. 17, 2026, DOI: 10.3389/fimmu.2026.1752471) by Nurittin Ardic and Rasit Dinc, examining the bidirectional interaction between neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) and microglia/macrophages in both ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Stroke is the second leading cause of death worldwide; ischemic stroke accounts for 80-85% of cases, with intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) and subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) comprising the remainder.
- NETs are chromatin-based structures containing histones, neutrophil elastase (NE), myeloperoxidase (MPO), cathepsin G, MMP-9, and antimicrobial peptides. They are released via two pathways: suicidal NETosis (PAD4-dependent, taking hours) and vital NET release (rapid, minutes, preserving neutrophil viability).
- NETs contribute to stroke pathology through: immunothrombosis, thrombus formation and stabilization, resistance to thrombolysis and thrombectomy, microvascular no-reflow phenomenon, blood-brain barrier disruption, hemorrhagic transformation after tPA, and impaired neurovascular repair.
- NET formation peaks within 6-24 hours after stroke onset; microglial activation evolves over days to weeks.
- The bidirectional NET-microglia interaction involves: NET DNA activating microglial TLR9, cGAS-STING, NLRP3 and AIM2 inflammasomes; NET histones causing cytotoxicity via TLR2/TLR4; and microglia-derived IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-8/CXCL8, ROS, and ATP promoting further NETosis via P2X7-NLRP3 pathways—creating a self-reinforcing feedforward inflammatory cycle.
- In ischemic stroke, NET-rich thrombi are more resistant to recanalization; elevated plasma H3Cit-DNA and MPO-DNA levels correlate with larger infarcts, hemorrhagic transformation, and worse outcomes.
- In hemorrhagic stroke, NETs contribute to hematoma expansion, perihematomal edema, vasospasm, and delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI); prolonged heme/iron-induced microglial activation distinguishes hemorrhagic from ischemic stroke.
- Therapeutic strategies include: DNase I (promotes NET degradation and fibrinolysis), PAD4 inhibitors, NE/MPO inhibitors, histone neutralizing agents, NLRP3 inhibition, CSF1R modulation, and TREM2 agonism—with combination and temporally phased regimens showing promise.
- NET biomarkers (H3Cit-DNA, MPO-DNA) in plasma and thrombus specimens offer potential for patient stratification and personalized immunotherapy.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"NET-microglia interactions create a self-amplifying inflammatory cycle that exacerbates BBB damage, enhances infarct expansion, and facilitates hematoma toxicity in ICH."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Functional dynamics of neutrophils after ischemic stroke - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6993940

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article titled "Functional dynamics of neutrophils after ischemic stroke," published in Translational Stroke Research (2019 Mar 07; 11(1):108, doi: 10.1007/s12975-019-00694-y). The study was conducted by researchers from the Third Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University (China), the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, and Ohio State University College of Medicine.

**Key findings:**

1. **Patient data:** The study analyzed 225 acute ischemic stroke (AIS) patients (68 female, 157 male; mean age 64.87) admitted within 24h of symptom onset, plus 56 healthy controls. Neutrophil counts and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) in peripheral blood increased soon after stroke onset. In AIS patients without infection, NLR positively correlated with higher NIHSS scores (R²=0.07, P=0.0006). In patients with infarction >1.5cm, both neutrophil counts (R²=0.07, P=0.0208) and NLR (R²=0.07, P=0.0447) positively correlated with infarct sizes. In mice pretreated with antibiotics, neutrophil frequency and NLR in blood positively correlated with infarct volumes at 1d after tMCAO.

2. **Temporal dynamics in mice:** Neutrophil percentage in peripheral blood peaked at 12h after cerebral ischemia, followed by a 1-2d spike in brain lesions. Bone marrow neutrophils dropped before 12h, recovered at 1d, then steadily increased until at least 7d. Spleen neutrophils peaked at 12h then declined by 2d. Neutrophil-attracting chemokines (CCL5, CXCL1, CXCL2, CXCL3) peaked at 12h. Notable neutrophil infiltration in the brain was detected at 12h and was prominent at 1-2d, with few remaining before 7d.

3. **Neutrophil phenotypes and clearance:** The percentage of CD206+ N2 neutrophils in the ischemic brain was relatively stable over time, slightly increasing at 7d. Neutrophil clearance by microglia/macrophages started at 12h, peaked at 2d, and continued until at least 7d. Engulfed neutrophils (F4/80+) showed higher CD206 and lower MPO expression over time.

4. **N2 neuroprotection:** N2 neutrophils facilitated macrophage phagocytosis in vitro and did not further induce neuronal death after ischemic injury compared with N0 or N1 neutrophils. Treatment with N1 conditioned medium exacerbated post-OGD neuronal death, while N0 or N2 CM did not. Injecting TGFβ (2ug/mouse) 1d before tMCAO to skew neutrophils toward the N2 phenotype reduced infarct volumes at 1d.

5. **NETs formation:** Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in ischemic lesions peaked at 2-3d after stroke, detected via co-labelling citrullinated histone H3 (CitH3) and Ly6G, Sytox green/neutrophil elastase staining, and scanning electron microscopy at 2d. The paper notes this is the first documentation of NETs formation in ischemic brain.

6. **Inflammatory mediators:** mRNA levels of NE, MPO, MMP3, TIMP1, and IL-12 elevated in ischemic brain at 1d; MMP10, NLRP3, and BAFF at 2d; and MMP2, MMP8, MMP9, MMP13, IFNγ, IL-23, TLR7, TLR9, and PAD4 at 3d after tMCAO.

**Conclusions:** Neutrophil function has an important impact on stroke outcomes. Peripheral blood neutrophil frequency could serve as an early indicator of stroke outcomes. N2 neutrophils facilitate macrophage phagocytosis and are less harmful to ischemic neurons. Directing neutrophils toward the N2 phenotype could be a promising therapeutic approach for ischemic stroke.

**Keywords:** brain ischemia, neutrophils, extracellular traps, neuroprotection.
</summary>

N2 neutrophils facilitate macrophage phagocytosis and are less harmful to ischemic neurons. Directing neutrophils towards N2 phenotype could be a promising therapeutic approach for ischemic stroke."

--- SOURCE 7: Immune Cell Infiltration into the Brain After Ischemic Stroke in Humans Compared to Mice and Rats: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12975-021-00887-4

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents an open-access systematic review and meta-analysis published in Translational Stroke Research (Volume 12, pages 976-990, 2021) titled "Immune Cell Infiltration into the Brain After Ischemic Stroke in Humans Compared to Mice and Rats." The study, led by Carolin Beuker and Jens Minnerup and colleagues, sought to compare the spatial and temporal distribution of immune cell infiltration after ischemic stroke between humans and rodents, given that anti-inflammatory strategies have shown benefit in animal models but failed to demonstrate clear clinical benefit in patients.

METHODOLOGY: Following PRISMA guidelines, researchers searched PUBMED from inception to February 2019, screening 17,463 studies (7,076 after removing duplicates). They included 205 eligible studies: 188 rodent studies and 20 human studies (with 3 overlapping). Inclusion required quantification of lymphocyte, macrophage, and/or neutrophil infiltration via immunohistochemistry or flow cytometry. Rodent studies used permanent/transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (pMCAO/tMCAO), photothrombotic, or other focal stroke models. Data were extracted from control groups only. Random-effects meta-analysis (DerSimonian-Laird) was performed using the metafor package in R, with heterogeneity quantified via I². The study is registered with PROSPERO (CRD42019142603).

KEY RESULTS:
- In both humans and rodents, macrophage and neutrophil infiltration preceded lymphocytic influx, with macrophages and neutrophils being the predominant immune cells within 72 hours after infarction.
- In human stroke, mean patient age was 73.5 years (SD 7.8), 55% were women, and the middle cerebral artery territory was most commonly affected. Macrophages accumulated early (day 1), neutrophils peaked at days 2-3, and lymphocyte numbers were lower overall.
- In rodents, neutrophils appeared within 24 hours, peaking at day 2 (FACS) or day 3 (histology), with decline from days 4-7. Macrophages showed an early peak at day 2 and a second peak at day 4/5. T cells appeared in small amounts within 24 hours and plateaued by day 4.
- Immune cell infiltration extent in rodents depended on duration and location of vessel occlusion and species. Neutrophil counts in the infarct core were higher in rats than mice; macrophage counts in the penumbra were slightly higher in rats.
- The density of infiltrating immune cells was correlated with infarct volume (meta-regression), though no significant association was found.
- The temporal profile of poststroke immune response was comparable between patients and rodents, despite high heterogeneity across studies.

DISCUSSION AND IMPLICATIONS: The study's main findings are: (1) temporal dynamics of immune cell infiltration are comparable after human and rodent stroke; (2) macrophage and neutrophil infiltration preceded lymphocytic influx in rodents, with these cells most numerous within 72 hours; (3) immune cell infiltration was highly heterogeneous across both human and rodent studies; and (4) macrophage counts were higher in proximal transient compared to proximal permanent stroke models at days 1 and 7. The authors suggest that the overall heterogeneity of the post-ischemic immune response—including differences in occlusion patterns (transient proximal occlusions dominate in animal models vs. more permanent occlusions in patients), the use of young healthy animals versus aged comorbid patients, and variable experimental conditions—may contribute to translational failure in stroke research. They propose that including selected, homogenous stroke patients similar to animal study conditions and using noninvasive inflammation imaging might improve patient selection for clinical trials.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We here performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to summarize and compare the spatial and temporal distribution of immune cell infiltration in human and rodent stroke."

--- SOURCE 8: Hypoxic-ischemic brain injury in neonatal mice ... ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-65517-1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in *Nature Communications* (volume 16, article 9696, 2025) investigating the role of neutrophils in hypoxic-ischemic (HI) brain injury in neonatal mice. The study was conducted by an international team of researchers including Mathis Richter, Eva Diesterbeck, Josephine Herz, Oliver Soehnlein, and colleagues.

**Key Findings:**

1. **Biphasic neutrophil infiltration**: Neutrophils infiltrate the HI-injured brain in a biphasic pattern, peaking at 1 day and 7 days after HI. This was confirmed by flow cytometry and 3D whole-brain light sheet imaging. Early neutrophils (day 1) showed a hyperactivated phenotype with high ROS production, while late neutrophils (day 7) exhibited an angiogenic phenotype with high Siglec-F expression.

2. **Dichotomous function**: 
   - Early brain-infiltrating neutrophils aggravate tissue damage (neuronal death, oligodendrocyte loss, glial activation) and contribute to the development of hyperactivity in adolescent animals.
   - Late-infiltrating neutrophils promote neurological recovery by supporting oligodendrocyte regeneration and vascular remodeling/angiogenesis, and attenuate anxiety-related behavioral alterations.

3. **Experimental methods**: The researchers used neutrophil depletion via anti-Ly6G combined with anti-rat IgG at either 24h (early) or 7 days (late) after HI in neonatal mice (HI induced at P9). They assessed long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes at 5 weeks (Open Field and Elevated Plus Maze tests), tissue atrophy, neuronal/myelination markers, oligodendrocyte proliferation, and vascular parameters using light sheet microscopy and VesselExpress analysis.

4. **Molecular findings**: The HI-injured brain undergoes disease-stage-dependent changes in protein expression. Osteopontin, myeloperoxidase, Chitinase 3-like 1, and CCL6 were upregulated at both 24h and 7d. Chemokines CXCL-2, CXCL-10, CCL5, CXCL-5, Lipocalin-2, and MMP-9 were specifically induced at day 7. Angiogenesis-promoting proteins (Chemerin, Angiopoietin) were elevated at day 7, while VEGF recovered from day 1 suppression by day 7.

5. **Vascular findings**: Neonatal HI impairs developmental vascularization, particularly affecting small vessel (<7 µm) development. Late-infiltrating neutrophils promote endothelial cell proliferation and vascular remodeling in the sub-acute phase.

6. **Conclusion**: The disease stage-dependent neutrophil diversification reveals that early neutrophils aggravate tissue damage while late neutrophils contribute to neurological recovery, offering new possibilities for disease-stage-specific therapeutic targets in neonatal encephalopathy.
</summary>

"Neonatal encephalopathy caused by hypoxia-ischemia (HI) leads to a strong neutrophil infiltration. The long-held assumption that neutrophils act exclusively as tissue-damaging cells, is challenged by increasing evidence of a profound neutrophil heterogeneity."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Frontiers in Immunology (14 July 2021, Volume 12) titled "New Insight Into Neutrophils: A Potential Therapeutic Target for Cerebral Ischemia" by Ran Chen, Xu Zhang, Lijuan Gu, Hua Zhu, Yi Zhong, Yingze Ye, Xiaoxing Xiong, and Zhihong Jian from the Department of Neurosurgery and Central Laboratory at Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University, China.

**Main Topic:** The review examines the dual role of neutrophils in ischemic stroke, from their production in bone marrow to their functional differentiation in the brain, and proposes targeted neutrophil-based therapeutic strategies for cerebral ischemia.

**Key Points:**

1. **Background:** Ischemic stroke is a major cause of permanent disability in adults. After stroke, immune cell infiltration can both aggravate ischemic injury (via neuronal apoptosis) and promote neuronal repair and regeneration. Neutrophils are the first immune cells to enter the brain from the periphery after ischemic stroke, accumulating within minutes.

2. **Dual Role of Neutrophils:**
   - **Harmful effects:** Neutrophils release proinflammatory factors, ROS, proteases, and MMPs (especially MMP-9) that damage the BBB, cause edema, and aggravate neuronal injury. They form neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) that directly damage neurons and induce thrombosis. Neutrophils can cause the "no-reflow" phenomenon by blocking microvessels.
   - **Beneficial effects:** Neutrophils participate in angiogenesis via FPR2 activation, promote reendothelialization, and N2 neutrophils (analogous to M2 macrophages) release anti-inflammatory mediators and have neuroprotective effects.

3. **Spatiotemporal characteristics:** Neutrophil numbers in the ischemic brain peak on days 1-3, then gradually decrease. Neutrophils are predominantly found around pia mater and blood vessels, with only some reaching brain parenchyma (related to basement membrane integrity loss). VLA-4-mediated neutrophil entry into the brain is a key factor in behavioral injury after cerebral ischemia.

4. **Production and Migration:** Neutrophils are produced in bone marrow (1-2 × 10^11 cells/day in adults). G-CSF regulates production through the IL-23–IL-17–G-CSF axis. After stroke, sympathetic nervous system activation increases bone marrow neutrophil output. CXCR4 retains neutrophils in bone marrow, while CXCR2 promotes their release. NF-κB and p38MAPK signaling are rapidly activated in bone marrow after ischemia.

5. **Phenotypic polarization:** TLR4 deficiency increases N2 neutrophils and is associated with neuroprotection after stroke. N2 polarization is induced by IL-10, TGF-β, IL-13, and IL-4, while N1 polarization is facilitated by IFN-β, IFN-γ, and IL-12. PPAR-γ agonist rosiglitazone promotes the N2 phenotype.

6. **Mechanisms of injury:**
   - ROS overproduction via NADPH oxidase (NOX2) damages surrounding tissue
   - Neutrophils accelerate atherosclerosis by promoting monocyte recruitment, LDL oxidation (via MPO), foam cell formation, and NET-driven macrophage activation
   - MMP-9-mediated ECM degradation leads to hemorrhagic transformation

7. **Therapeutic implications:** The authors propose local targeting of neutrophils at the onset of cerebral ischemia rather than nonselective overall inhibition. Potential targets include VLA-4 blockade, CD39 expression (inhibits neutrophil invasion), CXCR4 regulation, and TLR4 modulation. Anti-TNF-α therapy has proven beneficial in autoimmune diseases and may have relevance.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Neutrophils are the first group of immune cells to enter the brain from the periphery after ischemic stroke, and their exact role in cerebral ischemia remains to be further explored."

--- SOURCE 14: Neutrophil extracellular traps in ischemic stroke - PMC - NIH ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12463598

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Frontiers in Neurology (September 12, 2025, Vol 16, article 1641985) examining the role of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in ischemic stroke. Authors Wenbo He, Zuoli Wu, Ying Liu, and Ziming Ye (from Nanning, China) review the mechanisms, clinical implications, and therapeutic potential of NETs in stroke pathology.

Key findings from the review:

**What are NETs?** NETs are web-like structures composed of decondensed DNA, histones, and granular enzymes released by activated neutrophils. While essential for host defense, their dysregulated formation in the cerebral microvasculature drives a vicious cycle of tissue injury.

**Core detrimental effects in stroke:**
1. **Promoting stable, lysis-resistant thrombi** - The dense DNA/histone/enzyme scaffold creates physically robust thrombi resistant to fibrin-centric lytic agents like recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (r-tPA). High NET content in retrieved thrombi is significantly associated with unsuccessful recanalization (mTICI <2b) and prolonged procedure times during mechanical thrombectomy.
2. **Compromising blood-brain barrier integrity** - NET-associated proteases (neutrophil elastase, matrix metalloproteinases) degrade tight junction proteins and basement membrane; NET histones are directly cytotoxic to endothelial cells.
3. **Amplifying neuroinflammation** - NET DNA and histones act as DAMPs, activating microglia and astrocytes, triggering a cytokine storm that recruits more neutrophils, perpetuating a vicious cycle.

**Mechanisms of NETosis:**
- Upstream triggers: ROS burst from ischemia-reperfusion, DAMPs (especially HMGB1), and platelet-neutrophil interactions
- Two pathways: (1) NADPH oxidase-dependent classical lytic pathway; (2) PAD4-dependent pathway involving histone citrullination and chromatin decondensation

**Clinical evidence:**
- NET levels are significantly elevated in acute ischemic stroke patients, particularly those over 65 with atrial fibrillation or cardioembolic sources
- NET formation peaks within 24h post-stroke, declining by 48h in murine models
- Older, more organized thrombi contain higher NET burdens; thrombus age was the sole independent predictor of NET content
- Systemic comorbidities (diabetes, obesity) "prime" circulating neutrophils, making them hyper-responsive and predisposed to exaggerated NETosis upon stroke onset via gut dysbiosis and meta-inflammation mechanisms

**Therapeutic strategies (Table 1):**
1. Inhibiting NET formation - PAD4 inhibitors (e.g., chloroquine), tetrahydroisoquinolines
2. Degrading existing NETs - DNase I (but limited efficacy in fibrin-rich thrombi as monotherapy)
3. Physical removal - therapeutic apheresis for circulating NETs
4. EV-based indirect modulation - astrocyte/microglia-derived extracellular vesicles that can cross the BBB

**Biomarkers:** NET markers (H3Cit, cfDNA, NE-DNA, MPO-DNA), NLR (neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio), NHR (neutrophil-to-HDL ratio), and MHR (monocyte-to-HDL ratio) show prognostic utility in stroke.

**Future directions:** Research led by China and the US; key controversies include the potential "double-edged sword" nature of NETs - whether they may have reparative roles in subacute/chronic recovery phases. Major translational challenges include ensuring therapeutic specificity and defining the optimal treatment window.

The review concludes that targeting the thrombo-inflammatory functions of NETs represents a paradigm shift from a purely fibrin-centric view of stroke, opening new avenues for more effective therapies.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"NETs are not mere bystanders but active drivers of stroke pathology... targeting the thrombo-inflammatory functions of NETs represents a paradigm shift from a purely fibrin-centric view of stroke, opening new avenues for developing more effective therapies."
</key_excerpts>
