## Introduction

The peripheral immune system plays a crucial and indispensable role in shaping the development and various functions of the central nervous system (CNS). It also contributes to the pathogenesis of CNS diseases, from the initial stages of acute injury through the subsequent recovery process [[1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B1),[2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B2)]. Strategies involving the regulation of the peripheral immune system for the intervention in CNS diseases hold significant research value [[3](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B3)]. Aging inevitably impacts nearly every component of the immune system, which in turn influences the genesis and progression of CNS diseases [[4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B4)–[6](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B6)]. However, the specific changes that aging induces in the immune system—a phenomenon known as immunosenescence—and their subsequent effects on the physiological functions and pathological processes within the CNS remain largely unexplored.

Immunosenescence is inherently complex and variable, with different immune cells displaying diverse responses to aging [[4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B4),[7](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B7)]. For instance, aging markedly alters the functionality and quantity of both neutrophils and natural killer (NK) cells. It reduces the microbicidal activity of neutrophils and diminishes the cytotoxic capabilities of NK cells, which, in turn, exacerbates infection and tissue damage [[7](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B7)–[9](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B9)]. Furthermore, the aging process shifts the inflammatory response by altering the composition of T cells and reducing the ratio of naive to memory T cells [[10](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B10)]. Despite these insights, research has largely been focused on macro-level changes in specific immune cell types, with scant attention to the nuanced alterations in various subpopulations.

Ischemic stroke is a cerebrovascular disease primarily affecting the elderly population [[11](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B11),[12](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B12)]. Previous studies have demonstrated that in the context of aging, resident brain immune cells—microglia—exacerbate functional impairments following ischemic stroke [[11](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B11),[13](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B13)]. Similarly, the aging process also has a significant impact on peripheral immune cells, affecting the prognosis of ischemic stroke. Specifically, aging increases the presence of procoagulant neutrophils, which obstruct cerebral microcirculation in ischemic regions and worsen outcomes. Aging also amplifies the infiltration of CD8 T cells, thereby potentiating the inflammatory response [[14](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B14)–[16](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B16)]. However, comprehensive studies investigating aging-induced changes in peripheral immune cells and their subsequent impact on stroke recovery are conspicuously absent.

In this study, we explored the intricacies of immunosenescence in the peripheral blood of aged mice, focusing on accelerated neutrophil aging, enhanced antigen-presenting functions in monocytes and macrophages, and shifts in T cell-mediated immunity. Notably, these age-associated changes are not confined to the circulatory system but are also manifest when these immune cells infiltrate cerebral ischemic regions following a stroke event.

## Results

### Immunosenescence hallmarks and the impact of aging on peripheral immune cell infiltration and functionality in post-stroke mice

We initially utilized cytometry by time of flight (CyTOF) to comprehensively assess alterations in peripheral immune cells in aged mice (Fig. [1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F1)A). Using specific marker antibodies, we identified the main immune cell subsets, including neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages (MM), T cells, B cells, NK cells, and a minor population of dendritic cells (DC) (Fig. [S1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)A). A decline in the proportion of lymphocytes, specifically T cells, B cells, as well as NK cells, was observed in the aged mice. In contrast, the proportion of myeloid cells increased, with neutrophils showing a particularly notable rise (Fig. [1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F1)A). Subsequent SPADE (Spanning-tree Progression Analysis of Density-normalized Events) analysis [[17](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B17)], employing CD11b as a myeloid cell marker, also suggested the expansion of neutrophil clusters (CD11b+Ly6G+) in the peripheral blood of aged mice (Fig. [1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F1)B).

![Image 10](https://spj.science.org/cms/10.34133/research.0287/asset/b8ecfc82-e6df-4d7a-ba73-d65ec71a5fee/assets/graphic/research.0287.fig.001.jpg)

Fig.1. Characteristics of peripheral blood immune aging in mice and its impact on the immune microenvironment of the ischemic brain. (A) Peripheral blood immune cells from aged (_n_ = 4) and young (_n_ = 3) mice were isolated and subjected to CyTOF analysis (top). Proportion of various immune cell subsets within peripheral immune cells for each group (bottom). (B) Representative SPADE results of mass cytometry data with cluster size indicating cell proportion and color denoting CD11b expression levels (left); in the SPADE results, representation of neutrophil cell proportions in aged and young mice is displayed, identified by Ly6G as a marker (right). (C) Peripheral blood immune cells from aged and young mice, as well as CD45hi immune cells from both groups at 14 d post-MCAO, were sorted for scRNA-seq (left); UMAP projection plot showing cell clusters of immune cells in the periphery and ischemic brain of aged and young mice (right). (D) Flow cytometry analysis of the infiltrated immune cell populations in the ischemic brain of aged (_n_ = 4 to 5) and young mice (_n_ = 5 to 6) at 14 d post-MCAO. *_P_< 0.05, **_P_< 0.01, NS means not significant, Student _t_ test. (E) Up-regulated functional pathways in neutrophils, MM, and T cells in the aged group compared to the young group. (F) Antigen-presenting functions and interferon pathways were significantly up-regulated in various immune cell populations in the periphery of aged mice compared to young mice. _P_ ≤ 0.0001 in all immune cell clusters, Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon rank sum test. (G) Schematic of the experimental procedure in which recipient mice received peripheral immune cells from either aged or young donor mice; right panel: mice that received immune cells from aged donors showed larger infarct volumes 14 d post-MCAO compared to mice that received immune cells from young donors. _n_ = 4 per group. **_P_< 0.01, Student _t_ test. (H and I) Rotarod (H) and adhesive removal tests (I) suggest that mice received aged immune cells (_n_ = 7 for Rotarod; _n_ = 8 for adhesive removal) exhibited worse long-term sensory and motor function recovery than those received young immune cells (_n_ = 6 for Rotarod; _n_ = 7 for adhesive removal). *_P_< 0.05, 2-way ANOVA repeated measurement.

To more explicitly understand the impact of aging on peripheral immune cells, as well as how these alterations affect the immune microenvironment following middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO), we isolated total blood immune cells from both young and aged mice as well as the CD45hi immune cells in both age groups at 14 d post-MCAO, for subsequent single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) (Fig. [1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F1)C and Fig. [S1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)B and C). After quality control, 45,649 cells were subjected to downstream analyses. Unsupervised clustering revealed 7 major cell groups: MM, B cells, T cells, neutrophils, NK cells, and 2 DC subsets (cDC and pDC) (Fig. [1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F1)C and Fig. [S1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)D) (Table [S1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)). We observed that most immune cell types exhibited varying degrees of infiltration at 14 d post-MCAO. Notably, B cells, which constituted a higher proportion in peripheral blood, were underrepresented in the brain at 14 d post-MCAO. In contrast, MM, which were less prevalent in the periphery, made up a higher proportion of brain-infiltrating immune cells. Additionally, T cells and neutrophils were highly represented among brain-infiltrating cells, suggesting they may play significant roles at this stage (Fig. [S1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)E). Moreover, when comparing the proportional changes in the number of infiltrated immune cells between aged and young mice, we identified an interesting “amplification” phenomenon. Trends observed in peripheral blood cell numbers were magnified in the aged brain. Specifically, aged mice exhibited a higher proportion of neutrophils and MM, and this increase was more pronounced in the brain. Conversely, the proportion of T cells and NK cells declined in peripheral blood in aged mice, and this decline was more marked in the brain (Fig. [S1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)E). We further performed flow cytometry to validate the differences in immune cell populations in the brain. The results indicated that following stroke, the brains of aged mice exhibited an increased infiltration of neutrophils and MM, while the infiltration of NK cells significantly decreased. These findings were consistent with the results obtained from scRNA-seq. We did not observe a significant difference in T cells infiltration between the aged and young groups (Fig. [1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F1)D).

From the perspective of cell subset functionalities, we observed a similar “amplification” or correspondence effect with the quantitative change. Specifically, immune cell functions such as antigen presentation, cytotoxicity, and cytokine signaling pathways were markedly heightened in both the aged peripheral blood and brain tissue as compared to their young counterparts (Fig. [1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F1)E). Additionally, we observed an up-regulation of antigen presentation capabilities and interferon signaling pathways across all immune cell subsets in the aged group, encompassing both blood and ischemic brain samples (Fig. [1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F1)F). Interestingly, these widespread functional alterations were already manifest in the peripheral blood of the aged mice (Fig. [S1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)F). These findings indicate that such changes may represent hallmark features of the aging process.

Subsequently, we further evaluated the impact of aged immune cells on stroke outcomes. Peripheral blood immune cells from either young or aged mice were transferred into the recipient young mice (Fig. [1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F1)G). Notably, we found that mice received immune cells from aged donors had larger infarct volumes compared to those received immune cells from young donors (Fig. [1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F1)G). Through behavioral assessments, we observed that mice received aged immune cells demonstrated a poorer trend in sensory-motor functional recovery (Fig. [1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F1)H and I). Furthermore, these disparities remained evident at day 14, a phase commonly acknowledged as the post-MCAO repair phase. Additionally, this increase in infarct volume and impaired functional recovery were accompanied by a higher infiltration of neutrophils, MM, CD4 T cells, and CD8 T cells, suggesting an intensified inflammatory response (Fig. [S1](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)G).

### Peripheral neutrophil senescence intensifies with aging and was amplified in the brain post-stroke

As mentioned above, we observed an increased proportion of neutrophils in aged mice. Further, we employed flow cytometry to quantify the neutrophil counts in the peripheral blood of mice. We discovered that aged mice exhibited higher neutrophil counts compared to their young counterparts (Fig. [2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F2)A). Utilizing scRNA-seq, we observed not only an increased proportion of neutrophils among peripheral immune cells but also a shift toward a “senescent” phenotype, as indicated by the elevated aging score in neutrophils from aged mice (Fig. [2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F2)B). CD62L protein expression was used as a marker to assess neutrophil aging [[18](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B18)]. Upon evaluating the expression levels of this molecule in the peripheral neutrophils of mice, we found that aged mice exhibited lower levels of CD62L expression compared to young mice, suggesting a higher propensity for aging (Fig. [2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F2)C). Additionally, scRNA-seq data revealed that, neutrophils from aged mice exhibited diminished Cxcr2 expression but enhanced Cxcr4 expression compared to those from young mice, and other genes associated with advanced neutrophil maturation stages, such as Ifitm1 and Wfdc17 (Fig. [S2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)A), were also up-regulated, suggesting an accelerated senescence process in peripheral neutrophils of aged mice [[14](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B14),[19](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B19),[20](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B20)]. In alignment with previous findings [[18](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B18)], we identified an association between neutrophil senescence and elevated inflammatory factor production (Il1b) as well as enhanced vascular injury function (Mmp9) in the peripheral blood neutrophils of aged mice (Fig. [S2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)B). Overall, relative to young mice, aged mice exhibited an increased count of peripheral blood neutrophils that manifested a senescent phenotype. This senescent state predisposed the neutrophils to be more activated, with augmented inflammatory and antigen-presenting capabilities (Fig. [S2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)B).

![Image 11](https://spj.science.org/cms/10.34133/research.0287/asset/a797f62d-8895-49e0-9146-e647c4cf1287/assets/graphic/research.0287.fig.002.jpg)

Fig.2. Aged mice exhibit accelerated neutrophil aging. (A) Schematic diagram illustrating the gating strategy for neutrophil quantification using flow cytometry, where neutrophils were identified as CD11b+Ly6G+ cells. Results indicate an increased number of peripheral blood neutrophils in aged mice (_n_ = 4) compared to young mice (_n_ = 5). *_P_< 0.05, Student _t_ test. (B) Left panel: scRNA-seq indicating that the proportion of neutrophils among immune cells increased in the aged blood. Right panel: Violin plot showing elevated neutrophil aging scores in aged mice. ****_P_ ≤ 0.0001, Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon rank sum test. (C) Flow cytometry indicating that aged mice express lower levels of CD62L in peripheral blood neutrophils than young mice, _n_ = 4 per group, *_P_< 0.05, Student _t_ test. (D) Immunofluorescence staining showing that at 14 d post-MCAO, aged mice (_n_ = 4) had more neutrophil infiltration in the ischemic brain compared to young mice (_n_ = 5). Scale bar = 50 μm, **_P_< 0.01, Student _t_ test. (E) scRNA-seq at 14 d post-MCAO suggesting an increased proportion of neutrophils among immune cells in the ischemic brain of aged mice; violin plot showing elevated peripheral neutrophil aging scores in aged mice. ****_P_ ≤ 0.0001, Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon rank sum test. (F) Ridge plot indicating down-regulated expression of Sell in neutrophils of aged ischemic brain. (G) Pseudotime trajectory of peripheral and ischemic brain neutrophils analyzed with Monocle3. (H) UMAP plot of peripheral and ischemic brain neutrophils from aged and young mice (left), and stacked bar plot showing the proportion of the 3 clusters (right). (I) BrNeu2 exhibited higher levels of chemotaxis, secretion, and antigen presentation-related genes. (J) Feature plot displaying the BBB permeability regulation score. (K and L) Immunofluorescence staining indicating that at 14 d post-MCAO, aged mice have more extravasation of endogenous IgG and neutrophils (white arrow) (K) as well as lower Occludin/CD31 area ratio (L) in the ischemic brain compared to young mice. _n_ = 5 per group. Scale bar = 25 μm. **_P_< 0.01, Student _t_ test. Pre-Neu, neutrophil precursor; BldNeu, peripheral blood neutrophils; BrNeu, neutrophil in the ischemic brain; DAPI, 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole.

We then sought to further dissect the maturation stages of these cells in peripheral blood. Using the presence of Pre-Neu, a precursor of neutrophils, as a developmental starting point, we employed Monocle3 [[21](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B21)] to discern the maturation trajectory (Fig. [S2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)C and D). As a result of this comprehensive analysis, we categorically distinguished neutrophils into 3 distinct groups based on their maturity. The first group comprised the aforementioned Pre-Neu, representing the earliest stage of development. Subsequently, 2 mature stages were identified: BldNeu1, indicative of early-stage mature neutrophils, and BldNeu2, representing the later stage of maturation. In addition, we observed an increase in the proportion of BldNeu2 in the peripheral blood of aged mice (Fig. [S2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)E), suggesting an age-related inclination toward the advanced neutrophil maturation phase. Neutrotime depicts a continuous developmental trajectory of neutrophils [[22](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B22)]. We observed that Pre-Neu distinctly expressed genes associated with early neutrotime, while in contrast, BldNeu2 prominently expressed genes characteristic of late neutrotime (Fig. [S2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)F). Interestingly, as a representation of a later neutrophil development state, BldNeu2 demonstrated a higher aging score compared to BldNeu1 and (Fig. [S2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)G). These findings lead us to postulate that neutrophils experience a systematic senescence during their developmental and maturation phases—a process seemingly intensified in the peripheral blood of aged mice. This senescent state of neutrophils is marked by enhanced adhesion, antigen synthesis, increased cytotoxicity, and bolstered immune responses (Fig. [S2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)H).

Subsequently, we investigated alterations in the neutrophils within the aged brain and their relationship with the senescence of peripheral neutrophils. Immunofluorescence staining highlighted that there was a greater infiltration of neutrophils in the brains of aged mice 14 d post-MCAO compared to the young mice (Fig. [2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F2)D). Under aged conditions, the proportion of neutrophils among immune cells following MCAO was elevated. Furthermore, paralleling our observations in the periphery, neutrophils in the aged brain exhibited a more pronounced aging phenotype than those in young brains, with this trend being more evident than in peripheral blood (Fig. [2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F2)E). The expression of CD62L (encoded by Sell) in neutrophils from the ischemic brain of aged mice was also found to be lower compared to that in young mice (Fig. [2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F2)F). We employed Pre-Neu as a starting reference to illustrate the pseudotime distribution of neutrophils from the peripheral blood and those infiltrated in the brain (Fig. [2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F2)G). Based on this distribution, we defined Pre-Neu and early-evolutionary stage neutrophils as BldNeu, given that they predominantly originated from peripheral blood. Neutrophils that appeared most mature in the pseudotime developmental trajectory were categorized as BrNeu1, as they were almost exclusively mapped to the ischemic brain. Other neutrophils distributed within the brain were collectively designated as BrNeu2 (Fig. [2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F2)H). The above results also suggest that neutrophils infiltrated the brain positioned at a later pseudotime endpoint compared to their peripheral counterparts. We observed that a group of BrNeu1 neutrophils could be mapped to the peripheral blood. These neutrophils exhibited a later developmental state on the pseudotime trajectory compared to other circulating neutrophils, suggesting that they may represent a more senescent population of neutrophils in the blood. Moreover, this subset of neutrophils also showed an increase in the peripheral blood of aged mice (Fig. [S2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)I).

BrNeu2 resided at the furthest endpoint in the pseudotime developmental trajectory (Fig. [2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F2)G) and exhibited lower expression levels of Cxcr2 and Sell, suggesting a potential senescent state (Fig. [S2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)J). Moreover, BrNeu2 was more prevalent in the brains of aged mice (Fig. [2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F2)H). Compared to other neutrophils, BrNeu2 had elevated expression of cytokine genes and genes associated with neutrophil degranulation (Ccl3, Ccl4, Cxcl2, lamp1, and Tnf), as well as adhesive function-related molecules (Icam1 and Spp1). Intriguingly, BrNeu2 also displayed increased expression genes-related antigen presentation (H2-Eb1, H2-Ab1, H2-Aa, and Cd74) (Fig. [2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F2)I). Furthermore, what’s of greater significance is our discovery that BrNeu2 has a substantial impact on the blood–brain barrier (BBB) permeability (Fig. [2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F2)J). We then assessed the BBB permeability in aged and young mice 14 d post-MCAO. The results indicated more pronounced extravasation of endogenous immunoglobulin G (IgG) and neutrophils, along with reduced tight junctions in endothelial cells in the brains of aged mice, indicating a more pronounced disruption of the BBB (Fig. [2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F2)K and L). Furthermore, vascular coverage in aged mice was lower than in young mice, suggesting impaired vascular repair in the elderly environment (Fig. [S2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)K).

Our findings suggest that, aged mice display more senescence characteristics in peripheral blood neutrophils compared to young mice. This may contribute to the increased senescent neutrophils observed in the brains of aged mice following ischemic stroke. Such senescent neutrophils appear to be more inclined toward a destructive state, potentially exacerbating unfavorable outcomes after stroke.

### Functional shift in MM toward enhanced antigen presentation in aged mice

We observed a notable shift in the overall gene expression profile of MM in the peripheral blood. Specifically, there was an enhanced expression of antigen presentation-related genes, while the expression of classical MM genes, such as Ccr2, Ly6c2, and Trem2, was markedly reduced (Fig. [S3](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)A). This suggests a functional transition toward antigen presentation of MM in aged mice blood. Three distinct clusters emerged within the blood MM population. BldMM0, indicative of the classical MM characterized by Ccr2 and Ly6c2 expression, having a reduced proportion in aged mice. In contrast, BldMM2, characterized by a diminished Ly6c expression and enriched of nonclassical monocyte markers Eno3, Ear2, and Ace [[23](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#B23)], maintained consistent across both age groups. Interestingly, BldMM1, a subset that highly expressing Fcgr4 and Ly6a, scarcely found in young mice but abundant in the aged, demonstrated heightened expression of antigen-presenting genes, including H2-Aa, H2-Ab1, and H2-Eb1 (Fig. [3](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F3)A and B). The results from CyTOF also confirmed that the proportion of Fcgr4+MM (one of the marker genes for BldMM1) significantly increased in the peripheral blood of aged mice (Fig. [3](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F3)C). Functional enrichment analysis further revealed that BldMM1, in comparison to other peripheral macrophages, distinctly showcased enhanced antigen-presentation capabilities (Fig. [3](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F3)D).

![Image 12](https://spj.science.org/cms/10.34133/research.0287/asset/84ef6cc2-f7be-49bf-894c-8ffc0d99aab1/assets/graphic/research.0287.fig.003.jpg)

Fig.3. Changes in MM functional states in aging. (A) UMAP plot of peripheral MM from aged and young mice showing increased proportion of BldMM1 in peripheral blood of aged mice. (B) Dot plot of marker genes for the 3 MM subclusters. (C) CyTOF results indicating a higher proportion of Fcgr4+ MM (gated from CD45+CD11b+Ly6g-Ly6c+F4/80+ cells) subgroups in the peripheral blood of aged mice (_n_ = 4) compared to young mice (_n_ = 3). *_P_< 0.05. Student _t_ test. (D) Enrichment of several antigen-presentation functional pathways in BldMM cell population. (E) Violin plot showing up-regulated genes in peripheral MM of aged mice (left) and antigen presentation function (right) were both elevated in the infiltrated MM of the aged mice compared to those of young mice at 14 d post-MCAO. ****_P_ ≤ 0.0001, Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon rank sum test. (F) UMAP visualization showing the distribution and proportions of the 3 distinct MM subsets in the ischemic brain. (G) Scatter plot showing the up-regulated DEGs with a log2(fold change) > 0.25 in BrMM1 (top) or BrMM2 (bottom) compared to BrMM0, with the percentage difference along the x-axis and log2(fold change) along the y-axis. The combined _z_-score of percentage difference and log2(fold change) is shown in the color scale. (H) Dot plot illustrating representative functional terms of BrMM1 and BrMM2 by GO enrichment based on _z_-score and significance (−log10[adjusted _P_ value]). (I and J) Quantitative comparison of the numbers of MHC-II+ (I) or Gpnmb+ (J) MM in the ischemic brain between aged and young mice. Scale bar =100 μm. Three-dimensional constructed image showing the morphology of MHC-II+ and Gpnmb+MM. Scale bar = 5 μm. _n_ = 4 per group. (I and J), **_P_< 0.01, Student _t_ test. BldMM, peripheral blood monocytes/macrophages; BrMM, monocytes/macrophages in the ischemic brain.

Further, we probed if this peripheral MM functional transition influenced the MM’s role in the brain at 14 d post-MCAO. Our findings resonated with our earlier observations: genes up-regulated in peripheral MM of aged mice comparted with young mice, as well as the genes related to antigen-presentation function were up-regulated in MM in the aged mice’s brain (Fig. [3](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F3)E). In the brain, we identified 3 MM subtypes: BrMM0, the classical MM with a Ly6c+Ccr2hi profile; BrMM1, showing a preference for antigen-presentation genes; and BrMM2, distinguished by Gpnmb and Trem2 markers (Fig. [3](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F3)F and G and Fig. [S3](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)B and C). In alignment with peripheral findings, there was a significant increase of antigen-presentation related BrMM1 (Fig. [3](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F3)F and H and Fig. [S3](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)D). In contrast, BrMM2, representing a distinct subset of MM known for its pronounced phagocytic and reparative capabilities, exhibited a reduced presence in the aged brain (Fig. [3](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F3)F and H).

Finally, performing immunofluorescence staining, we observed an increase in the number of antigen-presenting MMs in aged brains (Fig. [3](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F3)I). Conversely, the quantity of BrMM2 (Gpnmb+MM) notably decreased (Fig. [3](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F3)J).

### Altered T cell composition and increased T cell activation with aging

T cells play a pivotal role in adaptive immunity. In the peripheral blood, based on characteristic marker genes and cell surface molecules (Fig. [S4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)A), namely Cd4, Cd8, sell, ccr7, cd44, and klrb1c, we delineated various subsets of T cells. These subsets include CD4 naive, CD4 effector/memory (CD4 E/M), CD8 naive, CD8 effector/memory (CD8 E/M), and NKT cells. Additionally, the peripheral blood comprises a minority of T cells that respond to interferons, termed IFN-T cells, characterized by their expression of genes such as Ifit1, Ifit3, and Isg15. We also identified cycling T cells, marked by Mki67, Ccnb2, Cdca3, and Ccna2, as well as γδT cells, indicated by the presence of Trdv4 and Trdc genes (Fig. [4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F4)A and Fig. [S4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)A and B). Among these cells, we observed a significant decline in the proportions of both CD4 naive and CD8 naive T cells in the peripheral blood of aged mice. Conversely, CD4 E/M and CD8 E/M, exhibited a pronounced increase in their numbers (Fig. [4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F4)A). Flow cytometry analyses also confirmed an increase in the proportion of CD4 memory and CD8 memory (Fig. [4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F4)B).

![Image 13](https://spj.science.org/cms/10.34133/research.0287/asset/ce37640c-2da8-4069-8e76-e0c1ba5b974d/assets/graphic/research.0287.fig.004.jpg)

Fig.4. Altered subgroup composition in T cells due to aging. (A) UMAP plot of peripheral T cells from aged and young mice (left). Bar plots showing the proportions of the different T cell subsets (right). (B) CyTOF results indicating a significant increase in the proportion of memory cells expressing CD44hi of CD3+CD4+T and CD3+CD8+T cell populations in aged mice (_n_ = 4) compared to young mice (_n_ = 3). *_P_< 0.05, **_P_< 0.01, Student _t_ test. (C) Bar graph showing the number of DEGs in each subgroup in the peripheral blood of aged and young mice, with a log2(fold change) > 0.25 and adjusted _P_ value < 0.05. (D) Display of genes up-regulated in CD4 E/M and CD8 E/M cells in aged mice compared to young mice. (E) UMAP plot of peripheral and brain T cells from aged and young mice (left), along with the proportion of these T cell clusters in aged and young ischemic brains (right). (F) Mice that received aged T cell showing larger infarct volumes at 14 d post-MCAO. _n_ = 4 per group. **_P_< 0.01, Student _t_ test. NS means not significant. (G and H) Rotarod (G, _n_ = 7 per group) and adhesive removal tests (H, _n_ = 8 per group) suggest that mice receiving aged T cells exhibit worse neurological outcomes than those receiving young T cells. *_P_< 0.05, 2-way ANOVA repeated measurement. IFN-T, T cells that respond to interferons; Non-T, MCAO mice did not receive T cells; Young-T, MCAO mice received young T cells; Aged-T, MCAO mice received aged T cells.

Subsequently, we delved deeper into examining the gene expression differences of each T cell subset between the aged and young mice. The findings indicated that CD4 E/M and CD8 E/M displayed the most pronounced differences. For other T cell subsets, including NKT, we did not observe significant gene expression variations (Fig. [4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F4)C). CD4 E/M cells exhibited significant up-regulation of genes related to adhesion, differentiation, and secretory factor functions (such as Itga4, Stat1/4, and lgals1/3) as well as T cell survival associated genes (Bcl2 and Hif1a). In contrast, CD8 E/M cells displayed prominent up-regulation of genes associated with cytotoxicity, exhaustion (like Fasl, Eomes, and Tox), and chemotactic functions (such as Ccr5, Ccr2, and Ccl4). Furthermore, several genes were up-regulated in both cell types, with their functions relating to cytokine release, cytotoxicity, T cell adhesion, and T cell proliferation, reflecting attributes of activated T cells (Fig. [4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F4)D and Fig. [S4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)C). We named these genes that up-regulated in both CD4 E/M and CD8 E/M as common up genes (Table [S2](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)).

Integrating our observations from the peripheral blood T cells with those from the brain post-MCAO, several T clusters were identified (Fig. [4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F4)E and Fig. [S4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)D). The increase in the proportion of E/M cells with aging, as seen in the periphery, was consistently reflected post-stroke in the aged brain (Fig. [4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F4)E). We then assessed the expression of the common up genes within infiltrated T cells and found that these genes were predominantly expressed by CD4 E/M and CD8 E/M in the brain. Interestingly, while these up-regulated genes were primarily concentrated in these subsets, almost all of T cell groups in the aged brain demonstrated an increased expression of these genes compared to their young counterparts (Fig. [S4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#supplementary-materials)E and F). This observation further underscores the pervasive influence of aging on shaping the functional landscape of T cells.

Finally, to verify the impact of aged peripheral T cells on the prognosis of MCAO in mice, we isolated T cells from aged or young mice and transferred them into young mice, which were subsequently subjected to MCAO. The outcomes revealed that mice received young T cells did not result in a significant change in infarct volume (Fig. [4](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.34133/research.0287#F4)F). This webpage presents a peer-reviewed open-access research article published in the journal *Research* (11 December 2023, Vol 6, Article ID 0287, DOI: 10.34133/research.0287) titled "Age-Related Alterations in Peripheral Immune Landscape with Magnified Impact on Post-Stroke Brain." The study investigates immunosenescence (aging-induced immune system alterations) in peripheral blood of aged mice and its impact on the cerebral immune environment after ischemic stroke.

**Methods:** The researchers used a combination of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), cytometry by time of flight (CyTOF), flow cytometry, immunofluorescence staining, and various immunological assays. A total of 45,649 cells were analyzed after quality control, identifying 7 major immune cell groups. Middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) was used to model ischemic stroke.

**Key Findings:**

1. **Overall immune changes:** Aged mice showed increased neutrophil counts, elevated myeloid cell proportions, and declines in T cells, B cells, and NK cells. These peripheral changes were "amplified" in the ischemic brain after stroke. Functional changes including antigen presentation, cytotoxicity, and cytokine signaling were heightened in both aged blood and brain.

2. **Neutrophil senescence:** Aged mice exhibited accelerated neutrophil aging characterized by reduced CD62L expression, diminished Cxcr2 and increased Cxcr4 expression, and elevated aging scores. A distinct senescent neutrophil subpopulation (BrNeu2) in the ischemic brain showed enhanced chemotaxis, degranulation, adhesion, and antigen presentation functions, plus significant impact on blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability. Aged mice showed more IgG extravasation, reduced tight junctions, and impaired vascular repair.

3. **Monocyte/macrophage (MM) shift:** Aged mice exhibited enhanced antigen-presentation capabilities in MM, with a novel BldMM1 subset (expressing Fcgr4 and Ly6a) abundant in aged mice. In the brain, antigen-presenting BrMM1 increased while reparative/phagocytic BrMM2 (Gpnmb+) decreased in aged brains.

4. **T cell alterations:** T cell profiles shifted from naive to effector/memory (E/M) states with aging. CD4 E/M cells showed up-regulation of adhesion, differentiation, and survival genes; CD8 E/M cells showed up-regulation of cytotoxicity, exhaustion (Fasl, Eomes, Tox), and chemotactic genes. A decline in regulatory CD8 T cells (Klra+) and expansion of exhausted-like CD8 T cells retaining proinflammatory functions were observed.

5. **Functional validation:** Transfer of aged immune cells (or aged T cells alone) into young recipient mice resulted in larger infarct volumes, worse sensory-motor functional recovery, and increased infiltration of neutrophils, MM, CD4, and CD8 T cells at 14 days post-MCAO.

**Conclusion:** The authors provide comprehensive insights into key attributes of peripheral immunosenescence, offering a vital theoretical foundation for understanding ischemic strokes and other age-associated diseases. The study demonstrates that age-related immune disparities not only persist but are amplified within ischemic hemispheres following stroke.
args.key_excerpts: "Immunosenescence refers to the multifaceted and profound alterations in the immune system brought about by aging, exerting complex influences on the pathophysiological processes of diseases that manifest upon it."

## Abstract

* * *

The peripheral immune system plays a critical role in aging and in the response to brain injury. Emerging data suggest inflammatory responses are exacerbated in older animals following ischemic stroke; however, our understanding of these age-related changes is poor. In this work, we demonstrate marked differences in the composition of circulating and infiltrating leukocytes recruited to the ischemic brain of old male mice after stroke compared to young male mice. Blood neutrophilia and neutrophil invasion into the brain were increased in aged animals. Relative to infiltrating monocyte populations, brain-invading neutrophils had reduced phagocytic potential, and produced higher levels of reactive oxygen species and extracellular matrix-degrading enzymes (i.e., MMP-9), which were further exacerbated with age. Hemorrhagic transformation was more pronounced in aged versus young mice relative to infarct size. High numbers of myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils were found in postmortem human brain samples of old (> 71 years) acute ischemic stroke subjects compared to non-ischemic controls. Many of these neutrophils were found in the brain parenchyma. A large proportion of these neutrophils expressed MMP-9 and positively correlated with hemorrhage and hyperemia. MMP-9 expression and hemorrhagic transformation after stroke increased with age. These changes in the myeloid response to stroke with age led us to hypothesize that the bone marrow response to stroke is altered with age, which could be important for the development of effective therapies targeting the immune response. We generated heterochronic bone marrow chimeras as a tool to determine the contribution of peripheral immune senescence to age- and stroke-induced inflammation. Old hosts that received young bone marrow (i.e., Young → Old) had attenuation of age-related reductions in bFGF and VEGF and showed improved locomotor activity and gait dynamics compared to isochronic (Old → Old) controls. Microglia in young heterochronic mice (Old → Young) developed a senescent-like phenotype. After stroke, aged animals reconstituted with young marrow had reduced behavioral deficits compared to isochronic controls, and had significantly fewer brain-infiltrating neutrophils. Increased rates of hemorrhagic transformation were seen in young mice reconstituted with aged bone marrow. This work suggests that age alters the immunological response to stroke, and that this can be reversed by manipulation of the peripheral immune cells in the bone marrow.

--- SOURCE 1: Functional dynamics of neutrophils after ischemic stroke ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6993940

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Translational Stroke Research (2019, Vol. 11, Issue 1, p. 108; doi: 10.1007/s12975-019-00694-y; PMID: 30847778; PMCID: PMC6993940) titled "Functional dynamics of neutrophils after ischemic stroke." The study was conducted by researchers from Sun Yat-sen University (China), the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, and Ohio State University, with corresponding authors Zhengqi Lu and Song Guo Zheng. Wei Cai, Sanxin Liu, and Mengyan Hu contributed equally as first authors.

**Abstract/Key Findings:**
The study investigated the temporal dynamics of neutrophils after ischemic stroke using both patient data and an animal (mouse) model of transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO). Key findings include:
- Neutrophil counts in peripheral blood increased soon after stroke onset in patients, with higher counts indicating detrimental outcomes
- In mice, neutrophil counts peaked at 12h after cerebral ischemia in blood, followed by a 1-2 day spike in brain lesions
- Neutrophil clearance peaked at 2 days after stroke; extracellular traps (NETs) were mostly detected at 2-3 days after stroke
- Expression of the N2 marker CD206 on infiltrated neutrophils was relatively stable
- N2 phenotype neutrophils facilitated clearance by macrophages and did not further induce neuronal death after ischemic injury (compared with N0 or N1 neutrophils)
- Skewing neutrophils toward the N2 phenotype (via TGFβ) before stroke reduced infarct volumes at 1 day after tMCAO
- Conditioned medium from ischemic neurons drove neutrophils away from the protective N2 phenotype and increased extracellular trap formation

**Patient Study:**
- 225 Chinese (Han ethnicity) patients with acute ischemic stroke admitted within 24h of symptom onset (Jan 2014–Aug 2018) and 56 healthy controls were analyzed
- 58 patients had infections (respiratory or urinary); 167 did not
- In non-infected patients with infarction >1.5cm, both neutrophil counts (R²=0.07, P=0.0208) and NLR (R²=0.07, P=0.0447) positively correlated with infarct sizes
- NLR, but not neutrophil counts, positively correlated with NIHSS scores (R²=0.07, P=0.0006) in non-infected AIS patients

**Animal Model:**
- 152 male C57BL/6 mice used in tMCAO model; mortality ranged from 0% (1h, 3h, sham) to 42.86% (7d)
- Neutrophil percentages in peripheral blood peaked at 12h-1d, then declined to Sham levels by 2d
- Neutrophil infiltration into stroke lesions first detected at 12h, prominent at 1-2d, few remaining by 7d
- Chemokines (CCL5, CXCL1, CXCL2, CXCL3) peaked at 12h post-stroke
- Neutrophil clearance by microglia/macrophages started at 12h and peaked at 2d
- NETs formation peaked at 2-3d post-stroke (confirmed by CitH3/Ly6G co-staining, Sytox green/NE staining, and SEM)
- TGFβ pretreatment (2μg/mouse i.v., 1 day before tMCAO) increased N2 neutrophils and reduced infarct volumes

**Methods:** Included flow cytometry, immunofluorescence staining, RT-PCR, primary neutrophil/macrophage/neuronal cultures, OGD (oxygen glucose deprivation) neuronal ischemia model, magnetic sorting, SEM, and statistical analysis (ANOVA, Student's t-test, linear regression; P<0.05 significant).

**Conclusions:** Neutrophil frequency in peripheral blood could be an early indicator of stroke outcomes. N2 neutrophils facilitate macrophage phagocytosis and are less harmful to ischemic neurons. Directing neutrophils toward the N2 phenotype represents a promising therapeutic approach for ischemic stroke.
</summary>

"Neutrophil frequency in the peripheral blood could be an early indicator of stroke outcomes. N2 neutrophils facilitate macrophage phagocytosis and are less harmful to ischemic neurons. Directing neutrophils towards N2 phenotype could be a promising therapeutic approach for ischemic stroke." (Abstract)
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Neutrophil Heterogeneity and its Roles in the Inflammatory Network ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10207908

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific review article published in Current Neuropharmacology (2023 Mar 8;21(3):621, DOI: 10.2174/1570159X20666220706115957) by Meizhen Xie, Yulei Hao, Liangshu Feng, Tian Wang, Mengyue Yao, Hui Li, Di Ma, and Jiachun Feng from the Department of Neurology and Neuroscience Center, The First Hospital of Jilin University, Changchun, China. The article reviews neutrophil heterogeneity and its roles in the inflammatory network after ischemic stroke (PMCID: PMC10207908, PMID: 35794770; received 2022 Mar 29, accepted 2022 Jun 13; licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0).

KEY FINDINGS AND CONTENT:

1. **Neutrophils in Ischemic Stroke**: Neutrophils are the first peripheral immune cells to enter the brain after ischemic stroke, crossing the blood-brain barrier (BBB) to reach the ischemic parenchyma. They are mobilized from peripheral immune organs (bone marrow and spleen) and participate in stroke-related neuroinflammation. Traditionally, neutrophils were believed to aggravate brain injury through release of proteases, reactive oxygen species (ROS), pro-inflammatory factors, and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs).

2. **Clinical Trial Failures and Heterogeneity**: Clinical trials targeting neutrophils for cerebral infarction treatment have failed, partly because only a subgroup of neutrophils ("harmful neutrophils") may cause damage. This has led to recognition of neutrophil heterogeneity.

3. **N1 and N2 Neutrophil Phenotypes**: Analogous to M1/M2 macrophages, neutrophils polarize into two functional phenotypes after ischemic stroke. N1 neutrophils (dominant during acute phase, within 3 days) promote inflammation and damage neural structures via proteases, ROS, and NETs. N2 neutrophils (increasing in later phases) are neuroprotective, releasing anti-inflammatory factors and neuroprotective mediators. N1 and N2 phenotypes are highly plastic and can transform into each other under certain conditions, making them promising therapeutic targets.

4. **Neutrophil Origins**: Bone marrow produces ~10^7 neutrophils/day in mice and ~10^11 in humans. Differentiation progresses through five stages (promyelocytic cells, bone marrow cells, mesenchymal cells, band neutrophils, segmented neutrophils) regulated by transcription factors (C/EBP α/β/ε, PU.1, Gfi-1) and G-CSF. Release from bone marrow is regulated by the CXCR4/CXCR2 balance (CXCR4 retains, CXCR2 promotes release via CXCL1/CXCL2). Extramedullary reservoirs exist in spleen, lung, and liver.

5. **Neutrophil Lifespan and Heterogeneity**: Historically considered short-lived (7-9 hour half-life), newer research shows human circulating neutrophils live ~5-5.4 days (18 hours in mice). Neutrophil aging (characterized by decreased CD62L, increased CXCR4) follows circadian rhythms, is regulated by microbiota, and involves the IL-23/IL-17/G-CSF axis. Neutrophil heterogeneity is confirmed by morphological characteristics (density gradients: HDD, NDN, LDN), surface markers, and single-cell transcriptomics.

6. **Single-Cell Sequencing**: Neutrophils form a single transcriptional continuum called "neutrotime" across tissues (bone marrow = immature end; spleen and blood = mature end). Unbiased clustering divides them into 8 clusters (G0-4 from bone marrow, G5a-c from peripheral blood). In cancer, human neutrophils resolve into 5 subsets (hN1-5) and mouse into 6 (mN1-6). Single-cell analysis of neutrophils has NOT yet been reported in ischemic stroke.

7. **Mobilization Dynamics**: After cerebral ischemia, activated neutrophils appear in peripheral circulation within 24 hours. Bone marrow neutrophil numbers increase 10 min-4 hours after tMCAO, then decrease within 12 hours. Spleen neutrophils peak 12-24 hours post-reperfusion and return to baseline by days 2-7. Mobilization is driven by: (a) the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis via norepinephrine and cortisol; and (b) immune signals from the ischemic brain including DAMPs (HMGB1, HSP72, S100A9, ATP), chemokines, and cytokines (IL-1, TNF-α, G-CSF, IL-8, CCL-2, LTB4, C5a).

8. **Skull Bone Marrow Pathway**: A novel pathway exists where neutrophils from skull bone marrow (connected to meninges via vascular channels) are preferentially mobilized to the ischemic brain compared to peripheral blood neutrophils, likely due to anatomical proximity and direct vascular connections.

9. **Peripheral Blood Neutrophils and NLR**: Blood neutrophil count peaks 24 hours after stroke and high early counts correlate with larger infarct volume, worse symptoms, and poorer prognosis. The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) is a strong predictor: NLR >3.5 at admission predicts worse 3-month prognosis; high NLR within 48 hours predicts poorer outcome and higher death risk; high NLR predicts stroke-associated pneumonia and delirium; higher NLR at admission in endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) patients predicts cerebral hemorrhage, worse outcomes, and higher death risk.

10. **Neutrophil Chemotaxis (Adhesion Cascade)**: Infiltration involves capture, rolling adhesion, and crawling, mediated by E-/L-/P-selectins, PSGL-1, ESGL-1, β2 integrin/LFA-1, ICAM-1, Mac-1, and VLA-4. Platelets contribute via P-selectin release, GPIb (binding Mac-1), and secretion of chemoattractants (CXCL1, CXCL2, CXCL5).

11. **BBB Breakdown and Infiltration**: BBB disruption involves tight junction (claudin, occludin, JAMs) damage and basal lamina degradation. Caveolin-1 mediates occludin and claudin-5 separation from the cytoskeleton via endocytosis. TJ integrity is damaged 30-60 minutes after ischemia/reperfusion. Neutrophils mainly infiltrate the brain parenchyma (confirmed in pMCAO models and stroke patients).

12. **Therapeutic Implications**: Promoting N2 polarization or inhibiting N1 polarization has improved outcomes in animal stroke models, laying the foundation for polarization-based clinical treatments. However, temporal details and specific factors mediating N1/N2 polarization after ischemic attack remain unknown.
</summary>

"As the first peripheral immune cells to enter the brain after ischemic stroke, neutrophils are important participants in stroke-related neuroinflammation."

--- SOURCE 3: New Insight Into Neutrophils: A Potential Therapeutic Target for ... ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2021.692061/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Review Article: "New Insight Into Neutrophils: A Potential Therapeutic Target for Cerebral Ischemia"

**Publication Details:** Published in Frontiers in Immunology (Sec. Multiple Sclerosis and Neuroimmunology), Volume 12, July 14, 2021. DOI: 10.3389/fimmu.2021.692061. Authors: Ran Chen, Xu Zhang, Lijuan Gu, Hua Zhu, Yi Zhong, Yingze Ye, Xiaoxing Xiong, and Zhihong Jian (Department of Neurosurgery, Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University, China).

**Core Topic:** This review examines the dual role of neutrophils in ischemic stroke—both as drivers of brain injury and as potential contributors to tissue repair—and proposes neutrophils as a promising therapeutic target for cerebral ischemia.

**Key Findings:**

1. **Neutrophil Timing and Role in Stroke:** Neutrophils are the first immune cells to accumulate in ischemic brain regions, appearing within minutes of injury. They peak in the ischemic brain on days 1-3 and then gradually decrease. They enter via the blood-brain barrier (BBB), are attracted by chemokine gradients, and migrate through endothelial vessel walls. Enzmann et al. showed neutrophils are mainly confined to the lumen surface or perivascular space (neurovascular unit) rather than brain parenchyma.

2. **Dual (Beneficial and Harmful) Roles:** 
   - **Harmful effects:** Release proinflammatory factors, ROS, proteases, and matrix metalloproteinases (especially MMP-9), which damage endothelial cells, disrupt the BBB, cause edema, and aggravate neuronal injury. Neutrophils also induce the "no-reflow" phenomenon, release elastase, produce NETs (neutrophil extracellular traps) that damage neurons, and accelerate atherosclerosis.
   - **Beneficial effects:** N2 neutrophil phenotype promotes reduction of inflammation via anti-inflammatory mediators. Neutrophils participate in angiogenesis (via FPR2, VEGF, EGF), and N2 polarization is linked to neuroprotection.

3. **Neutrophil Polarization (N1 vs N2):** N1 polarization is driven by IFNβ, IFNγ, IL-12 (pro-inflammatory), while N2 polarization is induced by IL-10, TGF-β, IL-13, and IL-4 (anti-inflammatory). TLR4 deficiency increases N2 neutrophils and is associated with neuroprotection after stroke. TGF-β, mainly upregulated in microglia and macrophages after ischemia, induces N2 differentiation. Rosiglitazone (PPAR-γ agonist) promotes N2 phenotype and increases phagocytosis of neutrophils by microglia/macrophages.

4. **Production and Migration from Bone Marrow:** Neutrophils are produced in bone marrow (1-2 × 10^11 cells/day in adults). G-CSF regulates production. The IL-23–IL-17–G-CSF axis is the main regulatory feedback circuit. CXCR4 retains neutrophils in bone marrow, while CXCR2 promotes their release. Sympathetic nervous system activation after stroke increases hematopoietic stem cell activity and neutrophil output.

5. **Mechanisms of Damage:** 
   - ROS production via NADPH oxidase (NOX2) damages tissue
   - MMP-9 degrades ECM and basement membrane (type IV collagen loss), leading to hemorrhagic transformation
   - Neutrophils accelerate atherosclerosis through MPO-mediated LDL oxidation, foam cell formation, and NETs activating macrophages (NLRP3 inflammasome → IL-1β)
   - VLA-4-mediated neutrophil entry into the brain is a key factor in behavioral injury; blocking VLA-4 inhibits neutrophil brain entry and reduces damage

6. **Key Therapeutic Insights:** The authors propose a new therapeutic strategy involving **local targeting of neutrophils at the onset of cerebral ischemia** rather than nonselective overall inhibition of neutrophil function. T cells contribute little to early behavioral dysfunction but play important roles in chronic recovery (Treg-derived osteopontin promotes microglia repair activity and oligodendrocyte formation).

7. **Important Contradictions:** Neutrophil depletion in WT animals reduces infarct size, but when combined with TLR4 deletion, depletion of neutrophils exacerbates brain injury—indicating that in the absence of TLR4, neutrophils are not harmful and may be necessary for the neuroprotective effect.

**Conclusion:** Neutrophils play a complex, time-dependent dual role in ischemic stroke—exacerbating acute injury while potentially supporting repair. Elucidating neutrophil characteristics and their regulatory mechanisms may lead to new therapeutic strategies targeting neutrophil polarization and function locally rather than globally suppressing them.
</summary>

"Neutrophils are the first group of immune cells to enter the brain from the periphery after ischemic stroke, and their exact role in cerebral ischemia remains to be further explored."

KEY FINDINGS:
- N2 neutrophils (a polarized, anti-inflammatory phenotype of neutrophils) protected against oxygen glucose deprivation/re-oxygenation (OGD/R)-induced primary cortical neuron injury via brain-derived neurotrophic factor/tropomyosin-related kinase B (BDNF/TrkB) signaling in vitro.

--- SOURCE 6: Monocyte, neutrophil, and whole blood transcriptome dynamics following ischemic stroke ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-023-02766-1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in BMC Medicine (Volume 21, article number 65, published February 20, 2023) examining transcriptome dynamics in monocytes, neutrophils, and whole blood following ischemic stroke. The study analyzed RNA-seq data from 38 ischemic stroke patients and 18 vascular risk factor controls (VRFC) at the University of California at Davis Medical Center, examining gene expression changes at three time points post-stroke (0-24h, 24-48h, and >48h) across three stroke etiologies (cardioembolic, large vessel, and small vessel).

Key findings include:
- Distinct temporal gene expression patterns were identified for each cell type. Monocytes showed generally downregulated genes (290, 645, and 352 DEGs at TP1, TP2, TP3 respectively), while neutrophils showed generally upregulated genes (508, 745, and 547 DEGs), and whole blood showed highest upregulation within the first 24 hours (610 DEGs at TP1, declining to 260 and 227 at TP2 and TP3).
- Pathway analyses revealed enrichment of interleukin signaling pathways at different time points. In neutrophils, IL-1, 4, 7, and 8 pathways were exclusively enriched at 24-48h, while IL-2, 10, and 15 pathways were only enriched after 48h.
- Whole blood showed no shared pathways across all time points, with many pathways specific to 0-24h including p53, AMPK, ATM signaling, and FXR/RXR activation.
- Monocytes showed most over-represented pathways predicted to be significantly suppressed, including chemokine, IL-8 signaling, and NO/ROS production.
- Self-organizing maps identified gene clusters with similar temporal trajectories for different stroke causes and sample types.
- Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) identified modules of co-expressed genes that significantly varied with time after stroke, including hub genes of immunoglobulin genes in whole blood. Networks were built using 14,955 genes across 35 IS samples (monocytes), 13,921 genes across 31 IS samples (neutrophils), and 15,360 genes across 37 IS samples (whole blood).
- This is the first study to analyze transcriptional profiles of monocytes, neutrophils, and whole blood using RNA-seq at times ranging from 0 to >48h after ischemic stroke.

Methodology highlights: Monocytes were positively selected using CD14 antibodies (>93% purity), neutrophils enriched by negative selection (>99% purity), RNA-seq yielded average 200M ± 10M reads per sample, differential expression used ANCOVA model with p<0.02 and fold-change >|1.2| cutoffs, and upstream regulators were identified including common regulators for monocytes (TNF, CSF2, ERK) and neutrophils (CSF3, TP53, dexamethasone).

The study concludes that the identified genes and pathways are critical for understanding how immune and clotting systems change over time after stroke, identifying potential time- and cell-specific biomarkers and treatment targets.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: Frontiers | Neutrophil dynamics and inflammaging in acute ischemic stroke: A transcriptomic review ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/aging-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnagi.2022.1041333/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience (December 22, 2022) titled "Neutrophil dynamics and inflammaging in acute ischemic stroke: A transcriptomic review" by Truong An Bui, Glen C. Jickling, and Ian R. Winship from the University of Alberta, Canada. The article examines how neutrophil-specific gene expression patterns contribute to poor treatment responses in stroke patients, and discusses age-related transcriptional changes that may lead to worse clinical outcomes in elderly stroke patients.

Key topics covered:

1. **Cerebral ischemia and ischemic cascade**: Stroke is among the leading causes of death and disability worldwide. Ischemic stroke (IS) is caused by artery blockage, with over half occurring in the middle cerebral artery (MCA). The ischemic cascade involves ATP depletion, anaerobic metabolism, lactic acidosis, cellular depolarization, Ca2+ elevation, free radical release, excitotoxicity, and cytotoxic edema. The gold standard treatment is recanalization via endovascular therapy (EVT) or IV thrombolysis with r-tPA.

2. **Collateral circulation**: Collateral circulation (primary arterial collaterals in the circle of Willis, secondary leptomeningeal collaterals) partially perfuses ischemic tissue. Good collateral status predicts better recanalization outcomes, smaller infarct volumes, and better functional recovery. Collaterals extend the treatment time window (up to 24h for some patients).

3. **Futile recanalization and "no-reflow"**: Clinical trials (MR CLEAN, EXTEND-IA, ESCAPE, SWIFT PRIME, REVASCAT) showed a 54% rate of "futile recanalization" even with optimal recanalization timing. No-reflow refers to inadequate microcirculatory perfusion despite complete recanalization of the large artery, largely driven by inflammation and neutrophil adhesion.

4. **Post-ischemic inflammation**: Acute inflammation begins within minutes after vessel occlusion. Cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and chemokines (MIP-1, MIP-2, MCP-1) activate microglia and upregulate adhesion molecules (selectins, ICAM-1, integrins), facilitating leukocyte infiltration. Neutrophils release MMPs, ROS, and other cytotoxic agents that damage the BBB and brain tissue. Anti-inflammatory clinical trials (HALT, ASTIN, Enlimomab, MINOS) failed despite promising preclinical data.

5. **Neutrophil stalls in capillaries**: Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells (50-70% of leukocytes) with a lifespan of ~10-18 hours. They can clog capillaries, causing microcirculatory failure. Neutrophil counts at admission correlate with poor outcomes, larger infarct volumes, and hemorrhagic complications. Neutrophil depletion reduces tissue damage in animal models.

6. **Neutrophil phenotypes**: N1 (pro-inflammatory, injurious) vs. N2 (anti-inflammatory, protective) neutrophils, plus a pro-angiogenic subtype (~3-5% of circulating neutrophils). N2 skewing via TGFβ treatment reduces infarct volumes in MCAO mice. The binary classification is now considered oversimplified.

7. **Neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio (NLR)**: Proposed as a prognostic marker for inflammatory responses and clinical outcomes, predicting hemorrhagic complications in MT patients and 3-month mortality.

8. **Inflammaging**: Aging exacerbates neutrophil pathogenicity. Aged individuals have hyperactive circulating neutrophils with decreased CXCR4 and CD44 expression (diminishing efferocytosis), and high CXCR1, CXCL1, and CXCL12 levels (keeping them in circulation), creating a pro-inflammatory microenvironment that increases susceptibility to cerebrovascular disease.

9. **Circadian patterns**: Neutrophil aging peaks in the morning; IS risk is highest between 6 a.m. and 12 p.m. and lowest at night (12 a.m.-6 a.m.). Ischemic events during sleep have the worst prognosis.

The review concludes that understanding the interactions between stroke injury, aging, and inflammation at cellular and molecular levels is crucial for developing effective protective treatments, especially given the aging global population and increasing stroke burden.
</summary>

</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 10: Harmful neutrophil subsets in patients with ischemic stroke ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>

**Study Objective:** To better understand the functional state of circulating neutrophils in patients with ischemic stroke (IS) to inform planning of future clinical trials targeting postischemic inflammation.

**Methods:** Flow cytometry was used to analyze activation state and distribution of neutrophil peripheral subsets in 41 patients with acute IS (sampled within 6 hours of admission) compared with 22 age-matched healthy controls. 1. **Basal neutrophil hyperactivation:** Patients with IS showed lower L-selectin (CD62L) expression, higher CD11b expression, increased ROS production (both unstimulated and stimulated), and greater circulating neutrophil elastase levels compared with controls.
2. **Deregulated neutrophil death:** Lower spontaneous apoptosis and increased necrosis (significant by D2) were observed; circulating NET levels were paradoxically LOWER in IS patients than controls, persisting through D2 and D7.

5. **Association with disease severity:** Neutrophil abnormalities (lower CD62L, higher elastase, higher ROS, larger senescent subset, higher sJAM-C, higher rTEM percentage) were significantly associated with higher NIHSS scores (severe stroke defined as NIHSS >12). **Conclusion:** Acute IS is associated with increased inflammatory properties of circulating neutrophils and expansion of harmful neutrophil subsets, which may contribute to systemic inflammation and blood-brain barrier breakdown. --- SOURCE 11: Targeting neutrophils as a novel therapeutic strategy after stroke - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8393299

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in the Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow & Metabolism (2021 Mar 10;41(9):2150–2161, DOI: 10.1177/0271678X211000137, PMC8393299, PMID 33691513) by authors from Renji Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, China. The article reviews the multifaceted role of neutrophils in ischemic stroke and proposes targeting neutrophils as a novel therapeutic strategy.

KEY POINTS:

1. **Role of neutrophils in stroke**: Ischemic stroke triggers brain release of "help me" signals (ATP, HMGB1, HIF-1α, S100β, brain-derived antigens) that activate immune cells. Neutrophils are among the first responders recruited to the ischemic brain and contribute to acute post-ischemic brain injury. They release MMP-9, causing BBB disintegration and exacerbating neuroinflammation. Elevated circulating neutrophils and high neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio correlate with stroke severity, infarct volume, and worse functional outcomes.

2. **Temporal and spatial distribution**: Neutrophil recruitment begins within 30 minutes to a few hours after focal cerebral ischemia/reperfusion in animal models, peaks in the first days, and declines thereafter. In a tMCAo model, neutrophils appeared in small amounts at 12-24 hours after reperfusion, increased steeply at day 3, and declined at day 7. In stroke patients, circulating neutrophils rise within hours and are recruited to the brain within 24 hours. Neutrophils are found in leptomeninges as early as 6 hours, perivascular space by 15 hours, and CNS parenchyma by 24 hours. NETs (neutrophil extracellular traps) form in the vascular cavity and perivascular space.

3. **Failed clinical trial**: The ACTION II trial of natalizumab (which neutralized neutrophils) failed in acute ischemic stroke patients, partly because the heterogeneous clinical population did not match animal models where the therapy was effective (only permanent MCA occlusion animals with small lesions benefited). This highlights the importance of matching animal models to clinical populations.

4. **Neutrophil functional plasticity**: Neutrophils exhibit N1 (pro-inflammatory, induced by IFN-γ) and N2 (anti-inflammatory, induced by TGF-β) phenotypes. IL-27 can push neutrophils toward protective phenotypes, delivering cytoprotective lactoferrin to reduce brain edema in intracerebral hemorrhage. TGFβ reduces neuroinflammation and improves recovery after ICH.

5. **Neutrophil heterogeneity**: Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals neutrophil diversity across maturation and differentiation. Subsets include CD14+Ly6Glo immature neutrophils (neuroprotective in nerve injury), PMNb (interferon-stimulated gene-expressing, combat pathogens), low-density neutrophils (pro-inflammatory, enhanced NETs), and tumor-associated neutrophils (N1 inhibits tumors, N2 promotes tumors). sc-RNA sequencing studies in stroke are still absent.

6. **Regulatory signals**: Transcription factors including PU.1, C/EBPα, C/EBPβ, C/EBPε, LEF1, GFI1, and IRF8 control neutrophil development. TGFβ acts as a reprogramming factor (N2 polarization); type I interferon induces N1 polarization. Neutrophil development requires lower PU.1 levels than macrophage development due to C/EBPα antagonism.

7. **Neutrophil-microglia interactions**: Microglia phagocytose neutrophils in the ischemic brain. When microglia are eliminated (targeting CSF1R), neutrophil numbers increase and brain lesions enlarge, suggesting microglial phagocytic function may be a therapeutic strategy.

8. **Therapeutic strategies** (Table 2):
   - PAD inhibition (targets NETs): increases neovascularization, improves functional recovery in mice
   - CypD depletion in platelets: enhances cerebral blood flow, improves neurological function, reduces infarct volume
   - BR (blood replacement) therapy: reduces MMP-9 levels, improves stroke outcomes
   - VLA-4 blockade: reduces ischemic tissue injury, improves behavioral impairment
   - CEACAM1 knockout: inhibits MMP-9-mediated BBB breakdown
   - IL-17A-blocking antibody: decreases infarct size, improves neurologic outcome

9. **Specific mechanisms**: NETs contain double-stranded DNA, histones, and granule proteins (neutrophil elastase, cathepsin G, MPO), peak at 3-5 days, and are linked to thrombosis and impaired neovascularization. PAD4 is a key enzyme in NET formation. Cyclophilin D (CypD) mediates platelet necrosis and platelet-neutrophil interactions that exacerbate brain injury. MMP-9 inhibitors (DP-b9938, KB-R778539, SB-3CT40, BB-9437) protect stroke outcomes; icariside II regulates MMP-9/TIMP1 balance. Blood replacement therapy with healthy donor blood reduces infarct volume and MMP-9 levels.

10. **Conclusion**: Neutrophil populations are heterogeneous and simple N1/N2 classification is limited. Future research should characterize phenotypic, transcriptional, and functional profiles of neutrophils in stroke. The concept of "brain cytoprotection" (rather than "neuroprotection") is proposed in the era of highly effective reperfusion. Neutrophil-targeted therapies may serve as adjunctive treatments to reperfusion therapy, given that nearly half of thrombectomy patients do not experience clinical improvement.
</summary>

Hence, the clinical population did not match the profile of the animals in which the therapy was effective."; "Given the highly successful rate of thrombectomy in patients with large vessel occlusions nowadays, however, nearly half of the patients do not experience clinical improvement."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 12: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in cerebrovascular disease mechanisms, detection, and therapeutic targeting ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0014488626000464

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a review article published in the journal Experimental Neurology (Volume 400, June 2026, Article 115683) titled "Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in cerebrovascular disease mechanisms, detection, and therapeutic targeting." The article is authored by Zhinuo Li, Shao-Huang Wu, Xinyue Zhang, Tianrun Li, Mingyuan Xin, and Fangxi Liu, and is available via DOI: 10.1016/j.expneurol.2026.115683.

KEY CONTENT:
The review comprehensively examines the role of Neutrophil Extracellular Traps (NETs) in cerebrovascular diseases, particularly ischemic stroke. NETs comprise decondensed DNA scaffolds and granular proteins including histones, myeloperoxidase (MPO), and neutrophil elastase (NE).

MAIN FINDINGS:
1. NETs play a vital role in cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury by enhancing the stability of immunothrombi through DNA-histone scaffolds, conferring resistance to thrombolysis.
2. NETs exacerbate blood-brain barrier (BBB) damage by degrading tight junction proteins via inflammatory cascades.
3. Persistent NET formation impedes vascular remodeling and neural repair, compromising long-term functional recovery.
4. NET interactions with coagulation networks within thrombi are associated with reduced effectiveness of tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) in thrombolytic therapy.
5. NETs form via two distinct pathways: suicidal NETosis (lytic process triggered by microbial pathogens or sterile stimuli via PRRs such as TLR4, TLR9, and CLEC5A) and a second pathway.

DETECTION METHODS (three categories):
- Histology and in vivo imaging (co-localization of extracellular DNA with MPO, NE, or H3Cit)
- Body fluid biomarkers (quantifying circulating complexes such as MPO-DNA)
- A third category of current methodologies

THERAPEUTIC STRATEGIES:
- Targeting NETs during the acute phase may enhance reperfusion efficiency and ameliorate neural injury
- Modulating NETs during the repair phase can promote tissue regeneration

CHALLENGES TO CLINICAL TRANSLATION:
- Narrow therapeutic windows
- Limited intervention specificity
- Risk of infectious complications
- Lack of biomarkers for patient stratification

The authors note NETs exhibit pathological duality: protective in the acute phase (sequestering pathogens and clearing necrotic debris) but harmful when excessive or persistent. The review has 91 references and has been cited 3 times. The article was supported by the Liaoning Provincial Doctoral Scientific Research Start-up Fund Program and China Medical University Undergraduate Training Program for Innovation and Entrepreneurship.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"During cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury, NETs enhance the stability of immunothrombi by forming DNA-histone scaffolds, thereby conferring resistance to thrombolysis. They also exacerbate damage to the blood-brain barrier (BBB) by degrading tight junction proteins via activation of inflammatory cascades."
</key_excerpts>
